C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about efficiency, zero-shot prediction, and learned biological hierarchy. The new benchmark supplies additional evidence without revising those core claims.

C2.justification: Figure 7's caption newly attributes the longest-context throughput decline to memory pressure, connects reduced memory use to longer-context feasibility, and interprets measured speed advantages as consequences of hierarchical compression. Existing biological interpretations and Section 5.1 limitations are unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 specifies the new benchmark's single H100 GPU, BF16 precision, and forward-pass workload. Existing architecture and training details remain unchanged. Benchmark batch size, timing warmup, and repetition details are not supplied.

E1.justification: GTDB pretraining and the MaveDB, DEG, and B. subtilis evaluations are unchanged. The added efficiency benchmark varies sequence lengths and model configurations without introducing a new biological dataset, population, or task.

E2.justification: StripedHyena2 and Transformer baselines remain in their existing comparisons. Appendix A.5 benchmarks the already-used StripedHyena2 family; its 100M, 167M, and 234M configurations do not introduce a new comparison method.

E3.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a hardware benchmark using BF16 forward passes on one NVIDIA H100, testing three dnaHNet variants and three StripedHyena2 sizes across lengths from 2^10 to 2^19 nucleotides. Throughput, peak memory, and latency supplement the existing FLOP evaluation; earlier protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new analysis tests whether theoretical FLOP savings translate into practical efficiency and examines how throughput, memory, and latency vary with sequence length and model scale. Existing hierarchy comparisons and biological segmentation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: No repeated-run counts, seed information, uncertainty estimates, or significance-testing procedures are added or revised. Figure 7 presents measurements without error bars or timing-repetition information.

E6.justification: Figure 7 substantially extends the efficiency evidence with the first measured throughput, memory, and latency results. Reported examples include dnaHNet-M exceeding 1.6 million tokens/sec and dnaHNet-XL using about 18 GB versus over 55 GB for SH2-100M at 2^19 nucleotides. The plots also show SH2 faster at short lengths. Existing scaling and downstream results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same hierarchical architecture, boundary routing, smoothing, compression targets, training objective, and inference procedure. The new benchmark evaluates existing model variants.

P1.justification: v3 adds a short Appendix A.5 and explanatory caption, updates author affiliations and dates, and corrects three figure references in Section 4.3. The existing prose and overall section organization are otherwise retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds the three-panel Figure 7 with legends and a detailed caption, and shifts Table 6 upward on the final page. Existing figures and tables retain their content and design; the front matter also undergoes limited reflow.

R1.justification: The cited works, related-work discussion, and positioning relative to H-Net and other genomic tokenization approaches are unchanged. Appendix A.5 introduces no additional citations.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, Equations 1–4, and hierarchical FLOP-scaling argument are unchanged. The hardware benchmark adds no mathematical definition, assumption, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: Appendix A.5 adds useful measured evidence for long-context efficiency beyond v1's FLOP estimates, and corrected figure references improve navigation. The benefit is limited by incomplete timing details and an overstated Figure 7 caption: its claim of higher throughput across all lengths conflicts with the plotted short-context advantage for StripedHyena2. Overall, the added evidence provides a limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe dnaHNet, with matching main sections and Appendices A.1–A.4. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison; v3 adds Appendix A.5 and Figure 7.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds measured GPU throughput, memory consumption, and forward-pass latency in Appendix A.5.

before.justification: v1 reports original scaling experiments, MaveDB variant-effect predictions, DEG gene-essentiality predictions, and biological segmentation analyses in Section 4 and the appendix.

title: dnaHNet: A Scalable and Hierarchical Foundation Model for Genomic Sequence Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same claims: Bayesian non-negative reward factorization, scalable Weibull inference, and improved robustness, interpretability, and generalization. New evaluations and appendix arguments support or elaborate these retained contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial interpretations concerning factor reproducibility, preserved expressiveness, minimal hyperparameter tuning, computational scalability, and resistance to open-ended reward hacking. It interprets the human evaluation as evidence beyond proxy rewards. New limitations acknowledge KL-coefficient tuning and untested multi-turn, tool-use, and long-horizon settings.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 adds a code-access URL. New Appendix C.2 specifies uniformly selecting floor(N × noise ratio) preference pairs and swapping their labels, clarifying an existing experiment rather than establishing a changed corruption procedure. Table 6 adds wall-clock training times; the earlier algorithm, software descriptions, and hyperparameter table are retained.

E1.justification: Section 5.3 adds Arena-Hard-v0.1 prompts for evaluating generated-response preferences, supplementing the existing reward benchmarks and downstream capability tasks. The factor-stability study reuses existing model and dataset coverage. Multi-turn, tool-use, and long-horizon scenarios are discussed as future work, not evaluated.

E2.justification: New Table 4 compares the BNRM-aligned policy against base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Mistral is newly used as a response-policy opponent; the earlier Mistral-based gold reward model served as an evaluator. Comparator membership in the retained reward-model and PPO tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds a materially different validation protocol: GPT-4.1 pairwise judgments and blind assessment of 50 randomly sampled Arena-Hard pairs by two experts, reporting win/tie/loss rates. It also adds factor comparisons across backbones and training datasets and a full-fine-tuning timing comparison. Existing training settings remain unchanged in v1 Table 6/v2 Table 9.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 adds a focused test of whether factor semantics recur across runs, backbones, and datasets, plus measured training overhead in Tables 6–7. Earlier noise, KL-sensitivity, convergence, debiasing, and Best-of-N analyses are retained. Expanded explanations of those retained analyses do not establish additional experiments.

E5.justification: Table 7 newly reports factor correspondences for the main run and two additional runs, described in Appendix A.3 as using different random seeds. This adds repeated-run reporting for interpretability, without establishing additional repetitions of the earlier accuracy experiments. Confidence intervals and quantitative uncertainty estimates are not added.

E6.justification: New results include Arena-Hard GPT-4.1 outcomes, human-average win/tie/loss rates of 51%/18%/31%, training times, and factor correspondences. Table 2 revises Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B's average from 92.5 to 93.1 while BNRM remains 93.6, shrinking its reported advantage from 1.1 to 0.5 points. Most earlier numerical results and plotted trends are unchanged.

M1.justification: The local/global non-negative reward factorization, Gamma priors, Weibull variational inference, KL-regularized objective, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The added appendix arguments explain and analyze the existing method rather than introduce a new procedure.

P1.justification: The original narrative is largely retained. v2 inserts Appendix A.3–A.5, moves the former A.3 to A.6, expands the sensitivity discussion, and adds limitations, acknowledgements, and an impact statement. It also makes localized terminology, affiliation, and publication-header edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for Arena-Hard/human evaluation, training time, and factor stability, while relocating and renumbering retained displays. Figure 7's KL-coefficient label changes from lambda to eta without changing its curves. The existing diagrams, plots, and table designs otherwise remain substantially intact.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting Arena-Hard evaluation, NMF identifiability, sparse-coding bounds, linear representations, and deep non-negative models. Appendix A.4 expands the comparison with the already-cited InfoRM. The central positioning remains unchanged; duplicate or publication-version reference changes do not constitute new research relationships.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 introduces an NMF formulation, selective-window and sparsity conditions, and a claimed uniqueness guarantee up to permutation and scaling. Appendix D adds a sparsity/incoherence-based generalization bound in Equation 11. These substantially extend v1's mathematical content, although the PDF does not demonstrate the required conditions or provide a complete derivation of the bound.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the human evaluation, factor-stability checks, measured overhead, and reproducibility disclosures provide useful additional evidence. However, v2 introduces uniqueness and distribution-shift guarantees without establishing their assumptions or derivations, and its claim that all seven semantic families recur across every setting exceeds Table 7's reported matches. These empirical benefits and new overstatements materially pull quality in opposite directions, preventing a reliable net improvement judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BNRM research, with matching authors, method, and core experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D support comparison, including material relocated or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds Arena-Hard judgments, human assessments, training-time measurements, and factor-stability results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model training and evaluation, PPO policy evaluations, noise and data-size experiments, debiasing analyses, and Best-of-N results.

title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in RLHF via Bayesian Non-negative Reward Modeling

C1.justification: The central HARPO and unified-model contributions persist. v2 expands the reasoning claim to five named interpretability properties and recalibrates multitask superiority: the headline gain changes from +16.85% to +12.02%, while the discussion changes from best on nine tasks to top-two on eight tasks.

C2.justification: v2 interprets prediction agreement, brevity and human preferences through explicit XAI properties. It qualifies the proposed connection between balanced learning and transfer as requiring further investigation, and explains why SFT/BAM classifier heads preclude zero-shot evaluation. Conversely, it removes v1's substantive AUT qualification that improved precision comes with lower recall.

D1.justification: New Appendix D documents decoding parameters, tokenizer-based length measurement, paraphrase controls, annotator backgrounds, masking and annotation instructions. v2 also supplies a model/code repository link and states that these resources are released, replacing v1's post-review availability promise. Existing training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are unchanged.

E1.justification: Table 2 expands held-out coverage from autism behavior recognition and speech emotion recognition to five contexts, adding in-the-wild depression recognition, social-media sentiment analysis and sarcasm incongruity recognition. The Human Behavior Atlas training coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds Gemma 4-E4B, OmniSapiens SFT, OmniSapiens BAM and EMAGRPO to the retained comparators. Gemma 4-E4B also joins the held-out comparison in Table 2. These additions substantially broaden both model and optimization comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces systematic reasoning-evaluation protocols: answer agreement, paraphrase agreement, reasoning-token counts and masked pairwise human judgments. Appendix D specifies decoding configurations, a 512-token generation cap, fixed instruction paraphrases and three non-author annotators. The existing training budgets, checkpoint selection and predictive metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds stochastic-consistency and paraphrase-robustness tests, efficiency measurements and human assessments of specificity, coherence and concision. The original component ablations and HUM/SAR reasoning analyses are retained, although relocated. The detailed AUT overprediction, abstention and precision–recall analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports five independently sampled inference traces per input for consistency and average-token measurements (Table 3 and Appendix D). This concerns repeated inference, not additional training replications. Neither version reports training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: New results include OmniSapiens scores of 72.43, 58.47 and 69.27 on IDR, SMSA and SIR, plus automated and human reasoning outcomes in Tables 3–4. Retained per-task scores are unchanged. Expanded comparator sets change the model's average rank from 1.20 to 1.90 and HARPO's algorithm rank from 1.70 to 2.10; these are not same-setting performance declines. AUT diagnostic result entries are removed.

M1.justification: The Qwen2.5-Omni-7B backbone, task/sample advantage modulation, geometric centering, inertial smoothing, rewards and optimization objective are unchanged. Appendix A's Algorithm 1 differs only in its equation cross-reference; moving the model setup into Section 3 does not change the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statement and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the model and its interpretability. Model setup moves from the experiments into Section 3; reasoning evaluation and algorithm analyses are reorganized; a new Appendix D shifts subsequent appendices. Affiliations, publication information and acknowledgements also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds two reasoning-evaluation tables and a boxed annotation guide, expands the main comparison and held-out tables, and enlarges the appendix comparison table. All seven figures are retained, but the main figures are reordered and relocated, including v1 Figures 1–2 becoming v2 Figures 4–5.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its social-intelligence and interpretability positioning, adding foundations such as Baron-Cohen and Goleman and XAI evaluation literature including Langer, Nauta and Turbé. It also introduces EMAGRPO through Feng et al. as a multitask-balancing comparator. Several earlier motivation references disappear, although the core reinforcement-learning related-work discussion remains.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix D adds mathematical definitions of agreement across sampled predictions and agreement under paraphrasing, in Equations 13–14. The existing GRPO formulation and HARPO geometric-mean derivation remain unchanged, moving from Appendix D to Appendix E.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical case by addressing limited held-out coverage and missing strong comparators, while adding documented automated and masked human reasoning evaluations. The broader comparison also appropriately reduces the headline multitask gain. These benefits outweigh the loss of the useful AUT recall qualification. Reporting weaknesses remain: human-study sample counts are unspecified, and some Table 4 win rates contradict Appendix D's formula—for example, 80.6% Tie+Win and 35.3% Tie imply about 70.0% wins excluding ties, rather than the reported 66.0%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniSapiens-7B 2.0 and HARPO. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds held-out results, additional baseline evaluations, automated reasoning assessments and a human evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original HARPO training comparisons, held-out AUT and SER evaluations, component ablations and analyses of reasoning and training dynamics.

title: OmniSapiens: A Foundation Model for Social Behavior Processing via Heterogeneity-Aware Relative Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The introduction removes the claim that this is the first BG formulation incorporating machine-learning potentials as importance-sampling target energies. The main contributions—CG sampling, ESFM-based PMF learning, solvent-mediated accuracy, and computational savings—are otherwise retained.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 explicitly acknowledges learned-PMF approximation bias. Appendix B qualifies larger-peptide convergence as primarily covering the targeted dihedrals, and Table 5 cautions about cross-paper runtime comparability. Section 4.2 adds an interpretation of coarser mappings as improving ESS while generally reducing reweighted accuracy.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D substantially expand experimental documentation with larger-peptide simulation recipes, explicit flow/PMF training sample counts, and center-of-mass preprocessing. Hyperparameters and checkpoint-selection instructions are revised. Some earlier reproducibility information is removed, including the dipeptide box size and trajectory-recording stride; hardware, software, and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds alanine tripeptide (42 atoms) and hexapeptide (72 atoms), extending molecular complexity beyond the retained Müller–Brown and 22-atom dipeptide systems. Tripeptide uses both CG mappings and hexapeptide uses Core Beta; evaluation focuses on selected dihedral pairs.

E2.justification: v2 Table 7 adds TarFlow and ECNF++ to the dipeptide accuracy/ESS comparison against the explicit-solvent reference. v1 compared accuracy with generalized Born baselines and included ECNF++ only in a runtime comparison. The new caption attributes the atomistic BG results to prior studies; it does not establish new baseline training.

E3.justification: Appendices C–D revise MB flow training from 2000 to 1000 epochs, dipeptide training batch size from 256 to 1024, ODE tolerances from 1e-4 to 1e-5, and PMF training from 250 to 300 epochs with changed decay and final-checkpoint selection. New peptide experiments introduce longer trajectories and targeted biasing protocols. Appendix B also replaces the stated implicit-solvent 2 fs/H-bond constraints with a blanket 0.5 fs/unconstrained setting. These are reported protocol revisions, not proof of reruns.

E4.justification: The clipping analysis expands from dipeptide to tripeptide and hexapeptide, with separate ablation tables and sensitivity curves for five system/mapping combinations (v2 Tables 7–9 and Figure 10). Resolution comparisons and structural diagnostics also extend to larger peptides. The short 10 ns unbiased-dipeptide sampling-failure illustration in v1 Figure 6b is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report uncertainty values and specify ten independent MB data-generation trajectories. v2 changes table notation from ± values to parenthetical digits, but introduces no stated uncertainty-estimation procedure, model-run count, confidence interval, or significance test. The origins of the reported uncertainties remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised and expanded. In Table 2, Heavy Atom dipeptide JS/PMF/ESS changes from 0.0075/0.2493/0.2325 to 0.0048/0.2005/0.5112. Unclipped dipeptide ESS changes from near-zero or unavailable values in v1 Table 6 to approximately 0.36–0.46 in v2 Table 7. Runtime values change, and larger-peptide and atomistic-baseline results are added. Changed protocols prevent interpreting these as controlled same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The ESFM-trained PMF, flow-matching proposal, importance reweighting, and 1% clipping procedure remain unchanged, as do the specified network architectures and Appendix F algorithms. Appendix C newly documents center-of-mass centering and noise, without establishing that this was a newly introduced procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, method exposition, simulation-free evaluation discussion, related work, and future-work paragraphs undergo extensive rewriting. Appendix G is reorganized around the expanded systems and analyses. These changes substantially revise the narrative and explanations while retaining the main section sequence.

P2.justification: Figures are extensively redrawn and regrouped: v1 Figures 3–4 become v2 Figure 2, the MB figure moves to Appendix G, and Ramachandran panels are consolidated and promoted into the main text. Dataset, runtime, and ablation tables expand across peptides. A new labeling inconsistency appears in v2 Figure 11, whose axes say phi despite its psi caption.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds constrained mean-force approaches and newer generative-sampling references, while explaining the relationship to already-cited Tamagnone et al. (2024) and Kohler et al. (2023). Future-work citations expand and the first-formulation novelty claim is removed, but the overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Equation (18) adds the 1/B normalization and explicitly defines ESS as a fraction in (0,1], correcting the mathematical definition to match fractional reporting. Propositions 1–3 and the Appendix A proofs are substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its scalability argument mainly with a toy potential and dipeptide. The larger-peptide evaluations, direct atomistic-BG accuracy comparisons, and expanded resolution/clipping analyses substantially strengthen evidence for the central claims. Explicit PMF-bias and targeted-dihedral qualifications improve their interpretation. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: larger-system validation remains limited to selected dihedrals, and Appendix G.4 retains blanket clipping-benefit statements that conflict with the revised dipeptide results in Table 7.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original CG-BG evaluations on the retained systems and on alanine tripeptide and hexapeptide, with quantitative results and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations and CG-BG evaluations on the Müller–Brown potential and alanine dipeptide, including accuracy, runtime, and clipping experiments.

title: Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators

C1.justification: The abstract, highlighted contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: suitable nonlinear autoencoders recover structure invisible to PCA, and reconstruction loss can misalign with representation quality. The introduction sharpens the framing without changing these claims.

C2.justification: Section 5 revises its discussion of replica-symmetric agreement around the rescaled-tanh examples while retaining the unresolved standard-tanh discrepancy in Appendix E.2. Section 6 and new Appendix E.5 extend the loss-versus-representation interpretation to changes in network width.

D1.justification: Appendix E.5 documents the two-unit reconstruction, independent Gaussian initialization of both weight vectors, and settings for the width experiments. Existing optimizer, numerical-solver, hardware, and paper-code access information is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic spiked-cumulant distributions with correlation exponents 2 and 3 and the same downstream classification task. The added experiments vary network configurations without introducing new data or task coverage.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain BO/AMP, linear autoencoders/PCA, and the same nonlinear activation families. Rescaling tanh and comparing single- and double-unit versions change configurations of existing methods, without introducing a distinct baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: Figures 1–2 replace standard tanh with tanh(x/4). Appendix E.5 adds one-versus-two-unit evaluations and measures maximum spike similarity across the two weights and their mutual alignment. Existing data-generation, optimizer, and testing procedures are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.5 tests how bottleneck width affects reconstruction loss, spike recovery, and alignment between neurons. The existing finite-size, low-sample-ratio tanh, additional-activation, and correlation-exponent-3 analyses remain.

E5.justification: Matched experiments retain their run counts and standard-deviation reporting, including 30 autoencoder instances and 72 AMP seeds in Figure 1. The new width experiments use the existing 30-instance reporting practice; no new uncertainty-estimation procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Main-text tanh curves are replaced by results for tanh(x/4), a changed configuration; the original loss comparison survives as v2 Figure 4. New Figures 9–11 report lower absolute reconstruction losses with two neurons, larger gaps relative to the corresponding linear model, and marginally reduced spike similarities.

M1.justification: The tied-weight autoencoder, reconstruction objective, and AMP procedure are retained. Appendix B already formulates matrix-valued autoencoder weights in v1; the new two-unit and rescaled-tanh experiments instantiate width and activation settings within this existing family.

P1.justification: The introduction and replica-symmetry discussion receive localized rewrites, Appendix E.5 is added, and wording and bibliographic details are corrected. The overall section sequence and narrative remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 receive updated tanh legends and axis ranges, and three width-comparison figures are added. The original Figure 2 is retained as v2 Figure 4, other appendix figures are renumbered, and Table 1 and several figures move within the layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds Tabanelli et al. on computational thresholds in multimodal spiked models and distinguishes that setting from its single-view model. The introduction also more explicitly separates known nonlinear expressivity from the paper's quantitative analysis of learning.

T1.justification: Several local mathematical errors are corrected: Appendix A.3 reverses an initialization-probability inequality; B.3 repairs replica summation indices, signs, and a completion-of-square factor; B.5 restores a matrix inverse; and D.2 restores the missing square in the q-hat expression. The principal theorem statements and asymptotic characterizations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 repairs concrete algebraic inconsistencies and adds a useful width sensitivity analysis, improving the reliability and breadth of the supporting evidence. The standard-tanh discrepancy remains explicitly documented, so agreement for tanh(x/4) does not resolve that limitation. The core theoretical scope and conclusions remain stable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same spiked-cumulant autoencoder study. Their text, equations, figures, table, and appendices A–E are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulations and adds results for rescaled tanh and comparisons between one and two hidden neurons.

before.justification: v1 reports original autoencoder and AMP simulations, including spike recovery, reconstruction losses, downstream classification, and supplementary analyses in Appendix E.

title: A Solvable High-Dimensional Model Where Nonlinear Autoencoders Learn Structure Invisible to PCA While Test Loss Misaligns With Generalization

C1.justification: Both versions claim the same three contributions: a unified forensic framework, the FSFR dataset with self-evolving reasoning generation, and balanced optimization through ARSPO. Performance and zero-shot generalization claims retain their scope.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning task difficulty, reward reshaping, iteration saturation, hindsight bias, hard-sample coverage, and backbone transfer are retained. Section 5.4 restates existing appendix explanations, while the dual-use qualification remains.

D1.justification: v3 adds a repository link and states that code and data are publicly available; acknowledgements also identify the university HPC platform. Existing implementation details remain unchanged. The retained academic application-and-review restriction leaves the precise dataset access conditions unclear.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same FSFR source datasets and classification/localization tasks. OOD evaluation still covers ISOT, CASIA2.0, MMFakeBench, and FakeSV, including the same held-out video-text scenario.

E2.justification: The evaluated MLLM, specialist, and RL comparators remain unchanged in corresponding experiments. Direct GT Injection and alternative reward comparisons are also retained. Newly cited works, such as ASAP, are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Dataset partitions, sample counts, training settings, model backbones, metrics, and zero-shot testing procedures are unchanged. The iteration and hard-sample experiments presented in v3 Section 5.4 already used the same settings in v1's appendices.

E4.justification: The iteration-saturation and Hard-CoT ablations move from v1 Appendices I and L into v3 Section 5.4. The hindsight-bias comparison is additionally summarized there. Reward sensitivity, single-task, backbone-transfer, human-validation, and case analyses are otherwise retained without new evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies repeated-training run counts, seed variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The human-validation proportions and the assertion that iteration differences are statistically negligible are unchanged.

E6.justification: Corresponding numerical and qualitative results are unchanged. For example, Table 2 retains localization scores of 54.26 IoU, 63.78 F1, and 59.22 tIoU. v1 Tables 6 and 9 reappear as v3 Tables 5 and 6 with identical results.

M1.justification: The self-evolving CoT pipeline, collaborative hard-sample synthesis, ARSPO reward mappings, and dynamic coefficient algorithm are unchanged. Moving Algorithm 1 and existing analyses does not alter the procedure.

P1.justification: Section 5.4 integrates and lightly rewrites existing appendix analyses, with corresponding appendix reorganization. Affiliations, publication information, disclosures, and acknowledgements are updated. Most prose is retained; Section 3.1 introduces an incorrect OOD cross-reference to Section 4.2.

P2.justification: The iteration and Hard-CoT tables move into the main text and receive smaller single-column layouts, revised captions, and highlighting. Algorithm 1 changes column placement. The four figures and illustrated cases retain their content.

R1.justification: Seven references are added, including ASAP, two 2026 forensic papers, DCP, and three sign-language studies; Langley's paper-writing reference is removed. These are chiefly introduction citation additions, without a substantial revision of research positioning.

T1.justification: The objectives, gradient derivations, differentiability assumptions, expected-capability definition, and total-derivative analysis remain unchanged in Section 4 and Appendices B-G. No mathematical correction or additional proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the existing data-generation validation easier to assess within the main narrative and supplies an explicit code/data access pointer. These modest presentation and documentation gains leave the scientific evidence unchanged. Their benefit is limited by unclear public-versus-reviewed dataset access and the erroneous OOD cross-reference in Section 3.1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniVL-Guard and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Material moved between the appendices and main text can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results, including benchmark comparisons, ablations, and appendix human-validation outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, backbone-transfer experiments, and human validation of generated reasoning data.

title: OmniVL-Guard: Towards Unified Vision-Language Forgery Detection and Grounding via Balanced RL

C1.justification: The benchmark contribution and main multilingual findings remain stable. Section 2 now explicitly claims Macaron uniquely satisfies seven design properties simultaneously, refining the earlier general differentiation through cultural reasoning and controlled templates.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that verifier agreement supports factual correctness, scoring differences show no systematic bias, and extraction failures have negligible effects. It attributes Llama 3.1's generation-scoring drop to formatting failures. The existing coverage and constrained-task limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds annotator demographics, verifier recruitment and adjudication details, and verifier compensation. Table 3 also explicitly explains overall-score aggregation. The evaluation/proofreading prompts and dataset access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions retain 1,977 bilingual scenarios, 11,862 instances, 20 cultural contexts, 20 languages/dialects, 10 scripts, seven reasoning types, and 22 cultural aspects. The new audits and detailed breakdowns use this existing coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains the same 21 model configurations. DeepSeek's two configurations move into the open-weight category without being added or removed. The scoring audit reuses existing models; additions to the related-work comparison table are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds generation-versus-log-probability evaluation, with six models documented in Table 8, exhaustive three-verifier MCQ assessment, and extraction-error measurements. Section 4 also changes the reported API scoring rule from log-probabilities when available to JSON generation for API-only models. The original zero-shot tasks and prompts remain; rerunning the main evaluations is not established.

E4.justification: New Appendices B, D, and E examine annotation reliability, sensitivity to scoring method, and answer-extraction failures. These substantially extend validation beyond v1's retained paired-True/False, reasoning-category, cultural-aspect, and template-difficulty analyses.

E5.justification: v2 first reports three-verifier unanimity agreement estimates for all 20 cultural contexts in Table 6. Neither version reports model-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: All individual Table 3 numerical rows remain unchanged. Closed-thinking and open-weight overall averages change from 79.3% to 80.8% and 55.2% to 58.0% because DeepSeek is regrouped. Substantial new results include agreement scores, generation-scoring comparisons, extraction errors, and per-model language/script breakdowns in Tables 6, 8–9, and 11–12.

M1.justification: The template-filling, bilingual translation, and MCQ-to-True/False construction remain unchanged. Section 3.6 replaces sampled cultural review with three independent native verifiers answering every local-language MCQ, followed by adjudication and gold-label correction. This revises the quality-control component of the retained construction pipeline.

P1.justification: The introduction is condensed, experimental setup is shortened, model citations move into Table 3, and existing appendix material is reorganized around new sections. Most methodological prose, the main section sequence, and conclusions remain intact.

P2.justification: v1's coverage map is removed, the curation diagram is redrawn with a verification stage, Table 1 is redesigned, and six tables are added. Existing result displays are substantially rearranged. The annotation screenshots and several charts are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around separating language and culture, particularly contrasting its construction with Ying et al.'s post-hoc decomposition. It adds culture-proxy, cultural-alignment, interpretability, and M3Exam references, and redesigns Table 1 around native authorship, cultural coverage, and joint reasoning–culture annotation.

T1.justification: The formal bilingual-item definition, metadata sets, and six-instance construction are unchanged. No new theoretical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs appear; the added agreement and error measures serve empirical evaluation.

improvement.justification: v2 adds valuable systematic verification, scoring/error audits, and detailed results. However, Table 3's DeepSeek regrouping conflicts with Tables 5 and 11–12, and the new local-overall results do not reconcile with Table 3: Gemini 3 Flash thinking averages about 89.3% in Table 12, versus about 84.8% implied by pooling its local MC/TF scores. These inconsistencies undermine the added evidence's reliability, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Macaron. All pages, including figures, tables, and image-based appendices, are accessible and support reliable comparison. The detailed results added in v2 are absent from v1, rather than lost during extraction.

after.justification: v2 retains those original evaluations and adds native-verifier agreement, scoring-method comparisons, extraction-error measurements, and detailed language/script results.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot evaluations of 21 LLM configurations, including accuracy, language gaps, paired True/False performance, and reasoning/template analyses.

title: Macaron: Controlled, Human-Written Benchmark for Multilingual and Multicultural Reasoning via Template-Filling

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the empirical applicability claims to non-IID partitions and language-model fine-tuning. The central threshold-watermarking contribution, scalability claim, and original removal-robustness claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the added experiments as showing limited sensitivity to label heterogeneity and applicability beyond image classification. Section 6 replaces the IID-only, image-only limitation with a narrower qualification that comprehensive evaluation of larger language models remains future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code repository link in the abstract and documents the balanced Dirichlet partition and language-model training settings in Appendix C. Existing image preprocessing, hardware, and training details are retained. The PDFs establish the new access statement, not the repository's contents.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's IID image-classification coverage, v2 evaluates CIFAR-100 with heterogeneous client label distributions and adds language modeling through GPT-2 Small fine-tuning on WikiText-2. These introduce a distinct federated data scenario and a new task domain.

E2.justification: The independent per-client watermark baseline in Figure 3 is unchanged. The new experiments use unwatermarked controls, extending an existing comparison type without adding competing watermarking methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds a balanced Dirichlet sweep with four concentration values and a language-model protocol using four clients, 20 rounds, AdamW at 0.0001, perplexity, and minimum-perplexity checkpoint selection. Appendix D.2 also replaces the estimated-key L1 penalty with absolute cosine alignment against model parameters. This is a reported attack-protocol revision; unchanged plots do not establish rerunning it.

E4.justification: New Section 5.4 tests sensitivity to client label heterogeneity at fixed K = 32 and c = 0.025. Appendix D.2 revises the existing adaptive-attack formulation, while the extensive original attack analyses and their plotted outcomes are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three seeds, 0, 1, and 2, retain the existing uncertainty summaries, and identify Figure 10 error bars as 95% confidence intervals. The new tables extend existing reporting practices without introducing additional runs or statistical procedures.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports non-IID z-scores of 12.58–12.72 and watermarked accuracy reductions of 0.16–0.53 percentage points. New Table 3 reports watermarked perplexities of 10.58–10.70 versus 10.52 without watermarking, with z-scores of 6.89–9.63. These substantively extend findings to new settings; existing Table 1 and result figures remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 adds a weighted-FedAvg adaptation that divides embedding shares by public aggregation weights to preserve the watermark direction. This changes the embedding procedure for weighted aggregation; the existing setup, uniform-aggregation algorithm, and verification procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 expands the method overview, inserts two experimental subsections, rewrites the adaptive-attack explanation and limitations, and replaces placeholder correspondence and preprint information. The overall section structure and most prose are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds result Tables 2–3 and expands the notation table, renumbered from Table 2 to Table 4. Figures and algorithm floats shift with the surrounding text, but all twelve existing figures retain their graphical content.

R1.justification: v2 adds Radford et al. (2019) for GPT-2 and Merity et al. (2017) for WikiText-2. Section 7 and the claimed relationship to earlier watermarking methods remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 introduces positive normalized aggregation weights, defines reciprocal-weighted embedding shares, and derives the cancellation identity preserving their aggregate direction in Equations 8–9. Existing secret-sharing arguments, verification mathematics, and dealer-free complexity analysis are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 partly addresses v1's explicit IID-only and image-only limitations with relevant new evidence, adds weighted-aggregation support, and makes the documented adaptive-attack penalty consistent with reducing alignment. The gains are bounded: language-model evidence covers detection and fidelity in one small-model setting, and unchanged attack plots do not establish renewed validation of the revised loss. Overall, the paper becomes more complete without substantially strengthening its central robustness evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Collaborative Threshold Watermarking by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and can be matched despite pagination changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds non-IID CIFAR-100 experiments and GPT-2 Small fine-tuning results on WikiText-2.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification experiments on watermark fidelity, scalability, and removal attacks, plus simulated dealer-free setup timings in Appendix B.

title: Collaborative Threshold Watermarking

C1.justification: The contributions shift from solver-inspired residual fitting toward a unified OCP framework, explicitly claiming a shared objective with TTT/GDN, the first Rank-L/parallel-scan combination, and backward compatibility with GDN. These strengthen the claimed theoretical relationship to existing methods. The central Rank-L expressivity and 174-fold throughput claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix I newly interprets the language-model results as favoring Rank-L injection over exact flow/preconditioning and residual iteration over direction multiplicity for generalization. Existing limitations concerning local proxies and fixed memory capacity remain. Some new interpretation overreaches: the claim that every ablation worsens perplexity conflicts with shared-key LAMBADA perplexity improving from 27.00 to 26.02.

D1.justification: v3 adds the SlimPajama token budget, tokenizer, parameter counts, and language-model configurations, and changes the supplied repository link. However, it removes v1's recommendation data provenance, item-frequency filtering threshold, and chronological leave-one-out instructions. It also omits the synthetic experiments' 10k-step budget and MoM four-expert configuration. These are substantive changes in reproducibility information, without establishing corresponding experimental changes.

E1.justification: Appendix I adds language modeling on SlimPajama and zero-shot evaluation including WikiText, LAMBADA, PIQA, ARC, BoolQ, and other benchmarks. This substantially expands coverage beyond the four recommendation datasets and nine synthetic probes retained from v1.

E2.justification: The recommendation and synthetic-probing comparator sets are unchanged. The new language-model comparisons add evaluated EFLA and PGDN baselines, alongside Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, which were already evaluated elsewhere in v1.

E3.justification: The new language-model experiments introduce approximately 130M-parameter models trained on 2B tokens, validation/test perplexity, and zero-shot evaluation. Separately, Section 5.1 revises the stated recommendation cutoffs from K=10 to K={100,200,500}, although both versions' tables already report 200/500. Table 3 relabels the unchanged single-step ablation scores from L=1 to L=0; a rerun is not established.

E4.justification: Appendix I.4 adds a substantial mechanism study comparing independent directions, shared keys, reuse of the GDN base key, removal of residual subtraction, and a single solver step. These test the contributions of direction diversity and iterative refinement to language-model generalization. The original recommendation ablation scores and synthetic probing results are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added language-model tables continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: v3 Tables 7-9 add perplexity, downstream accuracy, and ablation results; for example, final test perplexity is 23.13 for PRISM versus 23.28 for GDN. Numerical entries in the original recommendation, component-ablation, and synthetic-probing tables are unchanged. The new Table 8 averages are internally inconsistent with its displayed task accuracies, limiting interpretation of the reported aggregate gains.

M1.justification: The core architecture and recurrent update remain recognizable. However, v3 Equation 8 and Figure 1 change initialization from r=v-u to r=v, while Algorithm 1 still specifies V-U. Its new Gated DeltaNet base-case descriptions also conflict over L=0 versus L=1. These inconsistencies prevent reliably distinguishing an actual procedural revision from documentation errors.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, theoretical motivation, method explanation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Appendices are reorganized and proofs substantially compressed. The restructuring also leaves duplicated baseline sections and a repeated computational-complexity paragraph.

P2.justification: Table 1 is rebuilt around mathematical objectives, and recommendation tables are regrouped by rank and parallelism. v3 adds a structural-correspondence table and three language-model tables, updates and relocates Figure 1, and relocates Figure 2. Dataset statistics are displayed twice in Tables 10 and 13.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially reframed around OCP and a Rank-Parallel taxonomy, positioning PRISM as an amortized counterpart to TTT and a generalization of GDN. PGDN and Su's stability discussion are added, while the RetNet reference is removed. EFLA moves from cited background to an evaluated comparator.

T1.justification: Section 3 introduces a unified proximal-plus-nonlinear-retrieval objective. New Appendix B derives the TTT-MLP correspondence and shows that repeated updates with a fixed key remain rank one, motivating independently learned directions. It also adds GDN special-case arguments. The earlier degeneracy, spectral, proxy-error, and stability analyses largely remain in condensed, relocated form.

improvement.justification: Appendix I adds valuable evidence beyond recommendation and useful mechanism ablations. However, v3 introduces conflicting algorithm descriptions and unreliable aggregate reporting: Table 8's nine PRISM accuracies average approximately 41.19%, rather than the reported 40.1%. It also drops important preprocessing, split, and training details retained in v1. The broader evidence and explanatory additions coexist with losses in consistency and reproducibility, preventing a confident judgment of net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PRISM and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Their retained material can be matched reliably despite substantial rewriting and internal inconsistencies in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds language-model perplexity, zero-shot benchmark results, and language-model ablations in Appendix I.

before.justification: v1 reports original recommendation experiments, training-throughput measurements, component ablations, and nine synthetic probing tasks.

title: PRISM: Parallel Residual Iterative Sequence Model

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about context-dependent retrieval, DISBench construction, the ImageSeeker baseline, and current models' reasoning limitations.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 newly qualifies the embedding comparison as demonstrating DISBench's need for cross-image reasoning, rather than supporting replacement of embedding retrievers by agents generally. Appendix B's substantive limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V1's separate code, dataset, and leaderboard links become a single repository entry point in v2, changing the supplied access instructions without establishing resource withdrawal. Most implementation details remain unchanged, and Appendix D.2 is not reconciled with the revised main-text memory specification.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same YFCC100M-derived DISBench coverage: 122 queries, 57 users, 109,467 photos, and intra-event/inter-event retrieval tasks. Removing the geographic map does not establish a change in the underlying population.

E2.justification: Tables 1-3 retain the same ten agent backbones, Qwen3-VL-Embedding 2B/8B and Seed-1.6-Embedding retrieval comparisons, and component-removal variants. The newly cited works are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Sections 5.1 and Appendix D.4 retain the same evaluation metrics, 30-turn limit, 128K-token context limit, default temperatures, and retrieval/viewing limits. No revised experimental protocol is reported; whether the revised Section 4 memory description applies to these experiments remains unresolved.

E4.justification: Appendix C.4 loses the supplementary characterization of photo locations through v1 Figure 7 and its accompanying geographic-coverage discussion. The tool/memory ablations, test-time scaling, four-model error analysis, and two Appendix E cases are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same parallel-run counts in the scaling study and annotation agreement reporting, including IoU 0.91. Neither adds seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: All matched performance values in Tables 1-3, scaling curves, error percentages, and Appendix E traces are unchanged. The limited loss is the empirical geographic point distribution shown in v1 Figure 7 and its accompanying coverage summary; no performance gain or loss is reported.

M1.justification: Section 4 revises compressed memory from session/working summaries to global/local/tool-use summaries, adding explicit failure-history retention and an image-count trigger. This is a limited reported procedural revision, but v2 Appendix D.2 still specifies the original two-component design, leaving the implemented variant uncertain.

P1.justification: Edits are localized: expanded personal-album motivation, a rewritten memory paragraph, a renamed and qualified Section 5.3, grammatical corrections, conference publication text, and acknowledgments. The overall section and appendix structure is retained.

P2.justification: V2 removes the geographic map, relocates the dataset chart and results tables, swaps the numbering of the scaling and error plots, and expands their captions. Front-page links become a footnote, and the second qualitative case spans pages; the retained displays otherwise preserve their designs.

R1.justification: V2 adds Naaman et al. (2004) and Whittaker et al. (2010) to motivate contextual personal-photo retrieval, plus MR2-Bench and MC-Search in related work. These are limited additions; the central novelty positioning is retained.

T1.justification: The context-aware set-retrieval formulation, memory-graph definitions, and Appendix C sampling algorithm remain unchanged. Neither version introduces additional theorems, proofs, or formal derivations.

improvement.justification: The added references and Section 5.3 qualification improve framing, but v2 introduces a reproducibility inconsistency: Section 4 describes three memory tiers while Appendix D.2 retains two. It also removes geographic-distribution evidence. The PDFs do not resolve which memory design underlies the retained results, so the benefits and harms do not support a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepImageSearch/DISBench work and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and Appendices A-E. Content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains the original experimental results in Tables 1-3, the scaling and error-analysis plots, and Appendix E.

before.justification: V1 reports original DISBench agent and retrieval evaluations, component ablations, test-time scaling, error analyses, and qualitative experimental traces.

title: DeepImageSearch: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Context-Aware Image Retrieval in Visual Histories

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on an efficient board-game algorithm and empirical component validation. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion make stability and convergence characterization central contributions and explicitly locate novelty in theoretical and empirical understanding of existing regularization ingredients. The principal efficiency claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting efficiency to branching factors, architecture/computation tradeoffs, and alternative regularization results. It discusses multiplayer and infinite-horizon proof boundaries and possible stochastic/continuous-action extensions. The earlier spatial-complexity explanation for action-value learning and Retrace extension suggestion disappear; the asymptotic-performance caveat remains.

D1.justification: v2 describes the added shared-head and separate-network configurations and their computational implications. It removes v1's explicit n-step/lambda-return formulas and MLP-head description. Default hyperparameters, optimizer settings, parallelism, hardware information, and existing implementation/checkpoint references are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds Matching Pennies, a simultaneous normal-form game, in Section 5.1. The five principal board games, 19x19 Go, and Count Up game are retained; Count Up moves from v1 Appendix L to v2 Appendix D. Stochastic and continuous-action environments are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: Appendices I–J add evaluated Forward-KL, Entropy Reward, Discrete SAC, V-MPO, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO comparators. Table 2 also includes AlphaZero in the test-time MCTS comparison, whereas v1's corresponding 9x9 Go scaling experiment compared KLENT with Gumbel AlphaZero. The original principal baselines remain.

E3.justification: The original board-game protocols remain intact. Targeted additions include a five-game comparison using checkpoints trained with 800 million simulator evaluations and 800 test-time rollouts, a Matching Pennies regularization grid, and architecture controls including separate networks with approximately twice the computational cost.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic evidence: Figure 3 tests convergence boundaries, Figure 8 tracks policy-update KL divergence, Appendix H tests head/backbone sharing and an EMA variant, and Appendix I tests alternative regularization choices. Existing component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, rollout studies, and Count Up analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new MCTS comparison in Table 2 explicitly reports means and standard errors. The existing learning curves and search-scaling experiments retain three-seed means and standard deviations. No increase in repeated-run counts or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Principal learning curves and older appendix tables are retained, but substantial results are added. Table 2 reports MCTS average win rates of 32.2%, 53.6%, and 77.2% for AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero, and KLENT. At 800 million evaluations, Tables 6–7 report 61%, 14%, 2%, and 3% for Forward-KL, Entropy Reward, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO, versus KLENT's retained 89%. Architecture and convergence findings are also added.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the analytical policy update, policy/action-value networks, lambda-return targets, joint loss, and self-play/fitting procedure. The new architecture and regularization variants are experimental alternatives; the proposed KLENT procedure is unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work and the problem setting are reorganized, value-learning exposition is compressed, and the appendices are reordered into four thematic parts with a contents list. These changes reshape the narrative beyond simply inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, rearranges benchmark and ablation panels into horizontal rows, adds convergence and KL-divergence figures and comparison tables, and redraws Count Up results for the main text. The Go spatial illustration and ablation-configuration table disappear; existing branching-factor statistics are additionally displayed in Table 1.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work as extending regularized-policy and game-theoretic research, explicitly comparing its convergence condition with Sokota et al. It adds literature supporting Discrete SAC, V-MPO, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO comparisons, while trimming historical TD-learning and Q-learning discussion.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's analytical-update derivation and empirical equilibrium discussion, v2 adds Section 5 and Appendix C: local linear convergence under alpha(alpha + 2 beta) > ||R||_2^2/4, supporting Jacobian lemmas and proofs, a general-sum extension, and a bounded-horizon convergence argument. These constitute a substantial new theoretical component.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's mainly empirical justification through conditional normal-form convergence analysis, targeted architecture and regularization tests, and broader MCTS comparisons. These additions better explain the design and test competing explanations for its efficiency. The finite-horizon proof presumes value-estimate convergence, new baseline configurations remain sparsely documented, and some method detail is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in scientific support.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe KLENT and share the principal experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds Matching Pennies simulations, architecture experiments, and additional algorithm comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original board-game experiments, component ablations, computational analyses, and Count Up game simulations in Section 5 and the appendices.

title: Revisiting Regularized Policy Optimization for Stable and Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Two-Player Games

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about EFIM-based hypergradient approximation, parallel efficiency, sample complexity and empirical performance.

C2.justification: The result interpretations, Hessian–Fisher rationale and model-misspecification discussion in Remark 4.6 are unchanged. The conclusion retains the same future-work boundaries concerning single-loop algorithms and outer-variable-dependent data distributions.

D1.justification: Appendices A and E retain identical implementation details, hyperparameters, two-GPU A100 setup and code-source links. The new acknowledgment identifies support but adds no technical or resource-access information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MNIST label cleaning, Fashion-MNIST distillation and the same 2D heat-equation control problem. No dataset, task or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: The experiment-specific comparator sets are unchanged, including Neumann/CG, stocBiO, AmIGO, TTSA and SOBA where reported, and Broyden for PDE optimization. Appendix E retains the same explanation of stocBiO's equivalence to Neumann for five-sample-per-class distillation.

E3.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E retain identical metrics and settings, including 50% MNIST label noise, distillation with 5 and 100 samples per class, batch sizes, iteration budgets, network architectures and PDE sampling procedures.

E4.justification: The existing comparisons across Neumann/CG truncation counts and distillation sample counts remain unchanged. No ablation, robustness test, error analysis or case study is added or removed.

E5.justification: Tables 2–5 retain identical plus/minus reporting and descriptions of averaging over the last 50 epochs. There are no changes to reported seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: All experimental values, curves and reported findings in Section 5 and Appendix E are unchanged. For example, both report NHGD test accuracy of 0.9180 ± 0.0003 in Table 2 and PDE outer loss of 0.0266 ± 0.0005 in Table 5.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendices A and E retain the same NHGD updates, EFIM inverse approximation, cross-derivative estimators, parallel implementation and practical smoothing procedure.

P1.justification: v2 adds an Acknowledgment thanking the NVIDIA Academic Grant Program and UMN Data Science Initiative, corrects the malformed word in reference 34 and updates the version/date stamp. The scientific prose and appendix structure remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The acknowledgment occupies the former start of the bibliography on page 13, moving References to page 14 and reflowing entries across pages 14–16. Figures, tables, captions and appendix layouts are unchanged.

R1.justification: The same 41 cited works and research positioning are retained. Reference 34 corrects a malformed rendering of 'nystrom' in the existing title; this is a bibliographic correction, not a different citation or changed relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: Section 4 and Appendices B–D retain the same assumptions, Hessian–Fisher equivalence, approximation and convergence theorems, and proofs. No mathematical statement, bound or derivation changes.

improvement.justification: v2 adds support attribution and repairs one malformed reference title, providing small editorial refinements. The methods, theory, empirical evidence, interpretations and reproducibility information remain identical, including the appendices; the localized edits do not meaningfully alter the paper's overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same NHGD research work, with 41 pages and complete Appendices A–E. Text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable comparison of the methods, equations, proofs, figures and tables.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E retain the original experiments and reported outcomes for hyper-data cleaning, data distillation and PDE-constrained optimization.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original experiments on MNIST hyper-data cleaning, Fashion-MNIST distillation and heat-equation-constrained optimization, including accuracy, loss and runtime results.

title: Natural Hypergradient Descent:  Algorithm Design, Convergence Analysis, and Parallel Implementation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the claimed applications from contamination detection to information retrieval and paraphrase detection. The theoretical contribution is qualified through revised conditional bounds and acknowledged non-decaying cases. The central claim of fast semantic search over trillion-scale corpora remains.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges that the occurrence-ratio intuition underlying v1's theory fails empirically and discusses linguistic constraints and examples with r >= 1 (Section 4; Appendix M). It adds substantive explanations of beta-dependent ranking tradeoffs and insertion-related grammatical errors affecting quality judgments. The existing multiword-semantics and resource limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds GPT-5.4 judging and paraphrasing prompts, query-selection and exclusion instructions, and settings for the new evaluations. Appendix D documents hyperparameter rationales, while Appendix H explains frequently accessed versus example-retrieval index storage. Its proposed SSD/HDD configuration is deployment guidance, rather than a newly tested hardware setup.

E1.justification: v2 adds ORCAS search queries, information retrieval on TREC-COVID and SciFact, and source-document identification using GPT-5.4 paraphrases of FineWeb-Edu sentences. The existing seven-language corpus coverage and seven contamination benchmarks remain; v1's reference to six languages was inconsistent with its own Table 3.

E2.justification: BM25, previously discussed only as related work, becomes an evaluated comparator in retrieval and paraphrase detection (v2 Tables 17–18). The original comparisons with infini-gram, infini-gram mini, and SoftMatcha are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include cold-cache controls, order-swapped GPT-5.4 judgments, manually prepared retrieval queries with precision/recall metrics, and 400 paraphrase-source tests. The pruning-latency sample increases from 400 to 2,000 queries. Reported English seven/eight-token proportions change from 7%/5% to 6%/6%, and cache clearing changes from CPU-cache terminology to OS page cache; these revisions do not establish reruns of all retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's pruning ablations and output-size/threshold analysis, v2 adds smooth-minimum versus plain-minimum quality comparisons, beta sensitivity examples, cold/hot-cache robustness checks, and empirical validation of theoretical assumptions with and without insertions/deletions. Appendix K.3 also revises the existing pruning-latency analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix M newly reports log-shifted geometric means to reduce outlier influence. Appendix K.3 explicitly increases the query sample for more reliable p99 estimation. This concerns statistical estimation and query sampling, not additional independent runs; confidence intervals and significance tests remain absent.

E6.justification: v2 adds retrieval, quality-judgment, cache, real-query, and assumption-validation results. New paraphrase P@1 is 84.3% for Ours, versus 74.5% for SoftMatcha and 82.8% for BM25 (Table 18). The main 278.17 ms latency and contamination totals remain, while lookup growth changes from 2.27 to 2.30 per token. Under the expanded query sample, Figure 15 plots higher latency with all pruning techniques, contradicting the accompanying speedup claim.

M1.justification: The core suffix-array search, pruning techniques, similarity function, and adaptive thresholding remain. Appendix I adds document-scoring adaptations for downstream retrieval, including an explicitly tested IDF-weighted variant, Ours+IDF, for paraphrase source identification.

P1.justification: Related work moves partly to Appendix A, problem formulation becomes Section 2.2, and the method is reorganized into six subsections separating building blocks, pruning, indexing, similarity, and thresholding. The introduction and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten, and the evaluation, application, and appendix structures are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICML layout, restructures Table 2, moves the suffix-array diagram from v1's Appendix H into main-text Figure 3, resizes the contamination figure, and redraws Figure 15. It adds tables for downstream applications, cache conditions, real queries, quality judgments, beta sensitivity, and assumption validation.

R1.justification: New citations support ORCAS, retrieval benchmarks, BM25, and query-length rationales. Earlier Heaps-law references to Baeza-Yates/Navarro and van Leijenhorst/van der Weide are removed. Table 2 refines lexical-semantic versus coarse-topic retrieval positioning, but the central relationship to SoftMatcha and the infini-gram systems remains.

T1.justification: v1 derives a constant query-length bound from its corpus-occurrence hypothesis and a moderate-gamma condition. v2 replaces this reasoning with explicit growth assumptions permitting r >= 1 and the bound A*a*(1-r^m)/(1-r), constant only when r < 1. It revises the corpus-size proof and adds conditional analysis of adaptive thresholding and additional pruning in Appendix N.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for practical usefulness through real-query, cold-cache, retrieval, and paraphrase evaluations, while exposing weaknesses in v1's occurrence-ratio rationale and making the theoretical conditions more explicit. Expanded experimental documentation and clearer organization improve assessability. Figure 15's contradiction with its pruning-speedup claim is a material regression, and geometric-mean checks do not fully validate expectation-based bounds. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in empirical support and theoretical transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SoftMatcha 2 research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds real-query evaluation, cache experiments, retrieval and paraphrase results, quality judgments, and empirical checks of theoretical assumptions.

before.justification: v1 reports original latency measurements, pruning ablations, multilingual search results, and manually verified benchmark-contamination findings.

title: SoftMatcha 2: A Fast and Soft Pattern Matcher for Trillion-Scale Corpora

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the state-of-the-art claim from five to four X-to-English tasks. The claims about training without word-level translation alignments, BLEU-based reinforcement learning, the released benchmark and adaptation using less than 1000 hours remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.8 newly states that the quality/latency trade-off cannot be adjusted at inference time, alongside the retained accent-control limitation. The added Impact Statement discusses interpreter employment and argues that restricted output-content control reduces spoofing risk relative to ordinary TTS.

D1.justification: Section 4.2.2 newly specifies pretraining with eight audio codebooks, adding eight randomly initialized codebooks, and then duplicating weights for two streams. The introduction drops its explicit data-preparation-code release promise; model, inference-code and benchmark links remain. This does not establish any actual resource withdrawal.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same multilingual training coverage, Europarl-ST and Audio-NTREX-4L evaluations, and Italian adaptation. The added figures reuse existing languages and datasets. Changing the abstract from five to four tasks does not remove the Italian experiments.

E2.justification: Seamless and Hibiki remain the external baselines, and comparator membership in Tables 1–6 is unchanged. New Figure 5 reuses the existing long-form baseline comparisons while evaluating additional Hibiki-Zero operating points.

E3.justification: Section 4.2.2 changes the reported audio-pretraining budget from 1K to 1M steps, a substantial revision to the stated training setting; this does not establish that experiments were rerun. The reward-weight sweep also adds α = 0 and α = 1. Existing evaluation splits, metrics and human-rating procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The reward analysis adds pure intermediate-reward and outcome-only controls in Figure 4 and language-specific benchmark trade-offs in new Figure 5. Appendix Figures 9–14 add training-dynamics diagnostics and translation timeline case studies. These substantially extend the investigation of reward balancing beyond v1's validation trajectories; the existing alignment and reward-frequency ablations remain.

E5.justification: Table 2 retains identical MOS values and accompanying ± quantities. No new repeated-run counts, seed information, uncertainty definitions or significance tests are introduced. The ablation plots retain the existing trajectory-smoothing practice.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–6 are unchanged, but the reported results expand substantially. Figure 4 adds endpoint trajectories, with α = 1 reaching approximately 65 BLEU while text LAAL rises to approximately nine seconds. Figure 5 adds benchmark trade-off curves, and Figures 9–14 add training losses and qualitative outputs. These are additional results, not improved headline scores.

M1.justification: The multistream architecture, coarse alignment procedure, BLEU-based rewards, GRPO objective and inference procedure remain substantively unchanged. Expanded pretraining details document the existing pipeline; the PDFs do not establish a replacement method.

P1.justification: Focused rewrites clarify modeling, related work and pretraining. v2 adds conflict-of-interest and impact statements and changes the publication front matter. The main section sequence and most explanatory prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 revises Figure 2's stream labels, expands Figure 4's curves, axes and legend, and adds the benchmark trade-off plot plus appendix training plots and translation timelines. Original Figures 5–7 become Figures 6–8, and Table 4 gains numerical highlighting. This substantially expands the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds a specific criticism of tuning Seed LiveInterpret 2.0's multiple reward components. The background citation switches from Wahlster's 2000 book to Baldridge's 2004 review of it. The broader literature coverage and contribution positioning remain stable.

T1.justification: Equation 4 corrects the likelihood-ratio conditioning: both probabilities now condition on all previous output frames and earlier codebooks at the current frame, replacing conditioning on only the current codebook's past. This is a localized mathematical correction consistent with the retained architecture.

improvement.justification: The added reward controls and benchmark trade-off curves strengthen evidence for the existing latency-control claim. Equation 4's correction, fuller pretraining documentation, narrower abstract claim and explicit inference-time limitation improve precision and transparency. The deleted data-preparation-code promise modestly reduces release specificity. With the original benchmark tables and research scope otherwise unchanged, the net gain is useful but limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hibiki-Zero research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds reward-weight evaluations, training trajectories and translation examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original translation benchmarks, human evaluations, Italian adaptation experiments and ablations, including supplementary results in Tables 4–6.

title: Simultaneous Speech-to-Speech Translation Without Aligned Data

C1.justification: The central claims remain a first benchmark for agentic game development, deterministic verification of multimodal tasks, persistent weaknesses in multimodal understanding, and benefits from visual feedback. Updated task counts, models, and performance examples change the supporting evidence without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 drops v1's hypothesis that dynamically choosing between feedback mechanisms explains improved cost efficiency. It newly attributes lower full-set performance to multimodal variants, hypothesizes that Gemini 3 Pro's difficulty-split exception reflects stronger multimodal understanding, and interprets low transcript overlap as suggesting no systemic memorization. The new Impact Statement also explicitly bounds the tasks to using existing assets rather than creating assets.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new diagnostic procedures and supplies per-configuration median token consumption and costs in Table 4. It removes v1 Figure 6's disclosure that Gemini CLI costs were approximated using OpenHands, without explaining whether cost collection changed. Exact prompts in Appendices A–D and the public repository remain unchanged; the failure judge's identity and prompt are unspecified.

E1.justification: The main benchmark retains Godot 4 and the same four development skill categories; its larger task count does not establish a new development domain. Appendix J adds a distinct evaluation task: completing held-out tutorial transcripts to probe memorization.
