E2.justification: Table 2 substantially revises the evaluated lineup: GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4 Mini replace GPT-5.1-Codex-Max, Qwen3.5-397B replaces Qwen3-VL-235B, and Claude Opus 4.5 is removed. The OpenHands comparison also removes Claude Sonnet 4.5 while retaining Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash, and Kimi K2.5.

E3.justification: The evaluation changes from 115 base tasks plus 17 variants to 154 core tasks plus 179 variants. v2 adds core/full reporting and a human-labeled split of 131 easy and 202 hard tasks. New protocols include LLM classification of failures from four leading configurations and first-half-to-second-half continuation of 117 transcripts, scored with ROUGE-L and BLEU-4. The main pass@1 metric remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix H adds analyses of variant inclusion and human-rated multimodal difficulty; Appendix I supplements the existing qualitative failure discussion with quantified error categories; Appendix J adds a memorization probe. Feedback ablations are also revised: for example, Sonnet 4.5 loses its screenshot-only and video-only evaluations, while GPT-5.4 Mini receives both.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 6 reports a linear fit used to contextualize cost versus success; v2 removes that fitted statistical summary. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Appendix F retains the same mean, three-standard-deviation-filtered mean, median, and maximum reporting convention.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and supplemented. With both feedback tools, Table 2 reports Gemini 3 Pro at 54.5% in v1 versus 53.8% in v2, and Sonnet 4.5 at 46.2% versus 34.8%; these use different task sets and are not same-setting performance declines. Tables 4–8 add subgroup scores, token and cost values, failure frequencies, and transcript-overlap scores. Task statistics also change. Appendix G's new GPT-5.4 attribution is uncertain because Figure 11 still labels the example GPT-Codex-5.1-Max.

M1.justification: The task-construction pipeline, deterministic Godot testing, screenshot MCP, and runtime-video feedback mechanisms remain unchanged. Appendices A–D contain identical construction, refinement, annotation, and agent prompts apart from formatting. Difficulty labeling extends evaluation rather than changing the proposed solving method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and Appendices A–G are retained. v2 locally rewrites the abstract, results discussion, and conclusion, changes 'framework' terminology to 'harness,' adopts author–year citations, and adds acknowledgements, an Impact Statement, and Appendices H–J. Most construction, method, related-work, and prompt text remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text to a two-column conference layout with running headers, resizes and relocates existing displays, stacks Figure 5's panels, and substantially redraws Figure 6 with model-family groupings and harness encodings. It adds Tables 4–8. The task-example figures and Figure 11's underlying graphic are retained rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the SlideChat pathology-image reference with SlideGen for the slide-generation comparison and adds BenchLM.ai as a source for the Design2Code comparison. The broader positioning relative to software benchmarks, computer-use agents, game playing, and specialized game-development systems remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The added empirical metrics and subgroup comparisons do not introduce new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's empirical validation beyond v1's category-level comparisons and illustrative failure case. Core/full and easy/hard analyses directly examine the intended multimodal challenge, quantified failure categories improve diagnostic value, and the transcript probe adds a limited contamination check. These address substantive validation gaps rather than merely increasing task counts. The unspecified failure judge and contradictory model attribution in Figure 11 limit reproducibility and consistency, but do not outweigh the added evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GameDevBench and provide readable main text, tables, figures, and appendices. The retained sections and appendices can be matched despite substantial reformatting and additional evaluations in v2.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations on 333 tasks and additional core/full, difficulty, failure-pattern, and transcript-contamination results in Appendices H–J.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 132 game-development tasks, including agent success rates, feedback ablations, cost comparisons, and failure analysis.

title: GameDevBench: Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Through Game Development

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the three central contributions: stronger pretraining weight decay improves plasticity; minimizing pretraining loss need not optimize downstream performance; and representation, attention-rank, and overfitting effects offer potential mechanisms. The enlarged experiments strengthen support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix A explicitly distinguishes correlational mechanisms from the experimentally isolated weight-decay effect and discusses sparse model configurations and untested regimes. Appendix D interprets observed stability costs. Its claim that upstream performance is unaffected is overbroad: the listed OLMo-2-1B-140x accuracy falls from 0.61 to 0.56 across decay settings.

D1.justification: v2 adds project-specific Models and Code links, a direct MMLUProCoT source reference, explicit OLMo checkpoint selection for fine-tuning, and detailed sample sizes, safety-training mixtures, and hyperparameter grids. These substantially extend v1's documentation of basic training recipes and hardware. The PDFs establish the presence of access links, not their external availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds fine-tuning on HellaSwag, Winogrande, PiQA, Arc-Easy, and Arc-Challenge, plus safety alignment using Alpaca and safety instructions with evaluation on I-MaliciousInstructions (Appendix C.3–C.4). The original six CoT tasks, pretraining corpora, and SST/AG News probing tasks remain.

E2.justification: v1's Table 3 includes only positive pretraining weight-decay values. v2 adds an explicit no-weight-decay control, λ = 0, for all five model groups and reports its results in appendix comparisons. The existing model families and positive-decay comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces joint pretraining weight-decay/learning-rate sweeps and fine-tuning learning-rate/weight-decay/batch-size sweeps (Appendix E). New protocols include cloze accuracy, harmfulness scoring on 100 prompts with four safety-training sample sizes, and upstream evaluation before and after fine-tuning. The original CoT splits and default fine-tuning settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix E tests whether the plasticity effect survives changes to other pretraining and fine-tuning hyperparameters, including selection of the best fine-tuning configuration. Appendix D adds stability–plasticity and upstream-performance analyses, while Appendix F.3 adds layer-wise parameter-norm analysis. The original probing, attention-rank, and leave-one-out analyses remain.

E5.justification: The new safety-alignment plots include error bars around mean harmfulness scores (Figures 12–16), but their statistical definition and run/seed counts are unspecified. The existing Pearson leave-one-out analysis is retained as Figure 10, formerly Figure 9.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the new tasks, zero-decay controls, hyperparameter sweeps, stability trade-offs, and norm measurements. Existing results also change: the overall Greedy probing/downstream correlation is 0.93 in v1 Figure 15 and 0.87 in v2 Figure 25, alongside an expanded set of model variants. Figure 4(c)'s OLMo probing curves are also revised.

M1.justification: Both versions investigate AdamW pretraining weight decay followed by supervised fine-tuning using the same Llama-2 and OLMo-2 architectures. The added experiments do not introduce a new training algorithm, architecture, objective, or adaptation component.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and portions of the methods and results, particularly Section 4.3, and reorganizes fine-tuning and evaluation material into task-based Appendix C. It adds discussion and analysis sections, while preserving the six-section main narrative and much of the original prose.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to a two-column conference layout. Numerous new experimental figures are added; v1 Figures 10–14 are consolidated into v2 Figure 24. Figure 6 is redesigned to display training loss, validation loss, and their gap, with additional revisions to panels, axes, legends, and captions elsewhere.

R1.justification: The main related-work section remains largely unchanged. v2 adds references for the new benchmarks and safety setup, vision-pretraining findings, and compositional generalization. Appendix A sharpens the comparison with Kobayashi et al. and expands the connection to the already-cited Lee et al. study.

T1.justification: The AdamW equations are rearranged and reindexed but express the same combined update. The attention-rank argument, training–validation gap, and 95%-singular-value pseudo-rank definition are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that the plasticity finding extends beyond CoT tasks and is robust to other training choices. Appendix E directly addresses v1's reliance on mostly fixed hyperparameters, while stability analyses, explicit mechanistic limitations, and project access links improve interpretation and reproducibility. Undefined safety error bars and Appendix D's overbroad upstream-performance interpretation are weaknesses, but they do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same weight-decay and language-model-plasticity study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison across the 28-page v1 and 32-page v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds commonsense and safety evaluations, hyperparameter sweeps, stability analyses, and parameter-norm measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining and fine-tuning experiments, linear probing, attention-rank measurements, and training–validation gap analyses in Sections 4–5 and the appendices.

title: Weight Decay Improves Language Model Plasticity

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list and main conclusion retain the same claims about diffusion-native preference modeling, noise ensembling, competitive reward accuracy and efficient alignment. The new experiments supply additional support without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C.3 explicitly distinguishes reuse of the formulation across backbones from transfer of trained rewards within compatible latent spaces. Appendix D.2 discusses requirements for untested broader applications. The conclusion removes the specific grid-artifact observation and instead references reward-hacking patterns already documented in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds limited implementation descriptions for the comparison heads: direct pooling versus a lightweight transformer followed by pooling. The core hyperparameter tables, training and inference algorithms, hardware disclosure and project URL are unchanged; detailed implementation information for the added experiments remains limited.

E1.justification: Both versions use HPDv3 training data, the same four preference benchmarks and text-to-image alignment using Pick-a-Pic. Added SDXL and SD3.5-L experiments change model configurations within this coverage. Video, editing and audio-visual applications are discussed only as future extensions.

E2.justification: The main Table 1 comparator roster is unchanged. v2 additionally evaluates LRM-SDXL as an alignment comparator in Figure 5, whereas v1 compared it only on offline preference accuracy. Table 6 also introduces average-pooling and transformer-plus-pooling alternatives for the reward-head comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds a controlled SDXL ReFL comparison holding the generator and optimization configuration fixed while changing rewards, and an experiment transferring an SD3.5-M reward to SD3.5-L. These new alignment curves extend through 200 steps, alongside new head configurations. This substantially expands the evaluation design; the original 150-step SD3.5-M experiment and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds direct tests of reward-head aggregation, performance against LRM-SDXL with a matched backbone, and reuse of trained rewards across generators sharing a latent space. These address architectural dependence, backbone confounding and transferability. Earlier noise, layer-depth, uncertainty, Flow-GRPO and reward-hacking analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A retains the same 1,000 HPDv3 pairs, ten noise draws per pair, variation ratios, mean margins and score variances. The added experiments introduce no new seed reporting, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports 71.55% average accuracy for DiNa-LRM on SDXL against 61.73% for LRM-SDXL (Table 5). Table 6 adds pooling-head averages of 71.03% and 71.14%, alongside the retained 71.49% Q-Former result. Figures 5–6 add SDXL alignment and SD3.5-L transfer findings. Original numerical results remain unchanged; these are additional results, not improvements to the original experimental runs.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same noise-calibrated Thurstone formulation, fidelity loss, FiLM-conditioned gated Q-Former and multi-noise token ensembling. Additional backbone evaluations and alternative-head ablations do not revise the proposed default method.

P1.justification: v2 adds an appendix contents page, reorganizes Appendix C into four subsections, expands Appendix D and adds acknowledgements and cross-references. Most existing prose remains intact. Some reference edits introduce errors, including 'Table 5.3' and 'Appendix 3' where v1 correctly referenced Section 5.3 and Table 3.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evidence displays with new SDXL and transfer plots (Figures 5–6), comparison and head-ablation tables (Tables 5–6), and an SDXL row in the backbone table. Existing figures and tables are retained but relocated or reformatted; v1 Figures 5–7 become v2 Figures 7–9.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting broader application discussion, including Reward Forcing, UniC and AnyTalker, plus a Visual-aware CoT citation in related work. The central positioning against algorithm-specific, step-level diffusion rewards remains unchanged. Publication and bibliographic updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: The diffusion and flow-matching definitions, preference likelihoods, uncertainty calibration, loss, ensembling equations and appendix uncertainty formulas are unchanged. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's comparison with prior diffusion rewards used different backbones. v2's matched-SDXL accuracy and alignment comparisons substantially reduce this important confounding, while head ablations and shared-latent-space transfer provide direct evidence for architectural robustness and reward reuse. These additions materially strengthen the central empirical case and clarify its limits. Sparse implementation details for the new experiments and minor cross-reference errors temper, but do not outweigh, these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiNa-LRM research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds SDXL comparisons, reward-head ablations and an SD3.5-M-to-SD3.5-L reward-transfer experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original preference-prediction experiments, architectural and noise-schedule ablations, uncertainty measurements, and ReFL and Flow-GRPO alignment results.

title: Beyond VLM-Based Rewards: Diffusion-Native Latent Reward Modeling

C1.justification: The introduction's third contribution changes from revealing a planning mechanism to revealing a predictive mechanism, partially narrowing the interpretation of the correlation finding. The abstract still mentions planning, and the main dynamism, irreplaceability, and practical-utility claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations involving long-tail head participation, threshold robustness, and noise from selecting excess heads, plus proposed compression and hallucination-detection applications. Appendix C's statement that all methods worsen at larger k conflicts with its random-baseline results. The existing limitations are retained.

D1.justification: The new appendices document the exact threshold grids and identify Llama-3.1-8B as the model used for the downstream sweep. Existing hardware, decoding, probe architecture, optimizer, training, and split information in Appendix A remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate NIAH and HotpotQA. The new analyses vary head-selection thresholds within retained tasks; the proposed compression and hallucination-detection applications are not evaluated.

E2.justification: The original ablation comparators and all Table 4 strategies remain unchanged. New Table 6 uses the existing Static, Dynamic Random, and Fixed Random baselines rather than introducing another comparison method.

E3.justification: New analyses evaluate static-head cutoffs of 20, 50, and 100, and RAG head budgets of 5, 10, and 20 on Llama-3.1-8B. Table 1 also adds active-head and unique-head count metrics. Existing experimental protocols remain intact.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests sensitivity of dynamic/static head overlap to the static cutoff; Appendix C tests downstream robustness to the retrieval-head budget. These targeted checks supplement the retained ablations and correlation analyses.

E5.justification: Table 1 newly reports mean and standard deviation of active-head counts across timesteps, such as 12.97 ± 7.69 for Llama-3.1-8B. This describes temporal variability, not uncertainty in benchmark performance. Appendix A.1's five-run and twenty-run reporting remains unchanged.

E6.justification: The original numerical results are retained. Additions include unique-head counts, such as 238/1024 for Llama-3.1-8B, and Tables 5–6. Table 5 reports its Jaccard similarity falling from 0.3512 at k=20 to 0.1236 at k=100; Table 6 adds downstream results at k=10 and k=20.

M1.justification: The retrieval-score definitions, MLP probes, and attention-masking adaptation of DRAGIN remain unchanged, including Algorithms 1–2. The additional threshold sweeps evaluate existing components without introducing a new procedure.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in Section 3.2, the planning-to-prediction terminology, and the expanded conclusion. v2 adds acknowledgements and two appendix sections, shifting the existing appendix labels while preserving the overall narrative structure.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands from four to six columns with smaller text, and Tables 5–6 are added. Existing figures reflow and Figure 4's caption changes, but their graphical content remains identical. The appendix results and algorithms are retained in the same displays.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and cited works are retained. The positioning against prior static retrieval-head approaches and the claim of the first systematic dynamic study remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 removes v1's quantitative deduction that the Jaccard and entropy values imply at most 6–10 active static heads and at least 10–14 additional dynamic heads. It substitutes a broader conclusion supported by observed unique-head counts. The formal definitions and Appendix A derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The direct head-count statistics and threshold sweeps make previously fixed-cutoff findings easier to assess while preserving the original evidence. The gains are limited by the single-model downstream sweep and overstated interpretation: Appendix C says all methods decline with larger k, although Dynamic Random F1 rises from 0.3670 at k=5 to 0.3807 at k=10. Overall, the useful additional evidence provides a modest improvement despite this reporting weakness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and support comparison of the text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The original supplementary results and algorithms are retained, with Appendices B–C becoming D–E in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds head-utilization statistics and threshold-sensitivity results in Table 1 and Appendices B–C.

before.justification: v1 reports original NIAH and HotpotQA experiments, including head ablations, correlation analyses, learned probes, and Dynamic RAG comparisons.

title: Retrieval Heads are Dynamic

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same LoRA-specific LLM–BO framework, domain prompting, learned embedding calibration, proxy efficiency, and cross-model applicability claims. The headline claim of over 20% improvement using about 30 iterations remains, and the conclusion is substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands discussion of embedding geometry, optimization-cost tradeoffs, applicability beyond LoRA, operation without manual domain knowledge, and dependence on embedding-model choice. It interprets direct GSM8K results as evidence against transfer alone explaining the gains. It also newly says scale-matched configurations tend to perform best, although unchanged Table 8 frequently favors configurations transferred from the smaller model.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page pointer, conversation hyperparameters in Table 12, and LLAMBO's ten-prediction setting. It revises the Optuna configuration description but omits v1's explicit statement that BO/LBO inputs are five-dimensional. Existing backbone, hardware, training schedule, and prompt-template details are largely retained; the PDFs do not establish what resources the project page actually provides.

E1.justification: v2 retains MetaMathQA/GSM8K/MATH and CodeFeedback/HumanEval/MBPP, adds conversation training on WizardLM-Evol-Instruct with MT-Bench evaluation, and extends evaluation beyond LoRA to Bayesmark breast-cancer and Iris classification and diabetes regression. This substantially broadens the represented tasks and domains.

E2.justification: LLAMBO, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator in the LoRA math comparison in Table 18 and the optimization-time comparison in Figure 3. Random search, Optuna/TPE, BO, LBO, and NOMAD remain. The shortened Optuna label does not identify a different baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes Optuna's reported candidates from categorical to integer, and Table 1 corrects the dropout increment from 0.5 to 0.05; these disclosures do not establish that experiments were rerun. Added protocols include MT-Bench GPT scoring, direct GSM8K optimization, alternative embedding models, and timing that excludes proxy training. Bayesmark introduces classification accuracy and negative MSE curves extending to 50 iterations, beyond the retained 30-iteration LoRA setting.

E4.justification: v2 adds PCA-based analysis of embedding geometry, embedding-model sensitivity tests, direct-GSM8K optimization to examine dependence on transfer evaluation, and automatic-versus-manual prompting experiments. These test substantial additional questions about representation, robustness, and reliance on supplied knowledge. The earlier component ablations, proxy correlations, and transfer analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new plots also lack uncertainty bands. LLAMBO's disclosed ten Monte Carlo predictions per iteration describe its internal prediction setting, not uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds conversation, Bayesmark, timing, LLAMBO, embedding-choice, direct-GSM8K, and automatic-prompting results. Most earlier benchmark values remain unchanged. In Table 4, Optuna's GSM8K/MATH scores change from 37.38/4.74 to 54.13/10.50, with its selected configuration also revised in Table 13. These accompany the changed candidate encoding and therefore are replacement results rather than an established same-setting gain.

M1.justification: The default algorithm, learned token, projection layer, GP objective, and proxy evaluation remain unchanged. Appendix C introduces an optional automatic prompting procedure: the surrogate learns hyperparameter-performance relationships, and GPT converts those trends into domain-aware prompts. This is a limited procedural extension, evaluated in Table 21.

P1.justification: The title changes, wording is polished across the abstract and body, and explanations of the search grid and embedding extraction are clarified. Acknowledgments and an impact statement are added. The basic organization of Sections 1–5 and Appendices A–D remains intact.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from single-column to two-column conference formatting. v2 adds Figures 2–4, MT-Bench columns, and several appendix tables; merges v1 Tables A3/A4 into Table 13; and moves Table A8 into the main text as Table 9. Figure 1 retains its visualization but gains a clearer caption. These constitute substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for FedPara, WizardLM, MT-Bench, Bayesmark, and Rathore et al. (2025), while dropping the Qwen2.5 technical-report reference. It also explicitly contrasts its GP-based embedding calibration with LLAMBO's prompting approach. The central positioning as LoRA-specialized LLM-assisted BO remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The GP/deep-kernel formulation, marginal-likelihood objective, and Appendix A gradient derivations are retained. The acquisition symbol changes from alpha to a, and Appendix B adds the standard formula for the already-used Expected Improvement acquisition. These are notation and explanatory additions, without new theoretical reasoning or formal results.

improvement.justification: The LLAMBO comparison and embedding/prompt ablations in Tables 18, 19, and 21 address meaningful gaps in v1's validation, while conversation and Bayesmark tests broaden applicability evidence. The net improvement is limited by thin documentation of new evaluation protocols and absent run-level uncertainty. The new scale-matched-best interpretation also conflicts with unchanged Table 8, weakening an otherwise useful expansion of the evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoRA hyperparameter optimization framework. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and can be matched despite the changed title, formatting, and table numbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds conversation and Bayesmark evaluations, timing measurements, an LLAMBO comparison, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original math-reasoning and code-generation experiments, HPO comparisons, component ablations, and analyses of proxy training and hyperparameter transfer.

title: A Language-Guided Bayesian Optimization for Efficient LoRA Hyperparameter Search

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: recursive Bayesian navigation, prediction–correction decoupling, the attention/KDE relationship, drift mitigation, and data-efficient fine-tuning with improved generalization.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly interprets the retained 10% experiment as limited fine-tuning and adds explanations involving MLLM capacity, semantic correction versus geometric smoothing, and noisy memory anchors. It removes the appendix's sample-complexity, module-collapse, and landmark-failure explanations. The stated limitation concerning GRU information decay remains unchanged.

D1.justification: V2's abstract adds a project repository address with a promise of future code release. Existing hardware, backbone models, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and auxiliary-loss coefficient remain unchanged. The PDF does not establish that the promised code is already available.

E1.justification: Both evaluate continuous aerial navigation using TravelUAV's UAV-Need-Help dataset, retaining seen, unseen-map, unseen-object, Easy/Hard, and assistance-level coverage. V2's added experiments reuse L1 Test-Seen; the removed trajectory examples do not represent separate task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds TravelUAV + Post-KF, applying constant-velocity Kalman filtering to predicted waypoints (Table 6). It removes the MBGRU comparator from v1's structural-decoupling experiment (Appendix Table 5). Comparator membership in the main benchmark Tables 1–2 is unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds a distinct training condition using only 10% of trajectories without full-data pretraining, with uniform trajectory sampling and Easy/Hard distribution checks. It also introduces post-hoc filtering and memory-threshold evaluation settings. The original full-data initialization followed by 10% fine-tuning, benchmark splits, and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds controls testing dependence on full-data pretraining, whether output-space smoothing explains the gains, and sensitivity to memory insertion thresholds. It removes v1's structural-decoupling and auxiliary-loss ablations and the top-down/front-view failure analyses. The gain, memory-length, and aggregate drift analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Table 3 newly reports NeuroKalman means and standard deviations over three randomly sampled 10% trajectory subsets and states that sampling uses fixed seeds. This uncertainty reporting concerns the new experiment; no increased repetition count is reported for retained results.

E6.justification: The new no-full-pretraining experiment reports NeuroKalman NE 85.89 ± 2.71 and SR 22.70 ± 0.87, versus TravelUAV's 122.63 and 13.19 (v2 Table 3). Post-KF and threshold results are also added. MBGRU, auxiliary-loss ablation results, and two qualitative examples disappear. Tables 1–2, matched gain/memory-length tables, and Figures 3–4 retain their results.

M1.justification: The GRU prior, attention-based memory retrieval, confidence-gated storage, learned Kalman fusion, waypoint prediction, and auxiliary losses remain unchanged. The default memory insertion threshold remains 0.5; the added threshold experiments test variants of the existing method.

P1.justification: Most retained prose and the main section hierarchy are unchanged. V2 locally revises the data-efficiency discussion, adds experimental discussion and acknowledgements, removes the appendix structure, and updates affiliations, author-role markers, and publication text.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 3, 6, and 7 while removing v1's appendix Tables 5–6 and both multi-panel trajectory Figures 5–6. The retained fusion and memory-length tables are moved and renumbered, Figure 4 is relocated, and Figure 2's illustrative input labels are revised. The supporting visual material is substantially reorganized.

R1.justification: Four references supporting the removed appendix disappear: Bishop and Nasrabadi (2006), Miller and Hardt (2018), Savinov et al. (2018), and Guu et al. (2020). Section 2 and the main positioning against prior navigation, memory, and filtering research remain unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 removes Appendix A.1's error-dynamics assumptions, claimed bounded-error contraction argument, and covariance-weighted anchor-regularization formulation (v1 Equations 10–14). These are substantive theoretical removals without replacement. The main Bayesian, retrieval, and fusion equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The new experiment without full-data pretraining and its subset variability estimates strengthen the central data-efficiency evidence; post-KF and threshold controls add useful checks. These benefits are partly offset by losing direct structural and auxiliary-loss ablations and trajectory cases. The removed contraction argument was itself incomplete: v1's Equation 13 did not establish that the combined error-propagation factor was contractive. Overall, the empirical support improves, but the gains are limited by lost diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NeuroKalman work, and all supplied text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. V1 includes Appendix A; v2 ends after the references. These are identifiable content differences rather than extraction gaps.

after.justification: V2 retains original navigation experiments and adds low-data training, post-hoc Kalman filtering, and memory-threshold results in Section 4.

before.justification: V1 reports original TravelUAV/AirSim navigation results, component ablations, and trajectory analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.

title: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Continuous Navigation via Memory-Augmented Kalman Filtering

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: three-stage generative cyclization, efficient hierarchical sampling, and advantages in stability, diversity, secondary-structure recovery and efficiency. The new experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets physicochemical agreement as evidence of pharmaceutical relevance, attributes improved torsion fidelity to Cyclic RPE, and strengthens the argument that learned initialization enables structural recovery. Final limitations remain unchanged, but Appendix D.2 drops v1's explanation that some unfiltered CPSea structures can fail closure or force-field criteria.

D1.justification: The abstract newly supplies a MuCO demo repository link, and Section 3.2 identifies the CP-Composer/CPSea open-source pipeline underlying topology detection. Existing architecture details, hyperparameters, hardware, training times, data filtering and refinement settings are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same CPSea training population and CPTrans, CPBind, CPCore and CPSea-PDB evaluation subsets, with the same peptide-length coverage and cyclization tasks. The added evaluations use the existing CPSea-PDB subset.

E2.justification: Appendix F.2 and Table 15 add evaluated AlphaFold3 and ProteinZen comparators, substantially extending comparison beyond the original AF2-derived and geometric-regression baselines to additional end-to-end methods. The four original quantitative baselines remain, although Figure 5 removes AfCycDesign and WGFormer from its case comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds hydrogen-bond, radius-of-gyration and SASA deviation/RMSD metrics, plus JS similarity for torsion and secondary-structure distributions. It also introduces linear-versus-cyclic RPE and random-initialization control protocols. Existing data splits, training budgets, sampling configurations and physical-refinement criteria remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.4 adds two targeted analyses: Table 5 isolates Cyclic RPE's contribution to side-chain fidelity, and Table 6 tests whether CHARMM36 alone can recover secondary structure from random coordinates. These materially extend the retained stage-replacement, refinement and sampling analyses.

E5.justification: The new random-initialization control explicitly reports 20 independent trials and first-sample, average and best-of-20 summaries. This is new repeated-trial reporting, not an increase in runs for the original benchmarks. Confidence intervals and significance tests are not added.

E6.justification: Original table values are retained: v1 Tables 1–10 match v2 Tables 1, 4 and 7–14. New Tables 2, 3, 5, 6 and 15 add substantial results, including MuCO JS similarities of 0.589/0.479/0.852 and secondary-structure gain of 0.2759 versus the random-trial mean of -0.0241. Figure 5 removes AfCycDesign/WGFormer case results.

M1.justification: The backbone flow model, torsional side-chain flow with Cyclic RPE, topology detection, CHARMM36 refinement and hierarchical sampling remain unchanged. Equations and Algorithms 1–3 retain the same procedures. The new linear-RPE variant is an ablation, not a revision of MuCO.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. v2 makes grammatical and terminology corrections, updates affiliations, revises Appendix D's explanations, and adds acknowledgements, an impact statement and Appendix F.2. These are localized changes rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference-style layout, extensively resizing and repositioning displays. Five tables are added, Figure 5 is reduced from six columns to four, and the sampling table changes from side-by-side dataset panels to vertically grouped rows. Plot labels, legends and captions also receive revisions.

R1.justification: v2 adds the ProteinZen citation and comparison, and explicitly acknowledges CP-Composer/CPSea as sources for the topology pipeline. The related-work framework remains stable. CPSea's date and other publication-metadata updates refer to retained works rather than additional research.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds a mathematical definition for the newly introduced JS-similarity measure: one minus the averaged KL divergence to the mixture distribution, applied to marginal and joint distributions. The flow objectives, geometric constraints and other existing mathematics remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The new distributional metrics, targeted controls and end-to-end comparisons strengthen validation of the existing method, while the demo link improves access information. The gains are useful but bounded: the additions concentrate on CPSea-PDB, small RPE improvements lack uncertainty estimates, and Table 6's positive best-of-20 random gain qualifies the prose's categorical failure claim. Overall, v2 provides better support with some remaining overinterpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MuCO study. All 29 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including Appendices A–F, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables and figures despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds physicochemical and distributional evaluations, cyclic-encoding and random-initialization controls, and AlphaFold3/ProteinZen comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original CPSea experiments measuring cyclization success, energy, diversity, secondary structure and efficiency, with sampling analyses and component ablations in Section 4 and Appendix F.

title: MuCO: Generative Peptide Cyclization Empowered by Multi-stage Conformation Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract adds an explicit claim of favorable scaling behavior and narrows the first-architecture claim from adaptive mesh refinement generally to HR-adaptive simulations. The central claims about fused attention, mesh flexibility, super-resolution and cross-dataset learning remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new scaling results as showing further growth potential and explains MINO's ATES memory failure through its mesh-dependent latent size. Appendix D emphasizes that APT's advantage is strongest in heterogeneous subsurface settings. The conclusion newly acknowledges that scaling was demonstrated for one physics type and leaves multiphysics pretraining and transfer fine-tuning untested.

D1.justification: Appendices C.1.2 and C.2.1 substantially expand implementation documentation for the added baselines, including widths, layers, tokens, graph hierarchy, optimizer settings and training budgets. v2 also specifies timing batch size and hardware and documents scaling configurations. Existing APT implementation descriptions and the promise to release code and created datasets upon publication remain.

E1.justification: New Appendix D adds Airfoil, Darcy and Elasticity evaluations, covering compressible flow, linear porous-medium flow and linear solid mechanics. This substantially extends task coverage beyond the retained subsurface and CarBench experiments. The scaling studies reuse ATES.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Transolver, MINO, UPT and HOOD to the faulted CO2 comparison. Table 3 adds evaluated UPT and Transolver baselines on ATES and records an attempted MINO evaluation that exceeds memory capacity. These additions substantially broaden comparisons on existing tasks; the earlier comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.5 introduces controlled experiments with 40k, 120k and 161k training samples and 0.8M, 17.5M and 69.4M parameters, reporting the best test loss during training. New baseline experiments specify additional training budgets and configurations. The faulted-CO2 timing protocol changes its reported GPU from A100 to H100, except HOOD on A100, and newly specifies batch size 340; these are not directly comparable timing conditions across versions.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 and Table 7 add data-size and model-capacity sensitivity studies, testing whether additional data and parameters continue improving ATES predictions. Section 4.3 also expands analysis of accuracy, latency and memory tradeoffs. Existing branch ablations, super-resolution tests, geological distribution-shift tests and qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: No changed run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimators, confidence intervals or significance procedures are documented. The existing uncertainty descriptions and CarBench sampling-seed caveat remain. Changes to CarBench uncertainty values are numerical result changes, without evidence of a changed estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline, scaling, efficiency and PDE results while retaining the main APT accuracy scores. Table 7 reports losses falling from 0.1153 to 0.0812 with increased data and from 0.1167 to 0.0722 with increased model size. CarBench changes from 96.00±3.1 to 96.00±0.18 for R2 and from 0.1535±0.038 to 0.1535±0.0022 for relative L2. The timing table replaces APT's 0.017 s with 0.002 s under different hardware. New Table 17 places APT second on Airfoil and Elasticity but third on Darcy, contrary to its caption.

M1.justification: The fused global/local encoder, gating, latent approximator, decoder, temporal conditioning and training objective remain unchanged in Section 2 and Appendix B. The new scaling experiments vary model width without introducing a new APT component or procedure.

P1.justification: v2 adds focused efficiency and scaling subsections, a mesh-adaptivity subsection, Appendix D and a limitations paragraph. Existing prose and section organization are largely retained, with localized grammar, reference and conference-header edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds the accuracy–latency–memory plot in Figure 4 and new scaling and PDE tables, while expanding the baseline and timing tables with rows, groups and footnotes. Existing figures and most table designs are retained, with localized relocation, renumbering and page reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds HOOD and MINO citations and introduces Appendix A.5 distinguishing R-, H- and HR-adaptivity. It explicitly credits UPT's earlier ability to query different input/output mesh topologies, refining APT's novelty positioning. Other reference changes largely update bibliographic metadata or remove duplicate entries.

T1.justification: The operator formulation, loss, conditioning equations, metric definitions and governing-PDE assumptions in Section 2 and Appendices B–C are retained. The new mesh-adaptivity taxonomy is descriptive and introduces no new formal result, proof or derivation.

improvement.justification: The added mesh-native comparisons in Tables 1 and 3 address an important weakness in v1's evidence for its central subsurface claims: limited comparison with closely related operators. Scaling experiments, broader PDE evaluations and explicit applicability limits further strengthen the paper. These substantial gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including best-test-loss selection in the scaling study, Table 17's incorrect ranking caption, and unexplained CarBench uncertainty changes that conflict with the retained discussion of unusually large deviations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same APT study. The main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, scaling experiments, computational measurements and standard PDE benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original APT experiments, including subsurface prediction, architectural ablations, super-resolution, out-of-distribution evaluation and cross-dataset training.

title: Adaptive Physics Transformer with Fused Global-Local Attention for Subsurface Energy Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about container-free execution, storage and setup savings, comparable training performance, and flexible isolation. The additional experiment supports existing claims rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: Sections 6.4–6.5 and the new Limitations section substantially expand qualifications concerning two central properties: efficiency and isolation. They discuss compression tradeoffs, acknowledge Docker's advantage at extreme concurrency and imperfect scaling, and specify Linux, untrusted-code, kernel-operation, and networking boundaries. These interpretations and applicability limits were not comparably articulated in v1.

D1.justification: Section 6.4 newly discloses gzip compression level 6, without establishing a change to the implementation. Conversely, v1's poorly labeled training-hyperparameter Table 6 and its accompanying sentence disappear without replacement. The code link, hardware specifications, and cache-exception documentation remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use SWE-smith for training and SWE-bench Verified for evaluation, with the same represented tasks and documented exclusions. Adding an official SWE-Agent-7B checkpoint changes the model configuration, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 add SWE-Agent-7B-docker as the matched comparator for SWE-Agent-7B-MiniSandbox. In v1, that official checkpoint appears only in the verifier-agreement experiment in Table 5. Existing comparators remain; Issue Mirroring becoming Task Mirroring is a rename.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 extends RL experiments to the official SWE-Agent-7B checkpoint, described as fine-tuned on Claude trajectories. It uses the retained 1,600-instance, one-epoch protocol with batch size 16 and eight rollouts. Existing experiments' budgets, hardware controls, metrics, and evaluation procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The pressure tests, timing breakdowns, verifier-agreement analysis, and appendix error and tool-interaction case studies are retained. New Sections 6.4–6.5 discuss design choices and existing scaling results without adding ablations, robustness tests, or case-study evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run variability, seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The five-step averaging used for scalability measurements and the reporting practice for Reward MD remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 add SWE-Agent-7B results: 13.4→16.4 for Docker and 13.4→16.8 for MiniSandbox, with associated timing measurements. These are additional checkpoint results, not improvements over matching v1 runs. Section 5.2 corrects storage from 93 GB to 89 GB, matching the unchanged Table 1; earlier result rows remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The mount-namespace/chroot isolation, venv caching, bounded decompression, distributed integration, and reward procedure are unchanged. The additional checkpoint experiments and packaging explanations do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: Most prose and section order are retained. v4 adds two discussion subsections, Limitations, an Impact Statement, and acknowledgements; condenses the concurrency explanation; and updates author and publication information. It also corrects True Negative to False Negative for the same counted event.

P2.justification: Tables 2–3 gain checkpoint rows, Table 5's TN heading becomes FN, and the appendix training-details table is removed. Several tables and figures are relocated or resized, with subsequent appendix tables renumbered. All eleven figures retain the same image content; there is no substantial visual redesign.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning against container-based and image-reuse approaches remain unchanged. Adding a URL to the existing SWE-Swiss reference and renaming Issue Mirroring to Task Mirroring do not introduce new related work or alter research positioning.

T1.justification: The I/O-budget inequality and definition of maximum admissible concurrency are preserved; v1's explicit Equation 2 is restated in prose. The appendix reward definition is unchanged apart from renumbering. No new assumptions, derivations, or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: The added matched-checkpoint experiment strengthens evidence that efficiency savings preserve training performance, while the new scaling and isolation qualifications clarify applicability. Correcting the storage discrepancy and FN terminology improves consistency. Gains remain limited: broad efficiency and isolation claims persist, and the poorly labeled hyperparameter table is deleted without a usable replacement. Overall, the additional evidence and clearer boundaries provide a modest net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SWE-MiniSandbox and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Matching the retained and relocated material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original empirical results and adds training-performance and timing results for the official SWE-Agent-7B checkpoint.

before.justification: v1 reports original training and evaluation results, storage and timing measurements, scalability experiments, verifier comparisons, and appendix case studies.

title: SWE-MiniSandbox: Container-Free Reinforcement Learning for Building Software Engineering Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: transferable coarse-grained dynamics, improved generalization from pLM embeddings, data-efficient state-of-the-art equilibrium sampling, and non-Arrhenius kinetics. New experiments strengthen support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendices D.3–D.4 add interpretations linking the usefulness of larger embeddings to model capacity and the 100M model's degradation to insufficient data scaling. Appendix D.5 explains why high coverage can coexist with unrealistic conformations. Existing limitations concerning coarse-graining, missing guarantees, generalization, and underestimated timescales are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, pLM embedding dimensions, TITO+Struct hyperparameter information, and Appendix B.5's 50×50 binning and shared-support metric definitions. These extend existing reproducibility documentation. However, B.5 specifies two TICA components while Section 5.2 retains four, leaving the precise metric implementation inconsistent rather than establishing a clear protocol replacement.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same mdCATH training coverage, fast-folding proteins, temperature-dependent folding/unfolding scenarios, four cryptic-pocket systems, and domain-annotation study. The new experiments vary models and controls within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Emu, a Boltzmann-emulator control matched to TITO in architecture, data, and compute, to Table 1. It also adds ConfDiff and Str2Str to the fast-folder comparison in Appendix D.5 and Table 10, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives beyond BioEmu and the original variants.

E3.justification: New experiments independently vary pLM family/size at fixed model capacity and model capacity from 1M to 100M at fixed ESMC-6B, with matched data and compute controls. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Separately, the reference force-field label changes from CHARMM22 to CHARMM22*, and Protein G's reported inference parallelism changes from 5,000 to 4,000 trajectories; neither establishes a rerun of retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds structure-only conditioning and matched Emu controls, plus Appendix D.3–D.4 ablations separating pLM choice from trainable model capacity. These address attribution questions left unresolved by v1's joint increase in model and pLM size. Appendix D.5 also examines unrealistic basins underlying Str2Str's high coverage.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same uncertainty-reporting practices, including plus/minus entries for equilibrium metrics and Bayesian MSM posterior standard deviations for kinetic observables in Appendix B.3. The added rows introduce no new seed counts, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Retained Table 1 scores are unchanged, but substantial results are added for TITO+Struct, Emu, pLM choices, capacities, ConfDiff, and Str2Str. Emu's MAE/RMSE are 1.305/1.639 versus TITO's retained 1.068/1.382. Table 10 gives PLaTITO-19M the lowest errors, while Str2Str has higher coverage, 0.707 versus 0.666. Table 9 newly reports 36M-model errors of 0.811/1.066; these are additional configuration results, not improvements to the unchanged 19M result.

M1.justification: Section 5.1 adds TITO+Struct, a conditioning variant combining Proteina structure embeddings with the amino-acid sequence without pLM embeddings. The underlying flow-matching objective, two-stage transformer architecture, and rollout procedures remain unchanged. PLaTITO-Big becoming PLaTITO-19M is a rename.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely retained. Changes include grammatical corrections, standardized notation, the PLaTITO-19M rename, updated cross-references, an Impact Statement, and new appendix subsections. This is a localized expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the experimental displays with Tables 7–10 and Figures 11–12, adds rows to Table 1, and adds TITO+Struct columns to Figures 7–8. It also reformats plots and corrects apo/holo axis labels and captions in Figure 6 and the corresponding appendix figure. Existing dynamics and pocket figures remain present under updated numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations and comparative discussion for ConfDiff (Wang et al., 2024) and Str2Str (Lu et al., 2024). The broader research positioning remains stable. Publication updates for existing references, including earlier TITO work, do not represent newly cited research.

T1.justification: The mathematical framework and assumptions remain unchanged, with no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation. Replacing epsilon with z0 in the loss standardizes equivalent notation. Appendix B.5 supplies standard formulas and implementation definitions for existing evaluation metrics rather than new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v1's data-efficiency argument relied heavily on comparisons with differently trained BioEmu, while its scaling comparison changed model capacity and pLM size together. v2's matched Emu control and separate ablations address these important attribution weaknesses, and additional baselines strengthen validation. Code-access information and metric details improve documentation. The inconsistent TICA dimensionality and broad performance wording despite Str2Str's coverage advantage limit clarity, but the stronger controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PLaTITO research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–E are readable and support comparison, including matching renamed models and relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds controlled model comparisons, pLM ablations, and capacity-scaling experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original equilibrium-sampling, folding-kinetics, cryptic-pocket, and annotation-evaluation results in Section 5 and the appendices.

title: Protein Language Model Embeddings Improve Generalization of Implicit Transfer Operators

C1.justification: The same core contributions remain: the multi-objective formulation, retrospective and prospective behaviors, BAO training, and improved performance–engagement trade-offs. v2 foregrounds the Pareto framing in the abstract without materially changing these claims or the conclusion.

C2.justification: Section 3 adds sparse reward signals as an explanation for unsuccessful naive reward balancing. Appendix A.2 interprets λans variation as a smooth engagement–score trade-off, while A.3 addresses dependence on teacher capability. Existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents w=0, a 0.5 penalty for failing to complete initial-turn generation within the token budget, and numerical regularization settings in the new ablations. Existing training configurations, prompts, software, hardware and access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three UserRL tasks and feedback environments. The new appendix experiments vary penalty settings and the demonstration teacher within existing task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains exactly the same commercial models, raw Qwen3 models, UserRL baselines and BAO variants. The added teacher experiment retains UserRL as the comparator; GPT-4o-mini serves as a demonstration teacher.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 adds Function-Gym sweeps of λans from 0.0005 to 0.005 and λthink from 0.005 to 0.05. Appendix A.3 adds a Telepathy-Gym/Qwen3-1.7B comparison using GPT-4o-mini demonstrations with matched SFT counts and RL data. Existing experiment settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.2–A.3 tests sensitivity to both regularization coefficients and dependence on teacher capability. These are targeted additions to the existing component ablations, exploration analyses, reward-hacking tests and case studies.

E5.justification: Figure 5 retains its three-random-seed averages and standard-deviation shading. The new appendix tables provide point estimates without adding run counts, uncertainty estimates or statistical tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the existing plotted results are unchanged; new Tables 2–4 add sensitivity and alternative-teacher results. Under the new GPT-4o-mini-teacher setting, BAO versus UserRL achieves Pass@U-1 of 0.5122 versus 0.1707 and UR of 0.1423 versus 0.7619. These are additional-condition results, not revised original scores.

M1.justification: The behavior-enhanced SFT and behavior-regularized GRPO pipeline, behavior categories, prompts and Algorithm 1 are retained. v2 newly specifies w=0 and an initial-turn failure penalty as implementation details; this does not establish a revision to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, parts of the introduction, Section 3 and the opening of Section 4 are rewritten to clarify the Pareto framing. Two appendix subsections, acknowledgments and affiliation/publication-header edits are added; the overall organization remains intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 reorders its panels and adds an annotated infeasible region. Three appendix tables are added, existing configuration tables become Tables 5–6, and several figures relocate within the main text. The other displays retain their content and design.

R1.justification: v2 removes the Rahimi et al. (2025) citation and reference. It also explicitly contrasts BAO's inter-turn behavior emphasis with handcrafted reward balancing in Sun et al. (2025) and CollabLLM, while retaining the broader related-work discussion.

T1.justification: The contextual MDP, action-space decomposition, reward and engagement definitions, and Equations 1–5 remain mathematically unchanged apart from notation clarification. The rewritten Pareto discussion adds no substantive formal assumptions, derivations or proofs.

improvement.justification: The new penalty-sensitivity and teacher controls in Appendix A.2–A.3 strengthen empirical support, while the explicit implementation details improve reproducibility. These gains are bounded by their selected task/model settings; the main results and conclusions remain unchanged. The evidence supports a modest overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BAO study and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–D. Retained material can be matched reliably despite relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds penalty-weight sensitivity tests and an alternative-teacher experiment in Appendix A.2–A.3.

before.justification: v1 reports original BAO experiments on Function-Gym, Telepathy-Gym and Turtle-Gym, including component ablations, exploration measurements and reward-hacking analyses.

title: Pushing Forward Pareto Frontiers of Proactive Agents with Behavioral Agentic Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract qualifies its theoretical contribution from a causal inductive bias via latent interventions to a useful bias from controlling observability, bringing headline claims closer to qualifications already present in v1 Appendix B. The central method contribution and claims of roughly 20-point counterfactual gains and compact, efficient planning remain.

C2.justification: Appendix J interprets PHYRE rollouts and attention as evidence of interaction-aware prediction and explicitly excludes causal-graph identification. Appendix M.2 adds conditions under which predictive neighborhoods may align with physical interactions. General cautions about confounding and causal identifiability already appeared in v1 Appendix B.

D1.justification: Figure A3 adds a specific repository location for PHYRE visualizations, while Appendix C.1 removes the public evaluation-server link. Existing implementation, hyperparameter, hardware, and main code-access information is retained. PHYRE-specific training and sampling details are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 adds qualitative evaluation on PHYRE scenes involving gravity, momentum transfer, and multi-body collisions. This provides a limited extension beyond the retained CLEVRER reasoning and Push-T control coverage, rather than a new quantitative benchmark evaluation.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the CLEVRER and Push-T experiments, including reconstruction variants and DINO-WM variants. The PHYRE study extends the existing C-JEPA versus OC-JEPA comparison to another dataset; it introduces no new comparator.

E3.justification: The added PHYRE study introduces qualitative assessment through ground-truth versus imagined trajectories and cross-slot attention as an interaction proxy. Existing splits, metrics, training budgets, and MPC settings remain unchanged; both versions already evaluate CLEVRER on the held-out validation set.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix J add two illustrated PHYRE rollout cases and an attention comparison examining physical plausibility and reliance on relevant objects. Existing masking-budget, masking-strategy, reconstruction, and auxiliary-conditioning ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report planning-time averages across three seeds and the same fixed-seed information in Appendix H. v2 adds no repeated-run information, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and A2–A5 and the existing Figure 3 results are unchanged; for example, Push-T success remains 88.67% for C-JEPA and 91.33% for DINO-WM. New PHYRE examples show more plausible C-JEPA rollouts and more concentrated attention to relevant slots than OC-JEPA, adding qualitative findings without revising existing benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The frozen object encoder, identity-anchor masking, bidirectional predictor, joint history/future objective, auxiliary conditioning, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Recasting masking as control of observability does not change the algorithm.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Latent Interventions' to 'Latent Masking,' with selective abstract and explanatory revisions and updated author/publication information. Section 5.3, Appendix J, and two explanatory theory subsections are added; subsequent appendices are renumbered. Most existing prose and organization remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures A3 and A4 for PHYRE rollout sequences and attention maps. Tables A4–A5 move later in the appendix, Figure 2's caption changes terminology, and text reflows. Existing illustrations, plots, and table structures are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bakhtin et al. (2019) for PHYRE and connects the new attention analysis to the already cited SPARTAN work. The Push-T citation changes from Bekris et al. to Chi et al. for the same Diffusion Policy paper, constituting a bibliographic correction rather than a different cited work.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, four assumptions, lemma, theorem, corollary statement, and proofs are retained. v1 Appendices L.1–L.2 correspond to v2 M.1 and M.4. New M.2–M.3 paragraphs provide interpretation and shortcut explanations, not new formal results or corrected derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the headline causal framing more consistent with the observability-based qualifications already present in v1 and adds inspectable PHYRE examples supporting the proposed mechanism. These improve clarity and empirical illustration modestly. The gain is limited because the new evidence is qualitative, lacks PHYRE-specific training and sampling details, and leaves the quantitative results and formal analysis unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same C-JEPA work and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Existing content can be matched despite the title change, appendix renumbering, and layout shifts.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds PHYRE rollout and attention case studies in Section 5.3 and Appendix J.

before.justification: v1 reports original CLEVRER question-answering results, Push-T planning results and timings, and masking and auxiliary-conditioning ablations.

title: Causal-JEPA: Learning World Models through Object-Level Latent Masking

C1.justification: The central contributions—selective detection, control of endogenous confounding, and nearly minimax-optimal anytime tracking—remain intact. Section 1.2 removes the lower-order log-log qualification from its stated lower-bound contribution, giving a limited strengthening of that claim.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the broad claim that faster or slower threshold growth precludes optimal guarantees with a qualified explanation of controlled contamination and recovery. Section 4.3 softens the inference from the lower bound to sublinear-regret achievability. The conclusion adds substantive discussion of extension requirements, online variance calibration, dependent observations, and gradual drift.

D1.justification: Section 5 replaces v1's promise of future code availability with a statement of public availability and an explicit implementation repository link. This adds actionable access information; the repository's contents were not inspected. Most data-processing instructions and experimental hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Gaussian piecewise-stationary synthetic environments and NAB AWS CPU-usage series, including dense changes and adversarial scenarios. The additional discussion of exponential-family, regression, and dependent-observation settings proposes future extensions rather than reporting new evaluations.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain sliding-window and discounted-mean baselines, the same constant-threshold detectors, and the efficient ATC variant. Newly cited related methods are not added as evaluated comparators. The passive baselines' observation-timing revision is an evaluation-protocol change.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1.1 changes the sliding-window and discounted-mean formulas from including observations through t to using observations through t−1. This revises the reported prediction-time information available to those baselines. The sliding-window denominator and lower summation limit remain unchanged, leaving an indexing inconsistency. The PDFs do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The dense-change, passive-baseline, constant-threshold, variance-misspecification, adversarial-environment, and change-count analyses were already present in v1 Appendix A.1. v2 adds a main-text overview of these retained analyses without adding tests or case studies.
