title: LaCy: What Small Language Models Can and Should Learn is Not Just a Question of Loss

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about computational replacement, compact circuits, steering, and biological interpretability. The additional experiments support these claims without rewriting their headline scope.

C2.justification: v1 presents larger-model scaling as future work; v2 interprets 35M and windowed-CLT results as evidence of improved feasibility and an accuracy/compute tradeoff. It also adds global-functional-rule and circuit-stability interpretations, and explicitly identifies autoregressive and diffusion-model extensions as unresolved applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 documents 35M latent dimensions and sparsity, newly discloses explicit LayerNorm in the 8M implementation and its omission for 35M, and supplies window width and additional evaluation settings. Appendix G.3 and Table 10 add NVIDIA RTX A6000 hardware information, parameter counts, and training-time estimates, including extrapolations for larger models. Code and visualizer access information is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use UniRef50 training sequences, Swiss-Prot/InterPro family tasks, the same 12 ProteinGym assays, and the same seven steering assays. The new mutation-depth and stability analyses reuse existing coverage; larger backbones change model configurations rather than datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained PLT, CAA, and random-mutation comparisons, v2 evaluates ESM2-logit mutation selection on seven steering assays (Table 8) and PEX and GGS on the GB1 and HIS7 assays (Table 9). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds ESM2-35M configurations and evaluation protocols, including 1,024-example test subsamples for four assays and 128-example, fitness-balanced validation samples for multiple-mutant circuit discovery. It also specifies ten-round PEX/GGS comparisons and mutation-depth and circuit-overlap evaluations. Appendix A revises the reported auxiliary-loss setting from k_aux=floor(d_ESM/2) to 32, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds GFP prediction analysis stratified by mutation depth, circuit-node overlap across family inputs and training folds, and a windowed-versus-standard CLT accuracy/cost comparison. These test functional consistency, circuit stability, and connectivity tradeoffs beyond v1's retained replacement-model ablations and biological case studies.

E5.justification: Appendix E.1 newly specifies that the mutation-depth analysis uses the circuit discovered with the first random seed. Existing cross-validation, steering-trial counts, and uncertainty-reporting practices are retained; the revision does not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for ESM2-35M, windowed CLTs, mutation-depth retention, circuit overlap, and new steering comparators. For example, sequential 35M circuits achieve family F1 of 0.80 ± 0.12 and function Spearman correlation of 0.38 ± 0.19 (Appendix G). The original five tables and Figures 1–8 retain their results, while Section 3.1 changes the stated 8M function-circuit recovery from 74% to 76% without changing its reported correlation.

M1.justification: v2 introduces windowed CLTs, restricting each decoder to a width-w layer window instead of all preceding layers (Appendix G.3, Equation 14). This changes cross-layer connectivity and computational requirements; a width-four variant is trained and evaluated. The original circuit-discovery and steering procedures remain.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 adds focused discussion subsections and a scaling appendix, moves the SAE comparison from Appendix G to H, clarifies terminology, and updates the publication header and acknowledgments. This is a localized expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds mutation-depth Tables 3–4, comparator Tables 8–9, resource Table 10, and scaling/windowed-model Figures 15–16. Existing steering tables are renumbered, the SAE schematic becomes Figure 17, and appendix displays are redistributed and resized. The substantial change is new visual evidence, while Figures 1–8 and the interface screenshots are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ren et al. (2022) and Kirjner et al. (2024) for PEX/GGS comparisons, and Shu et al. (2026) as inspiration for windowed CLTs. These extend positioning toward protein optimization and scalable circuit tracing while retaining the existing SAE/transcoder framing.

T1.justification: Appendix F.1 corrects the edge-weight formula to use the target latent's encoder rather than the source latent's encoder. Equation 14 additionally defines the restricted decoder summation for windowed CLTs. These are localized mathematical changes; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's untested scalability limitation through actual ESM2-35M experiments and an evaluated windowed architecture that reduces parameters from 207M to 125M while retaining 82% versus 85% family-task performance. Broader comparators and circuit-stability checks strengthen validation. The gains remain substantial despite limitations: mutation-depth evidence uses one seed, larger-model timings are extrapolated, and Appendix G's latent-space percentages are inconsistent with its stated 12 × 4800 latent space.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ProtoMech research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds ESM2-35M experiments, windowed-CLT evaluation, circuit-stability analyses, and additional steering comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original protein-family classification, function prediction, circuit discovery, steering experiments, and biological case studies.

title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders

C1.justification: V1 claims to introduce a distinct alignment-risk category and broadly transferable exploit skills. V2 recasts the contribution as a controlled framework for vulnerable RL pipelines, explicitly limits transfer, and elevates task-dependent resistance to correction into the abstract and main contributions. This substantively narrows and redefines the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies explanations involving internalization, situational awareness, and capability-driven generalization. Sections 5.5–6 and Appendix A acknowledge reversed RL-versus-SFT comparisons, persistent tampering under both origins, nonmonotonic scaling, and limitations of loophole removal. New broad-alignment checks support a mostly task-bounded interpretation.

D1.justification: The code-access link changes from Capability_Oriented_Alignment_Risk to Capability-seeking-RL-risk. Removing v1 Appendix E.4 also removes a worked prompt/output example, although Appendix F retains the tampering templates. Existing audit settings, rewriting model pool, and processing details are largely preserved.

E1.justification: Appendix A.7 adds HarmBench and TruthfulQA checks of original and exploit-trained checkpoints, extending evaluation to broader alignment outcomes. The four vulnerability games and their existing BBEH, CNN/DailyMail, and LiveCodeBench coverage remain.

E2.justification: Appendix A.5/Table 12 adds initialization through SFT on correct, non-exploitative Reward Tampering solutions to the Qwen3-4B-Base sequential-training comparison. From-scratch and exploit-RL initializations were already evaluated; the existing main comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Table 2 and Appendix D replace the refusal-rate-difference definition with the fraction of paired refuse-audit/answer-user outcomes, resolving inconsistency with v1 Section 3.1. Appendix A.5 also introduces the non-exploit SFT initialization protocol. These reported changes do not establish that existing evaluations were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a source-exposure control, trajectories for the existing correction experiment, and broad-alignment diagnostics in Appendices A.5–A.7. These extend the transfer and persistence analyses without replacing them. V1's detailed E.4 Reward Tampering transcript is removed, while the separate illustrated tampering case remains.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Appendix A.1 retains 16 rollouts per prompt. The new correction curves show trajectories without introducing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Matched numerical entries in v1 Tables 3–10 and v2 Tables 4–11 are unchanged. New Table 12 reports 80.7% exploitation for the non-exploit SFT control alongside the existing 81.6% from-scratch and 89.8% exploit-RL results. Table 13 adds broad-alignment scores, and Figure 3 adds correction trajectories.

M1.justification: The four games, GRPO training, sequential RL, SFT distillation, and Safety GRPO remain unchanged. Protected score-field overwriting through insecure parsing was already described in v1 Section 3.4 and Appendix C.4; v2's revised summaries do not establish a new mechanism.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change throughout, with extensive rewriting of the abstract, introduction, result explanations, discussion, conclusion, impact statement, and analytical appendices. Research questions and headings emphasize discovery, bounded transfer, and persistence. This exceeds localized editing despite retaining the overall section hierarchy.

P2.justification: V2 extensively reformats the main text into two columns and changes table and figure sizing and placement. It adds conceptual Figure 1, correction Figure 3, and Tables 12–13; Table 3 redisplays existing results. V1 Figure 1 is retained as appendix Figure 4.

R1.justification: Section 2 now positions the study as complementary to prior reward-hacking and scheming research instead of encompassing those behaviors within a broader category. Section 6 adds connections to EVOL-RL and TTRL. References also add safety-related work and remove the earlier jailbreak-defense and semantically-aware-reward citations.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 corrects the self-grading argument: v1 checks whether overclaiming has nonnegative return, whereas v2 explicitly derives E_overclaim − E_honest = (1−q)(1−7p). This establishes the advantage over honest reporting for p < 1/7 and q < 1. The experimental audit probability remains 0.1.

improvement.justification: V2 makes the conclusions more defensible by acknowledging counterexamples in retained results and correcting Appendix C.2's reward comparison. New controls and broader alignment checks provide useful supporting evidence. The gains remain limited: the source-exposure control compares SFT with RL, so it does not fully isolate exploit experience, and the new evaluations lack detailed protocol and uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same vulnerability-game study despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing additions, removals, and relocated material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds a source-task exposure control, corrective-training trajectories, and HarmBench/TruthfulQA evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original RL experiments, cross-task transfer, SFT distillation, corrective training, and appendix controls using Qwen and Llama models.

title: Alignment Risks from Capability-Seeking RL Training

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the scheduling and switching contributions and the headline improvement of up to 2×, averaging 1.5×. The sensitivity study supplies additional support without redefining those core claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new sensitivity results as showing increasingly effective workload-aware deployment and assignment as heterogeneity grows, attributing the widening advantage to static deployments' increasing mismatch. Existing limitations and extensibility discussions are retained.

D1.justification: For the added sensitivity experiments, Tables 1–2 document exact SILO/LILO/SISO/LISO percentages and the ordering of workload mixtures used to construct temporal traces. Existing implementation, profiling, hardware, and code-link information is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds controlled Azure-derived test scenarios: five workload mixtures with different spatial skew and four temporal sequences of those mixtures. These extend input-condition coverage while retaining the existing datasets and workload types.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain vLLM (static), vLLM (reload), Llumnix, Dynamo+vLLM, and the existing predictor and exhaustive-search comparators. The added sensitivity study reuses vLLM (static).

E3.justification: The added sensitivity protocol evaluates Llama2-70B on 16 GPUs using controlled workload proportions and temporal transitions, characterized by spatial and temporal coefficients of variation. Previously reported experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 6.3 and Tables 1–2 add targeted analyses of how performance benefits vary with spatial skew and temporal workload changes. Existing component ablations, prediction comparisons, optimality checks, and homogeneous-workload analysis remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Existing statistical reporting is retained. The new tables add point speedups without repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates; their CV values describe workload variability, not uncertainty in measured performance.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add five spatial speedups ranging from 1.14× to 2.66× and four temporal speedups ranging from 1.23× to 1.98× over vLLM (static). Existing main-text and appendix results are unchanged; these are additional settings, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The two-level scheduler, k-means/LSTM workload predictor, greedy switching procedure, KV-cache handling, and appendix Algorithms 1–2 are unchanged. Moving the system overview into Section 3 does not introduce a method component.

P1.justification: The overview moves from v1 Appendix A into v2 Section 3 with light prose editing. Section and appendix references are updated, the publication notice changes, and a sensitivity-analysis paragraph is added; the remaining narrative is largely retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds two sensitivity tables and moves the overview diagram from Figure 16 to Figure 3, resizing it and correcting LiveServe labels and section references. Existing result plots retain their content, while figures, the case-study table, and surrounding text undergo relocation and reflow.

R1.justification: The reference list and substantive research positioning are unchanged. Extended related work moves from Appendix B to Appendix A without adding or removing cited works.

T1.justification: The flow-network constraints, capacity normalization, optimization objective, and appendix mathematical examples are unchanged. The added empirical CV descriptors introduce no formal theoretical development or proof.

improvement.justification: The sensitivity study supplements v1's trace experiments and ablations with targeted evidence about when OServe benefits most. Bringing the corrected overview into the main text also improves accessibility. The gain is limited: the new study covers one model/cluster configuration, and its tables do not clearly identify the performance metric underlying speedup or report uncertainty.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OServe system. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated between versions.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds spatial and temporal heterogeneity sensitivity experiments in Section 6.3.

before.justification: v1 reports original serving experiments, latency and throughput measurements, workload-prediction results, ablations, and appendix evaluations.

title: OServe: Accelerating LLM Serving via Spatial-Temporal Workload Orchestration

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: adversarial imitation for generative alignment, two optimization strategies, competitive results from 13K demonstrations, transfer to discrete images/video, and regularization against reward hacking. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of high-KL outliers as a source of PG instability, initialization dependence under policy–expert distribution shift, and differing data-scale effects on prompt-following and preference metrics. Its Impact Statement also introduces an explicit limitation concerning inheritance of expert-data biases and harmful content. These expand mechanisms and applicability boundaries beyond v1's retained discussion.

D1.justification: v2 documents the masking coefficient c=2, reconstruction sampling procedure, SigLIPv2 so400m feature extractor, MMD kernel bandwidths {1,2,4,8}, and measured per-step training costs. Existing hardware, optimizer settings, learning-rate tables, and code/data access statement are retained.

E1.justification: The image, discrete-image, and video tasks and their data sources remain unchanged. The new 4K/8K expert subsets and reconstruction/distribution analyses examine retained coverage rather than adding a dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the original experiments is unchanged, including RLHF-PD/PG, Online DPO, Reward Gradient, FPO, and the frontier-model comparisons. The added studies use existing methods and ablation controls, including removal of cold-start initialization, rather than introducing another competing method.

E3.justification: New protocols include PSNR/LPIPS reconstruction testing on 1,024 images with four sampled timesteps each, MMD/SWD evaluation using 1,024 expert samples and prompt-matched rollouts, fixed-budget 4K/8K data experiments, and matched 800-step initialization controls. The masking comparison adds an 800-step condition against the original 400-step baseline. Existing benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices B, E, and F substantially expand diagnostic evidence: they test one-step approximation accuracy across noise intervals, KL masking, expert-data scale, runtime components, cold-start dependence, and policy–expert distribution distance. These address previously untested design choices and failure conditions while retaining the original analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The four sampled reconstruction timesteps are part of an evaluation protocol, and the standard deviation in KL masking is an algorithmic quantity, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 remain numerically unchanged. New Tables 9 and 12–16 add substantial results, including overall reconstruction PSNR 32.55/LPIPS 0.083, masked FAIL-PG UniGen 65.49 at 800 steps, data-scale scores, runtime measurements, initialization effects, and MMD/SWD distances. These are new measurements or conditions; the masking result is not a same-budget improvement over the retained 400-step result.

M1.justification: Appendix E adds an optional KL-masking extension to FAIL-PG: samples exceeding the batch mean KL proxy plus two standard deviations are excluded from the normalized FPO objective. This changes the update procedure, while the original FAIL-PD/FAIL-PG algorithms and discriminator architectures are retained.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains largely verbatim, with a KL-masking pointer and updated appendix references. v2 adds appendix sections, acknowledgments, an Impact Statement, and conference publication information. Appendix G.1 introduces an incorrect Figure 4 reference for FAIL-PD and an unresolved 'Figure ??' reference for FAIL-PG.

P2.justification: Six new tables substantially expand the display of approximation, stabilization, scaling, timing, initialization, and distribution-distance evidence. Original Tables 1–8 and all five figures retain their content and designs; the two existing settings tables are renumbered, and the original visualization appendix moves later in the document.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Gretton et al. for MMD, Karras et al. for SWD, and Tschannen et al. for SigLIP 2. The main related-work discussion and research positioning remain unchanged; the Kurach reference is updated from its preprint to publication form.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds an explicit derivation of the existing one-step approximation by matching an Euler update to the interpolation path. Appendix E formally defines the KL threshold and masked objective. The original approximation formula and Appendix A KL derivation are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked reconstruction-error validation of its central approximation and quantitative feature-space checks of expert-distribution alignment. v2 supplies both, alongside controlled initialization/data-scale studies and measured training costs, substantially strengthening support for design choices and revealing practical dependencies. KL masking also provides evidence of improved training stability. Unequal training budgets in that comparison, continued absence of uncertainty estimates, and new figure-reference errors limit the gains but do not outweigh the stronger methodological validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FAIL research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original approximation-error, KL-masking, data-scale, timing, initialization, and distribution-distance measurements in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original FLUX fine-tuning experiments, discriminator and training-stability analyses, and discrete-image and video-generation results in Tables 1–8 and Figures 2–5.

title: FAIL: Flow Matching Adversarial Imitation Learning for Image Generation

C1.justification: The abstract changes the claimed benchmark count from eight to six, although the introduction still claims eight. The central contributions—unified discrete flow matching, separate adapters, and reference-based multimodal preference alignment—remain the same. The expanded mRef-DPO contribution statement largely restates its existing formulation.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking reflection to localization and preservation in complex edits, token-conditioning weaknesses to diluted signals, and AdLN weaknesses to disruption of pretrained normalization. Appendix D also attributes specific retained visual failures to individual alignment losses. The existing impact and applicability qualifications are substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly specifies lambda_KL = 1.8, and Section 3.2.3 explicitly states the Stage-II parameter composition. These are disclosures rather than demonstrated setting changes. Hardware, training schedules, data quantities, and the curation prompt are retained. The standalone OpenGPT-4o-Image dataset URL is removed while its paper citation remains.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on 200 PIE-Bench images covering add/remove, reasoning-based, scene-text, and multi-object edits. This extends the evaluated data within existing editing tasks. The earlier training datasets and benchmark coverage are retained.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds in-context token conditioning and AdLN as evaluated alternatives to the proposed time-step conditioning. Existing benchmark comparators and the DPO/uni-GRPO comparisons are retained; spelling changes such as BAGEL/Begal do not represent new methods.

E3.justification: The new PIE-Bench analysis compares reflection-enabled and reflection-disabled settings across four editing categories using PSNR, SSIM, structural distance, and CLIP similarity for edited and preserved regions. Existing training settings are unchanged. Section 4.1 corrects Qwen2.5-VL from 7B to 3B, matching Table 1 in both versions rather than establishing a changed experiment.

E4.justification: v2 adds targeted tests of whether reflection helps across editing complexities and whether token conditioning or AdLN can replace the proposed normalization (Tables 4–5). Earlier model-size, tokenizer, adapter, loss, training-token, and LoRA-rank analyses remain. The expanded discussion of Figure 14 interprets retained examples rather than adding a new visual ablation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's new description of results as averaged across benchmarks does not introduce repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: UniDFlow's GenEval position and color-attribute scores change from 0.97/0.93 in v1 Table 8 to 0.87/0.83 in v2 Table 9, losing leadership in those columns. The headline ablation DPG-Bench score changes from 91.91 to 91.19, although the Qwen3-4B row remains 91.91. New reflection and conditioning results are added; Tables 1–3, OCRBench scores, and the remaining matched benchmark entries are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.4 corrects the stated editing-loss target from preferred clean text tokens to preferred clean visual tokens. This is a limited correction to the written objective; the backbone, adapters, routing, training stages, and inference procedure remain unchanged, and an implementation change is not established.

P1.justification: v2 revises selected contribution and analysis paragraphs, standardizes terminology, updates author affiliations, and adds acknowledgments. It moves subject-driven generation into the editing discussion, reorders appendix sections, and retains the OCR discussion without its former standalone heading. Most explanatory prose and the main narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reformats the document into conference style, changing typography, headers, caption placement, spacing, and appendix column structure. It merges the detailed GenEval and DPG-Bench tables, adds the reflection table, expands the ablation display, and resizes or relocates numerous figures. The qualitative examples and existing plotted analyses are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ju et al.'s PnP Inversion citation for PIE-Bench and removes the standalone ChatGPT reference. The substantive positioning against autoregressive, hybrid, discrete-diffusion, and preference-alignment approaches remains unchanged; most bibliography changes are formatting or metadata updates.

T1.justification: The definition of Ledit immediately before Equation 9 changes its clean target from y_txt,0 to y_vis,0, repairing the text/visual mismatch in the mathematical objective. Other equations are substantively retained, with no new theorem, proof, or derivation.

improvement.justification: The new reflection and conditioning experiments provide useful support for existing design choices, while the corrected editing-loss target and disclosed KL weight improve specification. These are limited gains. Reporting inconsistencies remain: reduced GenEval scores are not reconciled with the retained uniform-improvement interpretation, and v2 Table 5 still gives different DPG-Bench values for its headline UniDFlow and Qwen3-4B rows.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniDFlow study. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including material relocated during v2's reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds reflection-complexity and time-step-conditioning experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original UniDFlow benchmark scores, component ablations, efficiency measurements, and qualitative generation and editing results.

title: Best of Both Worlds: Multimodal Reasoning and Generation via Unified Discrete Flow Matching

C1.justification: The central claims remain: adaptive merging improves over prompting, offers limited advantages over target-task fine-tuning, and often obtains similar gains from random adapters; relevant in-house adapters permit positive transfer. The regularization hypothesis disappears from the abstract but remains in the introduction and analysis.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries. It discusses structural regularization or implicit ensembling, small-budget overfitting and selection instability, and possible interference from Quasi-FIM-selected Qwen adapters. The conclusion adds alternative explanations involving inadequate selection or adapter incompatibility and identifies sparse metadata as an obstacle to distinguishing them.

D1.justification: V1 promises code and checkpoints without a project address; v2 supplies a repository address in the abstract. V2 also documents the new regularization grids and low-budget tuning procedure. Existing hardware, principal hyperparameters, and implementation adjustments in Appendices C–D are retained.

E1.justification: The 62 downstream tasks and their domain and language coverage remain unchanged. V2 additionally evaluates a separate population of 1,956 public Qwen3-based LoRAs alongside the original 958 Llama-based adapters, modestly extending source-adapter coverage.

E2.justification: Arrow is added to the evaluated comparator set in Figure 2 and Table 2, while existing comparators remain. New Figure 4 also compares regularized target-task LoRA variants against merging with randomly initialized LoRAs.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen3-4B experiments and a 10-sample protocol using 100 tuning steps without validation, beyond the retained 100-sample, 80/20 setting. It also introduces dropout, weight-decay, and batch-size sweeps and evaluation-based selection controls for non-adaptive methods. Appendix F.1's stated π-Tuning learning rates conflict with Appendix C.1, leaving that detail uncertain.

E4.justification: Figure 4 newly tests whether standard regularizers explain merging gains. Appendix F adds robustness analyses across model families and sample budgets, investigates π-Tuning's poor Qwen performance, and tests whether non-adaptive methods benefit from informed selection. The earlier coefficient-distribution, in-house-pool, and design-space analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five seeds for target-task LoRA training and three seeds for specified random-pool comparisons. V2 adds no new uncertainty-reporting procedure, confidence intervals, or significance tests; additional result rows do not change the reporting practice.

E6.justification: Existing Table 2 values remain unchanged, including Ours at 0.652/0.675 without/with target-task LoRA; Arrow adds 0.471/0.613. Figure 4, Table 6, Figure 13, and Table 7 supply substantial new results. These include the 10-sample finding that adding target-task LoRA can hurt performance. They are additional-condition results, not improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The proposed method retains evaluation-based selection, module-level coefficients, gradient-based optimization, and zero-initialized Leaky ReLU coefficients. Section 3's added equation documents this existing procedure. Arrow is an additional comparator, not a new component of the proposed method.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized introductory and concluding revisions, states two explicit research questions, expands the method explanation, and gives the existing coefficient analysis its own Q4 heading. It inserts Appendix F and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement, while retaining the overall narrative structure and most existing prose.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the comparative displays through new Figure 4, Figure 13, and Tables 6–7, and adds Arrow to Figure 2 and Table 2. Existing coefficient, in-house-pool, and appendix plots are retained with relocation or renumbering, rather than constituting new visual evidence.

R1.justification: V2 adds Ostapenko et al. and a description of Arrow. Most other reference changes update bibliographic metadata for existing works. The Qwen3 technical report was already cited in v1, despite the additional attribution in v2. The broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: No new assumptions, propositions, proofs, or substantive theoretical derivations are introduced. Equation 3 explicitly presents the previously described coefficient-weighted LoRA merging procedure.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's single-family, 100-sample evaluation, v2 better tests generality and alternative explanations through another model family, a smaller sample budget, and regularization and selection controls. However, reporting problems limit the gain: F.3 claims selection consistently improves results although Table 7 includes decreases, such as TSV with target-task LoRA from 0.522 to 0.502, and F.1's learning rates disagree with C.1. The additions strengthen the evidence, but their interpretation and reproducibility remain imperfect.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, framework, and retained experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds Arrow comparisons, regularization experiments, and model-family, sample-budget, and selection ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 958 recycled LoRAs across 62 downstream tasks, alongside selection, merging-design, and controlled-pool analyses.

title: The Appeal and Reality of Recycling LoRAs with Adaptive Merging

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims: persistent entity states bridge structure and sequence, counterfactual consistency addresses visibility bias, and EST improves diverse backbones with state-of-the-art forecasting performance.

C2.justification: v3 connects sparse state access and measured overhead to practical scalability, and interprets repeated visits to Iran as evidence in the worked query. Existing limitations concerning memory scaling, unseen entities and real-world nonstationarity are condensed rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies FP32 buffer storage and explains sparse indexing and in-place state updates, alongside additional resource measurements. It removes the code-repository link from the abstract without replacing it elsewhere. Appendix B's hardware, hyperparameters and optimization details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate temporal knowledge graph forecasting on ICEWS14, ICEWS18, ICEWS05-15 and GDELT. The new profiling and worked example use ICEWS14; the million-entity memory estimate is an analytical extrapolation, not an evaluated new dataset or scenario.

E2.justification: Table 1's comparator lineup is unchanged. v3 Table 4 newly compares EST-Mamba and EST-Transformer against matched w/o State variants for computational efficiency; v1's efficiency comparison included only the EST backbones.

E3.justification: v3 adds matched resource profiling using seconds per epoch, milliseconds per step and peak memory. Existing splits, training settings and truncation budgets remain unchanged. Although Section 5.1 changes the filtering terminology, Appendix B.3 retains the same explicit chronological, history-only rolling filter.

E4.justification: Adds an ablation isolating persistent-state computational overhead and an ICEWS14 case study tracing retrieved events and attention weights. Existing component, sensitivity, scorer and state-evolution analyses remain. The Mamba truncation analysis moves from Appendix E into Section 5.5 without new results.

E5.justification: No repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests are added. Existing gate mean and standard-deviation summaries are unchanged, and the new profiling results provide no additional uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark, ablation, scorer and truncation values are unchanged. v3 adds buffer-memory estimates, measured resource results and case-study attention weights. For example, Table 4 reports 60.77 versus 59.60 seconds per epoch for EST-Mamba and its matched stateless control.

M1.justification: The EST components, memory updates, loss and Algorithm 1 are retained. However, Eq. 7 replaces the previously undefined attention input e_t with the elapsed-time projection φ(Δt). The PDFs do not establish whether this changes temporal conditioning or merely clarifies notation.

P1.justification: Localized revisions rewrite an introduction paragraph and the sequence-backbone explanation, expand efficiency into Section 5.2.1, consolidate temporal-generalization discussion and introduce a worked-example Appendix E. The author/affiliation block and limitations wording also change; most of the document is retained.

P2.justification: Adds resource Tables 3–4 and worked-example Table 11. Former Figures 5 and 6 become one four-panel Figure 5, and existing appendix tables move and are renumbered. Table 1 is reformatted with shaded EST rows; retained plots and numerical displays otherwise preserve their content.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Spectron study. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across renaming and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds rank comparisons, runtime measurements, additional method comparisons and spectral diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original FineWeb pretraining results, downstream evaluations, ablations, spectral diagnostics and 39-run scaling-law experiments.

title: On Robustness and Chain-of-Thought Consistency of RL-Finetuned VLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, main contribution statements and conclusion retain the same central claims: polynomial-time regression with unknown outcome truncation under sub-Gaussian features, supported by efficient positive-only learning of unions of intervals. The added simulation does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: New Remark 3.2 explains the additional sample-complexity dependence through the precision required when learning the survival set. Section 4 also qualifies exact-set PSGD as an idealized comparator unavailable when the set is unknown, clarifying how to interpret the empirical comparison.

D1.justification: Section 4 adds a simulation-code repository link and a brief description of the synthetic setup, neither present in v1. This is a new evaluation design, rather than a revision or rerun of an existing v1 experiment.

E4.justification: The new simulation includes a limited diagnostic of truncation misspecification: PSGD with an incorrect survival set is compared with exact-set PSGD and the full algorithm. This examines the importance of estimating the set correctly, but adds no broader sensitivity sweep or robustness suite.

E5.justification: Figure 3 newly reports ten experiment repetitions, plotting mean Euclidean error with standard-deviation shading. v1 contains no empirical repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. The addition is confined to this single simulation.

E6.justification: Figure 3 supplies the first empirical results: the full algorithm's error decreases nearly alongside exact-set PSGD, while OLS remains substantially biased and incorrect-set PSGD retains much larger error. These are newly reported convergence findings, not performance gains over corresponding v1 experiments.

after.justification: v2 adds original synthetic-data experiments in Section 4. Figure 3 reports convergence results for four methods, aggregated over ten repetitions.

title: Exploring Accurate and Transparent Domain Adaptation in Predictive Healthcare via Concept-Grounded Orthogonal Inference

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about training-free MCTS slot planning, benchmark competitiveness, strategic non-sequential generation, and exploration breadth. The added evaluations support these existing claims.

It interprets the new controls as evidence against a compute-only explanation and adds qualifications about the speed–accuracy frontier and evaluation being confined to ReFusion.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GSM8K, MATH500, ARC Challenge, GPQA-Diamond, MBPP, and HumanEval. The added harness evaluations and compute comparisons retain these datasets and tasks.

P2.justification: Conference-style formatting substantially reflows the title, abstract, typography and displays. v2 adds Tables 5–9 and Algorithms 3–4, redraws comparator plots, places the training/inference charts together, and moves the vertically stacked main-text K-sensitivity plot to a horizontal appendix display.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for TUNA and DINOv2 and removes the EASE reference. The broader related-work organization and positioning of VILA against iterative and analytic CIL remain substantially unchanged; the switch to author–year citations is stylistic.

T1.justification: Proposition 3.1 becomes Remark 3.1, and Equation 3 drops the asserted proportionality between projection error and distribution distance. Appendix A.1 revises the associated derivation, introduces a normalized-target qualification and retains the projection-residual lower bound. This is a localized substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: The new rank, computational-budget and broader component controls improve scrutiny of v1's motivation and efficiency claims, while caching clarifies deployment costs. These benefits are qualified: DINOv2 substitution does not establish the claimed exclusion of pretraining leakage, and Tables 8–9 give unexplained differing DB+UGC results for ImageNet-R T=20 (84.95/89.50 versus 82.78/88.32). The added evidence therefore supports a limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VILA research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds rank-sensitivity, computational-budget, extended component-ablation and backbone-replacement experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original eight-benchmark evaluations, online-learning experiments, component ablations, case studies and efficiency measurements.

title: Advancing Analytic Class-Incremental Learning through Vision-Language Calibration

C1.justification: The central contributions—column-preserving encoding, theoretical support, and RDB prediction without additional training—remain intact. V2 qualifies the label-information wording in the abstract and introduction, and adds a concluding claim about possible advantages of transparent SQL-based features for agentic reasoning.

C2.justification: New Section 3.1 caveats acknowledge historical labels within encoder inputs and external metadata that could justify cross-column feature engineering. V2 also discusses leakage risks from LLM-assisted aggregation, interprets RandGNN findings, and extends the retained ablation's interpretation to competitive performance without validation-based selection.

D1.justification: New Appendix E documents DuckDB/FeatureTools implementation, API arguments, key mappings, cutoff-time semantics, a minimal usage example, and an affiliated skill installation link. These are additional disclosures rather than demonstrated implementation changes. The original repository link is relocated, while checkpoints, hardware, and context limits are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds five RelBench-v2 tasks: three binary classification tasks and two regression tasks, including beer-churn, brewer-dormant, and beer-ratings-total. This substantially extends the evaluated data coverage beyond the retained RelBench-v1 and 4DBInfer tasks. Rel-arxiv and rel-mimic are explicitly excluded.

E2.justification: RandGNN joins the existing RelBench-v1 classification and regression comparisons. Both RandGNN and Griffin are added to 4DBInfer, where Griffin was previously absent. The new RelBench-v2 comparison includes Griffin, RandGNN, and a supervised GNN; existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: V2 introduces an evaluation control coupling randomly initialized, untrained GNN encodings with the tabular ICL models used by RDBLearn. It also specifies evaluation of Griffin and RandGNN without additional training on RelBench-v2. Existing 10k context sampling, hop choices, development-set model selection, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new RandGNN comparison tests whether performance depends on JUICE featurization rather than merely a strong tabular decoder. Existing hop/backend ablations, synthetic feature-mixing tests, and supervised-versus-ICL analyses are retained. Appendix F.1 additionally mentions favorable preliminary tests with more aggregators, but supplies no supporting results.

E5.justification: Appendix B retains the same 100-trial averaging and identical error-bar plots. V2 introduces no additional seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-reporting procedures for the benchmark comparisons.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for RandGNN, Griffin on 4DBInfer, and five RelBench-v2 tasks. For example, new Figure 4 reports user-churn AUCs of 97.81 for RDBLearn and 94.27 for the supervised GNN. Existing RDBLearn scores remain unchanged, including 74.81 mean RelBench-v1 classification AUC; the added RandGNN mean is 70.02. The leakage discussion also corrects 99.61 to 99.62 AUC.

M1.justification: The column-preserving JUICE encoder, parameter-free aggregation procedure, temporal features, and single-table ICL prediction pipeline are unchanged. RandGNN is a comparator; the new usage documentation and prospective agent integrations do not establish changes to the proposed method.

P1.justification: V2 adds localized caveat and usage explanations, moves the existing stability discussion, renames Conclusions to Discussion, and distinguishes RelBench-v1 from RelBench-v2. Most existing prose and the overall argument structure are retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds the RelBench-v2 results display and usage-code figure, expands comparison displays with additional model columns, and redraws the 4DBInfer ranking chart. V1 Figure 10 becomes a reformatted Table 1 with added comparators; existing ablation and appendix plots are retained and relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused references and positioning concerning random-weight GNNs, LLM feature engineering and ReFuGe, RelBench-v2, DuckDB, and agentic database reasoning. The established positioning against supervised relational learning and existing RDB foundation models remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, propositions, equations, and derivations are unchanged. V1 Appendix F matches v2 Appendix G after renumbering. The new contextual caveats do not revise the formal assumptions or proofs.

improvement.justification: RandGNN strengthens empirical assessment of the encoder rationale, and RelBench-v2 broadens validation. The new caveats improve qualification of the argument, while Appendix E makes usage clearer. These provide an incremental overall gain: the added benchmark results remain preliminary and lack run-level uncertainty, and the new agentic and future-performance assertions are not experimentally established.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JUICE/RDBLearn research work. Their main text, equations, figures, results, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds author-executed RandGNN comparisons and evaluations on RelBench-v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original RDBLearn benchmark evaluations in Section 6 and an original synthetic feature-mixing experiment averaged over 100 trials in Appendix B.

title: No Need to Train Your RDB Foundation Model

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about internalizing contextual privacy, improving privacy-helpfulness tradeoffs and generalizing across tasks and agent topologies. The stated maximum leakage reduction remains 12.32%.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning cross-judge consistency, parameter sensitivity and b2-controlled privacy-helpfulness tradeoffs. The Impact Statement newly identifies limited direct applicability to closed-source models because fine-tuning is required. These are focused extensions of the existing interpretations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: The new appendix studies specify the additional judge, tested parameter configurations, attacker/defender models and deployment of trained verifier/refiner models. Existing prompts, training commands, batching, epochs, preference-dataset sizes and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix D.5 adds a compositional-privacy dataset with 119 scenarios evaluated under benign and adversarial conditions. Recovering sensitive information by combining individually innocuous responses substantially extends the evaluated threat scenarios beyond the retained PrivacyLens and ConfAIde tasks.

E2.justification: Table 9 introduces a Chain-of-Thought defense comparator for the new compositional-privacy evaluation. Vanilla LM, PPE and AIFC remain the comparators in the corresponding PrivacyLens comparisons; the original ConfAIde and topology comparator sets are unchanged.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce GPT-4o evaluation of the same outputs, additional reward-parameter configurations, and a paired benign/adversarial Overall Success protocol using a Llama-3.1-8B defender and Qwen3-32B attacker. Existing PrivacyLens splits, training settings and K=10 response sampling remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix D.3 adds a cross-judge robustness check. D.4 adds six alpha/beta configurations and expands the reported b2 settings from three to nine, substantially extending sensitivity analysis. The component ablations in Figures 3 and 5, topology tests and case study already appeared in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions retain K=10 response samples per test case, without adding training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. D.3 newly quotes human-agreement statistics from Shao et al. (2024); these are prior-work validation results, not a new statistical estimation procedure for PrivAct.

E6.justification: Tables 6-9 add alternative-judge scores, sensitivity outcomes and compositional-privacy results, including 42.39% Overall Success for CoT versus 46.34% with the b2=0.3 refiner. Table 5 also rescales average helpfulness from 0-3 to the documented 0-1 scale; these conversions represent unchanged outcomes, not performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same multi-agent generation, reward propagation, preference construction, DPO training and LC-ARS reward. Appendix D.5 evaluates previously trained verifier/refiner models in another defense framework without introducing a new training algorithm or method component.

P1.justification: Changes include localized metric explanations and attribution edits, reordered acknowledgements and Impact Statement, an expanded appendix outline, named D.1-D.5 subsections and a new Limitations section. The main narrative and method exposition are largely retained.

P2.justification: Four substantive tables are added for alternative judging, parameter sensitivity and compositional privacy. Table 5 is resized and the supplementary material is reorganized around subsection headings and wrapped tables. Figures 1-5 retain identical image content, and the original main-table structures remain intact.

R1.justification: v2 adds He et al. (2026) and Kim et al. (2026), and expands discussion of the already cited Patil et al. (2025) into an evaluated compositional-privacy setting. The ConfAIde reference update identifies the same work, while the principal novelty positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, preference construction and LC-ARS equation are unchanged, with no added proofs or formal propositions. The new benchmark's inherited Overall Success metric and empirical parameter sweeps do not revise the mathematical framework.

improvement.justification: The added judge check, sensitivity studies and compositional-privacy evaluation provide useful scrutiny beyond v1, while Table 5's normalization correction improves consistency. The gain is limited by overly broad judge-consistency language: the same Mistral-7B PrivAct outputs at b2=0.3 receive average helpfulness of 0.863 versus 0.472 under different judges. Overall, the supplementary evidence and clearer applicability limits improve the paper without fully resolving evaluation reliability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PrivAct research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, figures and tables can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds GPT-4o judging, hyperparameter sensitivity results and compositional-privacy evaluation in Appendix D.3-D.5.

before.justification: v1 reports original PrivacyLens and ConfAIde evaluations, component ablations, topology experiments and a qualitative case study, including supplementary results.

title: PrivAct: Internalizing Contextual Privacy Preservation via Multi-Agent Preference Training

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's four contributions, and principal concluding claims retain the same scope: avoiding reference contamination, conditional anytime validity, power and stopping-time guarantees, and improved empirical detection. The new qualifications concern interpretation and limitations.

C2.justification: v2 explains the initial standard-CTM advantage after a long null period and its subsequent loss through contamination. Section 5 newly states that mean-based betting can miss shifts preserving the p-value mean, and discusses ONS versus mixture martingales and the latter's unresolved power guarantees.

D1.justification: A new footnote in Section 1 provides a repository link for a software package implementing the method. This adds code-access information; the implementation details in Appendix H are unchanged, and repository contents cannot be assessed from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Gaussian immediate, delayed, and gradual shifts, Gaussian AR(1) sequences, and ImageNet-C corruptions. The revised change-point timing is a setting change within the existing delayed-shift task.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: standard CTM in the principal comparisons, invalid CTM in Figure 2, and pairwise betting in the AR(1) experiment. Newly discussed mixture martingales are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 and Figure 3 replace the delayed-change settings {200, 400, 600} with {200, 600, 4000}. The reference size, distributions, testing parameters, and other experimental protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The delay-sensitivity analysis now examines a substantially longer period before the shift, testing how accumulated null observations affect detection. The clipping ablation in Appendix F and other supplementary analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 trials for Figure 3 and retain the other simulation repetition counts. ImageNet-C still uses 10 seeds and the same standard-error reporting. No new uncertainty-estimation practice or significance test appears.

E6.justification: Figure 3 replaces the 400-step-delay results with 4000-step-delay results. In the new condition, standard CTM initially leads before conditional CTM overtakes it. The immediate-shift and gradual-shift panels, ImageNet-C results, and appendix figures are unchanged; this is not a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The fixed-reference construction, confidence-band correction, smoothed betting function, ONS updates, and clipping procedure remain unchanged. Algorithms 1-2 retain the same steps; mixture martingales are discussed only as future work.

P1.justification: v2 adds localized explanatory passages, expands the discussion, and introduces acknowledgments, funding disclosure, and an impact statement. The publication footer changes to conference proceedings information. The main section order and appendix organization remain stable.

P2.justification: Figure 3's middle panel has revised delay labels, curves, and a broader horizontal axis. Figure 4 moves from the left to the right column on page 8, with accompanying text reflow. Other figure contents and appendix layouts are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Clerico's two works, Gauthier et al., Kaufmann and Koolen, and Timans et al. These provide limited additional positioning around betting optimality, comparable stopping-time bounds, mixture martingales, and risk monitoring, without reorganizing the research framing.

T1.justification: The definitions, assumptions, theorem statements, regret analysis, and proofs in Appendices D-E are unchanged. The added explanation of conditional validity and remark comparing stopping-time bounds clarify existing mathematics without adding a formal result.

improvement.justification: Replacing the intermediate delay with a 4000-step stress test reveals an initial baseline advantage and supports a more nuanced empirical interpretation. The explicit limitation concerning mean-preserving shifts, additional theoretical context, and software-access link improve transparency and usefulness. These are limited gains; the method, formal guarantees, and most empirical evidence remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same conditional conformal test martingale research. The main text, figures, equations, and Appendices A-H are readable and can be matched despite pagination changes.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and reports a revised delayed-change experiment in Section 4.1 and Figure 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations of error control and detection power, ImageNet-C evaluations, and appendix experiments on clipping and pairwise betting.

title: Testing For Distribution Shifts with Conditional Conformal Test Martingales

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and central conclusions retain the same contributions: interpretable keyword-based stopping, Renewal and Maxwise rules, conditional false-positive control, and empirical efficiency and generalization. The additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the filtered GPQA results as evidence against label noise being the main source of detection power, discusses domain-dependent keywords and power/FPR tradeoffs, and concludes that Lmax sensitivity is limited. Section 4 also adds discussion of downstream policies and the user-experience consequences of premature stopping.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the new answerability judge as GPT-5.4 Pro and documents reuse of the keyword-extraction pipeline. Appendix A clarifies overlapping keyword categories, explaining 104 category memberships versus 102 distinct keywords, and specifies that the Qwen3-8B abstention detector serves prompting baselines. Hardware, generation budget, and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix B.2 expands keyword-extraction training from GSM8K alone to GPQA-only and pooled GSM8K+GPQA traces. GPQA already appeared in v1's evaluation, so this adds scientific-domain training coverage while retaining the existing evaluation domains and benchmarks.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain the same prompting, Length, DEER, Entropy, linear-probe, and diagnostic PLS methods. The additional analyses introduce no new competing method; GPT-5.4 Pro serves as an answerability judge.

E3.justification: New protocols evaluate a 50-item GPQA sample and its 43-item judge-filtered subset, and vary Lmax from the median to the 25th and 75th calibration-length percentiles. Appendix A.6 also narrows stated cold-start tuning from keyword/DEER/entropy signals to DEER/entropy only. This revises the reported protocol without establishing that the unchanged headline experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's keyword-category and bin-size ablations, v2 tests whether scientific results survive answerability filtering, whether performance depends on keyword-extraction domain, and whether Renewal is sensitive to its correction horizon. These additions in Appendices B.1–B.2 substantially broaden the robustness questions examined.

E5.justification: The existing cross-validation and averaging practices remain unchanged. The new analyses report point estimates without adding repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or another uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values and plotted results are retained. New results include 43/50 GPQA prompts judged unanswerable, filtered-subset performance, keyword-source FPR/power in Table 12, and Lmax sensitivity with average FPR of 1.87–2.37% and power of 61.86–64.61%. These supplement the results under altered subsets or settings rather than establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The Renewal and Maxwise algorithms, uncertainty score, keyword-selection pipeline, and matching procedure are retained. The new keyword-source experiments reuse the existing pipeline. The cold-start applicability revision concerns the reported experimental settings and does not establish a redesigned method.

P1.justification: The narrative and section organization remain largely stable. Changes comprise localized appendix additions, explanatory clarifications, notation cleanup, a deployment paragraph, and updated date and acknowledgements.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 12 and two small tables for GPQA filtering and Lmax sensitivity. Existing medical/scientific example boxes move beside their discussion in Appendix B.1, and appendix tables and figures are rearranged. Existing plotted graphics are unchanged; v1 Tables 12–15 become v2 Tables 13–16.

R1.justification: v2 removes the introduction citation and bibliography entry for Suresh et al. (2025), Compute When Worth It: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget. The remaining related-work discussion and research positioning are substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The definitions, guarantees, assumptions, and proofs in Section 2, Appendix A.4, and Appendix C are retained. Algorithm 1 and Proposition 2.1 receive equivalent notation changes. The added renewal-approximation sentence reinforces an existing caveat without revising the mathematics.

improvement.justification: The added analyses address previously untested sensitivity to keyword source and Lmax and partially validate the scientific benchmark's ill-posed labels. These strengthen the robustness evidence while preserving the original results. The gain is limited: GPQA validation covers only 50 LLM-judged items, and keyword-source variants sometimes exchange higher false-positive rates for higher power rather than uniformly improving performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Statistical Early Stopping for Reasoning Models. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated examples and renumbered tables.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds GPQA answerability validation, keyword-source comparisons, and stopping-horizon sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of stopping rules across 12 reasoning models, mathematical and scientific benchmarks, baseline comparisons, and ablations.

title: Statistical Early Stopping for Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The four central contributions and claims of generalizable conflict detection and improved KI-VQA remain. Although the abstract replaces 'state-of-the-art' with 'superior,' the introduction still explicitly claims SOTA performance, and the conclusion retains the same scientific scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of guidance precision and visual perturbation, interprets natural-conflict results as evidence against synthetic-artifact overfitting, and attributes robustness to intact visual evidence. Appendix C.3 asserts negligible error accumulation, while C.4 identifies intrinsic visual-language reasoning as a remaining bottleneck and advances causal interpretations. The original limitations paragraph is retained.

D1.justification: Dataset-construction details in Appendix A, implementation and hyperparameters in Appendix B, and prompt templates in Appendix D are unchanged after matching relocated content. No new code/data access information or implementation specifications accompany the added evaluation controls.

E1.justification: Appendix C.1 and Table 13 add conflict-discrimination evaluation on e-SNLI-VE with native contradiction labels and manually annotated InfoSeek-human. This materially broadens coverage to different conflict sources, beyond the retained REAL-VQA, E-VQA, ScienceQA, and MMKC evaluations.

E2.justification: The original benchmark comparators and Greedy/VCD/CAD comparisons remain. New diagnostic comparisons introduce uniform and random guidance, blank-image and Gaussian-blur alternatives, and oracle pivot signals in Tables 6, 8, and 15. Changed Prophet citations do not establish a changed evaluated method.

E3.justification: New experiments specify uniform token intervention, replacement of 50% of detected pivots, alternative visual perturbations, and two oracle controls. Existing splits, metrics, model sizes, retrieval settings, and training budgets remain unchanged; the additions are targeted evaluation variants.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component removals and decoding comparisons, v2 tests whether accurate detection signals drive gains, compares visual perturbation choices, examines imperfect versus oracle pivots, and decomposes errors into retrieval, extraction, mitigation, and visual-language reasoning failures (Tables 6, 8, 15–16). These substantially expand the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed counts, confidence intervals, variability estimates, or significance tests. The ten stochastic GPT-4o quality scores used during dataset construction were already documented in v1 and remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark scores are unchanged, but substantial results are added. Table 13 reports Qwen3-VL-8B zero-shot/RPA-SFT F1 of 71.6/80.5 on e-SNLI-VE and 63.4/75.0 on InfoSeek-human. Table 15 newly reports E-VQA accuracy of 39.3 under 50% pivot corruption versus 41.4 with predicted pivots. Tables 6, 8, and 16 add guidance, perturbation, and error-source results.

M1.justification: REAL-VQA construction, RPA-SFT, and RPGD retain the same procedures, components, and Algorithm 1. Section 3.3 adds conceptual distinctions without specifying an operational change to the method.

P1.justification: v2 adds Section 3.3, Appendix C.3–C.4, localized explanatory paragraphs, acknowledgements, and expanded affiliation/publication text. The main narrative order, method exposition, and most appendix prose remain intact rather than undergoing extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: New Tables 6, 8, 13, 15, and 16 display the additional experiments. Existing tables, Algorithm 1, and figures are repositioned as text flows, and Figure 8 adjusts failure-case image crops. The established table formats, figure content, and overall layout remain largely stable.

R1.justification: Section 3.3 adds explicit positioning against global graph indexing and sequential question decomposition. The references add e-SNLI-VE and replace the introductory LLaVA++ citation with DeepSeek-V3. These are limited changes within the retained research framing.

T1.justification: The reasoning-pivot definitions, conflict criterion, and decoding equations remain unchanged. Section 3.3 provides qualitative distinctions rather than new formal reasoning; Appendix C.3's oracle experiments do not introduce a mathematical proof or derived bound.

improvement.justification: The added guidance, perturbation, natural-conflict, and error analyses provide useful evidence beyond v1's existing ablations. The net improvement is limited by missing sampling/adaptation details for the new datasets and an unspecified error-attribution procedure. Table 15 also leaves its differing base scores unexplained relative to Table 5, and one corruption condition does not justify the broad claim that error accumulation is 'fundamentally negligible.'

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REAL framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A–E support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds conflict-discrimination evaluations, guidance and perturbation ablations, robustness tests, and error attribution.

before.justification: v1 reports original KI-VQA and conflict-discrimination experiments, component ablations, latency measurements, and supplementary experiments in Appendix C.

title: REAL: Resolving Knowledge Conflicts in Knowledge-Intensive Visual Question Answering via Reasoning-Pivot Alignment

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statement, and conclusion retain the same claims: CoCoEdit improves content consistency while maintaining competitive editing, supported by the curated dataset and mask-augmented benchmarks. Additional experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that consistency gains extend beyond reward metrics, 40K samples suffice, and RL contributes more than the curated data alone. It explains SFT's weaker editing scores through unfiltered ground-truth quality and clarifies the existing ablation baseline. Appendix D's limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 4.5 newly reports approximately 70 GB VRAM and per-step times of 10 minutes for Edit-R1 versus 12 for CoCoEdit. v2 also describes ground-truth retrieval and the consistency loss for the SFT control. Existing implementation settings, pseudocode, and the project link are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the OmniEdit/ImgEdit-derived training coverage and GEdit-Bench/ImgEdit-Bench evaluations, including local and global editing tasks. The new 120K experiment changes training sample count without establishing a new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands the comparisons with an SFT-on-40K control in Table 4 and FLUX.1-Fill-dev and ICEdit in Appendix C.4/Table 7. Existing model, RL, and commercial comparators remain. ICEdit was cited in v1 but was not an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 add LPIPS and DINO evaluation metrics. New Table 4 introduces 120K-versus-40K RL conditions and SFT using source ground-truth images with a non-edit-region PSNR/SSIM consistency loss. These extend the evaluation design; the original training and user-study settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of dataset-size sensitivity, SFT versus RL, and consistency under metrics excluded from the training reward, plus an efficiency comparison with Edit-R1. These address additional questions about sufficiency, attribution, and reward overfitting. The original component ablations, reward-ratio curves, and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: The user-study sampling seed, participant information, and correlation-reporting practices remain unchanged. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark, commercial-comparison, and component-ablation values are retained. v2 adds LPIPS/DINO scores, SFT/120K results, FLUX.1-Fill-dev/ICEdit results, and efficiency outcomes. For example, new Table 4 reports GEdit overall/PSNR values of 7.219/20.293 for SFT and 7.723/22.204 for 120K RL; these are additional conditions, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The CoCoEdit rewards, positive and negative regional regularizers, optimization objective, and inference procedure remain unchanged, as does Algorithm 1. Expanded explanations of instruction refinement and mask usage do not establish a procedural change; SFT is an added comparator.

P1.justification: v2 expands selected method and experimental explanations, adds subheadings within the ablation discussion, introduces Section 4.5 and Appendix C.4, and replaces the preprint footer with proceedings information. Most prose and the overall document structure are retained.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain LPIPS/DINO columns, and new Tables 4 and 7 display the added experiments. Existing tables are renumbered, and Figures 7, 13, and 14 move with text reflow. The figures themselves and the overall visual design are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to FireEdit and FLUX, and explicitly contrasts CoCoEdit's mask-free inference with spatially grounded editing. It also discusses the newly evaluated mask-guided and in-context alternatives. The main related-work survey and overall research positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, definitions, assumptions, and regional-regularization derivations in Section 3 and Appendix B remain unchanged. The added empirical metrics introduce no new formal definitions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens an already substantial empirical evaluation with metrics outside the training reward, dataset-size/SFT controls, additional baselines, and compute-cost disclosure. These provide useful corroboration and context. However, the SFT comparison does not cleanly isolate algorithm effects because v2 acknowledges that its ground-truth targets were not filtered for SFT quality. The net gain is positive but incremental.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoCoEdit work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including matching material across pagination and numbering changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds perceptual-metric evaluations, dataset-size and SFT experiments, additional baseline comparisons, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, qualitative outputs, correlation analyses, and a user study involving 30 volunteers and 100 sampled images.

title: CoCoEdit: Content-Consistent Image Editing via Region Regularized Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and three stated contributions retain the same claims: behavioral knowledge profiling, WikiProfile, near-saturated frontier-model encoding, a recall bottleneck, and recovery through thinking. The added introduction statement about scaling reiterates a finding already stated in v1 Section 5.1.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 and appendix B expand the mechanism discussion to distinguish diversity, inference, and recall facilitation, and qualify the training-specific interpretation with model-family confounding. Section 7 newly states Wikipedia generalization limits and the restricted coverage of the operational knowledge definition.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future benchmark release; v2 states that WikiProfile is available and supplies a dataset access link. It also adds text-length summaries and an approximately $500 frontier-model profiling cost with cost-reduction suggestions. Existing prompts and implementation settings are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 2,150 Wikipedia-derived facts and ten task variants. The new thinking analysis examines retained questions and conditions without adding a dataset, domain, or distinct task scenario.

E2.justification: The same 13 models and comparisons with versus without thinking remain. The Gemini-2.5-Pro versus GPT-5 grader comparison is also retained. The new diagnostic does not introduce a new comparison method.

E3.justification: Appendix B adds evaluation using correct≥p across correctness thresholds for 12 existing models, comparing availability with consistent correctness. The main evaluation retains eight responses per question, temperature 1, the same grading procedures, and the 0.5 profiling threshold.

E4.justification: New appendix B and Figure 12 add a focused diagnostic testing whether thinking gains reflect response diversity or more reliable correctness, including differences between native thinking and CoT prompting. Existing popularity, reversal, threshold, grader, and sampling analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix B.2 introduces binomial plug-in estimation of correctness in repeated samples and notes limited sensitivity to very low correctness probabilities. The existing eight-response count, 1,000 bootstrap resamples, 90% intervals, and FDR procedure remain unchanged; additional sampling runs are not established.

E6.justification: Figure 12 newly reports improved robustness for thinking-optimized models but degraded robustness for Gemma3 under CoT. Existing plots also revise small 'Knows' totals: Figures 1 and 4 change GPT-5 from 84.1 to 83.8 and Gemini-3-Pro from 87.7 to 87.5. It reverses the dep-cols interpretation from signal attenuation to excessive scores under signal and adds the limitation that similarity lacks a ground-truth scale.
