E1.justification: The RealCause datasets, TabArena regression datasets and two synthetic prior families remain. v2 extends incorrect-graph testing from v1's bivariate illustration to partially corrupted ancestry matrices on complex multivariate data. Appendix J also adds binary-treatment synthetic comparisons stratified by backdoor validity, extending scenarios within the existing causal-estimation domain.

E2.justification: v1's causal evaluations primarily compare the authors' own model variants. v2 Figure 18 adds evaluated comparisons against CausalPFN and CausalFM, and Table 3 adds CausalPFN, CausalFM and Do-PFN to the RealCause comparisons. Their citations in v1 did not constitute evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix E.1.2 changes the stated intervention-value distribution from uniform sampling over plus or minus four treatment standard deviations to the SCM's observational treatment marginal. This is a substantive reported protocol revision, without establishing which experiments were rerun. New experiments also introduce binary-treatment/backdoor stratification, observational–interventional discrepancy metrics, quantile-binned analyses and controlled ancestry-corruption sweeps.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of observational–interventional discrepancies and treatment–outcome correlations in Appendix E.3, relates graph-conditioning benefits to discrepancy strength in Appendix I, and tests backdoor-valid versus invalid cases in Appendix J. Appendix K adds quantitative hiding-versus-misspecifying experiments. v1's qualitative misspecification example is retained as Figure 19, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 adds Kolmogorov–Smirnov equality tests with reported p-values in Appendix E.3 and explicitly specifies paired bootstrap confidence intervals for comparator differences in Appendix J.1. Existing bootstrap reporting and Table 2's 100-run mean-and-standard-deviation reporting remain; an increase in repeated training runs is not established.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain identical numerical results, but v2 adds substantial new findings. Table 3 reports, for example, IHDP root PEHE of 0.58 for CausalPFN versus the retained 5.49 for Ancestral Info. New figures report prior discrepancies, conditioning benefits concentrated among larger discrepancies, comparator performance under backdoor violations, and substantially greater damage from incorrect than missing ancestry information.

M1.justification: The transformer, GCN/AdaLN components, loss and decoding remain recognizable. However, v2 Section 4.3 changes the ancestry indexing from T_ij to T_ji and describes adding biases to an already normalized attention matrix, while still calling them logit biases. Appendix D retains the earlier indexing and masking formulation. These conflicting descriptions prevent reliably distinguishing an actual attention-procedure change from an attempted clarification.

P1.justification: Targeted rewriting expands the attention and GCN explanations, introduces TFM-Prior/LinGaus-Prior terminology, moves the prior discussion from the experiments into Section 4.4, and folds consistency into Section 4.2. Copyediting, affiliation updates, acknowledgements and an impact statement accompany these changes. Much existing prose and the overall argument remain.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main paper and references to a two-column conference layout and adds Figures 6–9, 17, 18 and 20 plus the extended Table 3. Existing figures are resized and captions refined. v1 Figures 6–12 correspond to v2 Figures 10–16, and v1 Figure 13 becomes Figure 19; these are retained displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Breiman, Guo et al., Massey and TabICLv2, and removes Moor et al. It expands positioning against identification-specific CFMs through the new comparisons, while retaining the original distinction between restricted-prior and unrestricted-prior causal foundation models.

T1.justification: v2 adds Remark A.2, asserting that Proposition A.1's covariate-to-treatment/outcome paths can remain unspecified while preserving unconfoundedness. It also introduces the expected observational–interventional discrepancy definition in Equation 12. Proposition A.1 and the main consistency argument in Appendix B are otherwise substantially retained; the new relaxation receives no additional proof.

improvement.justification: The external CFM comparisons, quantitative graph-corruption tests and analyses of when conditioning helps improve empirical scrutiny beyond v1, including reporting CausalPFN's stronger overall RealCause performance. More qualified discussion improves transparency. These gains are tempered by conflicting attention specifications and Remark A.2's unsupported relaxation of ancestry conditions, which does not address post-treatment conditioning. The net improvement is therefore positive but limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same graph-conditioned causal foundation model research. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds prior-distribution analyses, comparisons with other causal foundation models, and quantitative graph-misspecification experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic graph-conditioning experiments, RealCause evaluations, predictive validation on TabArena datasets, and appendix ablations and case studies.

title: Use What You Know: Causal Foundation Models with Partial Graphs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: anti-distillation while preserving teacher utility, and reliable watermark detection with nearly zero false alarms. The headline 61.3-point student accuracy reduction is unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving rewriter error correction, degenerate repetition behind low baseline perplexity, and CDG-KD's mismatch with behavioral watermarks. Its answer-only interpretation is overstated: Table 4 shows one improvement over OPT, 6.5% versus 5.3% for Llama-3.2-1B on MATH. The main limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository URL in the abstract and identifies the reference, judge, and additional models used in the new analyses. Existing prompts, optimization settings, LoRA hyperparameters, preprocessing, and hardware disclosures are retained. Repository availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8K/GSM8K-Platinum, MATH, MMLU, and MMLU-Pro. The additions reuse these datasets and downstream tasks; they vary distillation procedures, model configurations, or measurements rather than introduce new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands the adaptive comparisons by evaluating KPOD against anti-distillation and CDG-KD against watermarking in Figures 5–7. Table 4 also introduces an answer-only comparator. ADS, DOGe, and the four existing watermarking baselines remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include perplexity and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judgments on 150 MATH traces, adaptive and answer-only distillation procedures, and varied teacher/rewriter configurations. The original dataset splits, standard SFT budget, and principal accuracy/detection metrics are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of trace quality, resistance to KPOD and CDG-KD, removal of reasoning supervision, and dependence on teacher/rewriter size. The Direct ablation and paraphrasing/filtering tests already existed in v1; their relocation alone is not an addition.

E5.justification: New Table 2 reports mean perplexity with standard deviations across 150 traces. This adds sample-variability reporting, not evidence of repeated training runs. Both versions retain the 100 independent trials per query budget for watermark detection.

E6.justification: The retained headline comparisons in Figures 2–3 and Table 1 are unchanged, but substantial results are added in Figures 5–7 and Tables 2–5. Examples include quality scores of 3.83 for OPT versus 4.01 for original traces, answer-only accuracies, and a 27.5-point student accuracy reduction with a 7B teacher and 7B rewriter.

M1.justification: The semantic and optimized prompts, gradient-based variants, HotFlip procedure, and watermark insertion method are retained. The added attacks and model-size experiments evaluate the existing proposed methods rather than change them.

P1.justification: Related Work becomes a standalone section, appendix robustness material is consolidated into Section 6.4, and new analysis subsections and acknowledgments are added. There are localized wording and author-line edits, while most existing prose and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 changes typography throughout, adds four tables, and relocates and expands v1 Figures 9, 14, and 15 into main-text Figures 5–7 with new attack series and revised legends/captions. The resulting display reorganization is substantial; other retained figures are principally renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds Feng et al. (2024) and Yi et al. (2025) for the evaluated adaptive methods, plus Hsieh et al. (2023) and Chen et al. (2025) for answer-only interpretation. The broader related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain stable.

T1.justification: The formal objectives, rewriting constraints, prompt-scoring expression, and gradient/HotFlip derivations are retained. The single-source assumption emphasized in v2 was already present in v1. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for central requirements that v1 evaluated incompletely: preserving trace quality and resisting adaptive distillation. Appendix B directly measures quality, Section 6.4 tests additional adaptive methods, and Table 5 establishes effectiveness beyond the original 7B-teacher/120B-rewriter pairing. These gains outweigh the limited overstatement of answer-only results, although that interpretation should acknowledge Table 4's exception.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same trace-rewriting study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds trace-quality measurements, adaptive-distillation comparisons, answer-only distillation, and model-size analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original teacher/student accuracy and watermark-detection experiments, including appendix ablations, additional benchmarks, and adaptive-distillation tests.

title: Protecting Language Models Against Unauthorized Distillation through Trace Rewriting

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about DRR, DRR-Net, VP augmentation, fidelity, and inference efficiency, including the up-to-27-fold speed claim.

C2.justification: Interpretations of refinement, augmentation, dataset geometry, and failure cases remain unchanged. Section 5 retains the same limitations concerning embedding structures, refiner architectures, and interpolation versus extrapolation.

D1.justification: Appendix B retains the same implementation, hardware, hyperparameter, normalization, sampling, and timing details. The stated code link and configuration/data-parameter access instructions are also unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Nyx, MPAS-Ocean, and Cloverleaf3D tasks, gigapixel reconstruction and super-resolution on the same two images, and novel-view synthesis on Lego and Drums.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain identical participants: K-Planes, FA-INR, and Explorable-INR for surrogates; the same augmentation and refinement variants; and the same Grid, MRGrid, TriPlane, NGP, SIREN, and NeRF comparisons in Appendix I.

E3.justification: Dataset splits, resolutions, model configurations, training budgets, preprocessing, sampling procedures, and metrics are unchanged in Section 4, Appendix B, and Appendix I. No evaluation protocol is added or revised.

E4.justification: The augmentation study, component ablations, positional-encoding and grid-resolution sensitivity studies, VP noise studies, and qualitative analyses are retained unchanged in Table 4 and Appendices C–H.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same point-estimate reporting and FLOP/timing averaging procedures in Appendix B.3. No seed information, repeated-training-run counts, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are added or revised.

E6.justification: Results in Tables 2–4 and 7–12 and the empirical figures are unchanged. For example, Table 2 reports Nyx DRR-Net PSNR of 44.69 and inference time of 10.7 seconds in both versions.

M1.justification: The DRR formulation, DRR-Net encoders and refiners, caching procedure, and VP augmentation remain unchanged. The redesigned Figure 1 illustrates the existing procedure rather than introducing a method component.

P1.justification: Figure 1's caption adds the terminology 'feature grid' and removes references to the former lettered panels. Its internal labels are rewritten, while the main prose, appendix prose, and section order remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces the horizontal architecture comparison and explicit preprocessing blocks with a throughput–expressiveness diagram and a two-stage DRR inset. Its narrower, taller layout causes subsequent reflow. Other figures and table structures are retained.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion, cited works, bibliography, and positioning relative to earlier INR and surrogate methods are unchanged; reference pagination shifts without changing content.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–7, including residual refinement, multi-resolution unification, and VP interpolation, are unchanged. Figure 1 introduces no new formal reasoning or theoretical result.

improvement.justification: The redesigned Figure 1 makes the existing two-stage workflow and throughput–expressiveness trade-off more explicit, but uses smaller, denser labels. This localized presentation trade-off leaves overall quality essentially unchanged; the methods, empirical evidence, limitations, and reproducibility information are identical.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same research work with complete, readable main text and Appendices A–I. Text, equations, tables, and rendered figures support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results in Section 4 and the appendices, including the scientific-simulation, image-representation, and NeRF evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original surrogate-model evaluations, augmentation and refinement ablations, sensitivity analyses, and gigapixel-image and NeRF experiments.

title: Refine Now, Query Fast: A Decoupled Refinement Paradigm for Implicit Neural Fields

C1.justification: The central clustering, description–history gap, explanation effects, and mathematical-training claims remain. V2 strengthens contribution positioning in Section 8 by claiming the first systematic behavioral taxonomy of LLMs and one of the first direct tests of competing explanations for behavioral variation.

C2.justification: Section 6.1 replaces the primary interpretation of humans as strongly risk-averse and probability-distorting with similar curvature and weighting parameters to LLMs but asymmetric gain/loss decisiveness. It explicitly attributes the specification-dependent interpretation to lambda–beta confounding. Section 4 also adds an argument against context-window capacity explaining the description–history gap.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2.3 supplies dual-beta initialization vectors and sampling ranges and specifies previously unstated random-initialization ranges for full standard prospect theory. Appendix B.2.1 replaces v1's inconsistent maximum-likelihood/35-lottery description with MSE fitting, aligning it with the procedure already documented in B.2.3.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three base prospect pairs, gain/loss frames, explicit descriptions, 20- and 100-outcome histories, and U.S. human population. The added prompt-wording checks retain the same risky-choice task and data coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 5 adds Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct to the open-model description–history comparison, although Appendix B.1 does not add it to the model inventory. The restricted prospect-theory and regret-model comparisons are retained, with their original numerical tables preserved.

E3.justification: Appendix B.3 adds a controlled evaluation of three introductory prompt phrasings using four reasoning and four conversational models. This introduces an additional testing protocol; the existing prospect construction, temperature, token limit, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantive comparison of dual-beta and standard parameterizations, showing that the interpretation of human behavior depends on model specification. It also adds prompt-wording robustness, a reported 10-versus-50-query check, and bootstrap assessment of clustering stability. Existing history-length, training-stage, and restricted-model analyses are retained or extended.

E5.justification: V1 already reports ten query repetitions and 1,000-replicate parametric-bootstrap confidence intervals. V2 adds a separate 1,000-resample bootstrap of behavioral metrics with significance reporting and describes a 50-query check. Appendix B.2.3 also changes the bootstrap binomial trial count from 10 to 20 without explaining its relationship to the ten repetitions still specified in Section 2.4.

E6.justification: V2 adds dual-beta fits and confidence intervals; explicit human choices now yield sigma=0.87 and gamma=0.79 under that specification, versus 0.04 and 0.13 in the retained standard fit. Figure 5 also revises existing implicit correlations, including Olmo-3-32B-Think's human correlation from approximately 0.36 to 0.15. V1 Tables 1–4 survive as v2 Tables 15–18, but the original standard-model checkpoint fits and confidence intervals are replaced.

M1.justification: The primary behavioral model changes from standard prospect theory with loss aversion lambda and shared decisiveness beta to a symmetric value function with separately bounded beta_gain and beta_loss. This changes the fitted analysis throughout Section 6 and Appendix C.4. The standard specification remains as an alternative in Appendix C.7.

P1.justification: V2 selectively rewrites the study-design explanation and behavioral-model discussion, clarifies description–history terminology, and adds acknowledgments. Appendix C is reorganized to separate dual-beta confidence intervals, alternative models, and retained standard-model results, while the main section sequence remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 1–6 and 13 are redrawn with revised typography, legends, axes, colors, and spacing. Appendix Figures 7–12 are substantially enlarged and relocated while preserving their image content. Fit tables are reorganized around dual-beta parameters and relocated standard results, producing substantial visual restructuring.

R1.justification: V2 adds Binz and Schulz (2023), Coda-Forno et al. (2024), and Hayes et al. (2024), and removes Chakravarty and Roy (2009). It also positions the dual-beta specification as a special case of Peterson et al.'s generalized power value model. The broader related-work discussion remains largely intact.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2.1 adds the domain-dependent decisiveness definition, the beta_loss/beta_gain loss-aversion proxy, and an argument that pure-loss choices identify the product beta times lambda. These are limited mathematical extensions to the existing prospect-theory framework; the standard and regret formulations are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful model-sensitivity and robustness analyses and makes the dependence of behavioral interpretations on model specification explicit. However, the revised bootstrap trial count is unexplained, and new estimates and confidence intervals show unresolved discrepancies: GPT-5.1's sigma is 0.87 in Table 1 but its interval is [1.28, 1.35] in Table 7. Together with unexplained Figure 5 result changes, these uncertainties prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same risky-choice study. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated results.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and reports additional behavioral-model fits and robustness checks.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM choice experiments, a 360-participant human study, behavioral correlations, and fitted behavioral models.

title: Mind the (DH) Gap! A Contrast in Risky Choices Between Reasoning and Conversational LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: unified Bayesian learning from heterogeneous feedback, scalable amortized inference, complementary reward information, improved downstream behavior, and interpretable uncertainty. Additional experiments do not redefine these stated core contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 now explains the noise-model and regularization parameters remaining despite avoiding cross-modal loss weights. Sections 6.2–6.3 add interpretations of ensemble failure, environment-dependent benefits under equal budgets, and compensation for corrupted feedback with demonstrations as a weakness. The earlier gradient-conflict discussion is removed, and dynamics-robustness discussion acknowledges advantages of demonstrations. The concluding simulated-feedback limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information with the Optuna sampler, startup trials, search ranges, allocation rules and caps, trial counts, validation objectives, and corruption parameters. It adds training-time comparisons and a repository link for code and trained models, replacing v1's supplementary-code statement. Hardware information remains essentially unchanged; actual repository availability was not checked.

E1.justification: The same six environments and four feedback modalities remain. v2 adds evaluation under corrupted preferences, demonstrations, ratings, and stop signals, individually and jointly, on the three grid environments. These extend the feedback conditions tested without introducing new domains or tasks. Grid-trap dynamics perturbations already appeared in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 introduces substantive comparisons absent from v1: MCMC on all three grid environments and Post-Hoc Reward Averaging on those grids plus LunarLander-v3. The existing feedback-subset comparisons and behavioral-cloning baseline in transfer experiments remain.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1 replaces fixed network widths and a two-value regularizer search with joint Optuna searches over widths, regularization, optimizer settings, and policy-training parameters. LunarLander preference and rating budgets change from 1024 to 256 each. Appendix A.2 changes rating generation from deterministic quantile assignment to stochastic cumulative-logit sampling. New equal-budget and corruption experiments introduce additional allocation and testing protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds an equal-total-budget ablation testing whether complementarity merely reflects more supervision, and individual/joint feedback-corruption tests examining compensation and failure modes. Dynamics-robustness curves are revised. Conversely, v1 Appendix E's extensive feedback-budget sweeps disappear. The qualitative reward-map analyses are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix C newly specifies 20 tabular and 10 non-tabular seeds per tuning trial. Main results and transfer figures retain n=10, and standard-error reporting continues. Table 4 also states n=10, leaving its relationship to the 20-seed tuning description unclear; the PDFs do not establish an increase in final evaluation replication.

E6.justification: Main returns, EPIC distances, and transfer curves change extensively. For example, full-feedback grid_cliff return changes from 90.8 to 100.0 and CartPole from 87.5 to 100.0, while grid_trap EPIC changes from 0.432 to 0.520. These are revised results under changed protocols, not isolated same-setting gains. Baseline, equal-budget, and corruption results are added, while the earlier budget-sweep entries are removed.

M1.justification: Section 5.1 changes the stated encoder input from (s,a,s') to (s,a), including its use in the TD likelihood. This is a limited specification correction: v1 Appendix A.1 already described state-only or state-action rewards. Algorithm 1, the shared variational objective, and the principal method components remain unchanged; an implemented redesign is not established.

P1.justification: Prose revisions concentrate on method properties and experimental interpretation, alongside shortened preliminary explanations, corrected terminology, and reorganized appendices. A generic Impact Statement and front-matter edits are added. The main section sequence and most introductory, related-work, and concluding prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, removes the original method-overview diagram, merges return and EPIC tables, and replaces bold/underlined ranking marks with shaded cells. It adds comparison and ablation tables and removes the six budget-sweep tables. Transfer plots are redrawn, including a four-panel main figure; existing qualitative maps are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Optuna citation, Akiba et al. (2019), and explicitly positions MAVRL against non-amortized MCMC and post-hoc averaging through new comparisons. The related-work discussion and relationship to AVRIL remain substantially unchanged. Publication and bibliography updates for existing works do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Section 4 corrects the ordered-logit definition from finite outer cutpoints to psi_0 = -infinity and psi_K = +infinity, ensuring the categories cover the full utility range. This is a mathematical correction beyond equivalent notation. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical scrutiny through direct non-variational comparisons, equal-budget controls, and corruption tests that expose limits of combining feedback. Expanded implementation details also help. These benefits are tempered by lost budget-sweep evidence and conflicting robustness-protocol descriptions: Appendix C attributes downstream tests to equal-budget checkpoints, while Section 6.3 describes fixed-allocation budgets. The added controls and qualifications support a modest net improvement, with reproducibility concerns limiting the gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MAVRL and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Content can be matched despite substantial reformatting and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across the same environments, including revised performance results and new baseline comparisons, equal-budget evaluations, and feedback-misspecification tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-learning experiments across six environments, including policy returns, EPIC distances, dynamics-perturbation tests, reward visualizations, and appendix feedback-budget sweeps.

title: MAVRL: Learning Reward Functions from Multiple Feedback Types with Amortized Variational Inference

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion withdraw v1's central claim that data scarcity is established as the binding constraint and that the data-to-parameter ratio determines scaling. V2 instead claims parameter scaling within one standardized setting, emphasizes test consistency and diagnostics, and explicitly limits the entropy estimate to task-specific remaining uncertainty.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the data-bottleneck and threshold interpretation with an interaction among data volume, effective epochs, and optimization budget. It corrects v1 Section 7.4.3's description of 2.3 bits as predictable information to remaining uncertainty. Residual heterogeneity now qualifies the Gaussian interpretation, and the new Broader Impact section discusses composition biases affecting the fitted floor.

D1.justification: V2 adds a dataset filename, configuration details for the supplementary experiments, the runs-directory location, and a manifest-filtering disclosure. Table 1 revises reported parameter counts, including TINY from 9,937 to 9,953 and L from 101,033,041 to 100,510,801. The repository and seed information remain; relocating reproducibility information to Appendix C is not a new code release.

E1.justification: V2 removes the 1,024-gene, 10,000-cell reconstruction setting, one of v1's two principal regimes, including its appendix coverage. It retains the 512-gene CELLxGENE task. The added 25k–200k subsets use the same gene set and preprocessing, so their sample-count variation belongs to E3.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally compares against external methods. scVI, scGPT, Geneformer, scBERT, and scFoundation remain related-work references, while the experiments compare sizes of the same transformer family.

E3.justification: V2 centers evaluation on the existing 18-run, 60k-step standardized sweep and removes the heterogeneous additional runs and XL setting. It adds reported held-out test evaluation, an M-model data-size sweep at fixed vocabulary and training steps, and XXS/TINY direct-NLL reruns. The original 90/5/5 split and canonical optimization settings remain.

E4.justification: New Section 7.3 and Figure 2 investigate data-size sensitivity and test the homoscedasticity assumption through per-gene held-out residuals. Section 7.5.3 and Appendix A add direct-versus-derived NLL calibration for XXS/TINY. V1 discussed these limitations without these empirical checks.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes from minimum–maximum seed ranges to means and standard deviations for validation and test MSE. The retained sweep still uses seeds 7, 8, and 9; this does not establish an increase in repetitions. No confidence intervals for scaling parameters or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: V2 removes Regime B results and the 21-run Regime A fit, replaces loss ranges with standardized means, and adds test results, including alpha=0.268, c=1.462, and R²=0.859. New findings include the nearly flat data-size fit, residual heterogeneity, and NLL calibration. The canonical validation fit and Table 4 entropy estimates remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The encoder, embeddings, mask token, prediction head, 15% masking, MSE objective, and scaling-fit procedure remain unchanged. Appendix B explicitly says the direct-NLL reruns differ only in additional validation logging. Revised parameter counts do not document a new architectural component.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, regime descriptions, results narrative, discussion, limitations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the standardized sweep. The dual-regime organization is removed, Broader Impact is added, and reproducibility moves to Appendix C. Citation formatting also changes from author–year to numbered references.

P2.justification: Tables 1–3 and Figure 1 are substantially redesigned around standardized validation/test comparisons. A new Figure 2 displays the data-size sweep and residual scatter; v1 Figure 2 is retained as Figure 3 with a revised caption. Typography, headings, title presentation, and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: The same 24 cited works and first-systematic-study positioning remain. However, v2 Section 7.4 drops v1's specific claim that its dual-regime behavior echoes Kaplan's parameter/data-scaling contradiction, replacing it with a qualified discussion of different scaling axes and insufficient evidence for an intersection analysis.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same mathematical content, including the scaling formulation and Gaussian entropy conversion. Homoscedasticity was already assumed in v1 Appendix A. V2 adds empirical checks and interpretive qualifications, without new proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves inferential reliability by withdrawing the unsupported causal conclusion from confounded regimes, correcting the entropy interpretation, and adding test confirmation and targeted diagnostics. These address central weaknesses while preserving the canonical scaling evidence. Coverage is narrower and entropy remains approximate. An unresolved discrepancy—Figure 2's 200k-cell M-model loss near 1.57 versus Table 2's 1.462 under apparently matching settings—limits the auxiliary sweep, but does not outweigh the stronger validation and more defensible conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scaling-law study. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching v1's canonical sweep to v2's standardized sweep.

after.justification: V2 retains the original standardized parameter sweep and reports held-out test results, a data-size sweep, residual diagnostics, and direct-NLL calibration outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports original transformer-training outcomes and fitted scaling laws for two CELLxGENE regimes, including seed-level loss ranges and entropy-floor estimates in Tables 2–4.

title: Scaling Laws for Masked-Reconstruction Transformers on Single-Cell Transcriptomics

C1.justification: The abstract, seven introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims about visual sensitivities, optimization, human preferences, interpretability, and partial mitigation. New appendix evidence supports these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v1 tentatively attributes product distillation failure to category heterogeneity; v2 claims corroboration and says category-specific distillation fixes it. Section 4.6 also extends the interpretation to unseen images. Appendix G attributes some matching failures to similar source images rather than optimization. The main limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix F explicitly identifies the original three-candidate setting and the one-proposal-per-round ablation after initialization. The first-page project address changes from the Vercel address to sahaslab.com/visualpersuasion. Existing algorithm and prompt documentation is retained, and both conclusions still describe code and data release as forthcoming.

E1.justification: The four datasets and agent-choice domains remain unchanged. Appendix G adds a distinct human identity-matching task, beyond the earlier preference judgments. The additional held-out images otherwise extend sampling within existing domains.

E2.justification: The new held-out distillation comparisons use original and zero-shot images as baselines (Figure 8 and Table 4), whereas the retained in-sample Figure 6 compares distilled images with zero-shot and final optimized images. The VTG/VFD/CVPO comparison lineup remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds substantive evaluation designs: distillation on 20 new base images per task, category-specific product distillation, and CVPO evaluation with one candidate rather than three. Appendix G introduces matching of all 400 original/CVPO-final pairs in ten-pair sets, with two matchings per pair. These supplement rather than replace the existing protocols.

E4.justification: New Appendices E–G test generalization beyond optimization images, whether product-category heterogeneity explains distillation failure, whether CVPO's advantage survives fewer image proposals, and whether edited identities remain recognizable. These substantially extend validation beyond v1's existing distillation and mitigation analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix G adds a participant-level binomial GLM relating matching accuracy to task duration, with a confidence interval for the odds association. Existing cluster-robust linear probability models and uncertainty-reporting practices are retained. Neither version reports optimizer seed replication.

E6.justification: v2 adds held-out results favoring distillation over zero-shot editing in three of four domains. Table 4 reports category-specific product choice estimates of 35.9%, 55.9%, and 59.2% for original, zero-shot, and distilled images. The k=1 experiment retains CVPO's lead over VFD and reports 17.9 mean rounds; Appendix G reports 11 of 400 pairs mismatched by both raters. Existing numerical results are retained.

M1.justification: Appendix E.2 adds a category-specific distillation variant that derives editing themes separately for each product category instead of pooling products. The core CVPO, VFD, VTG, normalization, and summarization algorithms remain unchanged; the one-candidate experiment varies an existing parameter.

P1.justification: v2 inserts three appendix sections and updates cross-references, with limited additions to the main discussion. It also adds equal-contribution and conference-publication text. Most existing prose and the main section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 8–9 and Table 4, adjusts Figure 2's proportions, and resizes or repositions several retained displays. Some captions now specify the 50% base rate. Existing appendix displays are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive related-work positioning are unchanged. Reference-list differences are attributable to layout rather than additions or removals.

T1.justification: The latent-utility formulation, pairwise preference model, identity-maintenance definition, and optimization and equilibrium reasoning in Section 3.2 are unchanged. The added identity study supplies empirical validation, not a revised definition or proof.

improvement.justification: The held-out tests, one-candidate ablation, and identity-matching study provide useful checks on weaknesses left largely untested in v1. Their value is bounded: Table 4's 59.2% versus 55.9% contrast has p≈0.1 despite the claim that category grouping fixes the problem, and successful identity matching does not establish that all substantive qualities remained unchanged. The additional validation nevertheless supports a limited overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across pagination and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds held-out distillation, category-specific distillation, a CVPO candidate-count ablation, and human identity-matching results.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments across four visual decision domains and nine VLMs, human choice studies with 154 participants, and interpretability, mitigation, and distillation results.

title: Visual Persuasion: What Influences Decisions of Vision-Language Models?

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: information geometry for softmax representations, distinct primal/dual interpolation semantics, and dual steering that minimizes off-target disturbance under the stated assumptions. The principal empirical controllability claim is unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 newly distinguishes the factorization assumption needed for the theorem from steering differences observed without it. Section 5.3 replaces v1's explicit explanation of possible target-steering failure and increased off-target distortion with an emphasis on empirical outperformance despite assumption violations. Appendix C.2 retains the evidence of probe mismatch.

D1.justification: Algorithm 2 and Appendix B.2 newly detail matrix-free conjugate gradient, suggest 20 iterations, and provide residual stopping and numerical safeguards. The top-20000 approximation, regularization value 0.005, data-processing instructions, and code-access link were already present in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions use C4 contexts for verb-form and English-to-French steering, synthetic color/shape images, and COCO object concepts. The appendix retains the same concept coverage; the new approximation test introduces no distinct dataset or task.

E2.justification: Euclidean steering remains the comparator, evaluated alongside dual steering with both Primal MD and Dual MD probes. Newly cited manifold-steering and concept-erasure methods are discussed but are not added to the experimental comparisons.

E3.justification: Table 1 introduces an approximation-evaluation protocol using Frobenius matrix error, K values of 1, 20, 2000, 20000, and 200000, and trajectory steps 0, 5, 10, 50, and 100. Existing data selection, steering metrics, and the 0.9999 stopping threshold are retained; the threshold was already documented in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds a top-K sensitivity check against the full Fisher information matrix in Table 1, quantitatively testing an approximation whose accuracy v1 only asserted. The existing regularization-geometry and probe-assumption analyses in Appendix C remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and SEM across test contexts using the same per-path probability-binning procedure, moved from v1 Appendix B.2 to v2 B.3. No new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are reported.

E6.justification: The quantitative robustness trajectories are substantively revised, particularly LLM rank differences. For English-to-French steering with Dual MD, Euclidean rank difference changes from an early plateau near 0.54 in v1 Figure 4 to a gradual rise exceeding 0.6 in v2 Figure 5; corresponding appendix trajectories also change in Figures 10 and 11, respectively. Table 1 additionally reports approximation errors, including values rounding to 0.0000 for K at least 20000. These are revised reported results, not an established performance improvement.

M1.justification: The dual-steering objective, probe constructions, and regularized Newton update in Algorithm 1 are retained. Algorithm 2 specifies conjugate gradient for the previously unspecified linear solve; this implementation disclosure does not establish a change to the underlying steering method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained, with limited terminology and explanatory edits. Appendix B gains a separate Metrics subsection, the stopping-rule paragraph moves within it, and v2 adds an Impact Statement and expands implementation and related-work passages.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reformats the main text into a two-column conference layout, changes typography and figure sizing, and rearranges displays throughout the paper and appendices. It adds the primal/dual-space schematic in Figure 4, Table 1, and Algorithm 2; existing figures are retained and renumbered rather than removed.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds focused discussion of concurrent manifold steering by Sarfati and Wurgaft and concept-erasure work by Bolukbasi, Vargas, Belrose, and Ravfogel. It also distinguishes Singh's affine steering using L2 distance from the paper's output-distribution KL objective. The broader novelty positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Sections 4.2 and B.2 add a computational-complexity argument contrasting explicit covariance computation and solution, O(kd² + d³), with conjugate gradient, O(nKd) after top-K truncation. The interpolation proposition, concept-factorization definition, steering theorem, and Appendix A proofs otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Algorithm 2 improves implementation reproducibility, while Table 1 quantitatively supports the approximation-accuracy assertion already present in v1. The expanded research positioning and geometric illustration also help. These targeted gains outweigh the softened failure discussion in Section 5.3, although Appendix C.2 still documents the violated probing assumption. The revised numerical curves alone do not establish improved empirical quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core arguments, experiments, and Appendices A–C. Text, equations, figures, and tables are readable; reformatting and renumbering do not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original steering and probing experiments and additionally reports covariance-approximation errors in Table 1.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original interpolation, probing, and steering experiments using Gemma-3-4B and MetaCLIP-2.

P1.justification: v2 adds short Practical Scalability passages, Appendix B.1 and corresponding-author contact information, alongside limited wording edits. Most prose and the main section sequence are retained.

T1.justification: The hierarchy constraints and other mathematical content are unchanged. v2 adds no formal assumptions, propositions, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: The new human audit provides limited evidence supporting the LLM judge, with sample IDs enabling scrutiny. The audit's small, manually selected sample limits the gain; the principal experiments and claims remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Mnemis research. Their text, figures, tables and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching across pagination and table-number changes.

P2.justification: Several existing figures are enlarged or relocated, including Figures 2, 4, and 5. Table 2 is widened with smaller text, and Table 5 expands to accommodate citations. Captions receive small edits; no figures or tables containing new results are added.

improvement.justification: More concrete abstract and finding summaries, larger key plots, and model-source citations modestly improve accessibility and attribution. The scientific evidence remains unchanged. Table 2’s smaller text and the uncertain meaning of the revised PROTEUS sampling window limit the overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same prescriptive-scaling study. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–J are available and support reliable comparison.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of interpretable reward decomposition, over 90% reward-behavior recovery, human validation, and latent-misalignment detection. Appendix A.7 newly discusses checkpoint-access and storage barriers and noisy trajectories from weak instruction-following models. A.5.1 also acknowledges Fixed-15 as a more competitive comparator.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the misalignment judge and supplies its full classification prompt in Figure 10. It also documents the corrective objective, realignment workflow, and negative-SFT-loss signal. Existing discovery hyperparameters, PPO/GRPO settings, and human-study instructions are retained.

The added reward-model comparisons vary alignment configurations rather than introduce competing discovery methods.

Appendices A.5.5–A.5.8 introduce corrective GRPO realignment, SFT-loss-based discovery, dataset comparisons holding the reward model fixed, and reward-model comparisons holding the dataset and policy family fixed. The informative-sampling and fixed-objective ablations receive expanded quantitative evaluation. The original static-checkpoint comparison is retained and relocated.

E5.justification: The misalignment comparison expands from four to 34 independent trials and adds a 95% confidence interval and pairwise p-values. The patching study reports ten audit trials, and the reward-model study reports three trials per model. Existing Model-Fit uncertainty reporting and human-study statistics remain.

E6.justification: v1's four-trial summary reports detection in 3/4 Obj-Disco trials and at most 1/4 baseline trials. The expanded LLM-judged evaluation reports 58.8% for Obj-Disco, versus 20.6% Iter-Filter, 0% Zero-Shot, 23.5% Fixed-3, 44.1% Fixed-15, and 5.9% Limited-Zero-Shot. P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the safety results and ablation discussion, adds four appendix subsections, and expands limitations. It also adds acknowledgements and a conflict-of-interest disclosure. The main exposition and overall section structure remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the misalignment-judging prompt display and before/after patching display, expands Figure 3's caption, and relocates existing figures. v1 Figure 6 becomes appendix Figure 25. Existing numerical plots and hyperparameter tables are preserved without a substantial visual redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds Dineen et al.'s QA-LIGN citation and Barto and Dietterich's supervised-learning/reinforcement-learning connection. Most other reference changes update publication metadata for existing works; the main positioning against prior discovery and interpretability approaches remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal objective definitions, Obj-Error and Model-Fit equations, trend functions, and submodular selection guarantee remain unchanged. The SFT discussion invokes an existing supervised-learning/reinforcement-learning connection without adding a proof or derivation.

improvement.justification: The 34-trial safety evaluation, uncertainty reporting, explicit judging prompt, and expanded limitations improve the assessability of v1's four-trial case study. The new applications add useful exploratory evidence. Gains remain bounded: the Fixed-15 comparison is not statistically significant (p = 0.33), and the patching study establishes no rediscovered misaligned objectives rather than independently verified removal of harmful behavior.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Obj-Disco research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

title: Discovering Implicit Large Language Model Alignment Objectives

C1.justification: The main framework and three-strategy contributions remain unchanged. The conclusion extends the performance claim to enhancement methods using task supervision, explicitly naming URIE and Dissen, while qualifying superiority as holding in most settings.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 and new Appendix E expand runtime interpretations and strategy-selection guidance, including immediate feedback in Parallel and fixed-hypothesis limitations in Alternating. v2 also explains the MNIST exception and explicitly limits the high-resolution study to a 10-class proof of concept. These extend interpretation without establishing new causal validation.

D1.justification: v2 adds relative runtime information: one signal evaluation on EARS reportedly costs approximately seven logit evaluations. It also explicitly documents deterministic clean-sample prediction. Existing architecture, training, sampling, and code-access information is retained; implementation documentation for the new comparisons remains limited.

E1.justification: Table 5 adds a standard-resolution ImageNet scenario at 224×224, extending image input conditions beyond the earlier downsampled ImageNet evaluation. Existing image and speech datasets and corruption types remain represented.

E2.justification: URIE is newly evaluated throughout the image comparisons in Table 1, and the Dissen enhancer throughout the speech comparisons in Table 2. Both works were already cited in v1, but these task-supervised enhancement comparators were absent from its reported comparisons. Their inclusion substantially expands comparison methods across both modalities.

E3.justification: The added ImageNet experiment uses a 10-class subset with a reported fixed sampling protocol and compares Parallel with Enhanced under the three existing corruptions. It supplements the retained 100-class, 32×32 experiment. Existing sampling budgets, classifier configurations, restricted-token speech decoding, and WER reference procedures are unchanged.

The existing sampling-step, guidance-source, DDPM/DDIM, and qualitative reconstruction analyses are retained.

E5.justification: There are no additions to repeated-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance testing. New table entries continue point-estimate reporting. Appendix E's discussion of implicit uncertainty is conceptual rather than a statistical reporting change.

E6.justification: Existing scores are retained apart from equivalent rounding. Substantial new comparative results include URIE leading on MNIST, with 99.5% under blur versus 99.3% for the best coupled strategy, and Dissen WERs of 7.96%, 6.46%, and 13.04% in Table 2. Table 5 adds Enhanced/Parallel accuracies of 92.1/94.0, 86.5/92.4, and 94.0/94.1 for 15% noise, 30% noise, and blur. M1.justification: The Parallel, Alternating, and Nested algorithms, training objectives, frozen classifiers, and sampling schedules are retained. The deterministic clean-prediction explanation clarifies the existing procedure; suggested acceleration techniques are not implemented method changes.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized notation and prose clarifications, adds a computational-complexity subsection and strategy-comparison appendix, and revises the conclusion. The audio appendix becomes Appendix F, and publication information and acknowledgements are updated. Most wording and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain comparator columns and revised captions, Table 5 is added, and Figure 4 gains horizontal baseline references and expanded legends while retaining the sampling curves. Other figures remain unchanged, with local float relocation and page reflow.

R1.justification: The new efficiency discussion adds references on faster solvers, distillation, DeepCache, flow formulations, and neural audio codecs. URIE and Dissen move from previously cited related approaches to explicit empirical comparisons. The foundational positioning against sequential enhancement, CARD, and joint energy-based models remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the evaluated task-supervised baselines in Tables 1–2 make the empirical comparison more informative, including the acknowledged MNIST exception. Table 5 provides a bounded resolution check, and notation and runtime explanations improve clarity. The gains remain limited because the new resolution study covers only ten classes, new experimental implementation details are sparse, and some added mechanism and runtime generalizations lack direct validation.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, standard-resolution ImageNet results, and an EARS computation-cost observation.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification accuracies, speech-recognition WERs, ablations, and qualitative reconstruction results in Section 4 and the appendices.

title: Joint Enhancement and Classification using Coupled Diffusion Models of Signals and Logits

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: logit distance controls linear representational similarity and concept preservation, KL provides weak practical guarantees, and logit-based distillation better preserves teacher representations. Additional evidence and qualifications do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands the applicability discussion. It explains that matching unlikely labels can transfer teacher noise, explicitly discusses unequal representation dimensions and large-model optimization, and clarifies the last-layer focus and exclusion of cross-modal comparisons. It also explains why maximal mCCA need not imply matching distributions and why linear-invariant similarity measures suit this identifiability perspective without being universally preferable.

D1.justification: The implementation sections match across v1 Appendix K and v3 Appendix L: architectures, preprocessing, learning rates, training epochs, batch sizes, software and drep subsampling are retained. Both versions provide the same code-access link.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Synth, CIFAR100 and SUB for classification, representational alignment and concept recovery. The added analyses use retained datasets; Appendix H adds a mathematical counterexample, and language-model experiments remain future work.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain KL-, L1- and L2-students with teacher references. Newly discussed similarity measures and distillation literature do not introduce evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: V3 adds a SUB protocol varying student dimension from 2 to 10 against a dimension-10 teacher, evaluating mCCA over the most aligned student-sized teacher subspace. It also evaluates the CIFAR bound at epochs 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. The original experiments retain their stated splits, architectures and training budgets.

E4.justification: V3 adds two substantive analyses absent from v1: the SUB dimension ablation tests how student capacity affects label accuracy, concept recovery and alignment (Appendix L.1, Figure 8), while the CIFAR checkpoint analysis tests the empirical behavior of Theorem F.1's bound (Appendix F.5, Figure 3). These substantially expand the targeted evaluation beyond fixed-configuration comparisons.

E5.justification: The original five-teacher, five-student-seed reporting and inverse-variance aggregation are retained. V3 separately specifies one teacher and five student seeds for the dimension ablation, reporting means and standard deviations, and displays five individual seed trajectories for the bound check. These are additional replication designs, not an increase in the original experiments' run counts.

E6.justification: Under unchanged reported settings, Table 4 revises SUB mCCA from 0.787 to 0.417 for KL, 0.996 to 0.993 for L1, and 0.997 to 0.994 for L2, retaining ±0.001. Table 2 likewise changes KL from 0.79 to 0.42. Figures 3 and 8 add bound-check and capacity-sweep findings; Appendix G adds KL values of 0.002 and 0.0017. The KL-alignment finding changes materially, although the reason for the score revisions is unspecified.

M1.justification: The model family, centered-logit construction, L1/L2 distillation objectives and linear identifiability dissimilarity are unchanged. The added student-dimension sweep evaluates existing methods under different model configurations.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. V3 adds explanatory passages, expands related work and limitations, introduces an Impact Statement and adds appendix subsections. Author presentation and citation formatting also change, without a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with new headers, reflowed equations and relocated tables. V3 adds Figure 3's bound plot, Figures 6–7's counterexample and Figure 8's ablation panels. V1 Figures 3–4 are retained as v3 Figures 4–5.

R1.justification: Appendix A expands positioning against orthogonal Procrustes, RSA and CKA invariances, and discusses further model families and multi-view research. New citations also support discussion of rank ordering, calibration and steering in Section 4. The central relationship to prior identifiability work remains unchanged; publication updates of existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: The central bounds and their proofs, including unequal-dimension Theorem F.1, are retained. V3 requires diversity of only one model in Theorem 2.2 and supplies its proof in Appendix C.1. Remark E.3 revises an example's constant and extends the tightness argument to Jensen–Shannon divergence. New Appendix H constructs models with maximal embedding and unembedding mCCA but different distributions.

improvement.justification: V3 provides useful additional evidence about student capacity and the theoretical bound, makes the identifiability argument more self-contained, and adds meaningful qualifications about noisy rare labels and applicability. These improve support and interpretation while leaving the central work intact. The gains remain limited by the single-teacher ablation and unexplained SUB mCCA revisions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the conference reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and additionally reports a student-dimension ablation and an empirical illustration of the canonical-correlation bound.

before.justification: V1 reports original distillation experiments on Synth, CIFAR100 and SUB, including classification accuracy, representational similarity and concept recovery in Tables 1–4.

T1.justification: The objective decomposition and Appendix D policy-gradient claim, proof and derivations are retained. Removing the extraneous argmax from Equation 2 is a notation correction, not a substantive theoretical revision.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central findings by testing dependencies on coding, probe extraction, training duration and the code-length incentive. Particularly valuable are the non-coding experiment and ten-seed demonstrations of detector benefits without a code-length penalty. Threshold checks and implementation disclosures also improve auditability. The new judge setup and bug-fix validation remain incompletely documented, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Obfuscation Atlas study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds Food-Sycophancy experiments, probe-stability controls and further robustness evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original RLVR experiments on four models, deception-probe evaluations, ablations and model-belief analyses.

title: The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes

C1.justification: v1's abstract claims unique reconstruction of the simplest physical law. v2 instead states reconstruction of a representable, regularization-minimizing admissible law, with recovery of the unique true law requiring an additional identifiability condition. The conclusion likewise qualifies statements about network limits, substantially narrowing the headline guarantee to match the retained theory.

C2.justification: Section 4.1.2 substantially expands discussion of regularity, measurement injectivity and applicability beyond the earlier brief remarks. New experiments motivate explanations involving architectural misspecification, enlarged search spaces and local minima. The conclusion explicitly acknowledges limited numerical performance and distinguishes the analytical contribution from a mature numerical framework.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial reproducibility information: early-stopping patience, regularization strength, derivative estimation, per-system architectures, restart and time budgets, forward solvers, grids and initial-condition generation. Tables 1, 3 and 6 organize these details. The documented code-access link also changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from two linear 1D PDE examples to seven Strogatz ODE systems, the 2D Brusselator and a 2D membrane-transport system. These introduce coupled nonlinear dynamics, Laplacian-dependent laws, and polynomial, rational, trigonometric and exponential recovery tasks.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates separate competing recovery algorithms. The new comparisons vary ParFam architecture and structural constraints as ablations; cited approaches such as SINDy and EQL do not become evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 10–80 ODE trajectories, system-specific architectures and optimization budgets, 64×64 and 32×32 PDE grids, and distinct measurement-resolution sweeps. They also introduce Savitzky–Golay derivative estimation and coefficient thresholding at 0.015 for error evaluation. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the original linear-PDE settings changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the original domain-dependent error analysis, v2 tests underspecified, default and extended architectures, and compares unconstrained recovery with additive diffusion constraints. Figures 3–7 also examine errors around trajectories and document difficult regimes, diffusion-coefficient recovery failures and variability across optimization runs.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run counts or uncertainty bands. v2 reports medians and interquartile ranges over 10 seeds for Figure 2, 15 seeds for the ODE experiments, and repeated-seed reporting for the 2D experiments. This establishes substantially stronger uncertainty reporting, without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: Figure 2 contains revised median curves, although the two displayed linear-PDE reconstruction formulas remain unchanged. Table 4 adds recovered ODE formulas and errors, including Lotka–Volterra errors of 0.14 and 0.11. Figures 4–7 add substantial PDE results, including unsuccessful diffusion recovery in the hard Brusselator regime and variable rational-term recovery in membrane transport.

M1.justification: The symbolic-network architecture, objective (Pm) and alternating optimization remain. Section 5.2.3 adds a constrained ParFam variant enforcing additive diffusion and excluding cross-terms between the Laplacian and state variables, a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially revised, related work becomes a separate section, and scope, novelty and organization receive dedicated subsections. Scattered assumption remarks become a structured discussion, and extensions receive their own subsection. This materially changes the narrative organization beyond simply inserting experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 3–7 and Tables 1–6, introducing extensive multipanel results, architecture comparisons and configuration summaries. Figure 2 is redrawn with uncertainty bands and revised captions. Wider text blocks and changed typography also substantially alter the document layout.

R1.justification: Six references are added, covering transport regularity, operator learning, variational regularization and Lasso; the earlier cited works are retained. Section 1.2 sharpens the distinction from existing all-at-once frameworks and ParFam/EQL by emphasizing the nontrivial verification of symbolic networks' function-space properties.

T1.justification: The principal definitions, assumptions, reconstruction theorem, identifiability corollary and Appendix A–C proofs are retained after renumbering. However, v2 drops v1 Remark 8's assertion that the sampling operators satisfy condition (5) while failing the stronger convergence conditions discussed there, removing a limited mathematical assertion.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation on two linear examples through nonlinear ODE and 2D PDE experiments, architecture and structure tests, and explicit uncertainty reporting. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility, while the abstract and conclusion better distinguish reconstruction from unique identification. The experiments still expose numerical failures, but reporting those failures and their variability makes the paper's practical scope considerably better supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same symbolic PDE recovery framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization and expanded experiments.

after.justification: Section 5 retains the linear-PDE experiments and reports original simulations and reconstruction results for seven nonlinear ODE systems and two 2D PDE systems.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figure 2 report original numerical reconstructions of two linear PDEs from simulated incomplete, noisy measurements.

title: Symbolic recovery of PDEs from measurement data

R1.justification: V2 adds the GELU and Swish references supporting its new comparisons. The Stuart-Landau citation retains the same work title with revised bibliographic information, rather than introducing a different research direction. The broader positioning remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–B. The retained material can be matched across section moves and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds ogbn-ArXiv results and activation/filter ablations. Baseline results attributed to other papers are distinguishable from the proposed models' results.

title: Beyond ReLU: Bifurcation, Oversmoothing, and Topological Priors

Appendix E adds a warning that new problems may require guidance retuning and explains excessive guidance as overwhelming diffusion regularization. The linear-FEM applicability boundaries remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project code-availability statement and repository address, revised guidance instructions, entropy calibration details and SAC implementation settings, including target entropy 4, discount 0.9 and 16 gradient steps per interaction. Existing architecture and hardware documentation remains; Appendix A still states that datasets and models cannot be publicly released.

Bayesian optimization and conditional diffusion remain. Unguided sampling and the projection variant were already evaluated in v1.

It also adds an RL protocol with ten-step episodes, one spatial arrangement during training, ten during evaluation and results from the 35,000-interaction checkpoint. Guidance settings change, while retained diffusion-training budgets, target selection and 200-sample evaluations remain unchanged.

Existing dataset-size, denoising-step, projection, density-weight and backprojection analyses remain, with updated evidence; projection results additionally appear by target.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages and appendix standard deviations over three seeds, with aggregate ablation deviations also spanning five targets. v2 extends this practice to additional results and metrics. No changed repeated-run count for retained experiments, new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is reported.

Projection changes from reducing average material coverage to increasing it. RL, entropy and target-specific projection results are added. These are revised-configuration results, not fixed-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 6.2 replaces v1's separate gradient multipliers for E and nu (0.5 and 0.02) with normalization-derivative scaling, gradient-norm clipping at 2.5 and clipping of the predicted clean sample during guidance. These refine inference within the retained diffusion/FEM/backprojection method; the architecture and objectives remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify material terminology, contributions and experimental findings. Model and training descriptions are combined, sampling details move to Appendix A, and evaluation details receive a dedicated Appendix B. The main section sequence and most methodological exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the result displays: separate 2D method and baseline tables become a unified comparison, 3D results receive their own table, and entropy columns extend the main and uncertainty tables. Figure 9 has different axes and content, Figure 10 adds three sensitivity plots, and qualitative sample montages are replaced.

It more explicitly acknowledges existing methodological components and distinguishes target-specific RL training from inference-time objective flexibility. The broader related-work coverage remains stable.

improvement.justification: The tuned RL comparison, full-parameter diversity metric and guidance-strength analysis strengthen evidence for the central accuracy-diversity claims. Performance changes are mixed under revised guidance, and the data/model-release restrictions remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 25 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including their appendices, equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original material-design experiments with revised guidance, an additional reinforcement-learning comparison, diversity measurements and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original FEM-based experiments on 2D and 3D inverse material design, baseline comparisons, ablations and supplementary analyses.

title: Guided Diffusion by Optimized Loss Functions on Relaxed Parameters for Inverse Material Design

C1.justification: The abstract and two introductory contributions retain the semi-analytical solver and tractable state-space analysis claims. It also qualifies numerical and scaling limitations using new evidence and discusses initialization-dependent missed equilibria/cycles and the restriction to shallow architectures.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository pointer, Latent ODE/Neural CDE tuning grids, explicit eigenvalue and perturbation thresholds in Appendix D.2, heartbeat selection/preprocessing instructions, and CPU/core information for cycle detection. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the perturbation strategy itself was already disclosed in v1.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original benchmarks and adds forecasting of irregular PhysioNet heart-rate series from ten subjects (Section 4.5, Appendix F.4), plus reconstruction of a stochastic Izhikevich neuron (Figure 6, Table 7). Table 3 describes 4/10 and 2/10 Euler runs as excluded rather than surviving. Prediction-time aggregation remains inconsistent: Table 1 specifies median/MAD, whereas Appendix G.3 specifies mean/standard deviation.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial benchmark, comparator, prediction-horizon and robustness results. Izhikevich results favor cPLRNN on Dstsp but standard PLRNN on DH (Table 7). Retained Lorenz P=10 cPLRNN Dstsp changes from 0.35±0.14 to 0.37±0.14, and Table 2 timings change. Appendix D.2 and Algorithm 3 detail the matrix-perturbation and gradient-discard fallback already described in v1 Appendix A. The mathematical corrections do not establish a changed implementation or new method component.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition and the main section order are retained. V2 makes local language, terminology and cross-reference corrections, updates front matter, and adds Section 4.5 and supporting appendix subsections. Figure 2 gains switching markers and a revised state-space projection. Existing appendix illustrations become Figures 4–5, with limited display corrections.

Unequal rollout conditions for new baselines and inconsistent prediction-statistic descriptions limit some comparisons, but the added evidence addresses important gaps in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same cPLRNN research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The core material and appendices A–H can be matched reliably; v2 adds further material, including appendices I–J.

title: Can Recommender Systems Teach Themselves? A Recursive Self-Improving Framework with Fidelity Control

Corrections include DeiT-Tiny FLOPs reduction from 38.5% to 41.5% in Table 1 and the DeiT-Base baseline from 81.08% to 81.80% in Table 2, with corresponding accuracy-difference corrections.

E5.justification: Head-sensitivity plots retain standard-error reporting, and the AIME table still averages four runs. The new benchmark tables provide point estimates without introducing seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-estimation practices.

M1.justification: The objectives, key-selection variants, bias/value fitting, head allocation, and chunked/online compaction procedures are retained. P1.justification: v2 adds Section 4.2, Appendix F.4, and Appendix G, clarifies Section 2, and makes terminology, cross-reference, grammatical, and publication-footer edits. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

T1.justification: The attention-matching equations, least-squares formulation, and Appendix A mass-preservation derivation are unchanged. Section 2 clarifies concatenated sequence lengths and illustrates the existing formulation without adding mathematical results or assumptions.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical case relied mainly on two multiple-choice datasets. v2 substantially strengthens it through generative QA and retrieval evaluations and a token-merging comparator, testing whether compaction preserves information beyond answer selection. LongBench v2 remains limited to a selected 47-context subset, and Appendix G's instruction-following and latency assurances lack dedicated tests. These limitations temper the new claims but do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fast KV Compaction via Attention Matching. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER, and KVMerger evaluations. Some additional RULER comparator scores are explicitly attributed to a leaderboard.

before.justification: v1 reports original QuALITY and LongHealth experiments, timing measurements, component ablations, and an online-compaction experiment on AIME 2025 in Appendix F.3.

P1.justification: The seven main sections retain their order and most methodological exposition. v2 edits terminology and tense, corrects 'CGB' to 'CGP', revises the contribution list and conclusion, reorganizes the appendices, and adds author-contribution and acknowledgement text. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's broad claims through direct comparisons with additional probing methods and BEATs, evaluations beyond classification, and measured computational costs. Undefined ± statistics, conflicting pretraining warmup descriptions, and an overbroad claim that CGP beats all probes despite the ESC-50 exception remain weaknesses. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BAT/CGP research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across the expanded appendices.
