C2.justification: Section 2.3 expands the justification for assuming directional convergence and explains that a positive limiting margin excludes asymptotic margin collapse, replacing the earlier momentum-history rationale. Section 6 more cautiously describes the largest observed margins rather than empirical maximization. The substantive non-smooth-model limitations remain.

E5.justification: Figures 1–2 change their shaded uncertainty bands from 95% confidence intervals in v1 to one standard deviation in v3. Both retain 10 random seeds. The new CIFAR10 figure also uses means and standard deviations over 10 seeds; no increased run count is reported.

E6.justification: Figures 1–2 present revised MNIST curves under changed reported settings while retaining the principal optimizer rankings. New Figure 3 reports CIFAR10 margins and alignment trajectories: NGD leads for the ℓ2 margin, Signum exceeds Adam for the ℓ∞ margin, and Muon-Adam leads for the hybrid margin. These are added or replaced results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The optimizer update equations, composite Muon procedures, and approximate-steepest-descent framework are retained. Both versions already analyze exponential and logistic losses. The different loss and network used experimentally change evaluation settings, not the analyzed algorithms.

P1.justification: The contribution framing, assumption discussion, normalized-descent introduction, and conclusion receive focused rewrites. The standalone main-text soft-margin theorem is omitted while its appendix treatment remains; Appendix D gains task-specific subsections and an Impact Statement is added. Most prose and the overall section sequence are preserved.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout with running headers. Figure 1 is relocated and resized; retained plots have revised axis ranges, legends, and uncertainty captions. v3 also adds the four-panel CIFAR10 Figure 3 and learning-rate Table 2.

R1.justification: v3 adds related-work discussion on Adam convergence and non-convergence, generalization, path-SGD, and tame geometry, with corresponding citations. Section 3.1 explicitly acknowledges that the normalized-descent result follows from Tsilivis et al. through time reparameterization. This refines novelty positioning while preserving the main relationship to prior implicit-bias research.

T1.justification: Most derivations are retained, including soft-margin monotonicity in Appendix C.9. However, normalized-descent and supporting results replace homogeneity degree L>0 with L≥1, and the initial-loss threshold changes from ℓ(0) to 1. Appendix Theorem C.30 also drops initialization assumption (A1), although main Theorem 3.5 retains it. These are substantive but localized assumption changes.

improvement.justification: CIFAR10 results, accompanying implementation details, and clearer novelty positioning improve coverage and clarity. However, v3 changes the loss threshold from ℓ(0) to 1 while Appendix C.9's unchanged proof still requires loss below ℓ(0); these differ for the explicitly defined logistic loss, where ℓ(0)=log(2). The omission of assumption (A1) from Theorem C.30 also leaves its invocation of Lemma B.9 unsupported as stated. These benefits and theoretical-consistency regressions prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work on the implicit bias of Adam, Muon, and related optimizers. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices A–D support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D report original MNIST experiments and an added CIFAR10 experiment with four-layer networks, including margin and directional-convergence results in Figure 3.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D report original MNIST experiments measuring optimizer-dependent margins and directional convergence, with results across 10 random seeds in Figures 1–2.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: STING exposes greater illicit assistance, lower-resource languages do not consistently increase success, survival analysis characterizes attack efficiency, and reasoning and defenses have mixed effects. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the low-refusal-recall discussion about potentially underestimated ASR with an interpretation that judge noise is unlikely to explain language findings. It adds the interpretation that strategist quality is the main bottleneck in the tested ablation and extends defense-tradeoff interpretations to Omni-Moderation and additional targets. Existing broader interpretations and impact qualifications remain.

D1.justification: The introduction newly states a code release and supplies a repository location; repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs. New analyses identify replacement-agent models and budgets, the multilingual-e5-small embedder, and moderation inputs. Existing hardware details, default hyperparameters, algorithm, and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: Section 6.1 expands human judge-validation coverage from Urdu and Telugu conversations to all seven study languages. The underlying AgentHarm task coverage, benign tasks, 44 base behaviors with 176 prompt variants, and overall seven-language attack suite remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Section 7.3 and Table 5 add OpenAI's Omni-Moderation as an evaluated defense alongside PromptGuard and the Safety Prompt. The single-turn and X-Teaming attack baselines remain unchanged. The additional target-model defense experiments retain the existing PromptGuard/Safety Prompt comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends evaluation design with phase-separation scoring, staged agent-model substitutions at Smax=5, native-language planning, token/embedding comparisons, and filtering both attacker messages and target responses. Human-validation samples increase from 83 refusal and 56 intent judgments to 570 and 260, respectively. The original Section 5.1 experimental setup is retained.

E4.justification: New Appendices A.4-A.5 test decomposition quality and sensitivity to strategist, attacker, and evaluator strength. A.8.1-A.8.2 examine English-plan dependence and cross-language divergence. Expanded judge validation, Omni-Moderation testing, and defense transfer to GPT-5.1 and Gemini 3 Flash provide substantial additional robustness and diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, Greenwood/log-log discovery-curve intervals, and Cox hazard-ratio reporting remain unchanged. No new seed, repeated-run, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are documented. The larger human-validation samples change evaluation design; the added appendix analyses generally report point estimates.

E6.justification: Original benchmark tables and figure results are retained, but substantial new results appear in Tables 6, 7, 10, 11, 13 and expanded Table 5. Examples include average AHS of 69.7% versus 58.8% after weakening all STING agents, native-language planning differences within 2.2 percentage points, and approximately 10% mean harmful-AHS reduction with Omni-Moderation. Judge precision/recall changes from 0.96/0.71 to 0.98/0.93 for refusals and 1.00/0.97 to 0.99/0.94 for intent on different validation samples, not matched-sample accuracy gains.

M1.justification: The four-agent STING procedure, phase progression, feedback, and success criteria remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and the strategist, attacker, and evaluator prompt templates are identical. Alternative agent models and planning languages are experimental variations rather than a revision of the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Localized edits expand the RMJD explanation, related work, validation discussion, and defense narrative. New appendix subsections reorganize multilingual analyses and renumber subsequent sections; acknowledgements and the equal-contribution footnote are updated. The main narrative is largely retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v3 substantially extends the tabular presentation with dedicated displays for phase separation, agent-model ablations, native-language planning, linguistic divergence, and defense transfer (Tables 6, 7, 10, 11, 13). Table 5 gains Omni-Moderation rows and a revised caption. Existing figures are unchanged images, although several figures and tables move.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds HAICOSYSTEM as an existing multi-turn agent-safety exception and distinguishes its broad safety simulation from budgeted red-teaming. References for Omni-Moderation and multilingual E5 are also added. The remaining research positioning is substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 introduces a quantitative definition of phase separation: the fraction of phase pairs with non-overlapping invoked-tool sets, averaged across behaviors and strategies. The reachability formulation, RMJD definition, Cox model, and Kaplan-Meier derivations remain unchanged; the expanded RMJD explanation does not change its mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the central multilingual findings: limited Urdu/Telugu judge checks become a larger seven-language audit, and native-language planning tests address dependence on English strategies. Component ablations clarify which agents drive effectiveness, while additional defense evaluations test generality beyond Qwen3-Next. These additions address important validation gaps without changing the established headline results. Pooled judge reporting and mostly point-only new appendix results leave uncertainty, but the gains in evidential support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same STING research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, tables, figures, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds strategist evaluation, component-model ablations, multilingual diagnostics, and additional defense experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original AgentHarm experiments, multilingual evaluations, judge validation, and reasoning, tool-knowledge, and defense ablations.

P2.justification: Algorithm 3's displayed pseudocode expands, and algorithm blocks and Figures 1-2 shift with text reflow. Table 1 and both diagrams retain their contents and captions; there are no new figures or tables.

improvement.justification: v1 asserts independence in its offline analysis after estimating transitions from complete trajectories. v2 explicitly addresses this issue with subsampling and retained-count lemmas, improving technical support and clarifying the contribution's scope. However, Algorithm 3 retains the all-N counting expression and returns D, while subsequent penalties still use unqualified counts. These inconsistencies limit the completeness of the correction, supporting a modest net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 26 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including Appendices A-D, are readable and support comparison of the algorithms, proofs, table, and figures.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical, including its appendices. The added 'Our focus' paragraph explicitly leaves empirical results for future work.

title: Improved Bounds for Reward-Agnostic and Reward-Free Exploration

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: hubness compromises evaluation, GICDM mitigates it through scaling and filtering, and suitable corrected metrics better align with human assessments. The qualification concerning robustness to real outliers remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of antihub blind spots and why removing central hubs does not solve hubness. Section 5.4 discusses the multi-scale intuition beyond Gaussian data and explains why violating the triangle inequality need not prevent evaluation. These extend the interpretation without replacing the existing limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix H newly documents runtime breakdowns, approximately 250 GPU hours for reproduction and 500 GPU hours for the overall project. v2 also replaces the anonymous code link with a named GitHub reproduction and usage link. These are documentation and access-information changes, not evidence of changed experimental budgets.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic scenarios, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN Bedroom, FFHQ and Free Music Archive data. The new convergence analysis reuses existing image dataset and encoder combinations without expanding task or data coverage.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain the same generative-evaluation metrics and hubness-reduction methods, including Sphere, MPGauss, LS, CSLS, DSL and NICDM. The new convergence analysis varies ICDM iterations rather than introducing a new comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix C introduces a convergence-evaluation protocol tracking maximum relative neighborhood-distance deviation over up to 20 iterations, with K=10 and K=100 across 16 dataset/encoder combinations. Existing benchmark settings, including the ten-iteration ICDM configuration, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C and Figure 8 test whether ICDM achieves pointwise convergence sufficiently closely within the chosen ten iterations. Existing component ablations, outlier analyses and qualitative cases are retained; the CIFAR-10 mode-dropping analysis receives a limited plot update.

E5.justification: Seed disclosure, Pearson p-values and significance reporting remain unchanged, with no added repeated-run counts or statistical estimation procedures. Changed shaded-band values in the mode-dropping plot do not establish a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–11 retain their numerical results. v2 adds convergence findings, including a reported maximum relative deviation below 0.17% after ten iterations, and reports computation times. The CIFAR-10 mode-dropping curves and shaded bands also change from Figure 12a to Figure 13a, while their pass/fail conclusions remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Equation 1 retain the same real-set ICDM, independent generated-point scaling and multi-scale filtering procedure. Added explanations of independence and filtered-point scoring do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: Related work moves before the GICDM section, and the density-estimator proof moves into Appendix B.1. Introduction, desiderata, filtering and experimental explanations receive targeted rewrites and terminology edits, while the overall narrative remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds the convergence plot in Figure 8, relocates existing displays and revises several captions. The mode-dropping panel, Figure 12a to Figure 13a, also changes its vertical-axis range. Existing tables and most figure designs are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Toeplitz (1911), Tucciarone (1973) and Komarov et al. (2013) to support the revised proof and complexity discussion. The central positioning relative to ICDM, NICDM and symmetric evaluation metrics is retained.

T1.justification: The density-estimator proof is substantially revised: v1's approximate KNN-based derivation becomes an explicit weighted-estimator consistency argument in Appendix B.1, with asymptotic conditions and Silverman-Toeplitz reasoning. Appendix H additionally derives O(N(TN+M)) computational complexity. The estimator formula and crossover proposition and proof are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies convergence evidence supporting the previously unexplained ten-iteration choice, a more explicit density-estimator argument, and useful runtime and code-access documentation. These improve assessability and reproducibility while leaving the central method and benchmark conclusions stable. The gains are limited by reporting inconsistencies in new Appendix C, which labels near-one ratios as relative deviations and gives conflicting first-iteration values.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GICDM research and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Moved and renumbered content can be matched, allowing reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds an empirical ICDM convergence analysis in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic benchmark experiments, hubness-reduction comparisons and analyses of generated images, including correlations with previously collected human ratings.

D1.justification: Appendices A-B retain the same pseudocode, architecture, hyperparameters, hardware, memory requirements and training-time information. The project repository link is also unchanged.

T1.justification: The diffusion, policy-gradient and reward equations in Section 3, graph definitions in Appendix B, and structural-metric formulas in Appendix C are unchanged. No theoretical result or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies more explicit support for the RL background and fuller, more consistent bibliographic information, including publication details for RhoFold and RhoDesign. These provide a limited improvement in context and reference usability; the scientific evidence, reproducibility information and limitations remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both readable, complete 27-page PDFs describe the same RIDER research, including Appendices A-E. Their text, equations, figures, tables and algorithms support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experimental results in Section 4 and Appendix D, including the benchmark comparisons, cross-predictor validation and ablations.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original RNA inverse-design experiments, including sequence recovery, structural similarity and AlphaFold3 validation. Appendix D contains original ablation and hyperparameter results.

title: RIDER: 3D RNA Inverse Design with Reinforcement Learning-Guided Diffusion

C1.justification: The main contribution now ties nonvanishing divergence to a positive score-error floor, replacing v1's broader non-summability claim. The introduction also withdraws the assertion that theoretical diffusion-retraining analyses are absent and positions this work as complementary, architecture-agnostic lower-bound analysis.

C2.justification: v2 explains that bounded score errors suffice for A3 but do not imply A4, interprets Figure 3's first-generation mismatch as a transient, and expands the argument for neglecting initialization bias at large diffusion horizons. These refine applicability and interpretation of the retained analysis.

D1.justification: Appendix G retains the same architectures, KDE bandwidth, optimizers, hyperparameters, sampling procedures, and metric-estimation details. No new implementation release or code/data-access information is provided.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same five-component, 10-dimensional Gaussian mixture, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, with the same recursive-training and controlled-perturbation scenarios.

E2.justification: The learned-score versus ideal/ablated-score controls and aligned, random, and time-only perturbation comparisons are retained. Newly cited theoretical works are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix G retains the experimental protocols: 100,000 GMM training samples, 20 generations, and 500 sampling steps; the image training budgets, DDPM sampling, and feature-space divergence estimation also remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The controlled perturbation study, generation-specific score-replacement ablations, memory-contribution analyses, and qualitative sample comparisons are unchanged. The new linear-Gaussian illustration is a theoretical derivation, not an additional empirical analysis.

E5.justification: The GMM experiments still report ten independent runs per configuration. The existing standard-deviation shading and uncertainty descriptions are retained, without new run counts, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

E6.justification: Figures 1–10 retain identical graphics and reported results; Appendix G's findings are unchanged, including CIFAR-10 observability around 0.25–0.35. The new discussion of Figure 3's initial discrepancy interprets existing evidence.

M1.justification: The real/synthetic mixture recursion, score-learning objectives, and reverse-diffusion sampling procedures are unchanged. The added linear-Gaussian example explains observability without introducing a new training or inference method.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, expands the abstract and explanatory passages, standardizes mathematical notation, revises Appendix A/B.1 exposition, corrects wording, and adds acknowledgements. The main Sections 1–5 and Appendices A–G retain their overall organization.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from single-column to two-column layout, substantially reflowing equations, captions, and figure placement, with Figures 1 and 2 reduced to column width. All ten figure graphics are retained; the appendices remain single-column.

R1.justification: The introduction adds Fu et al. (2024) and Cui et al. (2026) as existing architecture-specific theory and contrasts their upper bounds with this work's approach, substantially revising the stated research gap. Lewis et al. (2025) and Bakry and Emery (1985) are also added, while Chen et al. (2025) is removed. Duplicate-reference consolidation does not constitute removal of distinct works.

T1.justification: Proposition 4.1(i) removes v1's assertion that non-summable score errors prevent divergence from converging to zero; it now guarantees only non-summability of divergence. Theorem 3.5, formerly 3.4, explicitly requires uniformly positive observability for its equivalence statement. Section 3.2 also adds a linear-Gaussian observability derivation and sufficient-condition reasoning for A3. These substantively revise the scope and mathematical support of central results, although most appendix proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the precision of the existing theory by removing the overly broad nonconvergence claim in Proposition 4.1 and explicitly qualifying the equivalence in Theorem 3.5. Acknowledging prior theoretical work and explaining assumptions also improve credibility and readability. These are useful corrections and clarifications within a largely retained theoretical framework and empirical record.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same recursive diffusion-model study despite retitling and reformatting. Their text, equations, ten figures, and Appendices A–G are available and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the original simulations and image experiments, including their measured outcomes and generated samples in Figures 1–10 and Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-mixture simulations and Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10 experiments, including divergence estimates, observability measurements, and generated samples in Figures 1–10 and Appendix G.

title: Quantifying Error Propagation and Model Collapse in Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about inconsistency, unsupervised reliability-aware aggregation, performance benefits, and interpretable discriminators. The added experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds a logits-access limitation and develops the biased-majority limitation beyond v1's brief impact statement. Section 3.3 qualifies the calibration analogy. Appendix B.4 adds jury-size robustness interpretations, but its universal outperformance claim exceeds Table 6: with three judges, BT-σ scores 58.90 versus soft BT's 58.96.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies SciPy L-BFGS-B optimization, uniform initialization over [0,1), and typical convergence within 100 iterations. It also corrects the documented extraction tokens to A/B. These improve implementation documentation; the NovelEval prompt and exact retained-query identifiers are still absent.

E1.justification: V2 adds question-to-passage relevance assessment on NovelEval, extending coverage beyond summarisation and dialogue evaluation. This is a distinct evaluation task, although the reported experiment uses only 7 of its 21 queries (Appendix C).

E2.justification: V2 adds Crowd-BT as an evaluated reliability-aware comparator on SummEval (Figure 3a and Section 5.2). It explicitly does not report Crowd-BT on Topical-Chat. The existing comparator sets in the retained experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols select 7 NovelEval queries by excluding near-zero Avg-Prob SRC cases and evaluate representative judge subsets of sizes 2–8. Appendix D also changes the stated probability-extraction tokens from yes/no to A/B, matching the retained prompts; this reported correction does not establish that experiments were rerun. Existing complete-pair comparisons and SRC averaging are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix B.4 adds a substantive jury-size sensitivity analysis, testing aggregation with 2–8 judges. Section 3.2 additionally reports a qualitative check relating four-cycle and three-cycle rates, without numerical correlations. Appendix C adds judge-performance and inconsistency analyses on NovelEval; the earlier aspect-specific and hard-versus-soft analyses remain.

E5.justification: V2 first reports significance tests against Avg-Prob, including p < 0.001 for SummEval COH/CON and p < 0.05 for FLU/REL, attributed to hard BT-σ. Topical-Chat findings are described as mixed. The test procedure, repeated-run counts, and seeds remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their numerical results. Additions include Crowd-BT's SummEval SRC of 48.35, jury-size results, and NovelEval SRC of 46.92 for BT-σ versus 45.28 for soft BT and 43.59 for Avg-Prob (Table 8). The new eight-judge BT-σ entry of 59.92 in Table 6 conflicts with the retained 59.84 in Figure 3b, without an explained setting difference.

M1.justification: BT-σ, BT-σ-asp, hard BT-σ, and probability symmetrisation are retained. V2 explicitly writes the joint likelihood and discloses optimization details, but does not establish a change to the proposed aggregation procedure.

P1.justification: V2 consolidates baseline descriptions in Section 4, adds implementation and limitations subsections, expands appendix explanations, and moves the prompts appendix from C to D. Local language and bibliographic edits accompany these changes, while the overall narrative and most retained prose remain stable.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 6–8 and NovelEval Figures 9–10, and inserts a Crowd-BT bar into Figure 3a. V1's Topical-Chat Figures 8 and 9 become two panels of v2's Figure 8. Existing visual data are otherwise retained, with localized resizing, caption shortening, and repositioning.

R1.justification: V2 positions BT-σ against Crowd-BT, distinguishing binary mixture-based reliability from its soft-probability formulation. It adds references for Crowd-BT, NovelEval, and L-BFGS-B. Updates to existing preprint/publication records and Qwen authorship do not constitute new related works.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds the mathematical assertion that higher-order cycles decompose into three-cycles, providing an additional justification for the chosen analysis without supplying a proof. The expanded hard-BT and BT-σ likelihood displays otherwise restate the existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: V2 improves reproducibility through optimizer details and corrected token documentation, adds a relevant Crowd-BT comparison, and states concrete applicability limits. The additional validation is less conclusive than advertised: NovelEval selects 7/21 queries using baseline performance, significance procedures are unspecified, and Table 6 conflicts with some accompanying claims and retained results. These weaknesses limit the gains, but the clearer documentation and expanded comparison support a modest net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BT-σ study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: V2 retains these experiments and adds NovelEval results, a Crowd-BT comparison, jury-size experiments, and statistical significance reporting.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on SummEval and Topical-Chat, including aggregation performance, method variants, and analyses of judge reliability and cycle inconsistency.

title: Who can we trust? LLM-as-a-jury for Comparative Assessment

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about optimizer-dependent neural collapse, weight-decay coupling, momentum, and the NC0 diagnostic. The new Author Contributions section assigns credit rather than changing scientific contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4 retains the same interpretations of practical NC metrics, partial collapse, and generalization, together with the same limitations of the simplified theory and last-layer analysis. Appendix interpretations and qualifications are unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix D retains identical hyperparameters, implementation and code-source information, hardware, and training-time disclosures. The added affiliation, funding acknowledgment, and author roles provide no new technical or reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions retain MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet1K coverage, together with the separable-data and UFM experiments. No evaluated task, dataset, or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain SGD, SGDW, Adam, AdamW, Signum, and SignumW. Appendix comparisons are also unchanged, including Adam versus AdamW on ImageNet and Adam, AdamW, and SGD for vision transformers.

E3.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix D retain the same hyperparameter sweeps, training budgets, learning-rate schedules, metrics, and run-selection criteria. The distinct UFM, ImageNet, and vision-transformer protocols are also unchanged.

E4.justification: The weight-decay interpolation, extended-training, normalized-NC0, momentum, and zero-weight-decay ablations are retained unchanged. The correlation and singular-value analyses in Appendix D are likewise identical.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same standard-deviation bands across hyperparameter configurations. Table 6 retains the same regression sample counts, standard errors, confidence intervals, and statistical tests; no run-count, seed, or uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: Numerical entries, plotted results, and qualitative findings are unchanged throughout. For example, Table 2 reports NC0 of 0.34 for Adam and 5.33 for AdamW in both versions, and Appendix D.4.10 retains the best ViT test accuracy of 83.67%.

M1.justification: The optimizer update rules, architectures, training objectives, and Adam/AdamW weight-decay interpolation procedure in Section 3.4 are unchanged. No method component is added or revised.

P1.justification: v4 adds an IDEAS Research Institute affiliation and short Acknowledgments and Author Contributions sections before the references. It also clarifies Table 1's caption with 'on NC0'; the scientific narrative and appendix structure remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 1's caption changes, and the added affiliation and disclosures cause localized text reflow on the opening and reference pages. No figures or tables are added, removed, or redrawn; all appendix layouts are identical.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning, including Appendix C, are unchanged. References move between pages 11 and 12 because of the added disclosures; no cited work is added or removed.

T1.justification: Proposition 2.1, Theorems 3.1–3.4, the definitions in Appendix B, and the proofs in Appendix E are unchanged. Adding 'on NC0' to Table 1's caption clarifies its subject without revising mathematical content.

improvement.justification: v4 adds attribution and funding disclosures and slightly clarifies Table 1's caption. These localized editorial additions leave the scientific explanation, empirical evidence, mathematical arguments, reproducibility information, and limitations unchanged, so overall paper quality remains essentially the same.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with the same title, authors, and complete appendices A–E. Text comparison and rendered-page checks support a reliable comparison; all appendix pages are unchanged.

after.justification: v4 retains the same original empirical results, including the main optimizer experiments and the additional ImageNet, UFM, and vision-transformer experiments in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-network training experiments, optimizer comparisons, and neural-collapse measurements in Section 3, Tables 2–3, and Appendix D.

title: Optimizer Choice Matters For The Emergence of Neural Collapse

C1.justification: The four-dimensional framework and central claim that reliability gains lag capability gains remain. V3's introductory Figure 1 adds an explicit claim that the reliability plateau is industry-wide across providers. Its added positioning also expressly characterizes the contribution as a working operationalization rather than a redefinition of reliability.

C2.justification: New Appendix D.3 substantially clarifies applicability boundaries: failure semantics, operational profiles, and operating conditions needed for classical reliability guarantees remain unresolved. Section 6 and Appendix B newly acknowledge that zero-temperature evaluation may overestimate reliability at accuracy-maximizing temperatures. Section 4.2 also explicitly allows difficulty and evaluation protocol as alternative explanations for benchmark differences.

D1.justification: Appendix F.2 newly specifies that OpenAI models use the Chat Completions API. V1 does not specify this API choice, so this establishes additional disclosure rather than an API switch. HAL, Weave, hyperparameters, timeouts, retry settings, prompts, and judging details are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GAIA's 165 validation tasks and the verified 26-task tau-airline subset, with comparisons against the original 50 tasks. Prompt, fault, and environment perturbation scenarios remain the same. Updating the evaluated models does not expand task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison roster changes substantially. V3 adds GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.5 Flash, Claude 3 Haiku, Sonnet 4, and Opus 4.7; Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Sonnet 4.5 disappear. Figures 2–6 and the appendix comparisons reflect changed participant sets.

E3.justification: Table 2 revises the outcome-consistency metric, and the reported GPT-5.2 reasoning configuration on tau-bench changes from xhigh to medium. The spontaneous-abstention assessment is omitted. Dataset splits, paraphrase counts, fault probability, environment-perturbation intensity, and other stated evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1's spontaneous-abstention analysis, testing whether agents naturally decline likely failures, is removed (Appendix E.3, Figure 16). Detailed benchmark-error diagnostics in Appendix E.6 are also omitted. The main clean-versus-original comparison, confidence-based selective-prediction curves, difficulty analysis, and perturbation tests remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five runs with different random seeds and error bars showing plus or minus one standard error, clipped to [0,1]. No changed uncertainty-reporting procedure or additional statistical testing is documented.

E6.justification: Reported scores, rankings, and trend fits change widely. For example, Figure 4 changes GPT-4 Turbo's GAIA calibration from 0.69 to 0.60 and AUROC from 0.84 to 0.75. V3 adds results for the revised model roster and an Opus 4.7 underconfidence finding, while removing abstention and detailed original-tau-bench results. Changed metric definitions and model groups prevent interpreting aggregate differences as like-for-like gains.

M1.justification: The proposed measurement framework changes one computational component: outcome consistency is corrected in Table 2, affecting its contribution to consistency and overall reliability. The four dimensions, remaining components, aggregation rules, and agent scaffolds are retained.

P1.justification: Much of the main narrative is extensively condensed and rewritten. Detailed recommendations, limitations, future directions, and the real-world failure mapping move into reorganized appendices. V3 adds an appendix overview, an impact statement, and a dedicated classical-reliability discussion.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a substantially different conference layout and redraws plots for the updated model roster. Figure 1 becomes a compact four-panel display, with the full six-panel presentation in appendix Figure 7. Calibration and selective-prediction grids are rearranged; the failure-mapping table moves to the appendix; v1's abstention figure and six original-tau-bench figures are removed.

R1.justification: New Appendix D.3 develops a substantial relationship to classical reliability and dependability, including new references to Lyu and Musa and explicit distinctions from availability, maintainability, and trustworthiness. V3 also adds HELM and benchmark-reliability connections, while removing v1's explicit comparison with Qi et al.'s safety taxonomy.

T1.justification: Table 2 replaces outcome consistency based on unbiased variance divided by p_hat(1-p_hat)+epsilon with the average of (2p_hat-1)^2, corresponding to biased variance normalized by 0.25. This substantive definition correction eliminates the earlier formula's potential negative values. Other metric definitions and aggregation equations are retained.

improvement.justification: The corrected outcome-consistency formula resolves a concrete mathematical defect, while Appendix D.3 and the temperature limitation improve interpretation of the framework's scope. These benefits outweigh a limited loss of diagnostic evidence, particularly the spontaneous-abstention analysis. The improvement remains qualified because Appendix C retains the earlier accuracy-dependent normalization explanation, leaving some inconsistency with the corrected definition.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same agent-reliability study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V3 reports original evaluations of 15 model configurations on the same benchmarks, with updated reliability measurements and experimental findings.

before.justification: V1 reports original repeated-run evaluations of 14 model configurations on GAIA and tau-bench, including reliability measurements, perturbation experiments, and supplementary analyses.

title: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and efficiency claims, including GPQA sampling reductions of up to 75% offline and 55% online. Added experiments support the existing contribution rather than redefining its scope.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 newly interprets bin-count sensitivity as evidence that coarse difficulty grouping suffices, and runtime measurements as support for practical streaming deployment. Figures 16-17 frame Pass@1 and MV@128 as lower and upper reference bounds. The limitation concerning systematically incorrect population majorities remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Table 6 newly documents the timing experiment's 30 training questions, four warm-up samples, and offline configuration of B=16 with 500 Monte Carlo samples. The added ablation captions specify clustering and bin-count configurations. Existing implementation details and code/data access links are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GPQA-Diamond, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, BRUMO 2025, and HMMT February 2025 in offline and online settings, alongside the same simulations. The added analyses use existing datasets and task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds the DeepConf-based 'Conf. guided' comparator across all five datasets and five models in both Tables 2 and 3, substantially extending evaluation beyond uniform allocation and the online oracle. Figures 16-17 additionally include Pass@1 and MV@128 reference comparators. DeepConf was previously discussed but not evaluated as this allocation baseline.

E3.justification: Added experiments sweep oracle cluster counts of 2, 3, 5, and 8 and predictor bin counts of 2, 3, 4, and 5, measure allocation runtime, and evaluate single-sample and 128-sample voting references. The original benchmark protocol retains its 128-response pools and 64-trace finite proxy.

E4.justification: New Section 5.3 investigates sensitivity to oracle clustering and practical predictor discretization in Tables 4-5, and profiles allocation overhead in Table 6. These add direct evidence about parameter robustness and computational cost beyond the retained oracle comparisons and approximation simulations.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 30 subsampling repetitions, retain the appendix tables formatted as mean (variance), and show the same 95% confidence intervals in Figure 2. No new repeated-run counts, seed controls, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Existing PETS, Uniform, and oracle table entries are retained, while substantial results are added for the new comparator and analyses. For example, Table 2 adds 10,652 traces for confidence-guided allocation on GPQA/Qwen3-4B; Table 6 reports 4.73 seconds for the online predictor versus 212.2 seconds for offline OKG. Tables 4-5 and Figures 16-17 add sensitivity and reference-performance results.

M1.justification: The offline OKG procedure, online greedy allocation, Gaussian-probit surrogate, and four-response difficulty grouping are retained. The expanded Section 4.1 explains components already documented in v1 Appendices B.3-B.4 and D.2.

P1.justification: Focused revisions expand Section 4.1, polish proof prose, and replace the lengthy main-text related work with a summary plus Appendix A. Author affiliations and the equal-contribution footnote change, and an impact statement is added. Most scientific exposition retains its earlier wording and organization.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands result presentation: Tables 2-3 gain comparator rows, Tables 4-6 are new, and Figures 16-17 add multi-panel comparisons. Figure 1 is enlarged and several displays move. The original fifteen figures retain their content, and the full-result tables are renumbered as Tables 7-8.

R1.justification: The identifiable bibliography is unchanged, and most detailed related work is relocated. v2 adds a paragraph connecting crowdsourcing to uncertainty quantification and refines the main-text positioning, but introduces unresolved citation placeholders in Appendix A.

T1.justification: The self-consistency definitions, Bayes-optimal terminal rule, Theorem 4.1, Gaussian-probit approximation and concavity results, and asymptotic allocation derivations are retained. Appendix edits mainly add explanatory transitions and correct a proof cross-reference without changing mathematical substance.

improvement.justification: The evaluated confidence-guided baseline, discretization checks, and allocation timings strengthen empirical support beyond v1's uniform-baseline focus, while Section 4.1 becomes clearer. The gains are limited by sparse protocol details for the added experiments and new unresolved citations in Appendix A. The core method, theory, and earlier evidence remain intact.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PETS research and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. v1 Appendices A-D correspond to v2 Appendices B-E; much of the earlier related-work discussion moves to v2 Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds confidence-guided comparisons, difficulty-bin sensitivity results, allocation timings, and reference-performance curves.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original benchmark experiments on offline and online trajectory allocation, alongside simulations in Figures 2 and 5.

title: PETS: A Principled Framework Towards Optimal Trajectory Allocation for Efficient Test-Time Self-Consistency

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the claim that Label-Clustered CP consistently achieves superior or best substantive fairness to a claim about a favorable utility–fairness balance. The theoretical decomposition, evaluator contribution, and central set-size-versus-coverage claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly positions the evaluator as a first-pass aid for directing human studies. It discusses possible collider distortion, unstable ACSIncome interaction estimates, and the unsuccessful RAVDESS robustness fit. It also explains differing cluster-count optima and recommends downstream validation after screening by set-size gap.

D1.justification: New Appendix D.5 and Table 8 disclose total prediction counts, API costs, local runtimes, and RTX 5060Ti 16GB hardware, with a rationale for choosing repetition counts. Existing implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, and code-access information remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same four datasets, modalities, prediction tasks, and protected-group definitions. The added estimator and cluster-count checks operate within existing coverage without introducing new populations or input scenarios.

E2.justification: The CP comparator set and no-set control remain unchanged. However, v2 Appendix E.2 adds an evaluated alternative to the proposed fairness estimator: a GEE with adoption-by-group interactions, compared directly with the original GEE in Table 15.

E3.justification: v2 adds an expanded-GEE evaluation protocol and a single-split BiosBias experiment measuring downstream fairness across K=1–10. Existing benchmark settings and the ten-split set-size analysis remain unchanged; the newly disclosed repetition counts do not establish changed experimental budgets.

E4.justification: Appendix E.2 newly tests sensitivity to group-varying adoption effects. Appendix F.3 extends the existing cluster-count investigation to downstream maxROR, examining whether its optimum matches the set-size-gap optimum. These are targeted extensions of the existing analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds Wald z-tests at significance level 0.05 and associated p-values. Appendix D.5 first specifies repeated-prediction counts M=4, 5, or 8 across evaluation settings. The existing 1,000-resample bootstrap reporting is retained; no increase in repetitions is established.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark and bootstrap values are unchanged. New Tables 14–15 report interaction tests and expanded-GEE results, such as FACET Mondrian maxROR of 37.4% versus 37.7% under the original specification. Table 29 adds BiosBias results with minimum maxROR at K=6 (0.5%) but minimum set-size gap at K=2 (0.024).

M1.justification: The CP algorithms in Appendix B and primary LLM/GEE/maxROR evaluation procedure remain unchanged. The expanded GEE with adoption-by-group interactions is tested as a supplementary robustness alternative; it does not replace the primary estimator.

P1.justification: v2 expands the introductory fairness explanation, clarifies existing metric formulas, and adds focused appendix subsections and cross-references. It also adds acknowledgements and proceedings information. The overall narrative and section organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds compact tables for computational costs, interaction tests, estimator comparisons, and cluster-count sensitivity. Existing figures are retained, while figures and tables shift with text reflow and subsequent tables are renumbered. There is no broad visual redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds Kiyani et al. (2025) to situate downstream CP use within decision-theoretic research and more explicitly credits Cresswell et al. (2025) for Equalized Set Size. Other reference changes primarily update bibliographic metadata for retained works.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1, its assumptions, and the Appendix A argument are retained. Added formulas express existing fairness quantities; the expanded event-identity explanation and prediction-symbol correction clarify notation without introducing new mathematical reasoning or guarantees.

improvement.justification: v2 better aligns its headline claim with the retained results: Backward CP already had lower maxROR on FACET and BiosBias, making the revised utility–fairness claim more defensible than consistent superiority. Added computational disclosures and targeted robustness checks improve transparency and support practical guidance. The gains remain limited by the single-split sensitivity analysis and unstable interaction fits.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, Beyond Procedure: Substantive Fairness in Conformal Prediction. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–F are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds GEE specification checks, computational-cost measurements, and downstream fairness results across label-cluster counts.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM-in-the-loop experiments on FACET, BiosBias, RAVDESS, and ACSIncome, alongside numerical clustering analyses and bootstrap results in Section 6 and Appendices E–F.

title: Beyond Procedure: Substantive Fairness in Conformal Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions and headline claims: the QHFlow2 architecture, direct energy/force benchmarking, improved Hamiltonian accuracy, NequIP-level force accuracy, and favorable scaling. New supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains the energy–force error gap and why global Hamiltonian MAE can misrepresent downstream accuracy. It interprets large-molecule failures through orbital ill-conditioning and explicitly acknowledges that one-shot forces need not be conservative. These substantially refine the mechanism discussion and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds implementation disclosures about the single-Fock-build evaluation, B3LYP(VWN5) convention, SCF post-processing and H200 hardware, and two-H200/DDP training for ∇2DFT. The core architecture/training tables, software disclosures, and code-access information remain largely unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on drug-like molecules in ∇2DFT and zero-shot evaluation on PubChemQH molecules with 45–98 atoms. Geometry optimization and local potential-energy-surface evaluation also extend the task coverage beyond the retained snapshot-prediction benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 adds QHNetV2 to the QH9 comparisons in Table 2, trained eSEN baselines on rMD17 in Table 19, and xTB/MMFF comparators for geometry optimization in Table 25. HELM, SchNOrb, and PhiSNet were already compared in v1 Table 12; their appearance on ∇2DFT is an extension of coverage.

E3.justification: The reported SCF tolerance changes from 10^-13 in v1 E.4 to 10^-9 in v2 G.3. New protocols include a 1,920-GPU-hour ∇2DFT training cap, finite-difference force checks on 10 geometries per molecule, and BFGS optimization and Hessian evaluations with specified stopping thresholds and displacement steps.

E4.justification: v2 adds readout-degree and prediction-target ablations, large-molecule extrapolation, empirical error-scaling fits, analytic-versus-finite-difference force checks, orbital-subspace error decomposition, and geometry/PES diagnostics. These investigate substantial new questions. The original bond-stretching analysis is retained as G.10, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 introduces numerical ± summaries in Tables 23, 26, and 27 and fitted exponents with R² values in Table 22. The meaning of the ± quantities is not specified, and no increased training-run or seed count is established. The existing statement about fixing random seeds remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Most existing MD/QH9 scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results, including ∇2DFT accuracy, large-molecule failures, force-consistency measurements, and local PES errors. Figure 4 also changes: QHFlow2-l's SCF cycle ratio moves from 52.8% to 47.4%. Because the reported convergence tolerance changes, this is not a demonstrated same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The proposed SO(2) backbone, two-stage pair update, residual flow-matching formulation, priors, and training/sampling algorithms remain unchanged. The density-only and joint-output variants in G.11 are experimental alternatives; they do not replace the default Hamiltonian-prediction method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 rewrites the conclusion and bond-stretching discussion, adds explanatory cross-references, moves SCF documentation from E.4 to G.3, and updates publication and acknowledgement text. The extensive new scientific material does not constitute a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds twelve tables displaying new evaluations and analyses and expands Table 2 with QHNetV2 rows. Figure 4 is relocated and resized, Figure 6's reversed left/right caption is corrected, and the retained Figure 8 is integrated into a different appendix layout.

R1.justification: The new discussion in Section 3.3 and Appendix D.3 substantially expands positioning against HELM and QHNetV2, distinguishing their backbones, Hamiltonian readouts, pair refinement, and downstream energy evaluation. QHNetV2 is newly cited, while several ancillary reactivity references are removed.

T1.justification: G.8 adds a perturbative derivation of second-order energy error versus first-order force error, with particle-number conservation and nondegenerate/gapped-orbital conditions. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's snapshot accuracy and scaling results. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and qualification of the central claims.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds benchmark evaluations, force-consistency tests, geometry optimization, and further analyses in Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hamiltonian, energy, and force evaluations, scaling experiments, ablations, SCF convergence tests, and bond-stretching analyses.

title: Sonar-TS: Search-Then-Verify Natural Language Querying for Time Series Databases

Existing material is reflowed and renumbered. Figure 2 revises its navigation example; the other figures and original case-study displays are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims about simplicity bias, learned phase-consistent routing, expert specialization and parameter efficiency. It distinguishes transferring the architectural prior from transferring router weights, stating that distribution changes require router retraining, and extends the fragmentation interpretation to standard language models. Existing limitations are retained and expanded after relocation.

New Tables 13–23 add substantial findings, including 91.4% for capacity-matched single LoRA versus 93.8% for PA-MoE, 90.6% random and 92.2% fixed-interval routing success, approximately 0.30% inference overhead, and 93% within-segment token switching in the language-model diagnostic. Appendices J and R also introduce evaluated confidence-adaptive switching penalties and an optional inference bypass. These change training or inference procedures despite retaining the backbone and LoRA expert architecture.

P1.justification: Most retained prose and the main narrative remain substantially unchanged. v3 supplies numbered sections and lettered appendices, repairs previously empty cross-references, relocates limitations to Appendix A, and adds navigation sentences, an impact statement and acknowledgements. P2.justification: v3 adds eleven substantive result tables, Tables 13–23, and reformats the document with conference-style typography, running headers, linked references and revised float placement. Figures 1–5 and the original table contents are retained rather than replaced; the major visual expansion comes from the new tables and overall layout revision.

The revised router-training description is also not reconciled with the unchanged headline results. Overall, the additions help, but do not establish a major quality improvement.

before.justification: v1 reports original ALFWorld and WebShop experiments, ablations, expert-specialization measurements and failure analyses.

It also explicitly limits the compression method to training from scratch and explains why the results do not establish conversion of arbitrary pretrained checkpoints.

Figure 2(a) and Table 7 also add raw-weight approximation errors to investigate the sign component's role in compression difficulty.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes Section 4 around the complete from-scratch compression pipeline and integrates previously appendix-only compression evidence into the main narrative. P2.justification: V2 adds the explanatory sign-template Figure 5 and seven empirical tables, and redraws Figure 2(a) with raw-weight curves and revised legends. V1's six-panel Figure 20 is split between main-text Figure 8 and appendix Figure 22. Most other plots are retained and renumbered.

title: Sign Lock-In: Randomly Initialized Weight Signs Persist and Bottleneck Sub-Bit Model Compression

Appendix E.5 adds interpretations of the new sensitivity tests. Figure 3 also changes 'lossless' to 'near-lossless,' consistent with qualifications already present in v1's Appendix C.
