title: What Language is This? Ask Your Tokenizer.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central theoretical, methodological, and accuracy claims. The introduction slightly qualifies the cost claim, replacing zero additional inference cost for models with biases with a general negligible-cost statement supported by throughput measurements.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive arguments about approximate computational invariance, absence of harmful calibration overfitting, stable inversion, and practical inference overhead. Section 3.1 also corrects v1's claimed small-block advantage for full Hadamard transformations to an advantage for block Hadamard, removing the earlier explanation for the opposite trend.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies a 100-step warmup and regularization coefficient 0.1, documents multi-GPU resources and calibration lengths for larger models, and reports approximately two hours of Qwen3-14B training on four A100 GPUs. It also identifies the throughput hardware and vLLM implementation. Existing codebase references and folding instructions are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use WikiText2 and the same seven zero-shot benchmarks: ARC-E/C, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, BoolQ, and OpenBookQA. Larger models, NVFP evaluation, calibration sweeps, and throughput measurements extend configurations and protocols without adding datasets or language tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds OSTQuant to the main accuracy and WikiText2 comparisons. Appendix D.2 also evaluates original per-block FlatQuant alongside the retained global variant, now labeled FlatQuant†. These additions substantially extend comparisons beyond the modified baselines in v1.

E3.justification: Appendix D changes the reported QR training budget from 2,500 to 1,000 steps and expands the learning-rate range from 10^-5–10^-4 to 10^-5–10^-3. New 14B/32B configurations use shorter calibration sequences and proportionally more samples. V2 also introduces NVFP evaluation and hardware throughput protocols. These reported changes do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds orthogonal-plus-bias ablations, unquantized-model checks after transformation folding, condition-number tracking, SpinQuant loss comparisons, and sensitivity tests for calibration size/subset, training steps, regularization, temperature, and individual transformations. Conversely, the Qwen3-1.7B initialization results in v1 Table 4 are absent from corresponding v2 Table 7.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without comparable repeated-calibration uncertainty. V2 Table 10 reports means and standard deviations over five randomly selected WikiText2 calibration subsets for two models. This localized addition does not establish repeated-run averaging or increased run counts for the main comparisons.

E6.justification: Many retained scores change; for example, Qwen3-1.7B LATMiX-LU perplexity changes from 16.98 in v1 Table 3 to 15.11 in v2 Table 6. Numerous comparison, larger-model, NVFP, and analysis results are added. These are reported revisions, not established same-setting gains. Some revised aggregates are inconsistent: v2 Table 20 retains v1 Table 10's Qwen3-4B MXFP4 LATMiX-LU task scores but changes their stated average from 63.74% to 64.74%.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains LU/QR affine parameterizations, learned T1/T2 transformations, the online Hadamard T3, distillation plus volume regularization, transformation folding, and subsequent GPTQ. Additional ablations and quantization-format evaluations do not introduce a new LATMiX component.

P1.justification: V2 selectively rewrites the numerical-analysis and baseline-implementation discussions, clarifies MSE approximation assumptions, adds analysis subsections, and updates the affiliation. The overall section sequence, abstract, conclusion, and much of the explanatory prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the displays: Table 1 gains model columns, an FP16 row, and OSTQuant; Table 2 gains orthogonal-plus-bias rows; new tables present baseline controls and sensitivity studies. New figures show throughput and condition numbers, while Figure 2 is enlarged and gains a vanilla perplexity curve. The existing folding diagram is relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to OSTQuant, DartQuant, LLMQAT, and the vLLM serving work. Related work now distinguishes DartQuant's QR-derived rotations from LATMiX's affine parameterization. The broader positioning remains unchanged; the existing BRQ citation is merely relabeled Shao et al., 2025b.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.3's distribution-specific bound expands from sub-Gaussian variables to the broader psi_alpha class, including sub-exponential variables. Appendix A adds a tail-bound theorem and revises the maximum-moment lemma and derivation with alpha-dependent terms. The affine-folding derivations and KL/NLL proposition remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 adds valuable baseline controls, robustness and invariance checks, throughput measurements, and broader theory. However, it introduces material result inconsistencies absent from the corresponding v1 tables. The unchanged Qwen3-4B MXFP4 LATMiX-LU task scores average 63.74%, but v2 Tables 1 and 20 report 64.74%. For Llama3.1-8B-Instruct MXFP4, MR-GPTQ scores 68.93% in Table 1 versus 67.44% in Table 18, reversing its ranking against LATMiX. These conflicts undermine verification of the central comparisons; their impact prevents a reliable net quality judgment despite the substantial added evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LATMiX and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–F. Corresponding material can be matched despite v2's expanded experiments and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds larger-model results, calibration sensitivity studies, computational-invariance checks, and hardware throughput measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original quantization experiments, including zero-shot benchmark accuracies, WikiText2 perplexities, and transformation, initialization, and loss ablations.

title: LATMiX: Learnable Affine Transformations for Microscaling Quantization of LLMs

C1.justification: The principal claims about semantic reconstruction, improved topic quality and assignment, and useful retrieval representations are retained. V2 modestly broadens the contribution framing into a general DSL distillation framework with a Bayesian characterization. Retrieval becomes a separately enumerated contribution, but was already claimed in v1's abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds an implicit-to-explicit Bayesian interpretation and explains backbone-dependent trade-offs through a proposed mismatch between dense targets and FASTopic's transport solver. It recommends ProdLDA as the practical default and discusses FASTopic's retrieval failures. The impact statement additionally addresses biases inherited through LM distillation and limitations of using coherent topics in sensitive applications.

D1.justification: V2 supplies an implementation repository address, replacing v1's release promise and supplementary-code reference. It newly specifies single-token vocabulary filtering, retrieval KL direction and query exclusion, and integration settings for the added backbones. These improve documentation without establishing that the previously unspecified procedures changed; repository availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate topic modeling and label-based document retrieval on the same three datasets, with identical dataset statistics in Table 5. Additional model configurations and sensitivity experiments remain within this coverage; multimodal modeling is only proposed as future work.

E2.justification: The corresponding main and qualitative comparisons retain LDA, ProdLDA, CombinedTM, ZeroshotTM, ETM, BERTopic, ECRTM and FASTopic. Additional language models and DSL backbones are variants of the proposed approach, rather than additions to the external baseline set.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from one backbone with three language models to three backbones with five, adding Qwen3.5-0.8B and Phi-3-mini. New experiments vary hidden-state layers and target truncation. Table 4 changes from K=50 examples using a randomly selected seed to K=75 cases selected for the largest coherence margins. The main metrics and topic-count grid remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds layer-selection experiments in Appendix H and target-sparsity experiments in Appendix I, testing input representation and coherence–diversity control. Table 4 replaces the earlier qualitative examples and adds per-word leave-one-out coherence analysis. The original component ablations, prompt sensitivity, temperature analysis and vocabulary-size analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Five seeds per topic count, Welch tests and prompt-sensitivity ANOVA are retained; the new statement of 20 measurements per cell merely makes existing aggregation explicit. However, v1 Table 7 displays significance highlights that are absent from corresponding v2 Table 10, despite its caption still promising them. This is a limited loss of statistical reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive backbone/teacher results and new diagnostic results, and replaces qualitative topic lists. Retained values also change: Table 2 ERNIE StackOverflow P@5 changes from .588 to .754, while Table 1 Llama-1B 20NewsGroup Purity changes from .559 to .564. All 44 original per-topic-count rows and Table 3 ablation values remain unchanged. The revised objective prevents treating the retrieval changes as established same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The stated reconstruction objective changes from KL(prediction || target) in v1 to KL(target || prediction) in v2. V2 also extends the framework from ProdLDA to ECRTM and FASTopic while preserving their respective regularizers. These are substantive formulation and backbone adaptations; the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: Beyond the DSL-Topic title and terminology, v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, objective exposition, mathematical appendix and baseline documentation. It reorganizes metric explanations, moves the complete-results appendix from E to K, replaces the impact statement, adds acknowledgments and removes the AI-assistance paragraph. These constitute substantial editorial restructuring.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is replaced with a document-level example and Figure 2 is redrawn. Tables 1–2 gain backbone groupings, Table 4 introduces coherence scores and word-contribution coloring, and two diagnostic tables are added. The detailed results become four subtables across two pages. Figures 3–5 retain their plotted content despite relocation and resizing.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands the conceptual positioning through knowledge distillation and implicit Bayesian inference, citing Hinton et al., Xie et al., Wang et al. and Li et al. It also adds references for the new teachers and layer analysis while removing several earlier background citations. The existing topic-model related-work taxonomy largely remains.

T1.justification: V1 Appendix I develops a reverse-KL projection argument specialized to ProdLDA. V2 Section 3.4 and Appendix J introduce a broader structured model family and latent-concept posterior-predictive interpretation, replace the projection direction, and derive forward-KL equivalence to dense cross-entropy. V2 also makes the main objective's regularization sign consistent with the appendix.

improvement.justification: V2 provides useful evidence that the approach extends beyond ProdLDA, adds targeted design checks, and improves reproducibility documentation and consistency between the main objective and appendix. These gains outweigh limited reporting losses. However, unexplained revisions to retained retrieval scores, selection of favorable qualitative cases, and missing appendix significance highlights limit confidence in a larger overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same soft-label topic-modeling research, despite the DSL-Topic renaming. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of further model variants, hidden-state layers and target sparsity.

before.justification: V1 reports original topic-quality, retrieval, ablation and sensitivity results on 20NewsGroup, TweetTopic and StackOverflow.

title: Improving Topic Modeling by Distilling Soft Labels from Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, numbered introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about depth scaling, reasoning improvements, dense feedback, parity performance and generation efficiency. The added transfer experiment supports the existing contribution without redefining the paper's core claims.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges sequential prefill as an inference-latency bottleneck and expands the efficiency comparison with Universal Transformers. It also interprets competition results as correction of imperfect CoTs and argues for wiring robustness from minimal configuration search; these are new qualifications and interpretations.

D1.justification: V2 adds forward-pass pseudocode specifying caching, injection and extraction, plus an explanation of wiring selection. Section 4.4 specifies the existing GSM8K filter: over 168 Llama-tokenizer tokens, removing 44 of 384,620 examples. These supplement the already detailed connection lists, hyperparameters and CoT-training instructions.

E1.justification: V2 adds transfer evaluation on pooled 2023 AMC and 2024–2025 AIME problems. This extends the existing mathematical-reasoning coverage to a competition-test population using NuminaMath-trained checkpoints; the earlier datasets and tasks remain.

E2.justification: The standard Transformer and single soft-token comparators remain in their corresponding experiments. The new competition evaluation extends the existing baseline-plus-CoT comparison. Universal Transformers, feedback memory and Staircase Attention receive discussion but are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Section 4.8.1 adds a transfer-testing protocol using NuminaMath-trained checkpoints and the existing CoT-generation procedure with identical inference hyperparameters. Earlier splits, training budgets, model configurations and temperatures remain unchanged. The newly specified GSM8K filtering threshold clarifies an already reported preprocessing step.

E4.justification: The new competition-math experiment tests whether CoT-correction benefits transfer beyond the training dataset. Existing group-size and multiplier analyses, soft-token comparison, parity length-generalization experiment and discriminative-filtering analysis are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. V2's statement about zero or one wiring-selection trials concerns hyperparameter selection, not repeated measurements or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 5 adds AMC/AIME transfer accuracies of 2.00% for Baseline + CoT and 4.45% for TurboConn + CoT. Previously reported accuracies, training times, filtering measurements and Figure 4 curves are unchanged after matching v1 Tables 1/2 to v2 Tables 2/1.

M1.justification: The cross-token residual connections, projections, initialization, grouping mechanism and training objective remain unchanged, as do the listed model-specific connections. V2's Algorithm 1 and wiring-selection explanation document the existing procedure rather than establish an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely preserved. V2 makes localized grammar corrections, corrects the author name from Sidu to Sidi, adds explanatory subsections and an acknowledgment, and renumbers appendix sections after inserting the pseudocode section.

P2.justification: V2 removes the conceptual engine illustration, moves v1's architecture Figure 2 to Figure 1, renumbers the grouping diagram and adds a dense-connectivity Figure 3. It also adds an algorithm display, expands Table 5 and relocates tables, including exchanging the numbering of the main-results and efficiency tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds Fan et al. (2021) on feedback memory and Ju et al. (2022) on Staircase Attention, positioning TurboConn around augmentation of pretrained LLMs through zero-initialized additive connections. It expands the Universal Transformer comparison and adds sources for the competition datasets.

T1.justification: V2 formalizes the wiring heuristic as a connection-set definition in Appendix A.5. Appendix A.6.3 also corrects the Qwen parameter-count substitution from 17,772,768 to 10,367,448, making it consistent with the retained total of 141,111,768. The central computational-depth arguments remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 improves transparency through pseudocode, preprocessing and wiring-selection details, explicit acknowledgment of prefill costs, and closer positioning against earlier feedback architectures. It also fixes an inconsistent parameter-count calculation and adds limited transfer evidence. The new competition results lack a stated test-set size and uncertainty estimates, while wiring robustness is inferred from minimal search, so the overall improvement remains modest.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Turbo Connection research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete Appendix A are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and adds evaluation of NuminaMath-trained checkpoints on AMC/AIME competition problems in Section 4.8.1 and Table 5.

before.justification: V1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, accuracy and training-time measurements, ablations, parity length generalization, discriminative filtering and CoT experiments in Tables 1–5 and Figure 4.

title: Turbo Connection: Reasoning as Information Flow from Higher to Lower Layers

C1.justification: The title changes 'Prevents' to 'Mitigates.' The abstract replaces the assertion that Reference Resets implicitly use GR with an empirical statement that they find flatter regions with higher reward accuracy. The principal contributions and conclusion remain.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's existing caveats, v2 explains how strict answer formatting could violate reward continuity and how flat incorrect maxima could make GR cause hacking and gradient-norm monitoring misleading. Appendix D.6 also adds interpretations concerning action-reuse bias, resampling variance, and embedding-perturbation instability.

D1.justification: Section 5 adds an implementation repository link. Appendix C.2 clarifies that the KL penalty enters the loss rather than the reward; D.6 specifies importance-ratio clipping to [0.5, 1.5], and D.7 identifies hardware for the runtime comparison. One pseudocode backward-call typo is corrected.

E1.justification: Both versions use TL;DR, AlpacaFarm, GSM8K, and MATH with the same task coverage. The added ablations and runtime measurements use existing tasks; the stronger-judge experiments already appeared in v1 Appendix D.3.

E2.justification: New Tables 10–11 explicitly compare default GR with importance-sampling-corrected action reuse, action resampling, and perturbing all parameters. Comparator membership in the original benchmark comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix D.6 adds Pythia 1B TL;DR ablations across four GR strengths, and D.7 adds walltime-to-early-stopping evaluation for Qwen2.5-1.5B on AlpacaFarm. Existing benchmark splits and training settings are retained; the KL implementation clarification is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: Appendix D.6 adds targeted tests of whether action reuse needs correction or resampling and whether perturbations should include embeddings and output heads. D.7 adds computational-efficiency analysis. The existing judge, hyperparameter, reset-schedule, and reward-hacking analyses remain.

E5.justification: Table 3 newly reports three-seed means and standard deviations for the 0.5B GSM8K experiments; v1 gives point estimates without this information. This establishes new reporting, not an explicit increase from a stated earlier run count. D.6 specifies one seed per new ablation.

E6.justification: Table 3 replaces the 0.5B results with three-seed summaries: for example, LLM-judge No Reg changes from 2.0% to 20.7 ± 3.8%, and rule-based GR from 50.9% to 56.2 ± 1.0%. These are changed aggregates, not demonstrated method improvements. Tables 10–12 add ablation and runtime results; the 1.5B GSM8K values and Tables 1, 2, and 4 are unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed finite-difference GR procedure, action reuse, gradient clipping, and transformer-only perturbations are unchanged. The new ablations test alternatives without changing the adopted method.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized title, abstract, grammar, and publication-header edits, adds a limitations paragraph and two appendix subsections, and renumbers the retained reward-hacking example. Most prose and the overall organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 10–12, adjusts Table 3 for uncertainty reporting, and changes Figure 5's marker styling. New main-text Figure 9 redraws the existing judge comparison, which remains in the appendix as Figure 14. Other changes mainly involve reflow and renumbering.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning in Appendix A are retained. Reference URL replacements, removals, and bibliographic wording edits do not add or remove research works or revise the novelty positioning.

T1.justification: The definitions, assumptions, propositions, and derivations in Section 3 and Appendices B and E are unchanged. The expanded limitations do not introduce a new formal assumption, proof, or counterexample.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful evidence for existing implementation choices, uncertainty reporting for the 0.5B GSM8K results, and measured runtime comparisons. The code pointer, implementation clarification, and more explicit failure conditions improve reproducibility and claim calibration. These are bounded gains: the new design ablations use one seed each, while the central method, theory, and benchmark coverage remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gradient-regularization research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds implementation ablations and runtime comparisons in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original RLHF experiments on TL;DR and AlpacaFarm, reasoning experiments on GSM8K and MATH, and supplementary analyses.

title: Gradient Regularization Mitigates Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards

C1.justification: The central training-free sampling contribution and broad effectiveness claims remain. The abstract and conclusion revise the reasoning headline from a 3.6% gain in full-attention evaluation to 2.9–11.6 percentage points across full-attention and semi-autoregressive settings, and revise the creative-writing headline from 63.1% to 62.8%.

C2.justification: Section 3.2.4 qualifies state uncertainty as a proxy for proximity to the training manifold. Section 4.2 newly attributes advantages over LookUM on code and planning to the immediate-cost term. Appendix C reinterprets the retained distribution as proximity to an upper bound; Appendix F replaces the claim of fewer decoding steps with explanations involving batching, caching and bypass. Section 5's limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The abstract changes reported code availability from forthcoming to available. Section 3.2.3 and Appendix F explain shared prefix-and-suffix dual caching; Appendix A specifies negative-entropy LookUM without SMC/NIS; Appendix D corrects pseudocode polarity and distinguishes num_steps from K. Some quantified overhead summaries are removed. Hardware and the principal hyperparameter disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same math, code, Sudoku, Countdown, Alpaca-based writing, GenEval and ImageNet coverage, including the synthetic arithmetic and ultra-low-step scenarios. Added comparators do not introduce new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds adapted LookUM comparisons for Dream, SDAR and TraDo in Tables 2–3. AR, previously present in the binary-judgment case study, is additionally evaluated in the full-attention reasoning comparison and creative writing in Tables 2 and 5. This substantially extends comparison against alternative decoding strategies, including another look-ahead method.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 revises the beam-ranking procedure reported for the existing fixed-budget comparison. Other stated models, metrics, temperatures, block sizes, decoding budgets and sample counts remain unchanged. Figure 8's caption changes to ImageNet-512 while its plot title still says ImageNet-256, so an actual resolution change is not established.

E4.justification: The sampler-versus-beam-versus-Best-of-N study is revised through its reported beam-scoring rule in Section 4.3 and Appendix D. Figure 4 and its conclusions remain unchanged, without establishing new measurements. The other case studies, temperature analyses, low-step tests and empirical resource analyses retain their evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report reasoning accuracy averaged over five runs and retain the same correlation statistic, p-value and percentile-distribution reporting. No new run-count, seed, confidence-interval or significance-testing practice is introduced.

E6.justification: Table 3 replaces many K=1 accuracy entries under unchanged reported settings: Info-Gain averages change from 60.3 to 66.2 for SDAR and from 60.3 to 68.2 for TraDo, alongside substantial baseline revisions. Tables 2, 3 and 5 add comparator results. Writing's aggregate changes from 63.1% to 62.8% because AR is included; existing pairwise scores remain unchanged. The text also corrects entropy ratios against PC-Sampler to 65.9% and 62.0%. Corrections versus reruns are not explained.

M1.justification: The main objective and candidate-sampling cycle remain unchanged. The reported beam-search variant changes from cumulative entropy plus state uncertainty to accumulated Info-Gain plus a state score, with descending selection in Appendix D. The single-path argmin-to-argmax correction instead aligns its pseudocode with the main text's existing rule.

P1.justification: The abstract and mechanism explanation are condensed, the conclusion is rewritten, and terminology and notation receive local corrections. Affiliations and publication front matter are updated, and a generic Impact Statement is added. The main section sequence and appendix organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Tables 2–3 gain comparator rows, Table 5 gains an AR column, and Table 6 gains LookUM. Table 8's cache labels and several figure captions change. Appendix figures and code listings reflow across pages. All ten figures retain identical underlying image content; there is no graphical redesign or new figure.

R1.justification: v3 adds Lee et al.'s LookUM and Wei et al.'s TEAM references. It recognizes LookUM as concurrent look-ahead work and distinguishes Info-Gain through its immediate-cost term in the discussion and comparison table. This is a focused positioning extension; most related-work discussion and references are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix C aligns its conflicting definition with the main text: J changes from C−IG to IG−C, and its expected bound changes from nonnegative to nonpositive. The underlying information-gain inequality and proof are retained. Appendix F corrects beam-memory accounting to distinguish B caches from B×N candidate activations. Appendix A also changes KLASS's temporal index from t+1 to t−1 without explaining that revision.

improvement.justification: v3 improves comparison coverage through LookUM and AR, resolves several objective/pseudocode inconsistencies, corrects entropy-ratio arithmetic and clarifies caching. These provide concrete gains in consistency and reproducibility. However, the large Table 3 replacements remain unexplained, and LookUM excludes SMC/NIS, limiting conclusions about the full comparator. The evidence supports a bounded overall improvement, rather than treating higher revised scores as proof of substantially better paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Info-Gain Sampler research. All 19 pages of each version, including figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–F, are readable and support comparison. Remaining internal inconsistencies do not prevent matching the material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional comparator results in Tables 2, 3 and 5. Its appendices also retain original robustness and resource measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning, coding, planning, creative-writing and image-generation evaluations, together with case studies, ablations and low-step experiments.

title: Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion replace the central claim of a tractable event-prior KL upper bound with an IVP representation or regularizer. The introduction also shifts graph claims from cross-channel influence toward temporal ordering and alignment. These narrow important theoretical and mechanistic claims, while annotation-free recovery and superior classification claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly limits ERGs to sensor-space timing summaries, excluding source-level causal, anatomical, or synaptic interpretations, and identifies the event-prior term as a regularizer rather than an exact path-measure KL. It also explains baseline boundary-output limitations and Cohort B variability. Its new channel-representativeness discussion requires qualification: Table 9 supports generally higher HC frequencies, but AD–MCI ordering is mixed.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access URL, explicit auxiliary-weight sweep values, and updated regularizer pseudocode. Most architectural and optimization details in Appendix F are unchanged. Conversely, v1's explicit most-recent-event definition of cross-channel lags in Section 4.6 is no longer specified as precisely.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three synthetic frequency bands and EEG cohorts A and B, with the same participant groups. The added timing, weight-sensitivity, and channel analyses concern existing data and tasks; reporting more of the already-used 19 channels does not expand dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain NODE, ODE-RNN, and STRODE for synthetic comparisons and EEGNet, LCADNet, LSTM, ATCNet, ADFormer, and LEAD for EEG classification. The new runtime comparison uses the existing computational-comparison methods. Newly discussed point-process models are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds one-factor sweeps of three auxiliary weights on Cohort A while holding the remaining protocol fixed, and introduces per-window forward time as an evaluation metric. Existing subject splits, two-second windowing, normalization, aggregation, training budget, and classification metrics remain unchanged. Detailed runtime measurement conditions are not supplied.

E4.justification: Appendix E.5 adds systematic sensitivity studies for dLIF, ERG, and IVP-KL weights, extending the existing prior-removal ablation to regularization-strength robustness. Appendix E.6 additionally tests whether the four plotted frequency patterns represent all 19 channels. These substantially expand the supplementary analyses; the original prior ablation remains numerically unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions retain mean and standard deviation across five test folds and the synthetic event-rate intervals obtained through nonparametric resampling. The new runtime table also uses mean and standard deviation, without introducing a new uncertainty procedure or specifying repetition counts. No seed information or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Tables 3, 8, and 9 add substantial results on runtime, regularization sensitivity, and channel-wide frequency patterns. Examples include LERD's 9.209 ms mean forward time and ERG-weight sweep accuracies ranging from 63.73% to 75.03%. Fifteen previously unreported channels extend Figure 2; HC is highest in 18/19, with T4 an exception. All original benchmark, ablation, computational-cost, and supplementary diagnostic-metric values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The architecture and EPDE/MELP/ERG procedures remain largely unchanged, but the specified training regularizer changes. Section 4.3 and Algorithm 4 replace v1's U_epsilon upper-bound surrogate with a finite-horizon IVP integral using a normalized first-event prior. This revises one auxiliary loss; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted rewrites to the abstract, problem formulation, method explanations, visualizations, and conclusion. It relocates some theoretical setup, adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments, and updates author order, affiliations, and publication information. The overall main-section and appendix organization remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds runtime, sensitivity, and channel-frequency tables. Figure 4 retains the same plots but enlarges and rearranges them from two rows of three panels to three rows of two, pairing methods by frequency band. Other figures and retained tables largely preserve their displays despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds mechanistic Bayesian reasoning as context, citing additional Bayesian event/graph models, and contrasts LERD with observed-event point-process methods such as Smith and Brown and Truccolo et al. This expands the rationale for its annotation-free positioning while retaining the existing supervised-EEG and latent-dynamics literature structure.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 and Appendix B replace the claimed upper bound with a normalized finite-horizon KL representation, correcting the change-of-variable integrand and integration endpoints and stating an integrability assumption. V1's Corollary A.2 becomes A.3: general sub-Gaussian, zero-centered concentration is replaced by Gaussian concentration around the expected perturbation, with explicit bias and a revised matrix bound. Appendix D supplies a substantially revised proof.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs two central mathematical deficiencies: the incorrectly constructed finite-window KL bound and the uncentered concentration claim for nonlinear graph perturbations. The replacement results and explicit limits on causal and path-KL interpretations substantially improve soundness. Sensitivity tests and full-channel reporting also improve transparency without changing classification scores. Some lag-construction detail is lost and runtime documentation remains incomplete, but these limited drawbacks do not outweigh the corrections to the paper's theoretical foundations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LERD study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–F are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds measured inference times, auxiliary-weight sensitivity results, and additional channel-frequency summaries.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic event-recovery experiments, classification on two EEG cohorts, prior ablations, and analyses of inferred frequencies and graphs.

title: LERD: Latent Event-Relational Dynamics for Neurodegenerative Classification

C1.justification: The central claims about dense pretraining enabling flexible sparse inference remain intact. The abstract and introduction extend the accuracy-scaling claim from 2.6B to 7.6B parameters and advertise approximately one point of accuracy loss with 64-fold attention FLOP and KV-cache reductions.

C2.justification: v3 adds hypotheses explaining NoPE performance through shorter effective attention spans and limited RepoBench scaling through insufficient code data. It qualifies multi-dilation adaptation by the enormous hybrid-configuration space and expands proposed byte-level and parallel-reasoning applications. The central recurrence and sparsification interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code URL, documents the 7.6B model's dimensions and optimization hyperparameters, and clarifies adaptation learning rates in Appendix A.1. Conversely, it omits v1 Section 5.1's explicit instruction to always select the first and most recent blocks in top-k attention.

E1.justification: Both versions use FineWeb-Edu, PG19, the same six commonsense tasks, LongBench and RULER NIAH tasks. The PG19 experiment remains in v3 Table 11. Larger models and additional attention configurations do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds GQA/MQA comparisons (Figure 5), SnapKV and StreamingLLM to the NIAH comparison (Table 7), and Mamba2/GatedDeltaNet to the retained LongBench comparison (Table 5). Table 20 also introduces literature-reported Griffin/Pythia comparisons. Quest/MoBA comparisons already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v3 adds 7.6B-model training on 100B tokens, FLOPs-matched GQA/MQA configurations, a 1024-KV-entry NIAH comparison and a head-hit analysis over 500 examples. Appendix A.1 revises the reported smaller-model adaptation rate from an example of 2e-5 to 0.1 times the original learning rate, explicitly retaining earlier results; this does not establish rerunning them.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether recurrence improves block-selection hit rates (Table 9), whether one adaptation stage can cover multiple dilations (Table 10), whether positional encoding is necessary (Table 13), and whether dilation complements top-k attention (Table 19). Existing component, recurrence-placement and adaptation-curve analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new 500-example head analysis specifies a sample size, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial comparator and analysis results, plus 7.6B accuracy results: Table 8 reports commonsense averages of 64.4 for dense inference and 63.1 at D=64. Earlier 1.5B and latency results are retained, while v1 Table 13's detailed 2.6B commonsense results disappear. New Table 9 reports attention accuracy of 57.4 where Table 17 retains 63.2 for the same stated NIAH-MK-2 setting, an unexplained mismatch.

M1.justification: The full-sequence recurrence and active recurrence learning architecture remain unchanged. v3 adds procedural variants: joint adaptation across seven dilations (Table 10) and combined top-k/dilated inference, attending fully within selected blocks and using compressed representations elsewhere (Table 19).

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Efficiency and top-k discussions are reordered, positioning receives its own subsection, and the former appendices B–D are consolidated into experimental subsections. Existing design explanations and adaptation discussion also move between the main text and appendix.

P2.justification: v3 adds the GQA/MQA plot and multiple comparison and analysis tables, expands the scaling plot with a 7.6B curve and attention reference markers, and adds baseline rows to Table 5. Adaptation curves move into the main text, retained appendix tables are rearranged and compacted, and the detailed 2.6B table is removed.

R1.justification: New Section 5.3 and Table 6 substantially expand positioning against GQA/MQA, KV-cache eviction and other efficiency approaches, distinguishing their computational, storage and access properties. Additional citations contextualize NoPE, retrieval heads and larger-model comparisons. The Rae/PG19 citation disappears although the PG19 experiment remains.

T1.justification: The recurrence and dilated-attention equations and underlying mathematical formulation are retained. v3 adds empirical analyses and conceptual hypotheses, but no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important evaluation gaps: v1 provided 7B-scale throughput without corresponding accuracy evidence and lacked GQA/MQA and SnapKV comparisons. The new scaling results and controlled comparisons substantially strengthen support for the central efficiency–accuracy argument, while head-hit analysis tests the previously speculative block-scoring explanation. Removing detailed 2.6B results and introducing the unexplained Table 9/Table 17 accuracy mismatch weaken reporting, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantive improvement in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAT+ research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds 7.6B-model accuracy results, comparator evaluations and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining, adaptation, downstream accuracy, ablation and efficiency experiments, including additional results in its appendices.

title: RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference

C1.justification: The abstract, four introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: probabilistic model discovery, ModelSMC with LLM proposals, competitive discovery of interpretable mechanisms, and connections to SMC theory. Added analyses support these retained contributions without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking finite-model oscillations to random replacement and ESS, interprets channel-family rankings as reproducible posterior preferences, and interprets the ablations as robustness to design choices. Token-efficiency discussion changes from ModelSMC matching or sometimes exceeding baselines to acknowledging N=1's lower median curves while qualifying conclusions through overlapping intervals.

D1.justification: Where v1 refers readers elsewhere for full prompts, v2 supplies extensive Hodgkin–Huxley propagation and feedback transcripts, simulator code, input/output constraints and response schemas in Appendix H. It also adds a prompting diagram, prior-construction guidance, particle-classification procedures and ablation configurations. These substantially increase reproducibility information; the code-access location and hardware disclosure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 20-model, ten-dimensional Gaussian-mixture setting, synthetic SIR task, four kidney dietary scenarios and ten Allen database voltage recordings. The new analyses reuse these settings; changed target selections, particle counts and model configurations do not introduce new data or task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership remains FunSearch+ and ModelSMC N=1 for SIR and Hodgkin–Huxley, with only N=1 for kidney. However, the N=1 comparator explicitly shares the revised ModelSMC implementation, including the change from two feedback calls to one in Appendix D. This is a limited procedural revision of a retained comparator.

E3.justification: The default LLM changes from GPT-5 mini to Claude Sonnet 4.6. Discovery budgets, ancestry depth and FunSearch+ generation budgets change. Gaussian-mixture validation changes from copying-only propagation with up to 50 particles and 30 iterations to random replacement with 100 particles and 20 iterations. Reported likelihood metrics become totals rather than observation averages, and token-efficiency analysis switches from the best five runs to all ten.

E4.justification: Sections 4.5–4.6 add classification and analysis of 1,445 Hodgkin–Huxley particles, including channel-family rank stability, and ablations covering weighting, simulation budget, prompts, feedback, population size and LLM choice. Appendix G.1 adds weight-matrix and ESS diagnostics explaining finite-model behavior. These substantially extend the questions investigated beyond v1's existing examples and token analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions already report ten-run medians with 90% bootstrap intervals in Table G-1. v2 extends uncertainty reporting with bootstrap bands for token-efficiency curves and replaces Figure 2's mean/min-max presentation with medians and bootstrap intervals, labeled 100% in its caption. New ablations specify five seeds per variant versus ten for the default.

E6.justification: Main numerical results and rankings are replaced. For example, v1 reports average Hodgkin–Huxley marginal negative log likelihoods of 25.18, 28.96 and 25.95 for ModelSMC, FunSearch+ and N=1; v2 reports total values of 256.00, 254.58 and 243.27. These are under revised settings, not matched-setting performance changes. Conditional-likelihood result blocks disappear, while new ablation and posterior results are added. Figure 2 now shows oscillation below approximately 80% rather than concentration near 100%.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 replaces unconditional categorical resampling with ESS-triggered systematic resampling and replaces geometric-mean likelihood weights with likelihood products. Appendix D changes two-stage feedback generation to one combined LLM call and introduces posterior-sampling importance estimation of marginal likelihoods, used for kidney and Hodgkin–Huxley experiments. These revise the reported procedure, beyond adding implementation detail.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain recognizable, with localized rewriting and clarification. Appendix D reorders prompting before parameter estimation, an appendix contents page is added, and new analyses and prompt examples receive dedicated sections. This expands organization without extensively rewriting the retained paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 2 and Figures 5, D-1, F-2 and G-3, plus formatted prompt and code panels. Figure 2 is substantially redesigned. The token-efficiency display changes from v1's six-panel Figure G-1 to three panels with uncertainty bands in Figure G-4. Tables 1 and G-1 remove conditional-likelihood blocks and reorder columns; existing scientific figures are also redrawn.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Kitagawa's systematic resampling work and Claude Sonnet 4.6, and more explicitly positions the baselines as evolutionary versus sequential discovery paradigms. The broader related-work framing remains. Publication updates to existing references, including Jha et al., do not constitute new cited research.

T1.justification: The main consistency theorem and most of its proof remain, but Appendix C extends the resampling argument to adaptive resampling. v2 removes the geometric-mean formula from Appendix B, adds the posterior-sampling estimator in Eq. D-36, and derives the expected 81% target-model proportion in Appendix G.1. As printed, D-36 uses posterior/prior importance weights, opposite to the ratio required by its stated sampling distribution and marginalization target.

improvement.justification: The new ablations, explicit prompts and token-efficiency reporting across all ten runs improve transparency and empirical scrutiny. However, v2 introduces Eq. D-36 with a reversed importance ratio relative to Eq. 5, and Appendices F.3–F.4 explicitly say this estimator is used for the real-data experiments. The PDFs cannot establish whether this is only a formula typo or affects the updated results. That material reliability uncertainty prevents a confident net quality judgment despite the substantial additions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ModelSMC research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised and added content.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained tasks, together with new Hodgkin–Huxley ablations, particle classification and posterior analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-mixture validation, SIR model-discovery experiments, and kidney and Hodgkin–Huxley evaluations, including quantitative and token-efficiency results.

title: A Probabilistic Framework for LLM-Based Model Discovery

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same core contributions: online off-policy diffusion MARL, a tractable entropy surrogate, and coordinated optimization through a joint distributional critic. The headline claims of state-of-the-art performance across 10 tasks and 2.5-5× sample efficiency also remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit discussion of large-agent scalability limits, serial inference versus parallel memory costs, and the argument that sample efficiency offsets denoising overhead. It also explains the exclusion of SMAC. The continuous-action scope and concerns about the ELBO approximation gap were already present in v1.

D1.justification: Section 6 adds a code-access pointer. Appendix D.2 clarifies that the already reported rho = 0 produces hard target-network updates, and Appendix B expands the explanation of sampled diffusion trajectories and tractable Gaussian transitions. These are documentation additions, not demonstrated implementation changes.

E1.justification: Appendix D.3.3 adds 10-agent Cooperative Navigation, extending the existing 3- and 4-agent scenarios to a denser coordination problem. The HalfCheetah 6 × 1 task used for new ablations was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Appendix D.3.1 adds an evaluated standard Gaussian-policy comparator on 3-agent Cooperative Navigation. HATD3, HASAC, MADPMD, and MASDAC remain the benchmark comparators; applying that same set to the new 10-agent scenario does not introduce additional methods.

E3.justification: Section 6.2 changes the stated coverage-grid interval from 0.5 to 1.0, specifying integer centers and half-unit boundaries yielding 38 × 36 bins. This corrects the reported protocol without establishing that the experiment was rerun. New HalfCheetah sweeps also specify additional settings, including Vmax values from 2000 to 4000.

E4.justification: The appendix substantially expands diagnostic validation: a Gaussian-policy comparison tests the contribution of policy expressiveness, Tables 4-6 extend atom-count, value-bound, and entropy-coefficient sensitivity tests to HalfCheetah, and Table 7 adds an agent-scaling check. The original Ant ablations, exploration analysis, and qualitative demonstrations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five independent seeds, retain the ten-episode evaluation description, and report means with standard deviations. The additional results continue the existing uncertainty-reporting practice; no changed run counts, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: The original learning curves and all numerical entries in Table 3 remain unchanged. Added outcomes include Gaussian-policy return -26.1 ± 2.9, HalfCheetah sensitivity results in Tables 4-6, and 10-agent OMAD return -445.1 ± 3.3 in Table 7. These are additional experimental results, rather than revised scores for the original comparisons.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the proposed objectives in Equations 11-15 retain the same decentralized diffusion policies, centralized distributional critic, synchronized optimization, and temperature tuning. Expanded explanations and the added Gaussian-policy control do not revise OMAD itself.

P1.justification: v2 removes a duplicated introduction paragraph, expands selected method and appendix explanations, adds an acknowledgement, and divides Appendix D.3 into four named subsections. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The spacious single-column manuscript becomes a two-column conference main text with extensively reflowed equations, captions, and figure placement. Figures 3-6 are reduced to column width, Figure 1 gains data-flow labels, and four new appendix tables are added. Existing experimental figures are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds discussion and citations concerning diffusion-based global-state inference and algorithm-agnostic generative policies, including GORL, and sharpens the online/off-policy positioning. The former anonymous HAQO reference is updated to Lin and Lee's publication of the same work.

T1.justification: Equation 1 corrects the Bellman residual by moving the immediate reward outside the discount factor. The entropy lower-bound theorem and synchronized-objective derivation remain substantively unchanged; the added explanation of trajectory expectations does not introduce a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The added policy comparison, cross-task sensitivity tests, and 10-agent experiment provide useful support beyond v1's validation. Correcting the Bellman residual and grid specification, clarifying implementation details, and documenting code access also improve the paper. The gains remain limited because some new control and scalability settings are under-specified, while the original benchmark evidence and principal conclusions are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMAD research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-D are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds a Gaussian-policy comparison, HalfCheetah sensitivity experiments, and 10-agent Cooperative Navigation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MPE and MAMuJoCo experiments, including benchmark returns, exploration measurements, ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative trajectories.

title: Diffusing to Coordinate: Efficient Online Multi-Agent Diffusion Policies

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution statements and main conclusion retain the claims about transformer data inefficiency, weak cross-length sharing and recurrent induction bias. Added architecture experiments support or test these existing claims; they do not redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 extends the destructive-interference interpretation to Mamba and discusses its intermediate sharing behavior. The conclusion replaces confidence about slight model variations with more explicit synthetic-task limitations and unresolved transfer to realistic domains. Section 3 also clarifies that fitted curves are visual guides.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds Mamba implementation details, including expansion factor 2, state size 64 and convolution kernel size 4. B.4 specifies matched transformer dimensions, attention heads, MLP sizes and rotary positional embeddings. The stopping description and aggregate training-run count are also updated.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate modular addition, including parity, and S5 permutation composition. The supervision formats, length distributions and length-extrapolation task remain unchanged. New architecture experiments reuse these tasks; chess, code execution and embodied control are discussed without being evaluated.

E2.justification: The cross-length sharing comparisons expand substantially: Figures 6 and 7 add Mamba alongside the original transformer, LSTM and Dense-SSM, while Appendix B.4 compares GPT-2-style transformers with Pythia- and Llama-3-style variants on both tasks. Tables 1–4 retain their original comparator sets.

E3.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A.1 replace a fixed 250,000-step budget with at most 250,000 steps and early stopping upon meeting the validation-loss criterion. A.1 corrects the sample-space count to start at length 2. B.4 adds matched architectural controls. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix B.4 directly tests whether the central sharing findings are specific to GPT-2, using matched Pythia- and Llama-3-style architectures across both tasks and all three supervision formats. This substantially extends architectural robustness analysis. Existing length-generalization and smaller-model analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same five seeds, three learning rates and success criterion based on any successful configuration. Neither introduces confidence intervals or significance tests. The increase from over 190,000 to over 200,000 total training runs does not indicate increased repetitions per condition.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results, but Figures 6–9 substantially expand sharing results. Mamba's modular-addition sharing factors are 3.62, 0.30 and 2.56 for outcome supervision, CoT and ACoT. New Pythia/Llama-3 results include outcome-supervision factors of 2.60/5.79 and CoT factors of 0.22/0.36. These are additional model results, not improvements to retained models.

M1.justification: The binary–geometric search algorithm, sample-efficiency criterion, sharing-factor measure and supervision formats are retained. Added architectures serve as comparison models; they do not modify a proposed method. The revised training budget belongs to the experimental protocol.

P1.justification: v2 expands related work and the group-theoretic task explanation, rewrites the limitations paragraph, adds Appendix B.4 and makes local terminology and grammar edits. The main section order and overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The comparative visualization expands substantially: Figures 6 and 7 grow from three to four model columns, and new nine-panel Figures 8 and 9 compare transformer variants. Figure 2 extends its vertical scale from 10,000 to 50,000, revealing previously clipped observations. Existing tables are retained, while several figures move and observation boxes are restyled.

R1.justification: Related work adds substantive connections to Chang and Bisk's inductive counting study and Marchetti et al.'s sequential group-composition work. References for Mamba, Pythia and Llama 3 support the added comparisons. The overall positioning around in-distribution efficiency remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 1 revises the formal induction-bias condition: the right-hand conditional distribution depends on h_t alone in v2, rather than on both x_t and h_t in v1. Appendix A.1 also corrects the sequence-count summation's lower limit from 1 to 2. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The added architecture comparisons directly address v1's reliance on one transformer design, while clearer implementation information and synthetic-task limitations improve transparency. The gain is limited by incomplete reconciliation of the new evidence with retained claims: Figure 8 reports meaningful Llama-3 sharing, including 5.79 under outcome supervision, despite the broad claim of negligible transformer sharing. The revision strengthens the evidence more than it refines the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, tasks, methodology and original experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds Mamba, Pythia-style and Llama-3-style model evaluations in Figures 6–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original training experiments measuring sample efficiency, cross-length sharing and length generalization for transformers, LSTMs and Dense-SSMs, including appendix results.

title: On the "Induction Bias" in Sequence Models

C1.justification: v1 presents a general-purpose unified model for arbitrary incomplete scenarios and emphasizes a novel diffusion-transformer paradigm and demonstrated clinical applicability. v3 explicitly defines unification as a shared framework with task-specific models, positions MDiT3D as a tailored DiT conditioning interface, and qualifies clinical deployment as potential. These materially narrow the central scope and novelty claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning fixed modality vocabularies, compression-related detail loss, and hallucinated anatomy. Appendix D explicitly states that scanner, institution, protocol, and population shifts were not evaluated. It also explains how prompts complement available latents, while Appendix C.7 links completeness-prediction errors to contrast drift, modality bias, and blurred structures.

D1.justification: v3 adds CoPeVAE parameter/FLOP and wall-clock training costs, inference latency/VRAM, and measurement conditions in Section 4.5. It reconciles cardiac training details, including the main-text batch size with the value 64 already present in v1's appendix. Most architecture specifications, preprocessing, optimization settings, sampling details, and the code-access statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same brain and cardiac datasets are used. Downstream BraTS segmentation coverage expands from three real modalities plus one synthesized modality to one real modality plus three synthesized modalities (v3 Appendix C.8/Table 21), adding a more severely incomplete input scenario within the existing task.

E2.justification: The primary synthesis comparisons expand from six to nine baselines by adding DiffM4RI, APT, and ASLDM (v3 Tables 1–3). These methods also enter the retained single-synthetic-modality segmentation comparison (v3 Table 7 versus v1 Table 12). APT was cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: v3 adds MAE and FVD, lesion-restricted metrics, frozen nnU-Net anatomical evaluation with Dice/HD95, and pretext-task accuracy/macro-F1. New protocols exclude specified modality combinations from both training stages and standardize inference-cost measurements. The cardiac tokenizer's training-step table changes from 200k to 100k, resolving disagreement with v1's existing 100k prose; this does not establish that training was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing component, injection-position, backbone, and prompt-corruption analyses, v3 adds position-prompt replacement with mask codes, structured prompt interventions, unseen-combination robustness, lesion/anatomical fidelity, computational-cost analysis, perception accuracy, and synthesis errors grouped by prediction correctness. Figures 13–14 also introduce explicit failure analyses linking incorrect completeness predictions to degraded synthesis.

E5.justification: v1 includes ± values without an explicit multi-seed analysis. v3 Appendix C.2/Table 15 reports means and standard deviations across three independent seeds for CoPeDiT, M2DN, and ASLDM on two challenging brain settings. Figure 13 adds subgroup sample counts and dispersion. Conversely, the primary comparison tables remove the FID ± values reported in v1.

E6.justification: All 168 retained primary PSNR/SSIM/FID point estimates match, and the original segmentation results remain. v3 adds extensive baseline, metric, robustness, diagnostic, and computational results. Its new three-synthetic-modality segmentation experiment reports 87.70% average Dice for CoPeDiT, while APT slightly leads tumor-core Dice, 87.64% versus 87.49% (Table 21). These are new-setting results, not changes to v1's retained 90.23% single-synthetic-modality average. The original corruption-study SSIM/FID curves are omitted.

M1.justification: The CoPeVAE pretext tasks, prompt construction, alternating MDiT3D blocks, targeted prompt injection, and diffusion objective remain unchanged. v3 explains task-specific variants and conditioning more explicitly, but these procedures already appear in v1's methodology, architecture figures, ablations, and appendix.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Existing segmentation and prompt-sensitivity material moves into the main text, while injection-position and backbone ablations move to Appendix C.4. The experimental narrative is reorganized, prompt-token terminology is standardized, and dedicated limitations and discussion sections are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column journal format. The combined brain-results table is split, tables gain metric columns and comparator rows, and qualitative panels expand with error maps and additional examples. The motivation figure is redesigned, existing t-SNE and attention displays are merged, and new intervention, accuracy, failure-case, and segmentation figures are introduced.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands to broader medical image generation, reconstruction, and completion, incorporating works such as Text2CT, MAISI-v2, and DiffuX2CT alongside newer MRI methods. The introduction also explicitly repositions MDiT3D as an adaptation of DiT rather than a fundamentally new paradigm, substantially revising the novelty framing.

T1.justification: The sample partition, classification and contrastive losses, combined tokenizer loss, and diffusion objective in Equations 1–5 are mathematically unchanged. The x-prediction/x0-prediction terminology change is equivalent. Neither version supplies additional theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the unchanged method through additional competitive baselines, explicit three-seed checks, held-out-combination tests, lesion-level validation, and observed failure analyses. These address gaps behind v1's broad reliability and applicability claims. Clearer definitions of unification and explicit domain-shift limitations also improve claim accuracy. Removing primary-table FID uncertainty is a reporting loss, and seed coverage remains limited, but the stronger validation and better-qualified conclusions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoPeDiT for brain missing-modality and cardiac missing-slice synthesis. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, multi-seed experiments, unseen-combination tests, computational measurements, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original MRI synthesis comparisons, component ablations, prompt-corruption experiments, and downstream tumor-segmentation results, including supplementary material.

title: Exploiting Completeness Perception with Diffusion Transformer for Unified 3D MRI Synthesis

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about ReportLogic, specialized LogicJudge evaluation, and judge vulnerabilities. The additional evidence does not redefine or strengthen those central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds a rationale connecting auditability to decision-support use, attributes rubric schema compliance to constrained prompting and instruction following, and explains why ties count differently for targeted and surface-bias attacks. The limitations section and established explanations of judge failure modes remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a concrete code/data repository link, rubric-generator selection and verification details, and explicit attack-screening criteria covering isolation, minimal edits, and bounded strength. It also corrects the training-prompt example. These expand documentation of existing procedures; hardware, training budgets, and hyperparameters are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix C.4 changes targeted-attack success from preferring the attacked report to preferring it or tying on the targeted dimension. Section 5.1 also changes query counts from 1,319/847/915 to 1,204/1,262/1,198, matching the already-existing appendix table. These are reported protocol corrections; the PDFs do not establish reruns or changed data collection.

E4.justification: v2 extends the rubric analysis with per-dimension human agreement and qualitative generator-selection findings. New Table 5 provides five original/attacked report pairs illustrating three targeted defects and two surface manipulations. The existing rubric ablation, bad-case analysis, and attack suites remain.

E5.justification: The new dimension-level agreement rows use the existing Fleiss' kappa reporting practice. Neither version introduces different repeated-run or seed information, confidence intervals, significance testing, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: New Table 3 reports eight General-Rubric/Context-Aware kappa pairs, including Internal Consistency at 0.35/0.42 and Warrants at 0.73/0.73. Appendix C.2 adds qualitative generator rankings and reports no rubric JSON-schema violations. Table 1 and the existing performance plots retain their results; no plotted update accompanies the revised targeted-ASR definition.

M1.justification: The taxonomy, context-aware rubric pipeline, ensemble distillation, and SFT/GRPO training remain unchanged. Figure 12 replaces an illustrative Tie label with both good/both bad, aligning the example with requirements already present in v1 Appendix A.1 and Figure 12's constraints.

P1.justification: v2 expands related-work and appendix explanations, adds local subheadings, and corrects grammar and cross-references. The overall section sequence, central narrative, and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the per-dimension agreement table and paired attack-example table, with accompanying layout shifts. It corrects spelling in Figure 2, changes Figure 3's color-bar label from LogicBench to ReportLogic, and reformats Figure 12. Existing figures and tables are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 substantially expands positioning through dedicated discussions of rubric-guided evaluation and trained LLM judges. It distinguishes instance-specific rubrics from fixed schemes and LogicJudge from general-purpose evaluators, adding references to Prometheus, Generative Reward Models, Skywork-Reward-v2, and the MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena judging study.

T1.justification: Appendix C.4 revises the defined success event underlying targeted ASR: its numerator now includes ties on the attacked dimension. This is a limited metric-definition change. The SFT loss, GRPO objective, reward equations, and existing kappa formula remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 improves transparency through dimension-level annotation evidence, concrete attack examples, clearer quality-control documentation, an explicit code/data link, and corrected reporting. The gains are limited by an unresolved inconsistency: Appendix C.4 includes ties in targeted ASR, while Figure 5 retains its preference-only caption and unchanged plot. Overall, the additions modestly improve the paper without establishing stronger main performance results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReportLogic benchmark and LogicJudge study. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and additionally reports per-dimension human agreement and qualitative rubric-generator comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original judge-agreement results, a three-domain model leaderboard, human annotation experiments, rubric ablations, and adversarial evaluations.

title: ReportLogic: Evaluating Logical Quality in Deep Research Reports

C1.justification: The abstract reduces the headline APAVA improvement from 12.13% to 11.6% and specifies that it concerns the average metric. The conclusion adds the corrected 4.11% relative gain over Medformer. The central architectural, effectiveness, and linear-complexity contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: The explanations linking centralized communication to noise robustness, physiological coordination, and generalization are unchanged. Corrected numerical comparisons retain the same interpretations; no substantive applicability boundary or limitation is introduced.

D1.justification: The augmentation and preprocessing instructions, GPU information, hyperparameters in Table 6, pseudocode, and code/data access information are unchanged, including the appendix implementation details.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ADFTD, APAVA, TDBrain, PTB, PTB-XL, FLAAP, and UCI-HAR. The PTB noise scenario and Appendix C.6 centralization comparisons involving ETTh2, ETTm2, and Weather are also retained.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 retain the same ten baselines. Appendix comparisons also retain Leddam and TimeXer in Table 9, Medformer in Table 10, and MedGNN in Table 12, with unchanged comparator membership.

E3.justification: Subject-independent splits, preprocessing, six evaluation metrics, training settings, noise-testing procedure, and five-fold cross-validation remain unchanged. The revised numerical summaries do not establish a change to experimental settings.

E4.justification: Tokenization and CoTAR ablations, efficiency and noise analyses, token visualizations, cross-validation, and centralization analyses are retained. No analysis is added or removed; the revised efficiency percentage summarizes the existing comparison.
