It also identifies cross-cell-line limitations: simple mean and linear predictors can outperform AdaPert, with discussion of conserved perturbation effects and cell-state variation. These materially expand the mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds inference details including a four-layer GATv2 with concatenated skip connections, clarifies semantic embedding construction, and documents new graph and threshold settings. Conversely, it removes v1 Appendix E's training/model-selection description and Table 8's TxPert hyperparameter search space, including optimization budgets and validation-based selection information.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from K562 and RPE1 to include JURKAT and HEPG2. Appendix C also introduces a distinct transfer scenario: training on RPE1, HEPG2, and JURKAT while holding out K562 as an unseen cellular context.

E2.justification: The original six main baselines remain, but v2 Tables 9–12 add Context Mean, Linear-GenePT, Linear-OneHot, scGPT, and Geneformer to the reported comparisons. The new cross-cell-line comparison also includes Perturb Mean, substantially broadening the controls beyond v1's comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds cross-cell-line testing, MAE-based evaluation, and the Systema protocol with perturbation/control references, top-20-gene scores, and centroid accuracy. Appendix A/Table 5 changes reported effect-size grouping from fixed DEG-percentage bins to within-dataset DEG-count tertiles. Appendix D additionally specifies and sweeps FDR/LFC thresholds. These are substantive reported protocol changes, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices D–G add DEG-definition sensitivity, graph-source and density ablations, fixed versus adaptive neighborhood comparisons, attention-threshold sensitivity, and DEG/non-DEG error analysis. Pathway validation expands to 272 K562 perturbations and pathway-specific rankings. The original loss/context ablations and HIRA case study are retained.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies BH-adjusted Wilcoxon testing for DEG identification and 300 permutations for GSEA, extending statistical-procedure documentation. Existing mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remains unchanged; neither version provides explicit training seed counts, and v2 does not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–3 remain unchanged, but v2 adds extensive benchmark, transfer, Systema, ablation, and pathway results. For example, new Table 13 reports transfer Pearson correlation of 0.4601 for AdaPert, versus 0.5149 for Linear-GenePT and 0.6501 for Perturb Mean. Some appendix values differ from retained main results without reconciliation, such as K562 TxPert Pearson correlation of 0.5879 versus 0.580. v1 Table 10's RPE1 DES@100 and significant-gene Spearman entries are omitted.

M1.justification: The perturbation-conditioned subgraph selection, context aggregation, and three-term training objective remain unchanged in Equations 5–21. v2 clarifies GPT-4o versus text-embedding roles and documents inference architecture; these disclosures do not establish a changed underlying method.

P1.justification: The appendices are substantially reorganized: baseline and metric descriptions are consolidated under Experiment Settings, related work moves from C to H, and pathway discussion is consolidated within expanded case studies. v2 adds an appendix contents list, rewrites the abstract and portions of the introduction/data exposition, and adds Impact Statement and Acknowledgments sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds an inference schematic, benchmark and Systema charts/tables, threshold heatmaps, graph comparisons, error boxplots, and pathway-ranking displays. Original distribution Figures 7–8 are combined into Figure 6, and the HIRA display is retained as Figure 28. Dataset tables are expanded and restructured, while the hyperparameter table is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds application citations including Kim et al. (2024), Ishikawa et al. (2023), and Gonzalez et al. (2025), while removing Dunefsky et al. (2024) and Feng et al. (2024). The data-driven versus knowledge-driven taxonomy and positioning of AdaPert remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The numbered mathematical formulation and metric equations, Equations 1–30, are retained. v2 adds empirical evaluation procedures but no new theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation through simple mean/linear controls, fixed-neighborhood comparisons, DEG-threshold robustness tests, and pathway validation across 272 perturbations instead of relying on the HIRA example alone. The transfer study also exposes an important applicability limitation. These additions address significant gaps in v1's evidence for the proposed mechanism and biological utility. Removal of tuning details and unreconciled main/appendix results weaken reproducibility, but the broader, more diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaPert research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations on JURKAT and HEPG2, cross-cell-line transfer, graph and DEG-threshold analyses, and broader pathway experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original K562 and RPE1 prediction experiments, component ablations, regularization sensitivity, and HIRA pathway analysis.

title: Learning Adaptive Perturbation-Conditioned Contexts for Robust Transcriptional Response Prediction

C1.justification: The central efficiency and predictive-performance contributions remain. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now restrict comparable implicit Bayesianness to the tested one-at-a-time streaming protocol. The conclusion additionally highlights context ordering, without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies interpretation through the teacher-forced consistency scope, finite-sampling effects in ordering diagnostics, architecture differences affecting TNP-A runtime comparisons, and attention-dependent memory tradeoffs. Section 5.1 also explicitly discusses CNP outperforming vanilla incTNP and TNP-D in factorised temperature forecasting, including a possible underfitting explanation.

D1.justification: Appendix E.3.1 substantially expands reproducibility of the central KL diagnostic by specifying teacher-forced densities, canonical reordering of mixture parameters, and the estimator. Further disclosures cover filtering, random ordering, comparator parameter differences, and memory measurements using 16-bit floats and specified PyTorch backends. Core training details and code access remain available.

E1.justification: Both versions cover RBF and mixed-kernel GP regression, synthetic tabular data, the same four UCI datasets, and HadISD interpolation and forecasting. The 24-hour evaluation and kernel-distribution shifts already appear in v1. New diagnostics reuse this coverage with different ordering, aggregation, or computational settings.

E2.justification: V2 includes TNP-A in Table 1(b)'s static AR runtime comparison, reporting cost ratios of 1.04 for GP and 0.81 for temperature. Its predictive scores already appeared in v1 Table 2(b), and its streaming runtimes were already compared in Appendix E.2. Other baseline families are retained.

E3.justification: Added evaluation designs include gradient-noise measurements using 80,000 samples, context-permutation diagnostics, aggregation over K=1,2,10,100 orderings, and memory measurements comparing attention backends up to one million context points. Existing benchmark settings remain stable; the expanded teacher-forcing description documents the retained KL experiment rather than establishing a protocol change.

E4.justification: V2 adds unfiltered hyperparameter outcomes and measured gradient noise (Appendix E.1.3), AR target-order sensitivity (E.5), memory scaling (G), and extensive context-order, greedy-ordering, and aggregation analyses (H). These directly investigate robustness and computational tradeoffs. V1's distribution-shift analysis is retained as Appendix I.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly states that results generally use one training run and seed per model. Table 1 also specifies ties within one SEM. SEM reporting and Monte Carlo averaging already existed; the new disclosure does not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 3 retain their numerical results, but substantial new findings concern gradient noise, ordering, aggregation, memory, and TNP-A timing. For example, Table 8 reports a +0.0053 log-likelihood gain for incTNP-Seq on GP(64) when increasing aggregation from one to 100 orderings. Figure 21 shows higher incTNP memory use with FlashAttention despite linear scaling.

M1.justification: The core incTNP and incTNP-Seq procedures remain intact, but Appendix H adds substantive methodological extensions: greedy variance-based context ordering (Algorithm 2), incTNP-Prior with a learned token supporting empty contexts, and prediction aggregation across context permutations. These change training or inference procedures.

P1.justification: V2 selectively clarifies background, experimental interpretation, and conclusions; subdivides appendix discussions; updates affiliations and publication information; and adds an Impact Statement. Most existing prose and the overall introduction-background-method-experiments-conclusion structure remain, so the scientific additions do not constitute wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial visual material for unfiltered outcomes, gradient noise, ordering sensitivity, memory, and aggregation, including Figures 12–13, 19, 21–26 and Tables 6–8. Table 1 gains TNP-A columns and explicit SEM-based highlighting. Existing streaming and distribution-shift figures are retained with relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds Burt et al. (2020) to motivate variance-based ordering and Feng et al. (2024) for constant-memory alternatives, while removing Katharopoulos et al. (2020). The main positioning against existing NP and streaming methods remains. Consolidating duplicate Hollmann references does not remove a distinct cited work.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 4.2 for conditional regression with i.i.d. inputs and Proposition C.1 extending the decomposition to non-i.i.d. inputs, with proofs. Appendix G derives transient, persistent, and total memory costs, while Appendix H defines a context-permutation KL diagnostic. These substantially extend v1's exchangeability and runtime analysis.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's assessment of sacrificed context-order invariance and KV-cache memory costs through direct diagnostics and measurements. Conditional-regression proofs, a reproducible KL-estimator description, and narrower consistency claims substantially strengthen justification and transparency. The new analysis exposes higher memory use with FlashAttention, and single-seed evidence still limits robustness conclusions, but these limitations are now clearer without weakening the retained benchmark evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Incremental Transformer Neural Processes. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds original gradient-noise, memory, ordering-sensitivity, and prediction-aggregation analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original GP regression, synthetic and real-world tabular, and HadISD temperature experiments, including predictive accuracy, runtime, consistency, and distribution-shift results.

title: Incremental Transformer Neural Processes

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a three-regime, solver-verifiable induction benchmark and the finding that compact solutions generalize better. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the claimed evaluation scope to include symbolic synthesis alongside prompted models, without redefining the research question.

C2.justification: v3 develops universal-to-existential collapse as an explanation of structural failures, distinguishes GPT-5.4's FullObs/CI compactness gains from increased EC bloat, and interprets unified versus specialized symbolic search. It also corrects the equality-use discussion and adds specific limitations concerning bounded symbolic search, absent compactness-prompt ablations, and the limited renaming pilot.

D1.justification: v1's Software and Data statement postpones artifact release; v3 provides repository access information and states that datasets, code, cached outputs, and analysis artifacts are available. Appendix A documents symbolic encodings and search bounds, while Appendix C.1 adds target-pool construction steps, eligibility counts, and selection/reuse rules for the existing benchmark.

E1.justification: The original FullObs/CI/EC tasks, bands, and dataset sizes remain. Appendix B.6 adds a limited input-perturbation scenario: consistently renamed predicates and objects on 30 paired instances, ten per task.

E2.justification: v3 adds GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.5 Flash, DeepSeek4Pro, and Grok4.3 to the model comparison. Table 2 and Appendix A additionally introduce z3-prenex + rescue across the tasks, the FullObs-specific z3-ad-mix portfolio, and ilasp-frag for FullObs and CI, substantially broadening comparison beyond prompted models.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce a 30-minute-per-instance symbolic search protocol and a paired 30-instance renaming design. GPT-5.2's reported reasoning setting changes from 64k to med (v1 Table 23; v3 Table 29), without establishing reruns. EC best-completion diagnostic totals also change from 199–200 to 135–137 predictions (Tables 19 and 25), without explaining the smaller sample.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained family, lift-hard, equality, and bloat analyses, v3 adds systematic tests of existential versus mixed quantification, premise-only occurrences of x, helper-like relational structure, and universal-to-existential collapse (Appendix B.5). It also adds the renaming pilot, model/problem fixed-effects controls, and new paired and failure case studies in Appendix D.

E5.justification: v3 adds fixed-effects regression coefficients, standard errors, and p-values controlling for model and problem (Tables 4 and 26). Confidence intervals and paired-comparison p-values already existed, but v1 Table 20's explicit specification of 95% percentile-bootstrap intervals, 2,000 resamples, and one-sided binomial tests is omitted.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include 65.9% FullObs accuracy for z3-ad-mix, 100% EC success for the unified Z3 baseline, and 93.5% EC validity for GPT-5.4. Existing results also change: Opus 4.6 FullObs accuracy changes from 22.1% to 23.7%, and Grok4 coverage from 67.2% to 89.3%. Held-out estimates, error profiles, and example outputs are revised; EC diagnostic values involve changed samples.

M1.justification: The core task semantics, listed formula templates, distractor/trap generation, existential completion, and AST-based scoring are retained. Expanded target-pool documentation does not establish a changed generator. The newly introduced symbolic solvers serve as comparison methods.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, setup, results, limitations, conclusion, and appendix explanations are extensively rewritten. Evaluation and experiments are merged into Section 5, the appendices are reorganized, and terminology shifts toward input worlds and instance-correct solutions. Unresolved figure references in v1 are repaired.

P2.justification: v3 adds FullObs and CI generalization plots previously absent despite textual references, plus symbolic, structural-analysis, renaming, and target-pool tables. Existing charts gain model series and revised legends, tables are expanded and relocated, and qualitative-example tables are redesigned with separate prediction and gold-formula columns.

R1.justification: v3 adds ABD and PROOFGRID citations and explains their respective relationships to concept synthesis through default–exception abduction and formal deductive reasoning. The established ILP, synthesis, and reasoning-benchmark literature is largely retained, with positioning adjusted to include symbolic comparisons.

T1.justification: The finite-structure definitions and FullObs, CI, and EC correctness conditions in Equations 1–5 retain their mathematical meaning. New semantic examples and target-pool explanations elaborate the existing formalism; no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: Table 2 and Appendix A resolve v1's important lack of symbolic calibration, making benchmark difficulty substantially easier to assess. Structural analyses, robustness evidence, and detailed generation/access documentation strengthen interpretation and reproducibility information. These gains outweigh the unexplained smaller EC diagnostic sample, omitted bootstrap details, and the disagreement between FullObs prose and Table 4.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same INDUCTION benchmark. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains and updates those evaluations and reports original symbolic-baseline results, structural analyses, and a paired symbol-renaming experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on 375 FullObs, 200 CI, and 200 EC problems, including held-out generalization and appendix error analyses.

title: INDUCTION: Finite-Structure Concept Synthesis in First-Order Logic

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: context-conditioned evolutionary modeling, a first-order approximation guarantee, SHM-corrected VEP, and guided antibody optimization. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v4 replaces speculation that ESM2 helps mouse-antibody generalization with an interpretation emphasizing the evolutionary training objective. It adds explanations for failure at extreme branch lengths and expands the discussion of limited paired-chain training data. The principal limitations concerning approximation error and absent indels remain unchanged.

D1.justification: A new Reproducibility Statement supplies a COSINE code-and-data repository location. v4 also documents PRISM scoring modes, classical-model fitting details, and why the retained FLAb snapshot differs from another study's version. The original COSINE training hyperparameters, hardware, and preprocessing instructions remain intact; repository availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: v4 adds training and evaluation on approximately 15,000 TrRosetta general-protein family alignments, extending coverage beyond antibodies and synthetic codons (C.6). It also adds two Petersen MAGMA-seq binding assays with distinct antibodies, antigens, and assay technology (C.8). Existing coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds PRISM to the existing Spearman and Pearson VEP comparisons. It introduces a WAG-style model fitted on the antibody training transitions and fitted WAG and LG+G4 comparators for TrRosetta (Tables S2–S3). The CDR optimization comparator set was already present in v1 and remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include six VEP branch lengths from 0.01 to 10, an 8M randomly initialized model versus the ESM2-initialized model, and runtime sweeps over sequence length and sampling steps (C.9–C.12). The classical-model comparisons introduce matched-data fitting controls. Existing main VEP settings, data snapshots, and CDR optimization budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 substantially expands analysis of context dependence, branch-length sensitivity, dependence on pretrained initialization, and computational scaling (C.5, C.9, C.10, C.12). These address distinct questions about the source and robustness of performance. The SHM correction, paired-chain, SNR-weighting, and exact-versus-Taylor guidance analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three replicates per synthetic epistasis level, five tree simulations per guidance setting, and the 15-sample exact-versus-Taylor comparison with identical two-sided t-tests. v4 introduces no new repeated-run, confidence-interval, or uncertainty-estimation practice; its branch-length sensitivity range is not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results for new comparators, datasets, ablations, and runtime tests. Examples include TrRosetta test NLL of 1.027 versus 1.200 for WAG and 1.168 for LG+G4, and Petersen correlations of 0.504 and 0.328. Existing Table 1 scores are retained. Figure S4 updates Gillespie/matrix-exponential win fractions from 48.8%/40.2% to 52.0%/38.8% and plotted correlations from 0.62/0.53 to 0.64/0.56, although its caption retains the old correlations.

M1.justification: The COSINE rate parameterization, training objective, SHM-corrected selection score, and Guided Gillespie procedure remain unchanged, including Equations (2), (5), and (9) and Algorithms S1–S3. The new 8M model is an experimental ablation, not a replacement of the main model.

P1.justification: v4 locally rewrites related work, the CDR optimization discussion, and the impact statement, adds a reproducibility section, and expands the appendix organization. Most original prose and the overall background–method–experiments–conclusion structure are retained; the added scientific material does not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v4 adds six result tables and a branch-length sensitivity plot, expands existing VEP tables with PRISM, and redraws Figure S4 with revised axes and labels. It promotes v1 Table S4 to main-text Table 2 with a fuller caption and enlarges and rearranges the additional-antibody plots from Figure S8 into Figure S9. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 3 substantially expands positioning against germline-aware antibody models, including Im et al. and PRISM, and adds evolutionary translation work by Koehl et al. New Appendix A.4 distinguishes COSINE's biological transition modeling from discrete flow matching, citing Gat and Campbell. Shanker et al. is removed. Publication updates to existing references are not new research coverage.

T1.justification: The first-order approximation bound, Gillespie exactness lemma, mutation-selection derivation, and Appendix D proofs are unchanged. The added discussion of discrete flow matching and standard classical-model parameterization does not introduce a new theoretical result or revise the existing reasoning.

improvement.justification: The new context-independent controls, branch-length sensitivity study, and backbone ablation address important gaps in v1's evidence for the source and robustness of COSINE's performance (C.5, C.9–C.10). Additional antibody assays and general-protein evaluations substantially strengthen validation, while the code/data statement improves reproducibility information. The backbone comparison changes model size as well as initialization, and Figure S4 contains stale caption values, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COSINE study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, algorithms, and Appendices A–D support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds general-protein evaluations, antibody binding assays, and further controls and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-codon simulations, antibody transition modeling, variant-effect prediction, and guided antibody optimization experiments.

title: Conditionally Site-Independent Neural Evolution of Antibody Sequences

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction strengthen the maximum token-reduction claim from 36% to 47%, and the introduction specifies a 43% improvement over the best baseline. The underlying contributions remain unchanged; the conclusion still states 36%.

C2.justification: The new Impact Statement interprets token savings as sustainability and accessibility benefits and suggests applications beyond language reasoning. Removing Appendix C.5 also removes its assertion that sensitivity conclusions generalize across model–dataset settings. Most mechanism explanations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Implementation settings, hardware, software configuration, and code-access information are retained. However, v2 C.4 deletes v1 C.6's explicit identification of Table 6 samples as Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct outputs on GSM8K, slightly reducing experimental provenance.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GSM8K, MATH-500, DAPO-Math-17k, and CommonsenseQA. The human comparison and reasoning case studies also remain; no new dataset, domain, or task scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain DAPO, GFPO, GTPO, and S-GRPO, with the same base-model comparisons in Table 1. No baseline method is added or replaced.

E3.justification: Table 1 drops the stated rule withholding R@k when corresponding Pass@k underperforms the base model, changing the reported accuracy gate for efficiency comparisons. Dataset splits, model sizes, training budgets, and metric definitions otherwise remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 removes v1 Appendix C.4's expanded ablations, including the 1.5B and 7B comparisons, and C.5's multi-setting alpha/beta sensitivity study. The main 0.5B ablation and sensitivity plots are revised, as are training dynamics. Case studies and token heatmaps are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report plus/minus values and graphical uncertainty bands without specifying run counts, seeds, or confidence levels. Revised uncertainty magnitudes accompany changed results; no new statistical reporting procedure or significance test is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 3–5 and Figures 5–6 and 9–11 substantially revise results. For IAPO/Qwen2.5-7B on GSM8K, reported P@32 changes from 1.0000 to 0.9805 and L@32 from 111.83 to 83.97; on DAPO-Math-17k they change from 0.6889 to 0.4267 and 194.50 to 429.62. These are revised reported outcomes, not evidence of an improved method. CommonsenseQA and inference-time results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The three-component token advantage, conditional-MI estimator, KV-cache preloading, and chunk-wise forwarding remain unchanged. Appendix C.1's practical entropy substitution is already disclosed in v1.

P1.justification: v2 makes local wording and terminology edits, updates author/publication details, and adds conflict-of-interest, acknowledgements, and impact text. Appendix subsections are removed and renumbered, but the main narrative is largely unchanged.

P2.justification: The complete supplementary ablation and sensitivity figure sets are removed. Figures 5–6 and 9–11 are redrawn with revised axes, ranges, or labels, and some tables and equations are repositioned. The extensive token heatmaps are retained and renumbered from Figure 14 to Figure 12.

R1.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A retain the same research positioning. Bibliographic changes update publication metadata and remove the older RLAIF entry while retaining its corresponding 2024 publication; they do not introduce distinct prior work.

T1.justification: The covariance theorem, length-reduction corollary, exploration argument, and Appendix B derivations retain their substance. Replacing 'keyword' with 'informative' terminology and changing mathematical typesetting do not introduce new assumptions or reasoning.

improvement.justification: Useful disclosures and some clearer wording are outweighed by losing the larger-model ablations and broader sensitivity evidence from v1 Appendix C.4–C.5. v2 also introduces an inconsistency between its 47% abstract claim and unchanged 36% conclusion. Revised scores alone establish no quality gain. The methodological core and broad benchmark coverage remain intact, so the overall decline is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IAPO research. All 49 pages of v1 and 45 pages of v2 are readable, including equations, experimental figures, proofs, and extensive appendix case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and supplementary analyses, with revised mathematical benchmark results and training curves.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical and commonsense reasoning experiments, ablations, sensitivity analyses, inference-time measurements, and case studies.

title: IAPO: Information-Aware Policy Optimization for Token-Efficient Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the central claims: extending inverse distillation to discrete diffusion, establishing uniqueness, enabling stable gradients and achieving 4×–64× fewer sampling steps while preserving quality. The 128×/256× composed DCD comparisons already appear in v1 Figure 5.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations based on teacher-versus-fake advantages, sequence mixtures and uniform-process holding times, and interprets the new gradient ablations. Appendix D.2 newly acknowledges that the proof does not cover the experimental factorized sequence loss, a more specific limitation than v1's evaluation and scalability caveats.

D1.justification: v1's promise to publish code becomes a project-page announcement of code, checkpoints and tutorials. v2 Appendix E.2 documents conditional-data formatting, tokenizer, loss masking, optimizer settings, precision, four-GPU training, a 250,000-step budget and execution-based scoring. Explicit sampling pseudocode is also added.

E1.justification: v2 adds TinyGSM training and GSM8K evaluation for conditional generation of executable mathematical solutions (Section 5.2 and Appendix E.2). This substantially extends v1's unconditional OpenWebText evaluation. The original OpenWebText and SEDD coverage remains.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained teachers, SDTT and Duo-DCD, v2's OpenWebText comparisons include SDTT + Di4C2, DiDi-Instruct, D-MMD, ELF and FLM/FMLM (Figure 3 and Table 2). The new conditional comparison also includes autoregressive models and S-FLM. These are reported comparators, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: v2 adds MAUVE and Gradient Moment evaluation, an 863M model setting, and a conditional protocol using 512-token sequences, clamped prompts, execution-based exact-match accuracy and 32/64/128 reverse steps. These extend the evaluation design; the previously documented small-model OpenWebText settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: Appendix F.4 adds controlled comparisons of SUBS versus Gumbel/Argmax updates, full versus stop-gradient Duo updates, and Gaussian input noise for MDLM. Figures 14–15 and Table 4 investigate gradient stability and latent randomness, questions not experimentally isolated in v1.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates, whereas v2 introduces ± uncertainty terms for central IDLM GenPPL/entropy results and MAUVE comparisons in Figure 3 and Tables 2–3. Their meaning and repeated-run counts are unspecified, so additional runs or a particular uncertainty estimator cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: v2 adds conditional accuracies, 863M results, MAUVE/GM scores and ablation findings. Existing entries also change: 16-step SDTT GenPPL/entropy changes from 89.17/5.53 in v1 Table 1 to 61.34/5.36 in v2 Figure 3, without explaining the replacement. Appendix G also replaces full generations with shortened, partly reworded excerpts.

M1.justification: The inverse objective, alternating training, simplex relaxation, SUBS treatment and Gaussian reparameterization are retained. However, the printed MDLM objective gains a minus sign between v1 Equation (5) and v2 Equation (1), correcting its minimization formulation. The PDFs do not establish an implementation change.

P1.justification: The preliminaries and method explanation are extensively rewritten around masked and uniform diffusion. General SEDD material moves to Appendix A, related work moves into the main text, and a loss-intuition section and contents pages are added. The appendices are substantially reorganized and the qualitative material condensed.

P2.justification: v2 restructures the original quantitative table into comparison panels and separate tables with additional metric columns. It adds process and relaxation diagrams, a GenPPL–entropy plot and ablation plots, relocates existing SEDD and sampling-step figures, and replaces full-page sample listings with compact colored panels.

R1.justification: The broad acceleration survey in v1 Appendix A is replaced by a focused comparison in v2 Section 4, incorporating RSD, Di4C2, D-MMD, DiDi-Instruct and recent language flows. IDLM is now explicitly positioned through path-measure matching versus marginal matching and contrasted with consistency methods' factorization limitations.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix D corrects v1 Appendix C's interchange of optimization and expectation, keeping the optimization outside the population expectation. It adds explicit model-class/support assumptions and a gap-preservation lemma. It also restricts the sequence-level guarantee to the ideal full-sequence objective, explicitly excluding the practical factorized loss.

improvement.justification: Conditional accuracy, larger-model results and controlled ablations address important gaps in v1's evidence (Tables 1 and 3; Appendix F.4). The corrected proof and explicit restriction of its applicability also improve theoretical precision. Undefined uncertainty terms and partly rewritten qualitative excerpts reduce auditability, but the gains in empirical validation and mathematical clarity are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IDLM research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and relocated material, including the SEDD experiments, can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original distillation results and adds conditional-generation accuracy, larger-model experiments and ablations in Tables 1 and 3 and Appendix F.4.

before.justification: v1 reports original IDLM distillation experiments on OpenWebText, including GenPPL, entropy and generated samples for SEDD, MDLM and Duo variants.

title: IDLM: Inverse-distilled Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: Incremental sparse attention and competitive-to-cooperative dynamics remain the central contributions. v2 narrows the headline framing: the definite early-stopping regularization claim and broad reasoning implications give way to a controlled surrogate account and a suggested connection to effective complexity.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning non-identifiability and sparse-solution selection, the roles of isotropy and orthogonality, and hierarchical attention despite feature overfitting. It also explicitly distinguishes quantitative comparisons within regression from qualitative comparisons with classification transformers, clarifying the theory's applicability.

D1.justification: The documented code repository changes from ralvarezlucend/IL-SAP-Transformers to tml-epfl/sparse-attention-dynamics. Appendix D provides restart times and procedures for the new ODE comparison. Existing architecture, optimizer, data, and seed tables are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic Markov classification and positional regression, retaining finite/online data, reversed importance, non-uniform weights, and overlapping-interval scenarios. The new diagnostics examine these existing tasks.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 7 adds simplified stage-wise ODE trajectories as an explicit internal comparator to the full regression flow; v1 plotted only the full-flow trajectories. The restricted-context transformer comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The new Appendix D comparison initializes simplified ODEs at t = 25 and t = 300 and compares attention mass and value-matrix alignments. It also measures corresponding alignments in the classification transformer. Existing data and training settings in Tables 1–4 are unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds direct tests of whether the simplified dynamics track full regression flow and whether classification transformers exhibit the predicted value-matrix compensation (Figures 7–8). These substantially extend validation of the central mechanism. The original regression simulation and ablation suite are retained, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions list seed 0 and retain the same reporting practice. Neither introduces repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

It also updates the publication header and adds an impact statement. Most introductory, methodological and theoretical exposition is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material for runtime, cost decomposition, BCD convergence and smooth-activation experiments. Figure 4 becomes a two-dimensional heatmap, Figure 3 adds a smoothed presentation, and Table 1 changes its row membership and caption. Existing appendix performance figures are retained with renumbering and relocation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Adam, Muon, Shampoo, GELU, SiLU/Swish and gated activations, positioning optimizer combinations and broader activation support as future directions. Appendix N corrects ENorm's attribution to Stock et al. (2019). The central positioning against existing rescaling approaches remains.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the gradient-flow sign in Appendix B, replaces gradients with Hessians in Appendix C's equations (17)–(18), and corrects bias-path counting in J.2 and equation (92), changing a product's lower limit from k+1 to k+2. J.4 also corrects the cross-layer width ratio. The main theoretical framework and proof structure remain.

improvement.justification: v2 improves practical assessability through runtime and convergence evidence, explicit numerical limitations, additional implementation details and corrected formulas. The gain is limited by overbroad new summaries: Figure 7 shows deeper MLP rescaling exceeding one training epoch despite the broad overhead claim, and Figure 13 supports training acceleration only for GELU. Overall, the additions provide useful support while leaving some interpretation inconsistencies.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PathCond research. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, including Appendices A–N in v1 and A–O in v2. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds runtime measurements, coordinate-descent convergence experiments and smooth-activation evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy-network simulations, CIFAR-10 training experiments, MNIST autoencoder experiments and synthetic architecture/initialization analyses.

title: Path-conditioned training: a principled way to rescale ReLU neural networks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: an encoder-agnostic framework combining residual encoding, restriction, and bi-boundary optimization for detection under limited supervision. The new analyses do not redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds reasons for choosing normalizing flows. Appendix G interprets threshold responsiveness, explains high false-positive rates at low cutoffs, and discusses dependence on validation-based checkpoint selection. Appendix A's substantive limitations and future directions remain the same.

D1.justification: V2 adds a public code hyperlink, explicitly documents the 0.5 F1 threshold for existing validation and test evaluations, and specifies six coupling blocks with two-layer fully connected subnetworks and analytic log-determinants. These are disclosures; the PDFs do not establish implementation changes or verify repository availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same six datasets, real and synthetic anomaly types, unseen structural-anomaly evaluation, and S1–S3 supervision settings. The new threshold analysis reuses Wikipedia and UCI.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in all matched benchmark and ablation tables. The new threshold analysis compares against TCL, which already participates in the corresponding score-distribution comparisons.

E3.justification: New Appendix G evaluates test thresholds 0.01, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 using F1, TPR, and FPR, with checkpoints selected by validation F1 at 0.5. Existing protocols remain unchanged; Appendix C's newly stated default F1 threshold is additional documentation.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds a focused threshold-sensitivity analysis for SDGAD and TCL on two datasets. Existing component ablations, hyperparameter studies, loss-weight analyses, and distribution visualizations are retained, including studies moved from Appendix D into Section 5.5.

E5.justification: Appendix C retains the same five-independent-run, mean-and-standard-deviation reporting policy. No new seed, repeat-count, significance-test, or uncertainty-estimation procedure is specified; the added threshold tables provide point estimates without separate uncertainty information.

E6.justification: All ten original tables retain their data after matching renumbered tables. New Tables 7–10 add threshold results: on UCI, SDGAD reports F1 0.444444, TPR 1, and FPR 0.002298 at every tested threshold, while TCL reports zeros. These are additional results, not improvements over v1 under changed training.

M1.justification: Residual encoding, representation restriction, bi-boundary optimization, the combined objective, and anomaly scoring remain unchanged. Equation 6 introduces equivalent shorthand; newly specified flow implementation details do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: The hyperparameter discussion moves from Appendix D to Section 5.5, with appendices reorganized around new complexity and threshold sections. Localized prose revisions, equal-contribution and publication information, and acknowledgements are added; most narrative remains unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adds four threshold tables and rearranges existing tables and figures. The original hyperparameter Table 5 becomes main-text Table 4, and other displays are redistributed and renumbered. Existing figure graphics and retained table contents are unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 4.2 explicitly credits Zhang et al. (2024) for the two-hypersphere construction and distinguishes SDGAD through its dynamic, non-i.i.d., end-to-end setting. V2 also adds Hua et al. (2026), BAG; the Kong reference receives a publication update.

T1.justification: New Appendix D derives per-batch computational complexity for the baseline and SDGAD, accounting for encoder calls, projection, and flow blocks. The existing error-bound propositions and proofs in Appendix E.2 remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 improves transparency through the explicit F1 cutoff, flow implementation details, code link, complexity analysis, and clearer attribution of the hypersphere idea. Threshold experiments add useful evidence, although Appendix G overstates consistently favorable trade-offs: Tables 9–10 show lower SDGAD F1 than TCL at thresholds 0.01 and 0.1 on Wikipedia. The gains are therefore limited, with the central method, benchmark evidence, and existing proofs unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SDGAD research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds threshold experiments comparing SDGAD with TCL on Wikipedia and UCI.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations on six datasets, component ablations, hyperparameter studies, and score-distribution analyses in the main text and appendices.

title: Learning Discriminative and Generalizable Anomaly Detector for Dynamic Graph with Limited Supervision

The contribution list also adds an explicit novelty claim for the integrated PT+FT characterization. The central four-regime theory and initialization-dependent generalization claims remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 explains why weak pretraining reduces sensitivity to relative scale and why imperfectly learned features can benefit from refinement even under full task overlap. It also interprets SVHN as a lower-overlap proxy and suggests optimizer dynamics may explain nonmonotonic scaling effects. Most existing architectural and uncontrolled-overlap limitations move into Section 6.

D1.justification: Appendix D.8 adds Transformer optimizer settings, one-million-step pretraining and 32,000-step fine-tuning budgets, embedding-scaling instructions, and the source codebase used. Figure 11 supplies Adam regularization details. Existing Appendix E implementation information remains largely unchanged, while the addition-versus-multiplication inconsistency limits reproducibility of the new arithmetic experiment.

E1.justification: v2 expands beyond synthetic regression and CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-100-to-SVHN transfer and Transformer modular-arithmetic tasks with seen, shared-prime, and novel-prime moduli (Appendices D.5 and D.8). The arithmetic coverage is clearly new, although D.8 says addition while Figure 12 says multiplication.

E2.justification: Figure 11a introduces single-task ResNet baselines into the SVHN transfer comparison; v1's ResNet plots compare initialization scales without this baseline. Single-task diagonal-network experiments and the Lippl–Lindsey fine-tuning rescaling comparison were already documented, so the comparator expansion is limited.

E3.justification: New protocols include pretraining data scales below one, an additional CIFAR-100 60/40 class split, and Adam with pretraining weight decay and fine-tuning decay toward initial weights. Transformer evaluation introduces six pretraining targets, nine fine-tuning moduli, and specified training budgets. These supplement the retained protocols rather than establish reruns of existing experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds sensitivity to imperfect pretraining, a reduced-task-similarity probe using SVHN, optimizer and class-split robustness checks, and arithmetic-transfer comparisons organized by shared prime factors (Figures 4, 11–12). The original initialization sweeps and PR/ENSD representation analyses remain present.

E5.justification: Figure 12 specifies a new 25-seed protocol with one-standard-error bars for the Transformer experiments. Existing diagonal-network and ResNet run counts, Figure 3's two-standard-error reporting, and Appendix E's Monte Carlo uncertainty procedures are retained; additional runs of the original experiments are not established.

E6.justification: Figures 4, 11, and 12 add results on pretraining-strength dependence, SVHN transfer versus single-task learning, scaling effects under Adam and a 60/40 split, and higher errors for modular tasks involving novel prime factors. Original result plots are retained unchanged, including v1 Figure 4 as v2 Figure 5. These are additional results under new conditions.

M1.justification: The diagonal-network architecture, two-stage training, pathway rebalancing, readout reinitialization, and implicit penalty remain unchanged. Equations (2)–(3) are rewritten equivalently under symmetric initialization. The additional architectures and optimizer variants extend evaluation of the existing scaling interventions.

P1.justification: The overall section and appendix organization is retained. v2 reorganizes related-work paragraphs, expands replica-method and architectural explanations, brings representation analysis and limitations into Section 6, and revises the conclusion and publication front matter. Most existing exposition and proof text remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1 into separate training, teacher-task, and parameter panels and adds substantial multipanel displays for imperfect pretraining, ResNet robustness, and Transformer transfer (Figures 4, 11–12). Retained figures are relocated or renumbered, and the Appendix A plot is reformatted with a side caption.

R1.justification: v2 adds Jarvis et al. (2025), makes the integrated-characterization novelty claim explicit, and expands the explanation connecting diagonal-network dynamics to nonlinear networks. The positioning relative to Lippl and Lindsey remains substantially unchanged. Most other reference changes update publication metadata for retained works.

T1.justification: The central theorems, propositions, and derivations are retained, while Sections 3.3 and 5.3 explicitly extend analysis to imperfect pretraining. Appendix C.1 removes the detailed assumptions concerning deterministic limits, interchange of limits, and analytic continuation, retaining only a generic replica-assumption qualification.

improvement.justification: The new imperfect-pretraining, SVHN, optimizer/split, and Transformer experiments strengthen empirical support beyond v1's narrower validation. The central theory and original results remain intact. However, Appendix D.8 and Figure 12 disagree about the arithmetic fine-tuning task, and Appendix C loses explicit replica assumptions. These reporting weaknesses limit the overall gain despite the useful additional evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same central framework and corresponding Appendices A–E. Text, equations, figures, and implementation tables are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds imperfect-pretraining simulations, SVHN transfer, optimizer/split experiments, and Transformer modular-arithmetic results.

before.justification: v1 reports original diagonal-network simulations, ResNet experiments on CIFAR-100, and representation analyses in Figures 3–4 and Appendix D.

title: A Theory of How Pretraining Shapes Inductive Bias in Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The first history-aware HSM and MFAX contributions remain. However, v2 removes headline claims of state-of-the-art performance and first solving the partially observable macroeconomic game, emphasizing preservation of HSM convergence speed while learning history-dependent behavior.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies applicability: public-history sufficiency is presented as an additional assumption and an approximation in applications, with private-history omission potentially suboptimal. It also explicitly acknowledges missing convergence guarantees and explains why lower gradient variance need not produce lower across-seed performance variance. These materially sharpen the interpretation and limitations of the unchanged experiments.

D1.justification: v2 explains that one shared GRU embedding is computed per timestep and broadcast across states, defines the recurrent reset mask, and explicitly supplies the Macroeconomics AR(1) noise equation whose parameters were already listed. It also replaces the direct repository pointer with a project-page and usage-example pointer. Architecture sizes and hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same partially observable Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar, and Macroeconomics environments. The new two-state counterexample in v2 Appendix A is a theoretical construction, not an additional experimental scenario.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain SPG, IPPO, RIPPO, and M-OMD, with OpenSpiel and MFGLib retained in the library comparisons. v2 explains why AFP is excluded but does not evaluate it. Comparator membership in the retained figures and ablations is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.4 corrects Linear Quadratic's reported state count from 99 to 100 and its clipping boundary, removes a conflicting Beach Bar noise description, and adds principal wealth to consumption inside the Macroeconomics reward formula. These revise stated benchmark settings without establishing reruns. Evaluation metrics, hardware, budgets, and hyperparameter sweeps remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The SPG/RSPG memory comparison, ordinal-versus-categorical policy ablation in Figure 11, and supplementary policy and population visualizations are retained. The added counterexample supplies theoretical evidence rather than a new empirical ablation or robustness test.

E5.justification: Figure 2 retains the same uncertainty bands and reports 95% confidence intervals over 10 seeds in both versions. v2 shortens the caption but does not document additional runs, changed uncertainty estimation, or new statistical tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds explicit qualitative capability entries: all three libraries support analytic mean-field updates, while only MFAX is marked as supporting sample-based updates. Benchmark outcomes are unchanged: Table 2 retains its timing values, and Figures 2–11 retain identical graphics, rankings, and behavioral findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 gains an optional terminal-payoff initialization for the backward return, whereas v1 specifies zero initialization only. This is a limited correction to the stated procedure, consistent with the already-described terminal-reward environment. The recurrent policy, action parameterization, and blocking of gradients through mean-field transitions remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively rewritten and reorganized. Related Work moves before Preliminaries, the shared-observation argument is restructured around explicit assumptions, experimental subsections are consolidated, and Future Work becomes a separate section. Acknowledgements and revised author and affiliation text are also added.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, with substantial relocation of figures and tables. Figure 1 moves near the introduction, Figures 2 and 3 share a page, equation boxes are added, and Table 1 gains two capability columns. All eleven underlying figure graphics remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantially broadens its positioning to numerical solvers, common-noise theory, deep learning, and cooperative mean-field control, adding works such as Achdou and Capuzzo-Dolcetta and Carmona and colleagues. It explicitly acknowledges that model-free RL can incorporate recurrence, sharpening RSPG's distinction around exploiting known structure. These changes exceed the accompanying publication-year and bibliography corrections.

T1.justification: v1 Section 5.1 justifies restricting private history using shared observations alone. v2 introduces Assumption 6.1, requiring the public history and current individual state to contain the relevant aggregate-state information. New Appendix A proves that this condition is not automatic: full-history policies can obtain reward 1 while restricted policies obtain only 1/2. This materially corrects the theoretical scope of the policy reduction.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is correction of an important logical overreach: v1 treats shared observations as sufficient to discard private histories, whereas v2 states an additional informational assumption and demonstrates strict suboptimality without it in Appendix A. This substantially improves scientific validity and claim calibration. Clearer implementation details also help reproducibility, although the retained experiments do not validate the new assumption or establish reruns following the environment-formula corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RSPG method and MFAX framework. All 26 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, are available and readable; relocated content can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original benchmark results, timing measurements, and appendix ablations. Their retention from v1 does not change their empirical status.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar, and Macroeconomics, library timing measurements in Table 2, and policy-representation ablations in Appendix C.4.

title: Recurrent Structural Policy Gradient for Partially Observable Mean Field Games

C1.justification: The main dataset, verifiable benchmark, and emergent-generalization contributions remain. The abstract and introduction narrow the advertised task count from 200 to 150 and ground the taxonomy in cognitive and developmental psychology. References to increasing model scale become data scaling, and the conclusion explicitly emphasizes the persistent gap that data scaling alone cannot close.

C2.justification: v3 substantially revises the cognitive rationale toward operational capability dimensions and adds explanations for using abstract stimuli. Section 4.1 acknowledges incomplete separation of reasoning from generation quality. Appendix C.5 proposes text conditioning as a possible bottleneck, while C.6 adds caution about nine-model correlations and softens neuroscience parallels. Appendix D also explicitly acknowledges that G-16 scoring does not verify the full required ordering.

D1.justification: v3 replaces broad suggested scoring rubrics with detailed automated formulas, pixel thresholds, failure gates, and G-45 pseudocode. Appendix B.3.1 expands quality-control documentation, and D.1 adds task-selection rationales and explicit access information for the evaluator and selection records. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that the underlying implementation changed.

E1.justification: The complete 150-task taxonomy has identical task IDs, categories, and descriptions. Both versions use the same training tasks, ID/OOD evaluation coverage, and VBench-I2V benchmark. The headline count changes from 200 to 150, removing the description of 50 tasks reserved for future evaluation, rather than demonstrating removal of evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 retains the eight original model baselines and human reference while adding VBVR-LTX2.3. Table 9 also evaluates the LTX-2.3 base model against its fine-tuned variants. This is a limited comparator extension; the existing LTX-2 baseline remains separately reported.

G-45 changes from target identification/path validity/path efficiency/animation weights of 30/30/20/20 to movement/key collection/door reached/sequence weights of 30/35/25/10. G-31 replaces shortest-path and direction checks with color preservation, endpoint completion, and jump penalties. v3 also adds LTX-2.3 scaling settings. These are substantial reported protocol revisions, without evidence that retained results were recomputed.

E4.justification: v3 Appendix C.5 and Table 9 extend the central scaling analysis from Wan2.2 alone to the structurally different LTX-2.3 backbone, testing whether gains and saturation are architecture-specific. This adds substantive robustness evidence for the paper's scaling interpretation. Existing human-alignment, correlation, distribution, and qualitative failure analyses remain, including material moved to the appendices.

E5.justification: Both versions report five independent annotations per video, the same human-preference aggregation procedures, and the same task-level distribution plots. v3 introduces no new repeated-training-run, seed-count, confidence-interval, or significance-testing practice. Its caution about nine-model correlations changes interpretation rather than statistical estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds a new family of results for LTX-2.3: Table 9 reports overall scores from 0.355 at 0K to 0.516 at 500K, and Table 2 adds category-level results with ID/OOD averages of 0.580/0.453. These extend empirical findings to another backbone. Retained benchmark, Wan2.2 scaling, and VBench table values match v1. Figure 1's ID/OOD annotations change from 0.763/0.601 to 0.760/0.610.

M1.justification: The procedural generation approach and Wan2.2 training procedure remain unchanged, including the unmodified backbone and rank-32 LoRA adaptation. v3 explicitly applies the same procedure to LTX-2.3. Expanded generator and evaluator documentation does not establish a newly introduced training or generation method; reported scoring revisions are assessed under E3.

P1.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix A are extensively rewritten, the main data-curation subsections are compressed, and capability-correlation discussion moves from Section 4.4 to Appendix C.6 with substantial rewriting. Related work gains thematic subdivisions, and new appendix sections reorganize implementation and validation material. This is extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redesigned from ten examples to five explicitly labeled examples, and the foundational-faculties table is removed. The pipeline diagram and correlation heatmap move to appendices. The full VBench table is retained there alongside a new main-text summary. v3 adds the LTX scaling table and algorithm display and expands the main benchmark table. Appendix D's missing-image placeholders persist.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts substantially: philosophical and historical exposition is reduced, while operational cognitive-science grounding is emphasized. New discussion contrasts procedural supervision with Bee's MLLM-driven curation and connects VBVR to ARC, CLEVR, world-model limitations, and unified understanding/generation models. These are substantive additions and removals beyond bibliographic metadata updates.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix D introduces explicit mathematical definitions for custom scoring functions, including object fidelity, variance-based layout scoring, and trajectory penalties; Algorithm 1 formalizes the piecewise G-45 score. This is limited formalization of evaluation criteria. The residualized-correlation equations remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The second-backbone validation, explicit scoring implementations, and clearer cognitive rationale make v3 better supported and more auditable. The small-sample caution also improves interpretation. These gains remain limited by unreconciled scoring revisions alongside unchanged earlier results: some documented scorers omit constraints required by their task descriptions. Conflicting task counts and missing Appendix D illustrations also remain unresolved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VBVR suite, and their main text, results, equations, and appendices support comparison. However, both contain missing-image placeholders instead of the task illustrations in Appendix D, Figures 10–14, preventing comparison of those images.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds LTX-2.3 fine-tuning and data-scaling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, Wan2.2 data-scaling experiments, human preference annotations, capability correlations, and VBench-I2V results.

title: A Very Big Video Reasoning Suite

The central cross-chirality generalization, benchmark superiority, and first wet-lab-validated generative D-peptide design claims remain.

V2 retains that statement but materially qualifies the wet-lab interpretation by acknowledging comparable binding of both enantiomers and discussing flexibility or alternative binding modes. It also newly attributes random-plane representation deviations to PDB coordinate rounding and discusses broader applicability of scalar injection.

Existing splits, 100 designs per LNR target, evaluation metrics, and listed training epochs remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands supplementary validation: reflection robustness and latent equivalence tests (Tables S1–S2), mixed/scalar/single-injection ablations (Tables S8–S9), and L-enantiomer binding plus circular-dichroism controls (Appendix A.6, Figure S8). These address symmetry implementation, dependence on feature-injection choices, and stereoselectivity of the principal experimental binder.

E6.justification: V2 adds reflection and latent-distance results, mixed/scalar variant scores, and the consequential finding that L-1412 binds CD38 with affinity comparable to D-1412. Table S9 additionally reports raw D-chirality of 99.33% for triple_scalar versus 97.05% for triple_scalar_once. Tables 1–2 and all pre-existing diversity and Rosetta result rows remain unchanged; these additions are not performance gains for the original models.

P1.justification: Changes include targeted expansions of the wet-lab discussion and conclusion, new appendix subsections, clarified triple-product terminology, updated affiliations, and acknowledgements. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds four supplementary tables and the circular-dichroism plot in Figure S8, extends the Rosetta table, and shortens the hyperparameter table. Figure 1 moves earlier, Figure 5 gains a KD annotation, and running headers and page flow change. Existing visualizations are largely preserved.

R1.justification: V2 adds Newcombe et al. (2024) and Li et al. (2026) to contextualize limited stereoselectivity. It replaces the Tetra-DMPNN attribution to Du et al. (2024) with Pattanaik et al. (2020), and removes the ChiralCliff discussion and Schneider et al. (2018) citation.

T1.justification: New Lemma B.11 and its proof extend the inversion-discrepancy result to arbitrary improper orthogonal transformations. Equation (31) also gains a minus sign in the commutator identity. The existing chirality-separation and diffusion-stability arguments are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: The reflection proof/tests, additional ablations, and enantiomer/CD controls strengthen validation and make the biological interpretation more informative. The improvement is limited by qualitative-only reporting of L-1412 affinity, unspecified BLI repetition counts, and removal of scheduler details. The principal quantitative evidence remains intact, supporting a modest net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AFI/PepMirror research. Text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable matching across additions, moves, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds reflection tests, model-variant evaluations, and experimental enantiomer controls.

before.justification: V1 reports original latent-space analyses, LNR benchmark experiments, and CD38 binding assays for generated D-peptides.

title: Cross-Chirality Generalization by Axial Vectors for Hetero-Chiral Protein-Peptide Interaction Design

V2 also adds explanations involving cation–anion ordering, transformer computational efficiency, and scaling. It interprets the new training controls as evidence against destructive task interference and for the importance of decoupled time axes.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies fixed sinusoidal positional embeddings, lattice-length normalization by N^(1/3), and dataset-specific LogNormal parameters (Section 3.1; Table F.2). Table H.1 adds measured training and inference times with hardware and batch sizes. These improve documentation; the PDFs do not establish changes to the original implementation from these disclosures.

V2 introduces LeMat-Bulk as an evaluation reference and tests partially conditioned atom substitution on four MP-20 test crystals, fixing known species while generating masked species. The earlier guidance, permutation-space, scaling, and cumulative component analyses remain.

Its caption specifies variation across 2,500 generated structures, averaged over three MLIPs. This adds distributional dispersion reporting, but does not establish repeated training runs or uncertainty across training seeds.

Table 1 revises baseline scores: OMatG's MP-20 match rate changes from 61.88 to 63.75, with v2 specifying LinearODE, and CrystalFlow's single-sample MPTS-52 match rate changes from 22.71 to 21.00. Original MCFlow CSP and ATG entries largely remain unchanged; the new DNG numbers are not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: V2 adds a limited inference adaptation for atom substitution: each atom-generation step overwrites known sites with their given types while sampling masked sites (Section 4.3). The core architecture, flow objectives, ordering, augmentation, and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged. Newly specified positional embeddings and prior parameters are implementation disclosures.

P1.justification: V2 tightens the abstract, consolidates contribution bullets, clarifies method explanations, revises experimental discussion, and reorganizes Appendix H around tables. It adds a conflict-of-interest disclosure and updates publication information. The overall section sequence and most methodological and background prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Table 2 is extensively redesigned with new metric columns and pre-relaxation groups. V2 adds the substitution table and six Appendix H tables, relocates existing displays, and consolidates Algorithms 2–3 onto one page. Existing template-CSP and MPTS-52 tables survive as H.3/H.6. Captions are revised, and the retained scaling plot loses its correlation-coefficient annotations.
