R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning within static and dynamic scaling-law research, adding discussions of Bordelon–Canatar–Pehlevan, Cui, Spigler, Defilippis, Atanasov, and Paquette and collaborators. It explicitly distinguishes identical teacher/student features and Langevin dynamics from down-projected models and finite-batch SGD. Appendix I adds a detailed connection to Canatar's stationary theory.

T1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix G add explicit bias/variance scaling laws, finite-size corrections, and t* = βα/[2(1+α)]. Appendices B–C add arguments concerning concentration and Gaussian exactness. New Appendices H–J derive label-noise dynamics, a stationary-limit connection, and a nonlinear model formulation. These substantially expand the mathematical substance.

improvement.justification: v1 promises analytical scaling and optimal-stopping results but mainly supplies dynamical equations and illustrative learning curves. v2 supplies explicit predictions, derivations, and targeted simulations in Section 5, Appendix G, and Figures 4–5, addressing an important gap in the central contribution. The tested label-noise extension adds further substance. These gains outweigh localized inconsistencies, including Figure 2's outdated caption and Appendix I's final stationary-loss formula dropping the factor 1/2 present in Equations 79–80.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same teacher-student regression work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable: Appendices A–F in v1 and A–J in v2. Internal caption inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains simulation results and adds experiments on sample-size scaling, optimal stopping versus temperature, and static label noise, including Appendix H, Figure 6.

before.justification: Figures 1–4 report original numerical simulations of learning dynamics, generalization error, bias–variance decomposition, and regularization effects, compared with theoretical predictions.

title: Dynamics of neural scaling laws in random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about pattern-aware alignment, balanced reinforcement learning, superior TSQA performance, and generalization. Additional comparator evidence does not introduce a new core claim.

C2.justification: v1 Appendix F explicitly connects the failure case to local salient features overriding global direction and suggests stronger regularization for low-signal-to-noise sequences. v2 Section 5.8 retains the attention-bias explanation but omits that specific implication and proposed remedy.

D1.justification: v2 adds a PATRA GitHub repository link below the abstract, providing code-access information absent from v1. The PDFs do not establish the repository's contents or availability. Backbone, hardware, prompts, and disclosed reward settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage remains the four TSQA task categories, MTBench weather and finance tasks, the synthetic decomposition scenario, and common forecasting, anomaly-detection, and classification tasks. The downstream evaluations move from Appendix I to Appendix G without changing coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated TimeOmni-1-7B and ITFormer-7B baselines. Table 2 adds both models plus GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Pro, substantially broadening the comparisons with specialized time-series methods and proprietary models. Existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: The stated 90/10 TSQA split, task metrics, standardized prompts, deterministic decoding, and weather/finance training exclusions remain unchanged. The additional baseline comparisons introduce no documented revision to these protocols.

E4.justification: Component ablations, tuned-versus-zero-shot comparisons, reward balancing, training curves, success/failure cases, and latent-decomposition analysis are retained. Sections 5.9–5.10 relocate analyses already present in v1 Appendices E and G; the failure case also moves into Section 5.8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Deterministic decoding, training-reward smoothing, and the correlation-reporting practice in the decomposition analysis are unchanged.

E6.justification: New baseline results substantially extend Tables 1–2 and alter comparative rankings. TimeOmni-1 reaches 42.56% TSQA reasoning accuracy versus PATRA's 44.59%; ITFormer achieves better 7-day finance MSE, 0.174 versus PATRA's 0.191. Previously reported scores, including PATRA's and the appendix results, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 retain the same latent decomposition, learnable alignment tokens, attention-based fusion, supervised alignment stage, GRPO training, and balanced reward functions. No algorithmic or architectural change is documented.

P1.justification: The revision makes localized structural changes: appendix discussions move into Sections 5.8–5.10, related-work prose is expanded, and acknowledgements, an impact statement, and authorship notes are added. The introduction, methodology, and conclusion remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain baseline rows, and table shading and highlighting are revised. The existing reward-ablation table, failure-case figure, and decomposition figure move into the main text. The underlying diagrams, plotted analyses, and prompt illustrations are retained.

R1.justification: v1's short Appendix H becomes a substantially expanded Appendix F discussing reasoning versus forecasting, missing data and distribution shifts, graph/hypergraph methods, anomaly prediction, and broader multimodal learning. Numerous distinct works are added and several earlier references removed, beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The task formalization and mathematical definitions in Equations 1–14 are retained. Neither version adds or removes theoretical assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: The broader comparisons in Tables 1–2 make the empirical assessment more informative, and the repository link improves access information. Existing diagnostic evidence is also easier to find in the main text. These gains are tempered by shortened limitation discussion and an unrevised Section 5.5 claim of leading all finance metrics, now contradicted by ITFormer's 0.174 MSE versus PATRA's 0.191.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PATRA research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including material moved between appendices and the main text.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines to the TSQA and MTBench comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original TSQA and MTBench evaluations, ablations, a synthetic latent-decomposition analysis, and downstream forecasting, anomaly-detection, and classification results.

title: PATRA: Pattern-Aware Alignment and Balanced Reasoning for Time Series Question Answering

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate a specifically identified, causally steerable routing circuit to a central contribution. v1 leaves the coexistence of shared representations and game-specific predictions unresolved; v2 claims to resolve it through localized conflict processing and emphasizes distinct mid-layer reweighting and early-selection regimes.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a mechanism in which the layer-4 MLP constructs conflict features and layer-5 components route them, and develops the contrast between NoMidFlip reweighting and DelFlank selection. Appendix C.1 adds an explanation of final-layer Iago intervention behavior. It also removes v1's explicit warning that rotational isomorphism alone cannot distinguish one shared representation from multiple similarly structured representations.

D1.justification: v2 specifies component intervention sites, last-token-output zeroing, and activation readout locations for the new circuit analysis. Appendix A's architecture, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, probe-training details, and code/model/data access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use Classic, NoMidFlip, DelFlank, and Iago, including the same pure/mixed training coverage and ambiguous-prefix scenarios. The added circuit experiments investigate existing game and prefix conditions rather than introducing new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: The new circuit experiment compares full-circuit steering with routing-head-only steering and a runner-up layer-5 head using its own learned direction; Figure 6b labels the latter H0 control. Existing random-probe, one-hot-input, null-intervention, and matched/cross-probe comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Section 5.4.2 adds a substantial component-level evaluation protocol: separate direction-learning and held-out steering sets, readouts before attention/after attention/after MLP, and last-token component ablations. New measurements include signed game-ID margins, unique-move branch preference, and wrong-game probability mass. Existing model-training and benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 localized effective NoMidFlip steering to layer 5. v2 adds component and individual-head ablations, tile-conflict projection analysis, steering-strength sensitivity, and controlled circuit steering. These tests investigate which components construct and route game identity and whether the localized circuit causally controls branch selection.

E5.justification: The added circuit analysis reports 1,000 bootstrap resamples for head-ranking stability and a Mann–Whitney test with a rank-biserial effect size. Existing confidence-interval reporting and Appendix A.4's fixed seed 42 and single model-training run are retained; the bootstrap does not establish additional training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial circuit results, including Classic unique-move probability share changing from 0.48 to 0.68 or 0.01 under directional steering, and wrong-game mass increasing from 0.0001 to 0.0115 under ablation. All 12 Table 1 means and intervals and existing plotted results are retained. DelFlank accuracies of 77.4% and 75.8% are now correctly attributed in prose to layers 2 and 3, matching both versions' plots.

M1.justification: Section 5.4.2 extends the intervention procedure from residual-stream game-identity steering to learned component-specific directions applied jointly to the identified MLP–attention-head–MLP circuit. The game framework, transformer architecture, training, and original probing/alignment procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, related-work opening, ambiguity/OOD discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. Former Section 5.5 becomes 5.4.1 alongside the new mechanism subsection; v2 also adds Appendix C.1 and acknowledgments and edits publication information and terminology.

P2.justification: v2 adds a two-panel Figure 6 showing circuit readouts and controlled steering. Existing plots are retained, with some relocation/rescaling and subsequent renumbering; the DelFlank caption corrects layers 1–2 to 2–3. Table 1 is repositioned and its game-name capitalization standardized.

R1.justification: v2 adds Millière and Buckner, Mitchell, Schönemann, and Sikarwar et al., and removes Li et al. (2025) and Richens et al. It clarifies representational versus forward-dynamics meanings of world models while retaining the central positioning against vocabulary-only mOthello. Park et al.'s publication update represents the same work.

T1.justification: Section 3 corrects the stated move-set cardinality from '64 (or 65, including pass)' to 65 for the explicitly defined set containing all board positions and pass. The game-transition mathematics, Bayesian mixture derivation, and normalized-KL alpha score otherwise remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly leaves its central mechanistic puzzle unresolved after layer-level steering. v2's component ablations, matched head control, and held-out circuit steering provide substantially stronger causal evidence for a specific conflict-routing mechanism, materially strengthening the paper's explanatory contribution. Removing the useful Iago-isomorphism caveat weakens qualification, but the new controlled evidence provides a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MetaOthello study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds component-level circuit localization, ablation, and steering results in Section 5.4.2 and Figure 6.

before.justification: v1 reports original transformer-training results, probe measurements, representational alignment, and causal steering experiments in Table 1, Figures 2–6, and the appendices.

title: MetaOthello: A Controlled Study of Multiple World Models in Transformers

C1.justification: The core theoretical contributions remain the same. The abstract narrows the empirical-support claim from validating theoretical results to providing evidence consistent with their qualitative predictions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly qualifies the pretraining objective as an analytical surrogate, discusses prior instruction tuning as a limitation of the MMLU evidence, and limits task-similarity conclusions to the linear setting. It also clarifies multi-head applicability and acknowledges the small gap and limited settings of the new auxiliary experiment.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds a code-access link, and Appendix B.1 newly discloses that the existing two-head experiment does not share query/key parameters across heads. Existing hardware and fine-tuning hyperparameters are retained; repository contents were not inspected.

E1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a task predicting which of four word-count bins contains an MMLU question, replacing its original answer label while retaining the input distribution. Existing linear-regression tasks and MMLU category coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments, including Figures 4–8 and Table 2, is unchanged. The added word-count task reuses the existing full and value-matrix fine-tuning strategies.

E3.justification: The added auxiliary experiment introduces controlled relabeling into 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, and at least 30 words, with a zero-shot base-model check and seven-shot evaluation of fine-tuned models. Previously reported splits, budgets, metrics, and model configurations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new word-count experiment tests whether the fine-tuning trend persists under a task modification intended to reduce confounding by prior task learning. Existing architectural variants and in-distribution versus out-of-distribution analyses are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: The existing MMLU protocol still reports three repeated evaluations, mean accuracy, and standard error. The added word-count results provide point accuracies without additional task-specific run counts, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Appendix B.2 adds 26.67% zero-shot accuracy for the base model on word counting and seven-shot accuracies of 47.76% for value-matrix fine-tuning and 46.57% for full fine-tuning. These are new-task results; existing figures and Table 2 values are unchanged.

M1.justification: The linear-attention architecture, value-matrix fine-tuning strategy, training losses, minimal-update rule, and auxiliary-loss annealing remain unchanged. Separate query/key and two-head variants already appeared in v1 Appendix B.1.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized rewrites to the abstract, pretraining explanation, Section 4.4, experiments, and limitations. Section 5 becomes Experiments, an Architectural Variants heading is added, and publication metadata is updated; the overall narrative structure is retained.

P2.justification: All eight figures and both tables are retained. Figure 6 is relocated, Figures 7–8 and Table 2 move ahead of their appendix discussion, and Figure 1's caption corrects Theorem 4.1 to Corollary 4.1. The changes are limited layout and caption revisions.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive related-work positioning remain unchanged. Reference edits update formatting and bibliographic metadata, including the Matrix Cookbook citation, rather than introducing different research.

T1.justification: The formal definitions, equations, theorem statements, and Appendix A proofs are unchanged apart from citation metadata. The added shared-query/key multi-head discussion explains applicability without introducing a new formal derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the calibration of empirical claims and clarifies important applicability limits in Sections 3, 5, and 6. The auxiliary task provides a limited check on prior-learning concerns, while the code-access statement improves reproducibility information. These gains are modest: the core theory and existing results are unchanged, and the new comparison has a small gap without reported uncertainty.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds empirical results for an auxiliary MMLU word-count task in Appendix B.2.

before.justification: v1 reports original linear-regression experiments and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuning experiments on MMLU, including Figures 4–8 and Table 2.

title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

C1.justification: The abstract replaces the claimed theoretical guarantee of convergence to the exact data manifold with progressive agreement between data-consistency and prior variables. The efficiency discussion emphasizes inference efficiency. The central dual-feedback, SH, bias-reduction and superior-fidelity contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds an SNR/geometry explanation for differing CT, knee and brain gains, interprets high-budget behavior and residual trajectories, and explains computational tradeoffs. It explicitly separates PSNR-versus-NFE evidence from formal optimization convergence, qualifies the supervised comparison's scope, and discusses SH applicability beyond dual-coupled solvers.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 substantially expands baseline documentation with task-specific 10-slice validation, DAPS Langevin parameters and separate budget configurations, SITCOM optimization settings, and the MRI closed-form data-consistency implementation. Runtime hardware, batch size and memory details are added. The CT training recipe and code URL remain, although some new benchmark setups lack dataset/sample specifications.

E1.justification: v2 adds fastMRI brain reconstruction, AAPM and DeepLesion CT evaluation, and natural-image Gaussian deblurring, motion deblurring and 4x super-resolution. AbdomenCT-1K and fastMRI knee coverage remain; knee results move to Appendix B.1.

E2.justification: SITCOM joins the main quantitative comparison, and Appendix B.5 introduces the supervised ProCT comparator, substantially broadening comparison methods. The original four diffusion baselines remain in Table 3. Main CT qualitative panels replace DAPS with SITCOM, while DAPS remains evaluated elsewhere.

E3.justification: v2 adds recommended-budget comparisons: 100 NFEs for DDNM/DDS/DiffPIR, reported budgets of 5x200 for DAPS and 50x10 for SITCOM, and 50/100 NFEs for DC-PnPDP. The original uniform 50-NFE protocol remains in Table 3. New designs include a 200-slice brain subset, sweeps to 1000 NFEs, residual measurements and batch-10 runtime profiling.

E4.justification: The original component ablation and spectral diagnostic remain. v2 adds measurement-residual and dual-state trajectories, extends the budget analysis to examine high-budget plateaus, profiles runtime and memory, tests ProCT under in-domain/OOD conditions, and examines SH transfer to DDNM.

E5.justification: Unlike v1's point estimates, v2 Table 6 reports mean ± standard deviation for natural-image restoration. The aggregation unit, repeated-run counts and seeds are unspecified, so this establishes additional variability reporting, not additional independent runs.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 is preserved numerically as v2 Table 3, and the component ablation is unchanged. v2 adds substantial results under its expanded protocols: Table 1 reports LACT PSNR 39.46 versus DiffPIR's 34.70 at 100 NFEs, and brain AF=10 PSNR 30.91 versus SITCOM's 28.67 under their reported budgets. Runtime, cross-dataset CT, natural-image and extended-budget findings are also new; these are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core DC-PnPDP updates and diffusion-prior architecture are retained. Appendix B.6 adds a procedural adaptation that inserts SH into DDNM by replacing its standard DDIM re-noising step, although the authors present this as a scope diagnostic.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the empirical narrative into recommended-budget main results and controlled-budget appendix results, adds a dedicated Related Work section and structured diagnostic/discussion subsections, and rewrites the MRI and efficiency discussions. Much of the method and theoretical prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: The main table gains budget columns and separate DC-PnPDP rows; the original table and knee figure move to the appendix. Main qualitative examples are replaced, Figure 4 is redrawn over a logarithmic budget range to 1000 NFEs, and new runtime, residual, ProCT and natural-image displays are added. Appendix CT panels are also replaced and include SITCOM.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantially expands positioning against PnP-ADMM convergence, adaptation and stochastic methods, plus concurrent diffusion/ADMM approaches. It explicitly distinguishes SH from AC-DC's Langevin correction, stochastic generative PnP, dual-ascent diffusion and colored re-noising. These are substantive additions beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The explanation of Eq. (13) corrects the Fourier normalization convention from a unitary DFT to an unnormalized FFT, making the stated HW scaling consistent. The spectral-consistency proposition and bootstrap/fixed-point assumptions, theorems and proofs otherwise retain their substance; appendices B–D become C–E.

improvement.justification: v1 supported efficiency mainly through uniform 50-NFE comparisons and a short budget sweep. v2 preserves that control while testing recommended and larger budgets, adding residual diagnostics and measured runtime, and clarifying positioning against closely related work. These changes substantially strengthen evidence for the central benefits. Some added experiments remain underspecified, Tables 1 and 3 contain unreconciled 50-NFE CT scores, and convergence claims remain incompletely qualified, but the overall gain in validation and transparency is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DC-PnPDP work. Text, equations, tables, figures and all appendices are readable. Retained material can be matched despite substantial additions and relocation of the original main results.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and reports additional brain MRI, cross-dataset CT, natural-image restoration, residual and runtime results.

before.justification: v1 reports original CT and fastMRI knee reconstruction experiments, component ablations, spectral diagnostics and inference-budget results.

title: Plug-and-Play Diffusion Meets ADMM: Dual-Variable Coupling for Robust Medical Image Reconstruction

C1.justification: The central claims remain low-supervision alignment using a linear teacher, effective use of unpaired data, efficient KLOT differentiation and robustness across datasets and encoders. The contribution list and conclusion retain their scientific scope; the new experiments provide additional support.

C2.justification: v1 cautions that more encoder-pair observations are needed for firm conclusions; v2 presents mutual k-NN as a reliable diagnostic before alignment. v2 also substantially expands practical interpretations: teacher robustness is attributed to limited linear capacity and OT invariance, mismatched unpaired data are described as producing graceful degradation, and entropy/loss-weight choices receive mechanism-based explanations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and documents the WavLM-Large speech encoder, corruption construction and additional hyperparameter searches. Most optimizer, architecture, hardware and baseline implementation details in Appendix A remain unchanged. The conflicting teacher-temperature values in Section 6.1 and Appendix A.1 reduce the clarity of the new guidance.

E1.justification: v2 adds SkyScript satellite-image/text retrieval and LibriSpeech speech/text retrieval, substantially extending the evaluated domains and modalities beyond v1's general image–text benchmarks. It also introduces synthetic-noise scenarios for unpaired embeddings while retaining the earlier dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding existing comparisons retain their comparator membership and baseline implementations, including Tables 4–6 and Appendix A.2. The added domain experiments reuse previously evaluated CCA, SAIL and STRUCTURE. UOT-RCL is newly cited but is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols include SkyScript evaluation with 10k/30k test pools, LibriSpeech training with 1k pairs and 100k unpaired samples, weaker-encoder configurations, corruption sweeps and temperature searches using 500 Sinkhorn iterations. Section 6.1 reports teacher epsilon*=0.005, whereas v1 and the retained v2 Appendix A.1 specify 0.01. This leaves the actual default and whether retained experiments were rerun unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 adds teacher-pair corruption experiments, unpaired Gaussian-noise stress tests, loss-weight sensitivity across supervision/noise levels, and teacher/student temperature sweeps (Appendix B.2). It also adds Sinkhorn convergence analysis and extends encoder-similarity analysis to ResNet-50 and BERT. These substantially expand examination of robustness and design dependencies.

E5.justification: Both versions report spherical sliced Wasserstein distances as means and standard deviations over 20 seeds, using 100,000-sample subsets (v1 Appendix B.4/Figure 12; v2 Appendix B.3/Figure 15). No new run-count disclosure, significance test or uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented. Updated correlations are changes in results.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark tables retain their values, but substantial new results appear. v2 Table 7 reports SOTAlign SkyScript T2I/I2T R@10 of 27.3/27.4 and LibriSpeech S2T/T2S R@1 of 78.4/83.1. Table 8 reports 26.6 COCO MeanR@1 with 50% teacher-pair corruption versus 23.6 for SAIL. Expanded analyses report encoder-similarity correlation 0.95 instead of 0.83 and distribution-shift correlation -0.76 instead of -0.72.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same linear-teacher stage followed by alignment with supervised SigLIP and unpaired-data KLOT regularization. The corrected main-text gradient already appears correctly in v1's appendix; it does not establish an implementation change. The new modality experiments apply the existing framework.

P1.justification: Section 6 is reorganized into dedicated design-choice, supervision, data-source, encoder and benchmarking subsections, and Appendix B reorders distribution-shift and benchmarking material. Related work is tightened, local language is corrected, and affiliation/publication text is updated. Much of the existing prose and overall narrative is retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the experimental displays with convergence, sensitivity and satellite-retrieval plots plus new Tables 7–8. Distribution-shift and encoder-similarity plots are expanded and redrawn; the latter moves from v1 Appendix Figure 9 to v2 main-text Figure 7. Existing tables and several figures are also redistributed within the revised layout.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds UOT-RCL as prior OT-based frozen-encoder alignment addressing noisy labels and revises the CLIP background. References for the additional datasets and encoders are added. Positioning relative to OT-CLIP, S-CLIP, SUE and STRUCTURE remains substantially unchanged; the existing Assel/Monge Gap discussion moves from the appendix to Section 5.

T1.justification: Theorem 5.1, Equation 13, corrects the gradient denominator from teacher epsilon* to student epsilon, agreeing with Theorem C.4 and its proof already present in v1. Section 3.3 also corrects projection-matrix dimensions. The appendix's mathematical results and derivations otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by testing satellite and speech applications and examining teacher corruption, extreme unpaired-data mismatch and tuning sensitivity that v1 did not establish. These additions address important gaps in support for applicability and robustness. The corrected gradient statement and code-access information also help. The new inconsistency between teacher temperatures in Section 6.1 and Appendix A.1 limits reproducibility, but does not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SOTAlign work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds satellite-image and speech retrieval, corruption experiments and hyperparameter sensitivity studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval and classification experiments, alignment ablations, supervision sweeps and gradient-computation efficiency measurements.

title: SOTAlign: Semi-Supervised Alignment of Unimodal Vision and Language Models via Optimal Transport

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about delta actions, joint-space robustness, and task-space advantages in transfer and cross-embodiment learning.

C2.justification: The mechanism explanations and interpretations remain unchanged, as do Appendix B's limitations concerning fixed taxonomies, more complex morphologies/tasks, and broader transfer validation.

D1.justification: Section 3.2 newly identifies RoboTwin hard mode, and Appendix E.2 identifies the official RoboTwin-2.0 demonstration-generation tool. These clarify experimental provenance without establishing changed procedures. The code/data release statement remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same real-world tasks, ten RoboTwin tasks, robotic platforms, and transfer settings. Newly specifying simulation 'hard mode' does not establish that a different scenario was evaluated.

E2.justification: ACT/regression, DP/flow matching, and the four action-space configurations retain their comparison roles. The revised simulation table retains both ACT and DP; no comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: The main protocol and scaling plots remain unchanged. However, 79 of 80 task-level mean/error pairs in v2 Table 6 match means and standard errors calculated from the first three epoch-labeled columns of v1 Tables 9–10, now described as independent trials. The PDFs do not resolve whether this corrects labels or changes the evaluation design.

E4.justification: The scaling analyses remain in Appendix F.2 and Figure 10, alongside the other cross-validation studies. Removing v1 Tables 7–10 nevertheless removes task-specific data/compute sensitivity breakdowns, reducing the detail supporting those analyses.

E5.justification: v2 Table 6 adds task-level means and uncertainty summaries corresponding largely to point estimates previously tabulated under epoch settings. Both versions already specify three trials of ten rollouts, so additional runs are not established. The reinterpretation of the underlying observations as independent trials remains unexplained.

E6.justification: Appendix H removes v1's real-world across-setting summary (Table 6) and detailed simulation data/epoch grids (Tables 7–10), replacing them with task-level trial aggregates. This substantially changes the detailed numerical evidence. Main results remain unchanged: for example, Table 1 retains simulation delta-joint averages of 46.3 ± 1.9 for ACT and 48.0 ± 4.4 for DP.

M1.justification: The action representations, chunk-wise decoding, regression and flow-matching architectures and losses, and π0 fine-tuning procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Edits are localized: updated version dates, expanded EEF terminology, standardized RoboTwin naming, and a short demonstration-source clarification. The section organization and substantive narrative remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Appendix H's tabular presentation is substantially restructured: v1 Tables 6–10 disappear, and v2 introduces one table pairing ACT/DP rows by task with uncertainty values. Table 5 is repositioned on its own page. All twelve figures remain unchanged in content.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning are unchanged. Expanding EEF to End-Effector in Appendix C is a terminology edit.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, Proposition 4.1, and Appendix G's formalization, noise-amplification proof, and derivations are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 clarifies simulation provenance, removes duplicated ACT summary rows, and provides a more readable uncertainty table, but loses detailed scaling results. The epoch-versus-trial interpretation remains unresolved, and the new table's DP delta-joint task means average 47.3%, whereas its overall row reports 48.0%. These reporting concerns and the unexplained aggregation prevent a reliable net judgment against the gains in clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–H. The complete material supports comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original real-world robotic manipulation and RoboTwin simulation experiments, including action-space comparisons, scaling studies, and transfer learning.

title: Demystifying Action Space Design for Robotic Manipulation Policies

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about the sleep-text dataset, ReCoCa, language-grounded sleep understanding, and unseen-concept capabilities. The added comparisons support the existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: Appendix D.4 newly attributes foundation models' comparative strengths partly to parameter scale and transferable representations, discussing Chronos-2's strong fine-tuning performance. Table 6 interprets the older demographic skew as consistent with clinical prevalence. The stated clinical-validation and cohort-coverage limitations remain unchanged.

Appendix D.4 describes baseline pretraining alignment and Chronos-2 checkpoint use. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware, preprocessing, prompts, and code-access information are unchanged.

Appendix D.4 adds CFS evaluation with 10-shot and 50-shot linear probing and full fine-tuning, reporting AUC on its test split. It specifies shared pretraining splits for sleep models and use of Chronos-2's public checkpoint. These introduce substantial additional evaluation designs.

title: CARE: Confounder-Aware Aggregation for Reliable LLM Evaluation

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation and language-model experiments, training ablations, a 99-prompt human evaluation, and RTX 5090 kernel benchmarks.

improvement.justification: v2 identifies LittleBit-2 in the title and updates publication metadata, with minor reflow on pages 1–2. Existing reasoning and appendix scores remain numerically unchanged; these additions are new experimental results, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Section 5.2 and Algorithm 2 replace multiple windows covering all target tokens with one fixed-size window covering the most targets. The revised algorithm additionally requires more than one target within the window before activating PC guidance and changes the state-update rule to sample within that window while preserving positions outside it. The core architecture, training objective, and block-diffusion procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 separates reasoning benchmarks from a new natural-language experiments section, shifts subsequent section numbering, adds acknowledgements, and updates publication information. The relationship between the new 80-policy analysis and that 100-sample protocol is unexplained.

Appendix F examines selection effects through unselected and worst-architecture performance, while Appendix I quantifies architecture diversity under unconditional sampling. The histogram display is more compact, while existing diagrams, heatmaps, rollouts, and main result-table structures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the original novelty positioning remain unchanged. The appendix adds focused positioning against CLIP prompt learning, head adaptation and feature replay, with additional references for CLIP, SimpleCIL, RAPF, PROOF, self-supervised pretraining and the new datasets.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds proofs of Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 and a derivation of the general-subspace solution in Eq. 4. Section B.4 additionally develops a gradient-alignment expansion and a future-loss bound using a newly stated gradient-cone assumption with bounded residual. These substantially expand the formal analysis.

improvement.justification: Appendices A–C address substantial gaps in v1 by supplying missing derivations, making the training pipeline explicit, and extending limited sensitivity and backbone evidence with controlled analyses. This materially improves the method's inspectability and empirical support. New reporting inconsistencies remain, including the VPT-NSP discrepancy between Tables 6–7 and the UCF split mismatch, and the GAO argument is conditional on its cone assumption. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in explanation and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoDA research work and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. V1 ends after its references; v2 retains the main study and adds Appendices A–C. The added appendix is a substantive addition, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original sensitivity studies, CLIP evaluations, backbone and model-size comparisons, and loss-landscape analyses in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original continual-learning experiments on five datasets, component ablations, projection-energy analyses and computational comparisons in Tables 1–6 and Figures 3–6.

title: Task-Driven Subspace Decomposition for Knowledge Sharing and Isolation in LoRA-based Continual Learning

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion newly state that SPARe is independent of model architecture and inner parallelism topology. The central availability, 2–3× overhead, and 40–50% time-to-train claims remain unchanged; checkpointing complementarity is retained in Section 6.

C2.justification: v2 explains that heterogeneous or correlated failures can affect the accuracy of the closed-form averages while preserving survivor-set feasibility, and suggests placement across failure domains. It also adds explanations of gradient and optimizer-state preservation and the suitability of long-horizon simulation.

D1.justification: Section 2.1 newly spells out the mapping between N model-parallel replicas and M data-parallel communicators of world size N, clarifying communicator-level recovery and shrink-cost assumptions. Numerical settings and the supplementary reordering.ipynb access reference remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same simulated 600k-H100 pretraining scenario and Monte Carlo configurations with N = 200, 600, and 1000. Newly discussed correlated failures and other application domains are not added evaluation scenarios.

E2.justification: Section 5 retains Rep+CKPT and CKPT-only as the evaluated comparators. Systems added to the related-work discussion and alternative simulators discussed in Appendix F are not evaluated against SPARe.

E3.justification: Table 1 retains the same settings, including Weibull shape 0.78, 300-second MTBF, 3,600-second restart cost, and 10,000 training steps. Metrics and testing procedures are unchanged; the expanded topology and simulator descriptions clarify existing settings.

E4.justification: The redundancy sweeps and Monte Carlo validation are retained without additional analyses. The new correlated-failure discussion supplies no robustness tests, and Appendix F discusses prior simulator validation rather than reporting a new validation experiment.

E5.justification: Both versions report three discrete-event trials, three-trial averages in Table 2, and 1,000 Monte Carlo trials per configuration. Per-trial plots and uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: All result figures and numerical table entries match. Table 2 retains gains of 51.9%, 41.7%, and 39.6%, and Appendix C retains the same simulation values and formula-agreement statistics.

M1.justification: Appendix D introduces binary search as an optional replacement for HK-FREE's linear depth scan. This is a limited procedural alternative; Algorithms 1–2 retain their original steps, and the PDFs do not report adopting it in the experiments.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites Section 2.1, refines parallelism terminology across several sections, and adds a related-work section and simulator-choice appendix. These are localized expansions; most prose and the method–theory–evaluation organization remain intact.

P2.justification: All nine figure images are unchanged. Table 2 removes misleading '[days]' labels above normalized time-to-train values, while tables and Figure 9 are repositioned during reflow. Running headers and publication formatting also change.

R1.justification: The new Section 6 substantially expands positioning relative to storage-assisted recovery, TrainMover, Bamboo, ReCycle, and FT-HSDP, explaining their relationship to SPARe's abstraction layer. Appendix F additionally contrasts SimGrid with ASTRA-sim and Calculon and expands the simulator-validation literature.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds the HK-FREE monotonicity argument supporting an O(r)-to-O(log r) reduction in search calls. The stated condition for attaining Eq. (6) changes from instantaneous failure detection to detection before global all-reduce. The main formulas and Appendix B proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 improves clarity through the parallelism mapping and gradient-preservation explanation, adds useful qualifications about correlated failures, strengthens research positioning, and corrects Table 2's unit labels. These are supported improvements in exposition and interpretation; the empirical evidence and core proofs remain unchanged, and the broader applicability discussion adds no experimental validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPARe research work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including the additional Appendix F in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains the original discrete-event simulation results and Appendix C Monte Carlo results.

before.justification: v1 reports original SimGrid discrete-event simulations in Section 5 and Monte Carlo validation over 1,000 trials per configuration in Appendix C.

title: SPARe: Stacked Parallelism with Adaptive Reordering for Fault-Tolerant LLM Pretraining Systems with 100k+ GPUs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: two preference datasets, a unified compositional benchmark, a parameter-efficient reward model competitive with specialized baselines, and useful best-of-N filtering. Added analyses support these claims without materially changing their scope.

C2.justification: New Appendix D explicitly discusses reward-hacking limitations, incomplete separation of the scoring heads, and genre/language biases. The contextual-musicality discussion expands the earlier taste-anchor explanation into alternative hypotheses involving human judgment entanglement and statistical shortcuts. New ablation interpretations address teacher dependence and cross-modal fusion bottlenecks, substantially broadening applicability and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v3 adds a direct model-weights link and discloses listening-study counts of 50 prompts, 200 generations, and 300 comparisons. It documents configurations for the new ablations, transcription tie handling, and per-generator sample counts and ranking aggregation. The core implementation description and complete LLM-judge prompts are retained; several sample-count descriptions remain inconsistent.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and tasks remain CMI-Pref-Pseudo, CMI-Pref, PAM, MusicEval, Music Arena, and MusicCaps, covering musicality and text/lyrics/reference-audio alignment. AIME and MusicPref are added to descriptive comparisons but explicitly excluded from benchmark testing. The transcription analysis and generator leaderboard reuse existing data and conditioning scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 adds Omni-Reward to the main musicality and alignment comparisons and corresponding appendix breakdowns. Appendix I.1 additionally compares Whisper-derived WER preference prediction with CMI-RM on lyric-conditioned pairs. Existing comparators are retained, making this a focused expansion.

E3.justification: Table 4 changes Music Arena prediction from the combined musicality-plus-alignment score to musicality alone. Added experiments introduce 70k-Qwen/40k-Gemini supervision, three reward-head sizes, Flan-T5 substitution, WER tie exclusion, and prompt-wise round-robin generator ranking. These substantially expand experimental protocols. H.2 reports 2,800 objective-reranking prompts while Section 3.3.3 retains 2,183, leaving that sample count unresolved.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial checks of teacher dependence, mixed pseudo-label sources, model capacity, text-encoder substitution, and transcription as a preference proxy. It also analyzes listening behavior and re-annotates the test set to assess reliability. Earlier smoothing, data-size, mapping, prompt-conditioning, duration, and subgroup analyses remain, sometimes relocated or consolidated.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's agreement statistics and descriptive reporting, v3 adds Wilson 95% confidence intervals for test-label agreement, benchmark significance checks in H.1, and listening-test p-values with an explicitly stated one-sided binomial procedure in H.2. The benchmark test procedure is not specified, and some associated accuracies conflict with tables. No increase in reward-model training seeds or repeated runs is documented.

E6.justification: Most retained headline scores are unchanged, but v3 substantially expands results with Omni-Reward, re-annotation agreement, teacher and architecture ablations, WER prediction, and generator rankings. Table 4's Distill+Both Music Arena accuracy changes from 72.46% to 73.43% under the revised scoring rule, not a demonstrated same-setting gain. New results include 75.0% alignment and 75.2% musicality re-annotation agreement and 60.0% WER-based accuracy on 225 non-tied comparisons.

M1.justification: The proposed CMI-RM retains frozen MuQ-MuLan encoders, prompt and joint Transformers, two scoring heads, and the same two-stage training objectives and reranking procedure. New head sizes, Flan-T5 substitution, and mixed-teacher supervision are investigated as ablation variants; they do not replace the proposed pipeline.

P1.justification: v3 substantially revises the presentation of existing material: it clarifies training versus benchmarking data, compresses benchmark discussion and the conclusion, reorganizes appendix sections, and rewrites the contextual-musicality narrative. It also consolidates duplicated Music Arena discussion and adds a conflict-of-interest disclosure. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: v3 adds duration/listening-time histograms and a scatterplot, plus tables for reliability, new ablations, significance checks, and generator leaderboards. Table 1 gains dataset columns and an official-split row, while comparison tables gain Omni-Reward rows. The duplicated Music Arena regression table is consolidated. Existing main diagrams and preference heatmaps are retained, with caption and placement changes.

R1.justification: v3 introduces Omni-Reward as a general-purpose reward-model comparator and expands positioning against AIME, MusicPref, and SongEval, explaining their exclusion from the benchmark test sets. The central research gap remains unchanged. Numerous other reference edits correct or update citations for already-discussed models rather than introduce new research directions.

T1.justification: The model equations, Bradley–Terry formulation, regression mapping, and label-smoothing mathematics are retained. Equation 4 merely rewrites equal loss weights as an equivalent average. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v3's additions concern empirical evaluation rather than new formal theory.

improvement.justification: v3 provides more direct checks of benchmark reliability and teacher dependence, broader ablations, an additional relevant baseline, and clearer limitations. These improve the paper's evidential transparency. However, new inconsistencies limit the gain: H.1 reports 78.60% for the CMI-Pref model while Table 2 reports 77.80%, and A.3 describes four re-annotators while Table 7 specifies three. Conflicting reranking sample counts further weaken reproducibility. The net improvement is supported but limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CMI-RewardBench study. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial appendix additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds test-set re-annotation, teacher-source and architecture ablations, a transcription-based comparison, and generator rankings.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model evaluations, training ablations, human-preference analyses, and best-of-N generation experiments, including Tables 2–5 and Figure 3.

title: CMI-RewardBench: Evaluating Music Reward Models with Compositional Multimodal Instruction

C1.justification: The abstract, three stated contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about dense counterfactual credit, information-theoretic grounding, performance and generalization, including the claimed 14%–16% improvement over GRPO-based methods. The new diagnostics support these contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 explicitly states that InfoPO requires some task-relevant continuations and cannot recover useful structure from entirely degenerate trajectories or uninformative feedback. The new analyses also strengthen the interpretation of the reward as task-relevant sensitivity and of gating as protection against generic-question reward hacking. The existing limitations paragraph is retained.

D1.justification: Appendices B.5–B.6 add operational criteria for classifying action quality and question types and clarify that these labels are used only for analysis. These provide reproduction information for the new diagnostics, although implementation details remain limited. Existing hyperparameters, hardware, simulator prompts and code-access information are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same UserGym environments, ColBench backend programming tasks, tau2-Bench domains, Sokoban, WebShop and simulator-shift scenarios. The added diagnostics examine retained task coverage without introducing a new dataset or interaction scenario.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in the benchmark and generalization experiments are unchanged. The new reward-hacking analysis reuses the existing without-gate ablation. IGPO is newly discussed in related work but is not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendices B.5–B.6 introduce post-hoc protocols that stratify current and next actions by quality, inspect the highest-reward 10% of turns, and compare targeted versus generic questions after matching response lengths. Existing training settings, splits and benchmark evaluation protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations, masking sensitivity and interaction dynamics, v2 directly investigates whether information gain distinguishes useful from meaningless transitions and whether the variance gate prevents generic-question reward hacking. Tables 6–7 and Figures 10–11 substantially expand validation of the central reward mechanism.

E5.justification: Appendix B.5 adds a significance assessment comparing rewards for good and meaningless current actions, reporting p = 1.4 × 10^-108 without identifying the test. Existing three-seed mean-and-standard-deviation curves, four-run tau2-Bench evaluation and masking significance tests are unchanged.

E6.justification: The original benchmark results remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial diagnostic findings. Table 6 reports mean rewards of 0.380 versus 0.017 for good versus meaningless current actions. Table 7 reports length-matched targeted-versus-generic reward gaps of 0.319 for InfoPO and -0.055 without gating, alongside new question-frequency and interaction-length results.

M1.justification: Equations (2)–(6) and Algorithm 1 retain the same counterfactual reward, normalization, variance gate and policy objective. The added support discussion clarifies applicability; the new diagnostic labels are explicitly excluded from training.

P1.justification: v2 adds localized method clarification, diagnostic summaries, Appendices B.5–B.6 and an Impact Statement, with limited related-work editing. It also replaces the preprint footer with proceedings information. The retained prose and overall section organization undergo little rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds a substantial diagnostic display block: Tables 6–7 and multi-panel Figures 10–11 showing sensitivity distributions, threshold rates and action-quality transitions. Existing figures retain their content but move with the text; the earlier case-study and prompt Figures 10–18 become Figures 12–20.

R1.justification: Related work newly contrasts IGPO's answer-conditioned belief improvement with InfoPO's masked-feedback action sensitivity. The bibliography adds IGPO, two Kong et al. papers, AutoEnv and USM, and removes Zhao et al.'s preference-following paper. The broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Theorems 1–2, their proofs and the method's mathematical derivations are unchanged. Appendix B.6 adds the mathematical definition of a new diagnostic, the length-matched information-gain gap, as the expected reward difference over matched targeted-clarification and generic-question pairs.

improvement.justification: The action-quality analysis and length-controlled gate comparison provide more direct evidence against arbitrary-distribution-shift and verbosity explanations than v1's existing diagnostics. The explicit support requirement also clarifies a failure boundary. These additions strengthen the mechanism argument, although incomplete sampling, labeling and significance-test details limit their evidential strength. The improvement is therefore useful but bounded.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InfoPO study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds original action-quality and reward-hacking analyses in Appendices B.5–B.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original InfoPO evaluations, training curves, ablations and robustness analyses on UserGym, ColBench, tau2-Bench, Sokoban and WebShop.

title: InfoPO: Information-Driven Policy Optimization for User-Centric Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the central claims: synthetic data supports transfer to grounded environments, light prompt selection performs strongly, and heavier optimization encounters saturation or overfitting. The new end-to-end-framework wording summarizes existing contributions; added experiments provide further evidence rather than redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: v1 presents distribution mismatch and prompting limitations as possible explanations and suggests fine-tuning as future work. v2 argues neither alone explains saturation, discusses the DSPy objective mismatch, and adds interpretations of detection cues and failures. It also qualifies SFT as a limited lower-bound pilot, explains length-filtering comparability limits, and recognizes complementary benefits of trustworthy agent CoT.

D1.justification: Appendix F.5 adds substantial implementation information: Tinker access, rank-32 LoRA, AdamW, batch size, epochs, learning-rate selection, loss masks, reasoning-token handling and filtering counts. v2 also newly quantifies the existing unsuccessful-side-task exclusion at approximately 49% and states that synthetic data is shared selectively rather than publicly released.

E1.justification: Both versions cover STRIDE, Gloom and the same five ControlArena environments: AgentDojo, BashBench, Infrastructure-as-Code, RogueEval and SHADE Arena. The added experiments reuse this coverage; pooling, length filtering and using ControlArena for optimization change experimental protocols rather than introduce new tasks or domains.

E2.justification: Section 5.4 introduces supervised fine-tuning as an evaluated alternative to prompt sweep, human refinement and GEPA on the same Kimi base model, substantially broadening comparison beyond prompt optimization. Appendix E.2 also adds an action-plus-CoT comparator. The original comparisons, including MIPROv2, remain.

E3.justification: The new Kimi pilot pools 2,000 synthetic trajectories, reports an approximately 580-example validation split, and applies a common 24,000-token filter yielding approximately 6,700 test trajectories. It introduces fine-tuning budgets, learning-rate selection and inference-thinking controls. Section 6 separately reports optimization on 1,000 ControlArena trajectories. These are added protocols, not revisions established for the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 newly reports a dataset-size pre-study, an in-distribution optimization control, action-only versus action-plus-CoT monitoring, and qualitative inspection of detection cues and failures. Appendix F.5 adds SFT target and inference ablations, learning-rate sensitivity and score-collapse diagnostics. These substantially expand investigation of the performance ceiling.

E5.justification: The original bootstrap intervals and three-repeat inference analysis are retained. The new SFT pilot reports three-seed final runs, median-seed performance and seed ranges, explicitly identifies a one-seed ablation, and specifies stratified bootstrap with n = 2,500 in Table 6. This extends uncertainty reporting without establishing additional runs for existing results.

E6.justification: Original headline scores and result plots are retained. New Figure 7 reports Kimi pAUROC of 0.718 untuned, 0.907 for the best prompt, 0.906 for human refinement, 0.900 for GEPA and 0.907 for SFT. Tables 6 and 8 add ablation and environment results; Section 6 adds 0.81 [0.79, 0.83] for ControlArena-based optimization. The Kimi results use different models and filtering, preventing direct performance comparisons with v1.

M1.justification: v2 adds a weight-training approach to the previously prompt-optimized monitors: LoRA supervised fine-tuning of Kimi K2.6. Appendix F.5 specifies score-only and reasoning-containing targets, supervision at scores 1 and 10, and answer-only loss masking. This substantially extends the optimization procedures studied; STRIDE and Gloom generation remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized terminology and prose edits, clarifies contribution framing, expands the discussion, updates affiliation/publication boilerplate, and adds dataset-characteristics, pilot, diagnostics and impact subsections. The overall section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v1's Figure 3 test-generation illustration is replaced by a synthetic-trajectory walkthrough. v2 adds the Kimi comparison plot as Figure 7 and Tables 6–8, with accompanying caption and placement changes. Existing result graphics, including the Appendix H panels, are retained with renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.6 and Thinking Machines Lab's Tinker. Section 2 also clarifies that its constitutional approach uses a single scheming definition, distinguishing it from a multi-category threat taxonomy. The broader related-work framing is retained.

T1.justification: The scheming definition, monitor formalization and normalized partial-AUROC definition are unchanged. Neither version develops theorem-and-proof results, and the new empirical procedures introduce no substantive theoretical derivation.

improvement.justification: Where v1 leaves fine-tuning as future work, v2 supplies a controlled pilot, useful ablations and substantially clearer implementation and filtering disclosures. These strengthen support and transparency, but do not establish a general ceiling: the pilot is narrow and some additional controls are sparsely documented. Interpretation also occasionally overreaches; Table 8 calls methods essentially tied despite RogueEval scores spanning 0.655–0.788. Overall, the additions provide a limited net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, tables and Appendices A–H are readable and support reliable comparison across additions, relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds a Kimi K2.6 fine-tuning pilot, associated diagnostics and further analyses of monitoring performance.

before.justification: v1 reports original monitoring experiments on STRIDE, Gloom and ControlArena, including prompt optimization, scoring ablations and repeated-inference analyses.

title: Constitutional Black-Box Monitoring for Scheming in LLM Agents

C1.justification: The introduction revises advertised error-recovery success from 88.7% to 90.0%, alongside the newly explicit success definition. The training-free FSM and grounding contributions, abstract's 95.6% compliance claim, and conclusion about the necessity of symbolic safety interlocks remain.

C2.justification: Appendix G introduces reasoning-context overflow as a limitation of thinking-model backbones and emphasizes efficiency with lightweight models. Section 4.6 interprets the revised 0.782 ablation score as unchanged corrupted-input compliance. Appendix F adds trajectory-complexity arguments and repair limitations; the original simulation and hardware-registration limitations remain.

D1.justification: Previously absent appendices now provide tool signatures, expanded FSM rules, representative hardware schemas, metric weights and thresholds, benchmark composition, and planner, alignment, and baseline prompts. These substantially improve implementation and evaluation documentation. Existing code and project links are retained.

E2.justification: Section 4.2.4 adds Oracle-ReAct with forced verification, and Table 17 adds direct DeepSeek-V3.2-Think and Gemini-3-Pro-Think comparisons on Subsets C/D. These substantially strengthen the alternatives tested. Qwen and Kimi gain Table 3 rows but already appeared in v1's Figure 1.

E3.justification: Table 4 replaces Subset D sequence accuracy with correction success, explicitly defined as Cp > 0.8. Added experiments introduce forced-PASS termination for Oracle-ReAct and direct-versus-agent configurations for thinking models. Other newly supplied settings document existing experiments without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether mandatory verification rescues ReAct and whether stronger reasoning models replace or improve the framework. Appendix F.2 adds quantitative error-type breakdowns. Existing component ablations remain, with materially revised Subset D outcomes and explanations.

E5.justification: Both already report paired t-tests and cross-judge Pearson correlations. Tables 11 and 13 supply more detailed outcomes under those practices. No new repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or statistical estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Subset D Cp changes from 0.887 to 0.925. Table 6 changes w/o FSM from 0.000 to 0.782 and w/o Verification from 0.870 to 0.782. Added results include detailed judge/error breakdowns and Table 17's strong direct-model performance and agent-backbone failures. The new 90.0% correction success is a different metric from v1's 0.464 sequence accuracy.

M1.justification: The overall FSM, memory, and hierarchical verification architecture remains. The stated planner projection changes from symbolic keys alone to keys with semantic previews (Equation 2), and Equation 3 replaces the APPROVED-state execution condition with a verified-code condition.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most narrative remain. Localized rewrites expand memory/control explanations and revise error-correction and ablation passages. Grammar, affiliations, acknowledgments, and cross-references change, while the new appendices organize supporting material.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive appendix tables covering specifications, statistical checks, task complexity, error breakdowns, model scaling, and execution logs, plus boxed prompt listings. Table 3 expands and Table 4 changes its correction metric column. Existing figures are largely retained, with some displays relocated or elaborated.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds physics-aware rejection sampling through Hyun et al. New appendix citations include KeyBERT and Gemini 3 Pro. The broader research positioning remains; updates to SciAgents and other existing references principally correct bibliographic information.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces the five-bit signal space with mixed Boolean/ternary signals and revises formal grounding and execution definitions. Appendix E supplies custom score definitions, while Appendix F.1 adds a compounding-error calculation. The conditional safety assumptions remain, without a new safety proof.

improvement.justification: v1 directs readers to absent appendices for essential specifications and validation. v2 supplies much of that material and adds challenging controls that expose important strengths and failures, substantially improving reproducibility and assessability. Important issues remain: Appendix E.3 requires Cp = 1 for success, whereas Table 4 reports 100% success with Cp = 0.950, and Table 17's strong direct-model results qualify the retained necessity claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same BioProAgent study, with matching core sections, experiments, and figures. v1 ends after the references despite citing appendices; v2 supplies Appendices A-I. Newly documented material can be distinguished from retained content.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and reports additional Oracle-ReAct, error-type, and thinking-model evaluations.

before.justification: Sections 4.2-4.6 report original BioProBench simulation results, including benchmark comparisons, error correction, execution traces, and component ablations.

title: BioProAgent: Neuro-Symbolic Grounding for Constrained Scientific Planning

C1.justification: The headline attribution claim is redefined: v1's abstract states that 50% of misalignment variation is shared across models; v2 states that model/prompt selection reliably accounts for only 15% of measured error. The revised conclusion emphasizes evidence-conditioned higher-order interactions. The principal convergence, impact-misalignment, and ensemble-failure claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning prompt brittleness, shared error direction despite variable magnitude, and transcript-conditioned failures. Its new limitations qualify variance estimates by the sampled measurement design, and Appendix C.4 acknowledges confounding with true-score/VAM measurement error. These substantially extend and qualify v1's emphasis on systemic pretraining bias.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly specifies scaling by two standard deviations and supplies human-error model code. Figure 7 updates the fitting call and changes reported thinning from 25 to 20. Data, code, and model-output access links remain unchanged; the corresponding residualized-results table loses its N column in v2.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same NCTE fourth- and fifth-grade US mathematics classrooms and seven CLASS/MQI rating tasks, with four focal alignment tasks. The seven-item signed-error analysis in v2 reuses tasks already evaluated in v1; it does not introduce new classroom populations or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds an explicit human-expert error-decomposition comparator in Appendix C.6 and Table 8. Figure 4's caption also newly reports uniform and stratified random-score baseline outcomes. The main LLM, encoder, expert-rating, teacher-experience, and prior-VAM comparator lineup is retained.

E3.justification: The error-analysis protocol changes from regression residuals to squared standardized-score discrepancies, with additional signed-error fits over four and seven items. New decision studies vary the numbers of models and prompts averaged. The underlying classroom test set, 16-model evaluation, three prompt families, and temperature-zero querying remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds analyses of error direction, sensitivity to including all seven items, human-versus-LLM error structure, and reliability under different model/prompt averaging designs. Figure 12 adds noise-controlled ensemble alignment plots. The underlying BLUP and VAM residualization analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: v1 already includes correlation uncertainty and some aggregate variance intervals. v2 substantially expands reporting to component-level posterior medians, dispersion summaries, 95% highest-density intervals, additional intervals, and convergence diagnostics in Tables 1 and 4–6, plus posterior-derived reliability uncertainty. This is not evidence of increased independent LLM runs.

E6.justification: v1's residual-based decomposition reports model, prompt, and interaction shares of approximately 4.8%, 1.0%, and 1.4%; v2's squared-error analysis reports medians of 7%, 2%, and 2%. These concern different error definitions, not performance gains. v2 also adds signed-error, human-error, and reliability results, while Figures 3–4 and the existing residualized alignment estimates are retained.

M1.justification: The central measurement procedure changes: Section 3.3 replaces decomposition of regression residuals with decomposition of squared differences between standardized LLM ratings and VAM outcomes. Appendix C adds sign-preserving quadratic variants and posterior-based decision-study calculations. The LLM prompting and ensemble procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution framing, variance-analysis discussion, conclusion, and limitations undergo substantial rewriting. Appendix C is extensively reorganized, Appendix D.1 becomes a longer technical explanation, and the ethical discussion gains introductory framing. Terminology shifts broadly from foundation models to LLMs, and appendix headings clarify the two alignment targets.

P2.justification: v2 adds a main-text variance summary, detailed appendix variance and reliability tables, two reliability plots, and Figure 12's noise-controlled alignment display. Figure 7 is enlarged and its compact results table is separated out. Existing distribution plots and heatmaps are relocated or renumbered, and code listings and result tables are reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 adds statistical and psychometric references, including Bates, Vehtari, and Casabianca, expands instructional-coaching citations, and adds a coding-productivity example. Several scaling and emergence references disappear with rewritten passages. These refine supporting context without replacing the paper's relationship to prior classroom-scoring and alignment research.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds formal relative and absolute reliability definitions, a proof sketch establishing four-way interaction/residual non-identifiability, a controllable-variance upper-bound proposition, and a prompt-effect corollary. These extend substantially beyond v1's random-effects specification and variance-share explanation.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the central error analysis easier to assess through component-level uncertainty, signed-error and human-rater checks, and explicit identifiability and measurement limitations. These improve transparency beyond v1. The gain is limited because the revised analysis changes the error definition, and the abstract's specific 15% claim is not clearly connected to the displayed variance shares. The main alignment evidence remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same classroom-evaluation study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and reports additional signed-error decompositions, reliability analyses, and human-rater error comparisons in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 16 LLMs using three prompting strategies, including alignment with expert ratings and student learning, ensemble outcomes, and variance decompositions.

title: Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact

C1.justification: Both versions claim a role-agnostic benchmark, a 54-configuration empirical study, and a Communication-Reasoning Gap that worsens with scale and task complexity. Abstract and conclusion edits do not change these claims.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning information integration, coordination overhead, protocol suitability, and emergent-leader bottlenecks are retained. The limitations concerning protocol coverage, homogeneous teams, and model selection are unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code repository link in the abstract. Appendix C.3 changes the compute estimate from 500+ GPU-hours overall to that amount per experiment; other implementation and hardware disclosures remain unchanged.
