E3.justification: Agent scales, 128K context windows, the 100-round limit, metrics, and evaluation procedures remain unchanged. Appendix C.3 changes reported compute accounting without establishing a changed experimental budget or rerun.

E4.justification: The communication heatmaps, token-feasibility analysis, failure cases, leader-emergence analysis, successful coordination examples, and three prompt-scaffold ablations are retained without substantive revisions.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 still specifies one execution per configuration with fixed data-generation seeds. The annotation agreement, standard-deviation summaries, and percentile reporting are unchanged; no repeated-run or uncertainty analysis is added.

E6.justification: Benchmark scores, rankings, plots, and ablation entries are unchanged. However, Appendix C.3 changes 500+ GPU-hours equivalent from total compute to compute for each experiment, revising the scope of a quantitative resource-cost estimate.

M1.justification: The task-generation procedure, data partitioning, agent initialization, round-based execution, and three communication protocols are unchanged. Appendix B retains the same prompts.

P1.justification: Limited wording and punctuation edits replace several em dashes, refine terminology, and enumerate the three experimental axes. A corresponding-author email is added; section order and narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: All figures and tables are retained without redesign. Tables 6–8 are rearranged within the appendix, and text and references reflow, shifting the subsequent appendix pagination.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Ma et al. (2025), Talk2image, as an interactive image-generation example and Su et al. (2026), Difficulty-aware agentic orchestration, alongside Mixture-of-Agents. The broader research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: The task and metric definitions in Equations 1–5, communication-complexity characterizations, Relative Coordination Cost formula, and formal protocol specifications are unchanged.

improvement.justification: The new code-access pointer provides a concrete aid to locating the implementation, modestly improving reproducibility information. Scientific evidence is unchanged. This limited benefit is tempered by the unexplained switch from total to per-experiment compute in Appendix C.3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SILO-BENCH and contain the corresponding main sections, seven figures, 18 tables, and Appendices A–H. Text and rendered pages support a complete comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results, including the measured performance in Tables 1–4 and the detailed results and analyses in Appendices F–H.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 54 configurations across 30 tasks, totaling 1,620 experiments, plus single-agent comparisons, failure analyses, and prompt-scaffold ablations.

title: SILO-BENCH: A Scalable Environment for Evaluating Distributed Coordination in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same SFT-paradox claim, functional-alignment explanation, Faire contribution, and claimed benchmark advantages. Their scientific scope and strength are unchanged.

C2.justification: Interpretations of SFT failure, RL-induced functional grounding, entropy shifts, human agreement, and GGBench performance are retained. Appendix A's qualifications about surface-similarity metrics also remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 and Appendices A and C retain the same training settings, hardware/software disclosures, processing rules, and three verifier prompts. No implementation detail or code/data access information is substantively added or removed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Faire-Bench plane geometry, analytic geometry, and function tasks, together with GenExam and GGBench evaluations. No training domain or evaluation scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the main comparison, GenExam evaluation, and GGBench evaluation (Tables 2, 3, and 7). The switch to numbered citations does not introduce different baselines.

E3.justification: Both retain the 4,643/2,321/1,025 SFT/RL/evaluation split, Qwen3-VL-8B initialization, two SFT epochs, and seven GRPO candidates per prompt at temperature 0.9. Appendix A's evaluation metrics and procedures are unchanged.

E4.justification: The reward and training-paradigm ablations, token-entropy analysis, human-rating comparison, category-wise analysis, and geometry case studies are retained. Relocating their displays adds no new ablation, robustness test, or supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based variability, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both retain the same human-rating correlation, r = 0.9578, with unchanged statistical reporting.

E6.justification: Corresponding numerical results and qualitative findings are unchanged. Examples include Faire's 74.82 accuracy and 45.37 verification average in Table 2, 52.3 Math-Rel and 9.3 Math-Str in Table 3, and 63.13 overall GGBench score in Table 7.

M1.justification: The GeoGebra interleaved reasoning procedure, geometric/perceptual/semantic verifiers, SFT initialization, and GRPO reward and optimization formulation remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 revises affiliations and front matter, changes Section 5 from 'Experiment' to 'Experimental', adds an Appendix heading, removes the generic Impact Statement, and restyles citations and references. Scientific prose and the section sequence are otherwise retained.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column, ByteDance-branded design with a boxed abstract and blue headings. Figures and tables are extensively resized or relocated, and captions and appendix prompt boxes are restyled. Their scientific content is retained.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning relative to geometry solvers, interleaved generation methods, and existing benchmarks remain the same. Bibliography reordering and conversion from author-year to numbered citations are presentation changes.

T1.justification: Equations 1–14 retain the same trajectory definitions, entropy arguments, verification constraints, reward and GRPO objective, and evaluation definitions. No mathematical assumption, derivation, or proof is added or corrected.

improvement.justification: The method, arguments, empirical evidence, and reproducibility information are unchanged. The redesign enlarges some main-text graphics but separates appendix prompts and GGBench displays further from their discussion. These presentation tradeoffs, minor editorial edits, and removal of generic impact discussion leave overall paper quality essentially unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Faire research. The main text, equations, Tables 1–7, Figures 1–17, and Appendices A–F are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results in Section 5 and the appendices, including the ablations and GGBench evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original Faire evaluations, training and reward ablations, entropy analysis, and human-rating comparisons in Section 5, plus GGBench results in Appendix E.

title: How RL Unlocks the Aha Moment in Geometric Interleaved Reasoning

C1.justification: The system, HVR-loop and benchmark contributions and headline pass rates remain unchanged. However, v2's conclusion newly claims diagnostic proficiency equivalent to a junior forecaster; v1 only claimed useful assistance to human forecasters.

C2.justification: New Section 6 materially qualifies operational applicability: evaluation uses reanalysis, whereas biased live forecasts could cause cascading omissions or misdiagnoses, requiring expert interpretation and local observations. Sections 5.2-5.3 also expand explanations involving meteorological knowledge, tool adherence and visual occlusion. v1 lacked this substantive operational-data limitation.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the five-factor diagnostic target, 50-turn cap and 20-year climatological reference. It also states that evaluation events postdate model knowledge cutoffs and clarifies plotting-task matching and difficulty criteria. These disclosures improve specificity without demonstrating changed datasets or implementation; appendix prompts remain substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same five weather categories through 100 diagnostic events, 150 queries covering 30 indices, and 100 plotting tasks covering 20 figure types. Live forecasting systems mentioned in v2's limitations are not newly evaluated scenarios.

E2.justification: The evaluated models remain GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro-Preview-Thinking, DeepSeek-R1-0528 and Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct. Corresponding ablation configurations are also unchanged; newly cited agent systems are not added comparators.

E3.justification: The reported human-validation sample increases from 20 events (20%) to 30 events (30%). v2 also corrects the written numerical acceptance criteria to use absolute errors. These are reported protocol revisions; unchanged benchmark scores do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Both ablation suites and the difficulty-stratified analyses remain. Sections 5.2-5.3 add execution-log analysis describing abandonment of specialized tools after one or two repair attempts and plotting failures caused by layer-order occlusion. The existing human-validation analysis is also expanded and quantified.

E5.justification: v1 asserts high human-LLM score correlation without statistics. v2 specifies Pearson correlation and reports coefficients and p-values for five dimensions plus an average in Appendix Table 5. The observation and aggregation basis for these p-values is not explained clearly; neither version reports repeated-run variability.

E6.justification: Scores in Tables 1-4 and Figure 4 are unchanged. v2 adds human-automated correlations ranging from 0.81 to 0.98, averaging 0.88, and observations such as GPT-5 and Gemini completing HVR iterations within three rounds. Removed v1 Table 5 accuracy entries remain available in Figure 4.

M1.justification: The seven-agent architecture, knowledge-supported HVR loop and appendix system prompts are retained. Sections 3.1-3.3 revise the explanation and clarify agent responsibilities; the newly specified five-factor target and 50-turn limit do not establish a change to the implemented method.

P1.justification: Substantial portions of the knowledge-base construction, HVR explanation, benchmark description, results discussion and conclusion are rewritten. Section 4 gains separate workflow and subtask subsections; Limitations and Acknowledgements are added and the Impact Statement is removed. Terminology, the title spelling and author information are also edited.

P2.justification: Figure 1's arrows and Figure 3's error formula are redrawn, Figures 2-3 are relocated, and running headers are added. A new correlation table replaces the redundant appendix accuracy table, whose values remain plotted. Most figure designs and table structures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds meteorological diagnosis and forecasting references, a WeatherBench2 citation, and additional scientific-agent references including Guo, Liu and Pantiukhin. These mainly support existing statements; positioning relative to Zephyrus, ClimateAgent and EWE remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the mathematical acceptance rules from signed relative error to absolute relative error and from Reply < 0.05 to |Reply| < 0.05 when GT = 0. Figure 3 is corrected accordingly, resolving disagreement with v1's already absolute-error wording. No new theoretical results or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: Clearer HVR specifications, corrected error formulas, quantified human-validation reporting and the explicit reanalysis-versus-live-forecast limitation modestly improve transparency and reproducibility. Core benchmark evidence remains unchanged. Gains are tempered by the unsupported junior-forecaster equivalence claim and Table 5 p-values whose observation and aggregation basis is not reconciled with the stated 30-event sample.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HVR-Met. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable matching despite rewriting and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and additionally reports numerical agreement between human and automated evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 100 extreme-weather events, index-calculation and plotting tasks, and component ablations, including appendix results.

title: HVR-Met: A Hypothesis-Verification-Replanning Agentic System for Extreme Weather Diagnosis

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction recast the contribution as an operational, answer-level uncertainty framework. The claim of independent reasoning superiority over single-agent RL is replaced by a claim about post-debate performance and peer-information utilization. This materially narrows what the framework and training results are claimed to establish.

C2.justification: v2 expands the earlier proxy caveats, distinguishing latent beliefs, answer-level diagnostics, and training signals. It explicitly limits the heterogeneity theorem to information potential, acknowledges that the stronger agent is not uniformly improved, and discusses compatible model pairings. Appendix J adds substantive limits concerning mathematical tasks, answer equivalence, and extension beyond exact-match verification.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code location, documents the Single-GRPO training budget and AIME length exceptions, and changes the computational-resources training group size from 16 to five, matching Table 2 in both versions. Existing pseudocode, prompts, hardware information, and most hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions train on MATH and evaluate on MATH500, GSM8K, AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25. The homogeneous and heterogeneous Qwen/Llama diagnostic coverage is retained. The new ablations use existing tasks and model pairings.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Zero-Shot MAD and Standard IPPO. New Table 3 adds independently trained Single-GRPO Pair agents and Intrinsic-only and NLL-only variants, substantially extending the comparisons needed to distinguish debate co-training from standalone training and individual uncertainty components.

E3.justification: For AIME, v2 increases response/prompt limits from the previously stated 2,048/5,120 tokens to 4,096/9,216, materially changing evaluation conditions. The new Single-GRPO baseline receives 15 training epochs versus UMAD's retained two. Section 3.2 also changes the stated rollout count from 16 to five, although Appendix D.5 retains 16; the actual diagnostic sampling protocol remains inconsistent.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.1 and Table 3 separately test the intrinsic reward and NLL weighting and examine whether standalone GRPO training explains the gains. Conversely, v1's two dialogue case studies illustrating homogeneous failure and heterogeneous success are removed. The existing uncertainty trajectories, flipping analysis, and longer-debate evaluation remain.

E5.justification: v1's Table 1 provides point estimates without evaluation seed counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 adds uncertainty throughout Table 1 and specifies five evaluation seeds, while Table 3 reports three-seed means and standard deviations. Identical UMAD entries appear in both tables despite these differing seed descriptions, leaving their statistical provenance unclear.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially revises AIME results and heterogeneous UMAD scores. At T=5, UMAD's heterogeneous agent averages change from 50.6/57.7 to 66.5/65.8; the stronger agent now trails IPPO's 67.4 average. Table 3 adds component and GRPO comparison results. These are revised reports under changed AIME budgets and seed reporting, not demonstrated same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: UMAD retains the same GRPO-based training procedure, standardized NLL advantage weighting, and peer-correctness intrinsic reward. Algorithm 2 is unchanged. The revised descriptions of these signals as operational proxies do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theoretical exposition, method explanation, and results discussion are extensively rewritten. Related work is condensed in the main text and reorganized into Appendix A; limitations move from Section 8 to Appendix J. Dialogue examples are removed, an ablation appendix is introduced, and author/publication information is updated.

P2.justification: Table 1 is regrouped by debate round and gains comparison coloring and an expanded caption; Table 3 is added and the dialogue-example boxes disappear. All six figures retain the same underlying graphics, with localized caption and placement changes. The overall visual format remains stable.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of identity-aware debate, ModeX, and Tang et al.'s uncertainty-driven policy optimization, plus a Llama reference. It removes the Kadavath and Tomov references and the earlier first-work assertion. Most other bibliography changes concern the same works' publication metadata; the principal research positioning remains uncertainty analysis coupled with MARL.

T1.justification: v1's Theorem 3.3 claims a marginal information-gain ordering from a conditional novelty assumption, while its proof compares message pairs. v2 replaces it with homogeneous saturation Assumption 3.3 and Theorem 3.4, explicitly bounding the joint-information advantage by Delta, with a matching proof in Appendix B.3. The earlier individual-agent entropy/KL derivation is also removed.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects the central heterogeneity theorem's statement–proof mismatch, better distinguishes operational proxies from Bayesian quantities, and adds previously missing component and standalone-RL controls in Table 3. These changes substantially strengthen the paper's theoretical validity and empirical argument. Conflicting seed and rollout descriptions still limit reproducibility, and dialogue examples are lost, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantive improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UMAD research. Their main text, appendices, equations, algorithms, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses, revises Table 1 results, and adds component ablations and a Single-GRPO Pair comparison in Table 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original debate experiments, uncertainty and answer-flipping analyses, and UMAD training results, including Table 1 and Figures 1–6.

title: Epistemic Gain, Aleatoric Cost: Uncertainty Decomposition in Multi-Agent Debate for Math Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: training-free multi-instance generation using ISG and SGU, improved spatial fidelity, and efficient inference. The expanded conclusion restates these claims without materially changing their scope.

C2.justification: New Appendix B interprets the larger evaluation as evidence of reliability beyond a small example set and the Trellis results as evidence of applicability across backbones. It also qualifies absolute performance as dependent on backbone capacity. Existing mechanism explanations and the foundation-model bias caveat remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: The disclosed Hunyuan3D configuration, Grounded-SAM masks, guided layers and timesteps, smoothing strength, modulation strength, and momentum coefficient are unchanged. The added experiments provide no new implementation instructions, hardware information, or code/data access details.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the stated 3D-Front, real-world, and stylized image coverage. However, v2 does not identify the data source or composition of its new 500-sample and Trellis evaluations, so it is unclear whether represented data coverage changes beyond sample count and backbone.

E2.justification: Trellis, previously discussed as prior work, becomes an evaluated comparator against Trellis + TIMI in v2 Table 9. Hunyuan3D 2.0, DPA, and MIDI remain the comparators in the original benchmark and the new larger evaluation.

E3.justification: Appendix B adds a separate 500-sample evaluation beyond the retained 30-scene synthetic benchmark and introduces a controlled Trellis versus Trellis + TIMI comparison. This substantially expands evaluation scale and backbone settings; the original datasets' stated sample counts, metrics, and guidance settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new Trellis experiment tests whether TIMI's benefits extend beyond Hunyuan3D 2.0. Existing component and hyperparameter ablations are retained; the qualitative layer-selection and smoothing analyses move from v1 Appendix B into v2 Section 5.3 rather than constituting new analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v2 introduces 95% confidence intervals for all four methods and all six metrics in Table 8, substantially changing uncertainty reporting for the comparative evaluation. Interval construction, seeds, and repeated-run counts remain unspecified, so additional repeated runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Tables 1–7 and existing qualitative and user-study results are unchanged. New Table 8 reports TIMI's 500-sample LCD as 0.596 ± 0.023 and SSR as 0.705 ± 0.020, with the best point estimates across all six metrics. Table 9 adds improvements over Trellis, including LCD from 0.692 to 0.635. These are substantial additional results under new settings, not changes to the original benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The ISG separation objective and SGU smoothing, adaptive scaling, and momentum updates remain unchanged. Applying TIMI to Trellis is presented as testing the existing guidance mechanism, without introducing a new algorithmic component or architectural modification.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized language and notation corrections, expands related work and the conclusion, and integrates existing appendix ablation discussions into Section 5.3. It also updates author order, affiliations, correspondence and publication information, and adds acknowledgments. The overall narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8 and 9 and relocates v1's appendix Figures 9 and 10 into the main text as Figures 7 and 10. Existing figures retain their visual evidence, with associated renumbering, expanded captions, and table/page reflow rather than substantial redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to SEMV-3D, SAM 3D, and latent diffusion models and modestly revises the related-work discussion. TIMI's positioning remains unchanged. The Ardelean-to-Dogaru/Gen3DSR reference update concerns the same identifiable work rather than a newly introduced comparison method.

T1.justification: Equations 1–10 retain the same attention formulation, separation loss, update rules, and LCD/SSR definitions. Replacing the prose reference to scaling factor st with lambda_adap aligns notation with the unchanged equation; no mathematical assumption, derivation, or proof changes.

improvement.justification: The 500-sample comparison, confidence intervals, and Trellis test strengthen empirical support beyond v1's small main benchmark and single evaluated backbone. However, the new tests' data provenance and detailed settings, and the interval estimation procedure, remain unspecified. Table 8's substantially overlapping intervals also leave comparative significance unresolved. The additions provide a useful but limited overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TIMI and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices. Existing appendix material can be matched to its relocated counterparts in v2, allowing reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds a 500-sample quantitative evaluation and a Trellis backbone comparison in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative comparisons, qualitative generation results, a user study, and component and hyperparameter ablations in Section 5 and Appendix B.

title: TIMI: Training-Free Image-to-3D Multi-Instance Generation with Spatial Fidelity

C1.justification: The introduction qualifies the central Fuzzy-Trace Theory analogy as cross-modal fusion with predominantly visual/verbatim and textual/gist roles, replacing the more direct alignment framing. The principal contributions remain unchanged. The abstract's state-of-the-art wording repeats a claim already present in v1's introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 add explanations of changing modality dominance, sensory text as a visual label, and grounding links as multimodal pointers. Section 4.5 adds an interpretation of construction costs being amortized across queries. The limitations and Appendix F's weaker Movie-split findings remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents peak memory requirements and separate construction/inference costs, and explains unavailable efficiency measurements. The A100 platform, backbone, retrieval models, training and inference hyperparameters, prompts, and repository access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use Video-MME, MLVU, HD-EPIC++, and VStream-QA, including its Ego and Movie splits. The new efficiency study uses the existing Video-MME setting without subtitles and adds no distinct task or input scenario.

E2.justification: New efficiency Table 4 includes VideoAgent, absent from v1's reported comparisons, alongside existing comparators Qwen3-VL-8B, Video-RAG, and Vgent. Comparator membership in the retained accuracy tables and appendix experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 adds an efficiency protocol covering Video-MME's three length regimes without subtitles, measuring peak VRAM and construction/inference times normalized per minute of video. Existing data splits, training settings, accuracy metrics, and automatic judging protocols are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds an efficiency and deployment analysis examining construction cost, inference latency, and GPU memory requirements. Existing component ablations, memory-topology visualizations, qualitative examples, and Appendix F analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix F.2 retains the same repeated-evaluation uncertainty description and identical mean-plus/minus values. No new run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for the efficiency measurements are reported.

E6.justification: New Table 4 reports MM-Mem at 17.8 GB peak VRAM, 19.54 seconds construction time, and 5.35 seconds inference time per video minute; Vgent reports 18.7 GB, 20.18 seconds, and 7.38 seconds. These are newly reported measurements. Accuracy results in Tables 1–3 and Appendix F are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 replaces separately stored visual/textual traces with an integrated-memory description and explicitly includes visual pointers in symbolic-memory records. However, v1 already defines paired multimodal entries and grounding edges, while update actions, SIB-GRPO, and retrieval rules remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether storage or computation changed beyond the description.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites in the introduction, related work, memory description, and qualitative discussion, plus a new efficiency subsection and acknowledgments. Affiliations and publication information are updated. The overall narrative order and appendix organization are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with visual/textual artifacts at each memory level, revised labels, and a logo. Efficiency Table 4 is added, and existing displays are repositioned through reflow. The remaining figures and appendix displays retain their content.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to LicoMemory, VideoAgent, and the work on inducing high energy-latency with verbose images. It includes LicoMemory among text-centric agent memories and VideoAgent among long-video approaches. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The IB assumptions, variational bounds, optimization equations, entropy criterion, and Appendix A proofs are unchanged apart from numbering. Section 3.1 makes the existing grounding-edge neighbors explicit as pointer sets in the symbolic-memory notation, without adding a mathematical argument or formal property.

improvement.justification: The new efficiency study supplies concrete evidence for previously qualitative deployment claims, and Section 3.1/Figure 2 explain grounding links more explicitly. These are useful, limited gains while the accuracy evidence and proofs remain stable. Sparse profiling details and ambiguity about whether the revised memory description reflects an implementation change limit the overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MM-Mem and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–F. Corresponding content can be matched despite pagination and numbering changes.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds measurements of memory use, construction time, and inference latency.

before.justification: v1 reports original MM-Mem benchmark results, component ablations, memory visualizations, and SFT versus reinforcement-learning comparisons, including Appendix F.

title: From Verbatim to Gist: Distilling Pyramidal Multimodal Memory via Semantic Information Bottleneck for Long-Horizon Video Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about universal robustness asymmetry, its memorization connection, RA-Det, and detection superiority. The abstract's 7.81% improvement claim is unchanged; additional experiments support existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: Appendix D.2 reclassifies epoch-based evidence as a training-stage trend rather than a validated monotonic memorization proxy and interprets the new AMS associations as more direct support. V2 also discusses training-source independence, learned-probe necessity, inference overhead, and the limitations of single-generator training for real-world distributions. However, a retained paragraph and Figure 6's caption still describe epochs as a memorization proxy.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly identifies LSUN and AIGIBench/GenImage provenance and gives training-source sample counts. The stated hardware changes from four NVIDIA 4090 GPUs to eight H200 GPUs, and Table 5 reports compute, parameters, memory, and latency. Core training hyperparameters and the code link remain unchanged; the hardware revision alone does not establish reruns.

E1.justification: Table 4 adds seven generator columns: SDXL, SDv3.5, FLUX, FLUX1-dev, MJ-v6, Infinity, and VAR. This extends evaluation to newer synthesis systems and autoregressive generation. Appendix A also introduces diffusion-source and mixed-source training using SDv1.4 data from AIGIBench/GenImage. The original benchmark and CelebA-HQ study remain.

E2.justification: C2P-CLIP, previously discussed only in related work, becomes an evaluated efficiency comparator alongside UniFD in v2 Table 5. The detector membership in Table 1 and the JPEG/blur comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds SDv1.4-only training with 52,922 real/72,000 fake images and mixed-source training with 72,000/72,000, alongside the retained ProGAN 360,000/360,000 setting. It introduces fixed-probe controls, a five-value margin sweep, AMS-based evaluation, and matched-hardware efficiency measurements. Appendix D.2 also changes the stated epoch-analysis aggregation from epsilon values generally to small-epsilon values; the PDFs do not establish that the retained plots were recomputed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained backbone, loss, branch, and post-processing analyses, v2 tests learned probing against Gaussian noise, Gaussian blur, and resize residuals; examines margin sensitivity and training-source dependence; and analyzes computational cost. Appendix D.2 adds AMS-based validation of the memorization relationship, addressing a question previously investigated only through training epochs.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 6 already reports linear fits with slopes and R-squared values. V2 applies this estimation approach to AMS in Table 6, adding point-estimate results rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the retained ablation scores are unchanged, including RA-Det's 93.47% ACC/97.00% AP. V2 adds substantial results: for example, ProGAN-trained RA-Det scores 57.19%/61.50% on FLUX in Table 4, fixed-probe variants achieve 86.11–87.07% ACC in Table 3, and AMS regressions have positive slopes with R-squared values of 0.59–0.73. Efficiency results are new, and Figure 2 replaces the CLIP similarity distribution.

M1.justification: The frozen encoder, conditional-UNet probing module, semantic/discrepancy/residual branches, fusion, and composite loss remain unchanged. Alternative probes and contrastive margins are experimental controls, not revisions to the proposed detector.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and most introductory, methodological, theoretical, and concluding text remain intact. V2 locally rewrites ablation, robustness, and epoch-validation discussions; adds generality and efficiency subsections, acknowledgements, and an impact statement; updates the publication header; and reorganizes the appendices around the additions.

P2.justification: V2 adds four tables covering training-source summaries, detailed generator results, efficiency, and AMS regression, and expands/regroups the original ablation table. Figure 2 replaces the CLIP histogram and fixes panel labels; Figure 4 gains a detailed caption. Figures 5 and 6 are relocated, with their original plotted results retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for new generators and data sources, including Infinity, VAR, SDXL, FLUX, LSUN, AIGIBench, and GenImage. The appearance-versus-behavior positioning remains intact. Publication updates to existing references and consolidation of the duplicated Hounie citation do not represent newly introduced works.

T1.justification: V2 removes Appendix B.2's explicit inequality asserting that SIDE divergence strictly decreases with training epochs and withdraws its claimed theoretical justification. The central definitions, Assumption 4.1, Lemma 4.2, Theorem 4.3, and their proofs remain unchanged in Section 4 and the relocated Appendix D.1.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism: v1 lacked fixed-probe controls and relied on an asserted epoch-to-memorization relationship; v2 adds probing controls and AMS-based evidence. Training-source and contemporary-generator tests, together with measured computational costs, also improve assessment of applicability. These address important evidential gaps. The gains are tempered by Table 4's unclear averaging scope and the contradictory epoch-proxy wording retained in Figure 6.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RA-Det work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison. The original appendices are retained as Appendices C and D in v2, alongside new material.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds training-source comparisons, recent-generator evaluations, further ablations, efficiency measurements, and AMS-based memorization analysis.

title: RA-Det: Towards Universal Detection of AI-Generated Images via Robustness Asymmetry

improvement.justification: v2 slightly broadens attribution by citing BYOL-Explore, but adds no discussion that changes the paper's argument or positioning. The methods, evidence, theoretical analysis, reproducibility information and complete appendices are unchanged; the bibliographic addition and local reflow do not meaningfully alter overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same C-TeC research work and contain complete, readable main texts and Appendices A–M. Text comparison and rendered-page checks support a reliable comparison of equations, figures, tables and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results, including state-coverage comparisons, achievement curves and the appendix experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original exploration experiments in robotic environments, Crafter and Craftax-Classic, together with appendix ablations, noisy-TV experiments and toy-MDP simulations.

title: Temporal Representations for Exploration: Learning Complex Exploratory Behavior without Extrinsic Rewards

C1.justification: The central claims about exponential context savings and optimality among recursive agentic systems remain. The abstract and conclusion replace their SAT-focused emphasis on a 3B model outperforming frontier LLMs with claims spanning SAT fine-tuning and Go training from scratch. The introduction additionally claims improved length generalization against matched Go baselines.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes long computation from long-input access, using Needle-in-a-Haystack to explain an applicability boundary. It acknowledges storage and transfer costs outside the local-space measure and warns that correct Go labels can arise through shortcuts or invalid traces. Conversely, v1's explicit question-preservation limitation for shallow recursion is reduced to an appendix pointer without the same explanation.

D1.justification: New Appendix C documents Go trace generation and filtering, trace renderings, data splits, evaluation subsets, architecture, optimizer settings, precision, and attention masks. Section 5 adds a code-repository pointer and explains that scaffold-inserted tokens are excluded from the training loss. These substantially expand reproducibility information; Appendix B's SAT settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates SAT only. v2 retains SAT and adds 4x4 placement-Go position evaluation using exact-solver proof traces, with IID and longer-search test scenarios. Appendix C restricts supervision to finite traces querying Win/Lose states. This substantially expands the evaluated domain and reasoning requirements.

E2.justification: The SAT comparator roster in Table 1 is unchanged. v2 adds trained CoT and PENCIL comparators for Go, using the same small Transformer and proof supervision as the recursive model. These introduce direct comparisons against flat reasoning and single-context compression that were not experimentally evaluated this way in v1.

E3.justification: The SAT protocol is unchanged. The new Go protocol matches 3.18M-parameter models and 64K training updates, introduces IID and length-selected splits, and evaluates teacher-forced trace exact match on 1K roots per split, IID rollout metrics on 256 roots, and context lengths on 10K roots. Sections 5.2 and C.4 describe strict rollout validation, although the appendix does not explicitly enumerate the main text's child-label and parent-decision checks.

E4.justification: v2 adds length-OOD tests of extrapolation to longer searches, training-convergence comparisons in Figure 3, and rollout-validity diagnostics distinguishing correct binary answers from valid reasoning traces. It also compares context requirements across the three Go methods. The existing SAT context-efficiency analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new Go learning curves and accuracy entries do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: SAT Table 1 is unchanged, including recursive-model accuracies of 98%, 95%, and 64%. New Go Table 2 reports IID/length-OOD trace accuracies of 91.8%/38.5% for recursion, 73.4%/1.0% for CoT, and 71.0%/5.6% for PENCIL. v2 also adds rollout results, learning curves, and maximum visible contexts of 54, 16,356, and 595 tokens for recursion, CoT, and PENCIL respectively.

M1.justification: The call/return architecture and SAT implementation are retained. However, Equation 3 revises the formal prefixing procedure: v1 prepends the root prompt at every subsequent update, whereas v2 prefixes only non-root calls and removes that prefix before updating stored frames. Section 2 also makes malformed generator outputs undefined instead of applying the earlier fallback update. These are limited procedural refinements.

P1.justification: Beyond the added experiments, Sections 2–4 are extensively rewritten to explain generator execution, stack updates, resource accounting, and scaffold semantics. Notation changes from RCM to RM and individual recursive functions, related-work paragraphs are consolidated and reordered, and Section 5 is reorganized around two experimental settings.

P2.justification: v2 adds Go Table 2 and the training-curve Figure 3, expands Figure 2's caption, and relocates algorithm displays. The original SAT context plot is retained as Figure 4, and Table 1 retains its structure and values. These are localized display additions and layout adjustments rather than a broad visual redesign.

R1.justification: Section 7 adds an explicit distinction between this work's recursive reasoning and Zhang et al.'s long-input decomposition. Several diffusion-model references and the Winskel reference are removed. Most other bibliography changes update metadata or author attribution for the same works, rather than introducing new research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 makes targeted mathematical corrections while retaining the main complexity bounds and proof constructions. Definition 2 now counts transient generator outputs, including the final root return. TM(S,T) changes from an intersection of time and space classes to simultaneous bounds satisfied by one machine, with corresponding proof amendments. The least-fixpoint treatment also clarifies that undefined recursive calls are not observable oracle answers.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical argument relied on SAT fine-tuning compared with externally reported prompted-model scores. v2 adds Go comparisons with matched model sizes, supervision, and training updates, plus longer-search generalization and rollout diagnostics, substantially strengthening evidence for the proposed context organization. Targeted mathematical corrections and expanded reproducibility information further improve rigor. Go's primary metric is teacher-forced, uncertainty remains unreported, and strict-rollout criteria are not fully aligned between Section 5.2 and Appendix C.4. These limitations temper interpretation but do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same recursive-model framework and retain corresponding theoretical results and SAT experiments. All pages, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable. The theoretical appendices can be matched despite renumbering after the new Go appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains the original SAT results and adds original Go experiments, including trace accuracy, rollout accuracy, learning curves, and context measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original SAT accuracy for its fine-tuned recursive model in Table 1 and trajectory/context measurements in Figure 3. The comparator scores are separately attributed to prior work.

title: Recursive Models for Long-Horizon Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: independently controlled noise mechanisms, ELBO training with Bayes-derived sampling, and pretrained self-correction without remasking that improves parallel generation. The new experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets exact recovery as evidence of meaningful correction, discusses GIDD+'s creativity advantage, and attributes cross-ratio weaknesses to lower training-noise exposure. Appendix E.3 expands the explanation that likelihood-based benchmark accuracy does not directly measure iterative generation or self-correction.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link in the abstract and the judge prompt in Figure 4. Appendix E.1 corrects the swapped arithmetic expressions underlying the LM1B and OWT token totals; the stated budgets, architecture, optimizer, and hardware remain unchanged.

E1.justification: LM1B, OWT, Wikitext-103, and the seven commonsense benchmarks are retained. v2 extends evaluation to corrupted-OWT reconstruction and exact token recovery, including a cross-ratio scenario that exposes GIDD+ to stronger corruption than its training schedule.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged: MDLM, ReMDM-cap, ReMDM-confidence, and GIDD/GIDD+ at the same noise ratios. The added judge comparisons reuse GIDD+; the theoretical comparison in new Table 1 introduces no newly evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: v2 introduces GPT-5.4 judging of 256 paired OWT reconstructions from identical inputs corrupted to t = 0.8, across six sampling budgets, using five quality criteria and winner selection. It also adds single-step recovery evaluation with 5, 10, 20, or 50 corrupted positions and touch/recovery metrics. Existing training and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's correction counts and two noise-schedule ablations, v2 directly tests whether corrections restore original tokens and improve judged text quality. Matched-schedule and cross-ratio comparisons additionally examine correction quality under differing training-noise exposure. The original ablations remain intact.

E5.justification: v2 introduces paired t-tests for judge scores, binomial tests for win rates, and significance markers in Tables 4 and 9. Table 6 reports standard errors over 128 recovery samples. These substantially extend v1's averaging and Monte Carlo reporting; neither version documents repeated training seeds.

E6.justification: Existing perplexity, entropy, correction-rate, and zero-shot results are unchanged. New Tables 4 and 9 report SCDD win rates of 60.6% and 58.0% at 1024 steps, while GIDD+ scores higher on creativity. Table 6 adds 64.4%–69.4% exact recovery and a perplexity reduction from 154.8 to 25.5 at 50 corruptions; at five corruptions, perplexity instead rises from 22.0 to 23.8.

M1.justification: The intended SCDD procedure remains unchanged: absorbing-mask and uniform corruption, Bayes-derived reverse transitions, discrete-time ELBO training, and ancestral parallel sampling. The new generator representation and correction experiments do not establish an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and appendices A–G are retained. Changes include localized prose revisions, a reorganized GIDD proof, additional experimental subheadings, impact and acknowledgements sections, and removal of the contents page. Most existing exposition remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redesigns the main text and references into a two-column conference layout, with reformatted equations and tables. It adds four tables and the judge-prompt figure. Existing Figures 2–3 use identical images but are separated and relocated; retained tables are renumbered and restyled.

R1.justification: v2 adds Zhao et al. (2025), Rojas et al. (2026), Sahoo et al. (2026), and Zheng et al. (2026), while removing the Bie et al. (2026)/LLaDA2.1 discussion. It sharpens the GIDD comparison in Appendix D.2 and new Table 1. ReMDM's citation update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds a matrix-generator consistency proposition and proof. Revised Proposition 10 corrects v1's misleading identification of SCDD with GIDD by explicitly identifying the alternative nonabsorbing kernel. There are also local formula corrections. Conversely, v2 drops the explicit non-mask support factor from Equations (7)–(8), although Appendix B retains it.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's reliance on perplexity, edit counts, and illustrative samples, v2 provides more direct evidence that corrections recover content, alongside statistically assessed text-quality comparisons. The clarified GIDD proposition and added access information also help. Gains are tempered by reporting problems: Figure 4 does not specify pairwise winner selection, Appendix E.2 overstates significance relative to Table 9, and Equations (7)–(8) lose an explicit support factor.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCDD research, with matching authors, method, and retained experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–G support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds LLM-judged text comparisons and controlled recovery experiments on corrupted OWT sequences.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training and evaluation results, including perplexity, correction-rate experiments, noise-schedule ablations, and zero-shot benchmark accuracy.

title: Generalized Discrete Diffusion with Self-Correction

C1.justification: The abstract broadens its characterization of DiM from transport between equal-covariance unimodal Gaussians to distributions differing in their first moments. The principal CHaRS/PCT contributions and claims of improved behavioral control remain unchanged; the additional experiments mainly support existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds a possible limited-sample explanation for the diagonal-covariance variant's poorer performance and updates the corresponding limitation. Appendix E.7 interprets the throughput results as minimal additional overhead while explicitly qualifying comparisons with unsteered models because refusal responses are shorter.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link, specifies vLLM and a single NVIDIA H100 for the new throughput study, and explains estimation of diagonal covariances from cluster-assigned activations. It also clarifies which layer's centroids and coupling are used for directional ablation. These supplement the retained implementation details.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and tasks remain unchanged, including ADVBENCH/ALPACA, RealToxicityPrompts, language-utility benchmarks, and COCO-based cyberpunk and sketch generation. Sketch already appeared in v1's appendix. Human ratings, LPIPS, and throughput measurements assess retained coverage rather than introducing a new model task or input domain.

E2.justification: V2 adds nearest-neighbor and uniform coupling as evaluated alternatives to OT coupling in Section 5 and Table 5. The main ActAdd, DirAbl, and Linear-AcT comparisons are retained. ACT is newly discussed as related work but is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands evaluation procedures: a 44-participant two-alternative forced-choice study, LPIPS against style reference images, coupling comparisons at fixed K and over K=2–15, and throughput measurements on 100 harmless and 104 harmful prompts. These are new protocols; the original benchmark splits and evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained cluster-count and principal-component ablations, v2 tests whether OT matching outperforms alternative couplings, whether independently estimated diagonal covariances help, and whether CHaRS adds inference overhead. Section 5 and Appendices E.6–E.7 therefore add substantive tests of central design choices and computational efficiency.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly reports standard deviations for human preferences and LPIPS in Tables 4 and 8 and explains shared variance for complementary binary preferences. V1's Table 3 already contained uncertainty values, which remain unchanged. No new seed counts or repeated-run counts are disclosed, and the new uncertainty calculations are not fully specified.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their values. New results include CHaRS style preferences of 54.32% for cyberpunk and 78.94% for sketch, LPIPS of 0.67/0.69 versus Linear-AcT's 0.70/0.74, and tuned coupling ASRs of 95.19% for OT, 94.23% for nearest neighbor, and 87.50% for uniform coupling. Further results show lower ASR with diagonal covariances and throughput close to ActAdd. Section 4.2 also corrects the maximum zero-shot toxicity reduction from 38% to 42% and attributes the approximately 43% CLS reduction to Qwen2.5-7B.

M1.justification: The default CHaRS and CHaRS-PCT procedures remain unchanged. New Appendix E.6 introduces and evaluates a diagonal-covariance variant with affine component maps and piecewise steering-strength behavior, defined in Eqs. (29)–(30). The normalization clarification in Remark 3.2 already appeared in v1's implementation appendix.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Appendix B to main-text Section 6, with corresponding appendix renumbering. V2 adds acknowledgements and makes localized edits to the abstract, explanations, results discussion, and limitations. Most existing prose and the overall methodological narrative are retained.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the result displays with six new tables covering human preferences, coupling strategies, LPIPS, covariance configurations, and throughput. Existing figures are retained, with relocations such as Figures 4–5 moving to page 9. The notation table and appendix material also move, while the established visual style remains.

R1.justification: V2 adds Wang et al.'s ACT and distinguishes its paired-data requirements and per-cluster steering from CHaRS's unpaired matching and position-dependent field. Talamon et al. and Langley references are removed. Other title, year, and publication-detail updates largely concern the same cited works.

T1.justification: V2 corrects the Gaussian transport matrix accompanying Eq. (2) and an inverse exponent in the equal-covariance proof. Section 3.2 replaces isotropy alone with equal paired covariances as the justification for translation. Appendix E.6 adds the diagonal-covariance map and its geodesic interpretation; the main mixture-OT derivations and PCT rank argument are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens validation through human and perceptual checks beyond v1's CLIP-based assessment, direct coupling/covariance controls, and measured inference overhead. Mathematical corrections and code-access information also help. The gains remain bounded: the new mechanism tests cover one LLM, human-study uncertainty is incompletely documented, and Appendix Eq. (20) still conflicts with the corrected Gaussian transport formula.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CHaRS research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original human-preference, perceptual-similarity, coupling, covariance, and throughput results.

before.justification: V1 reports original jailbreaking, toxicity-mitigation, and image-style experiments, plus clustering and principal-component analyses in the appendices.

title: Concept Heterogeneity-aware Representation Steering

C1.justification: The central uncomputable-versus-exponential bound claims remain. v2 qualifies informal Theorem 1.1 with termination and Theorem 1.2 with worst-case necessity, and Section 6 explicitly positions the contribution as the first length-complexity bounds for entire transformer classes.

C2.justification: v2 adds a rationale connecting the idealized learner with complete bounded-length data and perfect optimization to practical learning difficulties. It identifies non-Lipschitz operations as a possible explanation for differences from Izzo et al., and distinguishes maximum training length from sample count, leaving potentially polynomial sample complexity open.

D1.justification: The precision representations, rounding rules, and simulation constructions in v1 Appendix C are retained in v2 Appendix B. No implementation instructions, hardware specifications, hyperparameters, or code/data access information are added.

E1.justification: Neither version conducts dataset-based training or evaluation. MAJORITY and bounded-depth Dyck languages remain theoretical examples, not added evaluation tasks.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods experimentally. The expanded comparison with Izzo et al. concerns theoretical assumptions, not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version reports an original experimental protocol. The settings listed in new Appendix A.2 describe prior theoretical models, not experiments conducted by this work.

E4.justification: No ablations, robustness tests, or empirical supplementary analyses are added or removed. The Dyck-language argument and its geometric illustration are retained; the new Lipschitz discussion is conceptual.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repetitions, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Section 6 revises cited length-generalization examples from N-to-3N and N-to-10N to 50-to-150 and 40-to-500, adding attribution to Deletang et al. These are changed literature examples, not original experiments or demonstrated same-setting performance gains. The paper's own bounds remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The C-RASP/C-RASP+ constructions and transformer computations are retained. Explicitly naming the two regimes as (1, log n)-precision and (1, 1)-precision replaces terminology already defined in v1, without changing the models or procedures.

P1.justification: v2 edits and condenses introductory material, expands the discussion, standardizes precision terminology, and updates publication and acknowledgement text. Lemma 4.5's proof moves into the main text, and the appendices are reorganized, while the main section sequence and most technical prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Lemma 4.2's inline bullet formulas become aligned display equations, and the relocated Lemma 4.5 proof changes from appendix to main-text formatting. Publication information and text placement change locally. Figure 1 and its caption are unchanged, and neither version contains experimental result tables.

R1.justification: The brief reference to Izzo et al. becomes a substantial comparison in Section 3.3 and new Appendix A.2, detailing both model variants and explaining possible compatibility with this paper's bounds. v2 also revises its positioning against Salzer et al., explicitly claiming a stronger undecidability result for a more restricted class. Deletang et al. is added, while several empirical-method and auxiliary references are removed; the Izzo publication update itself is not a new cited work.

T1.justification: The substantive definitions, undecidability reduction, exponential bounds, simulation proofs, and depth-two reduction are retained. Lemma 4.5's proof moves from v1 Appendix A into Section 4, and the Dyck definition added to Example 2.3 already appeared in v1 Appendix B. The new prior-work discussion supplies no new proof or formal separation.

improvement.justification: v2 improves clarity through explicit precision labels, termination and worst-case qualifications, and a detailed account of the assumptions behind potentially conflicting prior bounds. Moving Lemma 4.5's proof into Section 4 also improves accessibility. These are useful refinements to unchanged theoretical results; the Lipschitz explanation remains tentative rather than establishing a new separation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Length Generalization Bounds for Transformers by the same authors. Their main text, equations, Figure 1, references, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v2 remains a theoretical paper. The expanded discussion and appendix comparison summarize prior work without adding original experiments, simulations, or data analyses.

before.justification: v1 presents mathematical constructions, bounds, and proofs. Its empirical examples are attributed to prior publications; neither the main text nor appendices report original empirical results.

title: Length Generalization Bounds for Transformers

C1.justification: The original benchmark contributions remain, but v2's abstract footnote and Section 6 add a prominent claim of rapid benchmark saturation by Mythos Preview. This substantially changes the paper's capability assessment from an incompletely solved benchmark to every task being solved across five trials with the extended budget.

C2.justification: v2 removes the reassurance that correctly configured, up-to-date containers remain appropriate isolation and adds recommendations for hypervisor isolation and defence in depth. It also explains that crashes confound apparent capability plateaus, distinguishes mid-trajectory refusals from eventual task failure, and discusses nonuniform judge refusals.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds log-field definitions, refusal-detection criteria, scanner descriptions, clustering details and more specific completion/error reporting. Core prompts, generation defaults, VM providers and code-access information remain. Conflicting references to Opus 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 as judges limit reproducibility of the expanded analyses.

E1.justification: Table 1 retains the same 18 orchestration, runtime and kernel tasks, exploit conditions and canonical difficulty ratings. Renaming scenarios to tasks, evaluating newer models and increasing token budgets do not expand task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 2 expands the evaluated comparison from nine to fourteen models by adding Claude Mythos Preview, Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7, GPT-5.4 Pro and GPT-5.5. These models also appear in the expanded compute-scaling comparison.

title: Utonia: Toward One Encoder for All Point Clouds

E6.justification: Tables 19–21 add substantial new results: AlpacaEval shaping win rates range from 46.23% to 54.42%, and GSM8K mean best-of-N accuracy is 62.76% for shaping versus 62.06% for unmodified models and 61.20% for Huang calibration. M1.justification: Section 3.2 retains the same difference-of-means probes, final-layer activation extraction, Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization, and null-space intervention. P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 19–21 and Figure 10, repositions existing figures and tables, and adjusts labels and captions. The existing charts and principal table structures are retained, so the visual presentation is extended without a substantial redesign.

title: Old Habits Die Hard: How Conversational History Geometrically Traps LLMs

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Equation 1 retain the same Bernoulli/stratified knockout measurements, Lasso regression and selection of heads with the most negative coefficients. P1.justification: The seven-section main structure and much existing prose remain. C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the headline claims: unequal channel rates, the 0.255-bit information-theoretic gap, potentially unbounded GPTQ suboptimality, and state-of-the-art Llama/Qwen performance over 1–4 bits. The added experiments do not revise these central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of Gaussian applicability and query/key deviations, calibration-distribution mismatch, corpus-dependent fine-tuning benefits, and calibration-context tradeoffs. Fine-tuning is removed from the future-work discussion, although statements restricting the work to layerwise optimization and small-to-mid-sized models remain outdated.

D1.justification: v2 adds an implementation link and detailed fine-tuning instructions: AdamW settings, learning-rate schedule, four epochs, checkpointing, CPU caching, streamed integer codes and rescaler precision handling. It also reports four H100 GPUs for Llama-3-70B and documents the revised rate-search procedure. The linked resource's availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v1 uses WikiText-2 for calibration and perplexity evaluation alongside downstream benchmarks. v2 adds C4 perplexity evaluation, RedPajama calibration, and C4/RedPajama fine-tuning, substantially expanding corpus coverage and testing transfer beyond the calibration distribution. Existing downstream tasks remain.

E2.justification: The original comparison sets are retained. New longer-context comparisons include reported results for AQLM, DB-LLM, PV-Tuning, YAQA-B and QuIP (Tables 10 and 13). The new Llama-3-70B comparison additionally includes PB-LLM and OstQuant (Table 14); these are actual comparison entries, not merely citations.

E3.justification: v2 supplements the retained 2048-token evaluations with 4096- and 8192-token protocols, compares 1024 versus 2048 calibration contexts, and evaluates Llama-3-70B. It introduces fine-tuning budgets and controlled corpus comparisons using matched sequence counts. Appendix D also changes the reported mixing-search budget from 15 to 10 iterations.

E4.justification: The original component ablations remain. v2 adds Gaussian-versus-Laplace weight-distribution diagnostics (Figure 11), calibration-context sensitivity (Table 12), and calibration/fine-tuning corpus analyses across rates (Tables 15–16 and Figure 15). These test theoretical applicability and distribution sensitivity absent from v1.

E5.justification: Appendix E introduces distribution-fitting statistics: Kolmogorov–Smirnov distances to fitted Gaussian and Laplace distributions, averaged across layers with closer-fit counts. This adds statistical estimation and reporting, but neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Most original benchmark entries remain, while v2 adds extensive fine-tuned, C4, longer-context and 70B results. For example, Table 2 retains Qwen3-8B WaterSIC perplexity 11.37 at 2.125 bits and adds 10.18 for the separately trained WaterSIC-FT configuration. Figure 5 also changes its reported rate-distribution statistics.

M1.justification: Section 4 adds WaterSIC-FT, which freezes integer codes and trains continuous rescalers using teacher-student distillation. Rate assignment changes from binary search to a secant method, and Appendix D now matches the target rate at each adaptive-mixing candidate instead of reusing an initially selected scale.

P1.justification: v2 expands the introductory explanation, revises procedural prose, adds acknowledgements, and separates supplementary model evaluations into Appendix F while moving zero-shot evaluations to Appendix G. Most existing exposition, theory and prior-work text remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The model-size plot moves from v1 Figure 3 to v2 Figure 1 with a logarithmic size axis and additional curves. Main comparison plots become side-by-side displays; algorithms and appendix tables are relocated and compacted. New diagnostic figures and experimental tables substantially revise the presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning through prediction-based Gaussian rate-distortion theory (Zamir et al., 2006), outlier-safe pretraining (Park et al., 2025), and a source for 70B comparisons (Huang et al., 2024). The prior-work review is largely retained; most other reference edits update publication metadata.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the rate definition by adding 1/n, fixes the matrix-factor placement in Appendix B Equation (35), and restores the addition sign in Appendix C's regularized objective. The principal theorem, assumptions and proof strategy remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical assessability through cross-corpus controls, matched-context comparisons with stronger methods, and 70B evaluation, addressing gaps explicitly deferred in v1. Fine-tuning documentation and mathematical corrections also help. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, but reconciliation is needed: 1-bit Llama-3.2-1B fine-tuned perplexity is 30.47 in Table 1 versus 32.85 in Tables 7 and 16, and broad SOTA and scope statements are not fully aligned with the expanded evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WaterSIC research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds fine-tuning, cross-corpus, calibration-sensitivity and larger-model experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original WaterSIC perplexity, zero-shot accuracy, component ablations and compression measurements.

title: WaterSIC: information-theoretically (near) optimal linear layer quantization

Appendix B.1 attributes MMSI-Bench weaknesses and reversed scaling to limited training-data diversity. Existing limitations concerning task-specific training and missing perception CoT data are retained.

Appendix A's hardware, fine-tuning choices, and chunk sizes are unchanged, as is project-page access. Detailed implementation information for the added 8B experiments is not supplied.

E3.justification: Appendix B.1 adds evaluation of an 8B configuration alongside 4B and describes few-image inputs for the additional benchmarks. Existing experimental settings and metrics are retained; the new statement that VSI-Bench uses 32 frames does not establish a changed earlier protocol.

E4.justification: Section 4.4.2 and Figure 9 add an error-distribution analysis testing whether RFT reduces zero-overlap grounding failures. Appendix B.1 also investigates model-scale sensitivity across benchmarks, including reversed scaling on MMSI-Bench. These substantially extend the existing training-strategy, data-quality, and training-dynamics analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing training-curve reporting is unchanged. The new IoU density plot analyzes prediction errors rather than introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their results. New Table 5 adds benchmark and model-scale results: the 8B model scores 64.0 on VSI-Bench versus the retained 4B score of 62.8, while newly reported MMSI-Bench scores are 28.0 and 29.9, respectively. These are different configurations, not revised 4B performance. Figure 9 additionally reports reduced zero-overlap grounding errors.

M1.justification: The SFT-to-GRPO pipeline, original model components, task-specific rewards, and loss chunking remain unchanged. The added 8B evaluation documents a model-scale extension, without establishing a new algorithm or architectural component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related-work discussion receive localized revisions, with new Sections 4.4 and B.1. Appendix subsections are renumbered, the limitations text moves before the qualitative figures, and the publication header changes. The overall narrative structure is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the conceptual reward-surface illustration, IoU density plot, and Table 5. Existing figures retain their image content, with appendix Figures 8–14 becoming Figures 10–16. Table 4 and appendix material are repositioned, and grounding-example labels are restyled.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MMSI-Bench, All-Angles, and Chen et al.'s 2026 work on lifting unlabeled data for 3D understanding. It also explicitly positions the already-cited VST as concurrent generalist work and distinguishes 3D-RFT's focus on video-based RLVR.

T1.justification: Equations 1–16 and the mathematical formulations remain unchanged. Despite its 'Theoretical Analysis' heading, new Section 4.4.1 and Figure 8 provide a conceptual illustration of one-hot supervision versus geometric rewards, without adding formal assumptions, derivations, proofs, or counterexamples.

improvement.justification: The added evaluations make generalization and scaling limits more visible, including the MMSI-Bench weakness, while the ScanRefer error analysis supplies evidence beyond aggregate scores. Removing the priority claim also improves positioning. These are useful but bounded gains: the added evaluations remain sparsely documented, and the optimization explanation is conceptual rather than a formal demonstration.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3D-RFT work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds grounding error-distribution analysis and evaluations across additional benchmarks and model scales.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection, grounding, and spatial-reasoning results, alongside ablations, training curves, and qualitative examples in the main text and appendices.

C2.justification: The interpretations and limitations are unchanged. Section 4 still identifies the lack of exhaustive reward ablations and incomplete validation on fundamentally different GUI paradigms.

D1.justification: The v2 abstract adds a direct GitHub repository URL for WebFactory's code and resources. v1 already described an open-source release but supplied no project repository URL. Implementation details and hyperparameters remain unchanged.
