E4.justification: The knowledge/data ablations in Tables 1–2, foundation-model analysis in Figure 3, and action-distribution and transition analyses in Appendix F are identical. No ablation, robustness test, or supplementary analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Appendix I.3 retains the same 95% Wilson confidence intervals for the 90-task transfer evaluation. No repeated-run, seed, or uncertainty-reporting information is added or revised.

E6.justification: All numerical results and reported findings are unchanged. For example, Table 4 retains average transfer TCRs of 53.4% for WebFactory-3B and 37.0% for GUI-R1-3B; the results in Figures 3–5 also match.

M1.justification: Section 2 and Appendices C–G retain the same environment synthesis, task generation, trajectory filtering, action space, reward functions, and GRPO training procedure.

P1.justification: v2 appends one code-and-resources availability sentence to the abstract and updates the arXiv version/date stamp. The remaining wording and section organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: The expanded abstract changes line wrapping and pushes the final two lines of an introductory paragraph onto page 2, with corresponding spacing adjustments. All figures, tables, and layouts from page 3 onward are identical.

R1.justification: The references and Appendix B are identical, preserving the same positioning relative to offline benchmarks, live-web generation, and weak-supervision pipelines.

T1.justification: The action-space and reward definitions in Section 2.2.3 and Appendix G, including Equations 1–4, are identical. No mathematical assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies a prominent repository address where v1 only claimed an open-source release, modestly improving resource discoverability and reproducibility documentation. The scientific content and appendices are unchanged. The PDFs establish this documentation gain, but do not establish the linked repository's completeness or usability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same WebFactory study, with readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–I. Pages 3–22 have identical extracted text and rendered appearance; changes are confined to the first two pages.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and dataset analyses, including the offline benchmark, online-transfer evaluation, and public GUI benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original task-generation, trajectory-quality, and agent-evaluation experiments in Section 3, Tables 1–5, and Figure 3. Appendix F also reports analyses of the generated trajectory dataset.

title: WebFactory: Automated Compression of Foundational Language Intelligence into Grounded Web Agents

C1.justification: The three principal contributions remain, but the abstract, introduction, and conclusion explicitly scope the guarantees to a minimal stylized model and describe larger-model evidence as qualitative agreement. The claimed empirical reach extends from 1.5B to 8B parameters.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly states that the short-prompt construction abstracts away discourse, positional structure, and long-range dependencies, and positions deep linear networks as a limited illustration. It changes the depth interpretation from monotonic increase to approximate non-decrease and adds an explanation involving task-irrelevant shared components for Qwen-3-8B's weak raw feature separation.

D1.justification: Unlike v1 Appendix N.2, v3 Appendix O.2 specifies 10 fine-tuning epochs, per-device batch size 16, learning rate 1e-5, zero weight decay, and FP16 training. Section 8.2 also specifies the 20% activation-retention diagnostic. Existing synthetic hyperparameters are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic analogy/two-hop tasks, generated natural-language entity-category dataset, and orthogonal-input depth experiment. Qwen-3-8B extends model scale on retained coverage; renaming the natural-language experiment does not introduce a new dataset or task.

E2.justification: The joint-training, similarity-first, attribution-first, and identity-bridge controls remain in their corresponding experiments. Qwen-3-8B is an additional architecture tested under the existing curricula, rather than a newly evaluated competing reasoning method.

E3.justification: v3 introduces an 8B model configuration and a feature diagnostic retaining the top 20% of MLP activations at relational tokens. Earlier experimental settings are otherwise retained; the newly stated natural-language fine-tuning hyperparameters do not establish that earlier settings changed.

E4.justification: Section 8.2 adds a Qwen-3-8B diagnostic examining whether shared representation components obscure feature alignment, reporting weak separation with full representations and using filtered activations. Existing end-to-end/ReLU, premise-frequency, and layer-depth analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations for synthetic experiments and point estimates for natural-language results. v3 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: New Table 3 reports Qwen-3-8B feature similarity/success of 0.3785/84% for joint training, 0.3757/75% for late attribution, and 0.2704/34% for late similarity. Existing main and appendix numerical results and Figure 1 are retained. These are additional-model results, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The attention/value block, linear feature layer, cross-entropy training, curricula, and identity-bridge construction remain. Renaming the linear MLP and correcting cumulative training-time indices reconcile descriptions with the existing theoretical procedure; they do not establish a different core method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory framing, model description, experimental narrative, conclusion, and impact statement undergo substantial rewriting. Terminology is standardized around a minimal transformer-style block and feature layer, and a proof roadmap organizes the appendix arguments. Citation style, headings, and front matter also change.

P2.justification: v3 adds the compact Qwen-3-8B Table 3, corrects Table 1's two-hop success column from A to R, and fixes the one-layer-only appendix table caption. The unchanged Figure 1 moves beside its discussion. Existing table structures and plot design are largely preserved despite document reflow.

R1.justification: v3 adds focused deep-linear-network context in Appendix A, citing Saxe, Kawaguchi, Laurent and Brecht, Hardt and Ma, and two Arora papers. It also connects the analogy definition to Gentner's structure-mapping theory and refines the comparison with Huang et al.; the central research positioning remains.

T1.justification: The supporting mathematics is substantially revised. Theorem 6 replaces the 0.8 alignment lower bound with Omega(1), while Section 7 makes random orthonormal inputs independent of labels explicit. Its appendix proof revises Lemma 18, stage indexing, error bounds, and the previously omitted input residual. Other appendices restore missing representation-decomposition terms, revise the joint-training alignment bound, and replace the no-alignment derivations for Propositions 8 and 9 with inner-product bounds.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is improved mathematical consistency in this theory-centered paper: v3 replaces problematic no-alignment derivations, restores omitted representation terms, and revises the deep-linear proof and its overly specific 0.8 guarantee. Narrower assumptions and claims trade breadth for better alignment between statements and supporting arguments. The proof roadmap and disclosed fine-tuning settings further improve assessability. The added 8B experiment remains limited by filtered feature measurements and point estimates; it is supplementary to the substantial theoretical corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Feature Resemblance study. Their main text, equations, tables, figure, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching content across appendix and table renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds Qwen-3-8B results and an activation-based feature diagnostic in Section 8.2 and Table 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments, natural-language fine-tuning results, curriculum and identity-bridge comparisons, and appendix analyses of feature alignment.

title: Feature Resemblance: Towards a Theoretical Understanding of Analogical Reasoning in Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about curriculum reinforcement learning, state-of-the-art KB-VQA performance and generalization to unseen questions.

C2.justification: The explanations concerning sparse rewards, retrieval noise, observation propagation and training behavior are identical. Section 5 retains the limitation that retrieval manipulation only partially controls the distributional gap.

D1.justification: Implementation and reproducibility information is unchanged, including hyperparameters, retrieval-score fusion, graph construction, hardware, training times and the project-page address. Appendices A-C contain no revised disclosures.

E1.justification: Both versions use Encyclopedic VQA and InfoSeek for training and evaluation, ViQuAE for zero-shot transfer, and the same oracle-document scenarios. No dataset or task coverage changes.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged throughout the tables, including the zero-shot models, retrieval-augmented methods, ViQuAE reading-comprehension baselines, and SFT/DAPO ablations. Bibliographic edits do not add or remove evaluated methods.

E3.justification: The evaluation protocols, metrics, model sizes and training settings are identical. Both retain 20k training examples per main benchmark and separate 1k InfoSeek subsets for evaluation and hyperparameter selection.

E4.justification: Both retain the same component ablations, propagation-similarity comparison, training-dynamics analyses and hyperparameter sensitivity experiments in Section 4.5 and Appendix A. No analysis or case study is added or removed.

E5.justification: Appendix B reports three independent runs in both versions, with identical curves in Figure 5. Run information and statistical reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: All numerical tables and plotted results are identical, including the appendix results. For example, Table 1 retains Wiki-R1 7B scores of 37.1 on EVQA and 44.1 on InfoSeek, and Table 2 retains 55.6 F1 and 50.3 exact match on ViQuAE.

M1.justification: The retrieval-controlled data curriculum, sampling curriculum, observation propagation and training objective are unchanged in Section 3 and Algorithms 1-2. The revised citation in Section 3.4 does not change the procedure.

P1.justification: v2 updates NoisyGRPO from an arXiv reference to a proceedings reference, adjusts the Qiu citation suffixes, and merges Shi et al. 2025a/2025b into 2025. The arXiv version/date stamp also changes; substantive prose and section organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Citation edits cause small local changes in line wrapping, and the revised bibliography changes spacing on page 13. All five figures, eight tables, their captions and placements, and the appendix layouts remain identical.

R1.justification: The distinct cited works and research positioning are unchanged. NoisyGRPO receives publication metadata, while two identical Shi et al. entries are consolidated; these are bibliographic edits rather than additions or removals of prior work.

T1.justification: Equations 1-6, the task formulation, optimization expressions and propagation mathematics are unchanged. Neither version adds a theorem, proof or mathematical correction relative to the other.

improvement.justification: v2 removes a duplicate Shi et al. reference and unifies its citation labels, improving bibliographic consistency. The NoisyGRPO entry also gains publication details. These provide a small editorial improvement; the scientific content, supporting evidence and reproducibility information are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same Wiki-R1 paper, with 19 readable pages including Appendices A-C. Text extraction and rendered-page comparison establish that the equations, algorithms, tables, figures and appendices are available for reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the same original benchmark results, ablations and appendix experiments, including the independent-run results in Appendix B and Figure 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original Wiki-R1 evaluations on Encyclopedic VQA, InfoSeek and ViQuAE, component ablations, hyperparameter analyses and three-run training curves.

title: Wiki-R1: Incentivizing Multimodal Reasoning for Knowledge-based VQA via Data and Sampling Curriculum

C1.justification: v1 claims incompatible geometries, no common refinement and no procedure satisfying all four criteria. v3 instead claims non-nesting of componentwise classes, explicitly permits compatible guarantees and replaces 'No universal procedure' with 'No universal certificate.' The abstract also withdraws martingale necessity for general Blackwell admissibility and qualifies the coverage and approachability claims.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes empirical calibration from self-predictive martingale coherence and explains why calibration does not imply log-loss optimality. It interprets constrained Bayes as separate criterion-specific optimization problems and explains compatibility despite non-nesting. Applications become motivations, Gaussian extensions require further verification, and covariate-shift overcoverage is explicitly interpreted outside the exchangeability guarantee.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the clipping transformation and epsilon=10^-6, identifies simulated versus theoretical table quantities, and documents initialization and split-conformal rank/tie-breaking details. These improve technical specification; they do not establish how v1's computations were implemented. No code or data-access resource is added.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Bernoulli prediction and testing tasks and the same heteroskedastic Gaussian conformal scenarios involving Uniform and Beta covariates. The removed Gaussian location laboratory was analytical, not an additional empirical dataset or simulation.

E2.justification: The simulations retain Bayes versus plug-in MLE and likelihood-ratio e-process versus five-look z-testing. Clipping is presented as numerical handling of the MLE comparison. KT, discounted e-processes and dogmatic-prior predictors are theoretical witnesses, not new experimental baseline competitors.

E3.justification: The reported log-loss evaluation separates clipped numerical loss from theoretical unclipped risk, and the boundary diagnostic changes from an empirical frequency to an exact model probability. Sample sizes, testing thresholds, peeking schedule and conformal calibration/test sizes remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether v1 already used clipping internally.

E4.justification: v3 adds an analytical failure check for fixed clipping: Table 2 states that it destroys plug-in martingale self-consistency and permits CApp feasibility only on the restricted parameter interval. Section 8.1 also quantifies boundary events below Monte Carlo resolution. The existing conformal covariate-shift analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state 10,000 Monte Carlo replications. Neither reports seeds, confidence intervals, standard errors or significance tests, and v3 establishes no increase in repeated runs or new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The central risk table is substantially corrected: v1 Table 4 reports finite MLE risk, including 2.368 at n=5; v3 Table 3 reports clipped risk 1.286 and theoretical unclipped risk infinity at every n. These are differently specified quantities, not a same-setting performance gain. Under retained settings, e-process/peeking rejection rates change from 0.034/0.169 to 0.031/0.165, and conformal coverages change from 0.897/0.964/0.888 to 0.900/0.946/0.900.

M1.justification: The work remains a theoretical analysis of existing prediction and inference procedures. The predictive-system tuple and new separation witnesses revise the formal framework, without introducing a new predictive algorithm. The experimental Bayes predictor, likelihood-ratio construction and conformal procedure are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions and discussion are extensively rewritten. Sections 4–6 gain substantial explanatory structure, terminology and scope remarks; proofs previously deferred to appendices appear alongside revised statements. The Gaussian laboratory and duality subsection disappear, and Applications becomes Motivations and Interpretations.

P2.justification: Several diagrams are redrawn or relabelled, especially the explicitly schematic risk plot and simplified coverage plot. The procedure-to-geometry diagram is removed, and the constrained-Bayes diagram is reorganized. The extended classification table is removed, a separation-witness table is added, and the classification and log-loss tables receive substantial structural revisions.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from incompatible paradigms and a purported counterexample to martingale posteriors toward qualified, modular certificate transfer. v3 adds an explicit comparison with Choe and Ramdas on filtration transport and draws on Dawid, Krichevsky–Trofimov and misspecification literature. It removes the companion-paper framing and associated citations, alongside the Blackwell lecture framing.

T1.justification: v3 replaces risk-set closedness with upper-hull closedness, adds support/continuity conditions for Bayes admissibility, and replaces v1's varying-prior martingale equivalence under every true law with a single-prior implication under the prior predictive law. It revises AV dominance and restricts the martingale equivalence to point nulls. New definitions and proofs introduce rank-family coverage efficiency, the predictive-system space, active-coordinate separation witnesses and precise CApp feasibility. The Gaussian separation proposition and formal Lagrangian proposition are removed; appendix proofs are partly relocated and substantially superseded.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the alignment of claims, proofs and numerical evidence. It corrects v1's inference from non-nesting to incompatibility, distinguishes the laws supporting martingale statements, supplies missing qualifications for Bayes admissibility, and resolves the finite-versus-infinite MLE risk presentation. The explicit separation witnesses strengthen the central argument. Generality is reduced, including withdrawal of the Gaussian extension, but this trades unsupported breadth for more defensible conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. All supplied pages were inspected, including v1 Appendices A–B; their contents were matched to retained, revised or removed material in v3, which has no separate appendices.

after.justification: Section 8 retains the three original Monte Carlo studies and reports revised numerical results in Tables 3–5.

before.justification: Section 8 reports three original Monte Carlo studies of Bernoulli prediction, sequential testing and conformal coverage, with results in Tables 4–6.

title: Bayes with No Shame: Admissibility Geometries of Predictive Inference

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion more explicitly center the contribution on multi-chunk KV reuse where full-context prefilling remains feasible but redundant. Information flow is qualified as operational rather than formal causal analysis. The central attention-selection, positional-alignment, and reordering contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially refines applicability and interpretation: it qualifies information-flow claims, limits the motivation when exact prefilling is already cheap, and distinguishes attention fidelity from generation-oriented selection. Section 6.3 corrects the VLM budget interpretation and acknowledges the OCRBench exception, 842 versus CacheBlend's 845 at k=2. Section 8 also frames latency comparisons as implementation-dependent measurements rather than ideal compute costs.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents the common 15% recomputation budget, global first-stage selection without per-chunk quotas, normalized chunk scoring, and stable ordering of ties. It clarifies that VLM k denotes visual chunks and identifies FlashInfer-style kernels for irregular attention. These refine implementation and experiment documentation without establishing changed underlying settings.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds the LongBench v2 short-question subset, comprising 180 examples with reported context lengths of 10k-210k. The original four LongBench datasets, five VLM benchmarks, and Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation remain. This extends coverage within the existing long-context QA focus.

E2.justification: Tables 7, 8, 10, and 11 add evaluated comparisons with KVLink5, TurboRAG, PCW, BM25 Recompute, PyramidKV, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM. This substantially broadens comparison beyond the original recomputation baselines to training-based cache reuse, retrieval, and compression or eviction methods.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a Llama-3-3B comparison, accuracy evaluation on the selected 180-example LongBench v2 subset, attention-matrix MSE averaged across layers on 100 HotpotQA examples, and an ascending-versus-descending ordering control. These substantially expand the evaluation protocol. Explicitly stating the existing experiments' 15% recomputation budget does not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices D.3, E, and G add tests of full-context attention recovery, sensitivity to chunk-order direction, and component-level runtime overhead. These provide substantial new mechanism and efficiency analyses. The original RoPE, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and layer-selection analyses remain; Figure 4's corrected caption does not constitute a new experiment.

E5.justification: Both versions report median latency over 10 independent runs. v2 adds no accuracy confidence intervals, significance tests, seed information, or revised repeated-run practice. The new evaluation sample counts and averaged metrics do not provide uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 7-14 add substantial results for new comparators, longer contexts, and diagnostic analyses. For example, Table 9 reports accuracy of 0.2889 for Our, 0.2611 for CacheBlend, and 0.2056 for EPIC. Among retained results, Table 3 changes the LLaMA fixed-chunk NarrativeQA baseline from 0.1623 to 0.1862. Most original scores remain unchanged; Table 6's conversion from percentages to fractions is equivalent.

M1.justification: Attention-mass top-k selection, global RoPE reconstruction, full-layer KV recomputation, and two-pass chunk reordering are retained. Section 4.3 makes the global selection budget, normalized chunk score, and tie handling explicit. Figure 1 already depicts reordering by selected-token ratio in v1, supporting clarification rather than an established algorithm change.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain. v2 adds targeted explanations, revises terminology and section titles, updates author/affiliation and publication-header text, and reorganizes the expanded appendices, moving the original implementation appendix from B to F. This is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Tables 7-14 substantially expand the presentation of comparisons and diagnostic evidence. Existing displays also change: Figure 2 receives new colors and marker styling, Tables 5-6 are restructured, and several captions and highlights are revised. Figure 4's erroneous heatmap caption is corrected while its actual plot remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to SnapKV, KVLink, TurboRAG, and PCW, plus a RAG subsection explaining that the method operates after retrieval. Appendices B and D expand positioning relative to trained cache-reuse methods, passage retrieval, and complementary KV compression, while retaining the original training-free recomputation positioning.

T1.justification: The existing KV, RoPE, positional, and attention-selection mathematics is retained apart from notation clarification. Equation 9 expresses the selected-token-ratio reordering rule already depicted in v1 Figure 1. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central selection and efficiency claims through broader comparator families, attention-recovery and reversed-order controls, and longer-context evaluation. title: InfoFlow KV: Information-Flow-Aware KV Recomputation for Long Context

C2.justification: v1's claim of negligible computational overhead is replaced by acknowledgment of increased runtime and a memory/runtime tradeoff. Appendix E also explains the new baselines' failure mechanisms and describes text alignment as competitive rather than universally best. The original compatibility limitation and low-pass interpretation remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents the extension's candidate-mining and filtering process, new baseline compositions, the Wan prompting template, and hardware and resource measurements for the cost study. Original implementation defaults, visibility-mask details, and repository access information are retained. Specific mining-model identities remain unspecified.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same data sources and task types, including extreme occlusion, semantic branching, and conflicting-condition examples. The new 100-case AmbiSem-3D-Ext split uses ObjaverseXL and emphasizes view-induced ambiguity, which v1 already explicitly includes. It expands sampling within existing coverage rather than establishing a distinct domain or task.

Original comparators remain; the change from '2D Edit' to 'SDXL' in Table 2 identifies the existing baseline more explicitly.

Additional comparison protocols introduce video/multi-view generation followed by reconstruction and direct text-image fusion. Original benchmark settings, metrics, defaults, and user-study design are retained.

E4.justification: The original component, hyperparameter, prior-count, and prior-source ablations and RelaxFlow conflict cases remain unchanged. Figures 9–11 add diagnostic case studies of alternative pipelines' branch misalignment, reconstruction inconsistency, and attribute leakage; Table 6 adds computational-cost analysis.

Runtime measurements report 2.46× and 1.82× backbone costs for SAM3D and TRELLIS respectively.

M1.justification: The dual-branch procedure, multi-prior conditioning, attention-logit smoothing, temporal schedule, and visibility-aware fusion remain unchanged. The new direct text+image fusion procedure is a comparison baseline, not a modification of RelaxFlow.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization are retained. Changes include grammar fixes, a clearer Section 5.4 title, affiliation and publication-status updates, acknowledgements, an impact statement, and a new Appendix E with subsequent appendix renumbering.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 and the visual ablation are reformatted as larger, full-width displays. v2 adds dataset galleries in Figures 7–8, baseline visualizations in Figures 9–11, and Tables 3–6. Existing supplementary figures are retained and relocated, with extensive reflow of the surrounding layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Wan, MV-Adapter, Nano Banana Pro, and additional completion, affordance, and visual-token research, while extending discussion of alternative conditioning routes. The central novelty argument remains unchanged. Interp3D and optimal-transport bibliographic updates refer to already cited works.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A retain the same mathematical definitions, spectral assumptions, stability analysis, and Wasserstein bounds and proofs. Typographical corrections and an optimal-transport citation update do not change the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility through four additional comparison families and evaluation beyond the original 21 manually curated ambiguity cases. It also corrects the unsupported negligible-overhead assertion with measured costs and exposes text-alignment tradeoffs. Missing uncertainty estimates and incomplete new configuration details remain limitations, but the broader validation and more accurate account of practical costs resolve important weaknesses in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RelaxFlow. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, a 100-case evaluation, and runtime and memory measurements in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, component and sensitivity ablations, qualitative experiments, and a 32-participant user study in Section 5 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original answer-decoding, inflection-point, and early-exit experiments, plus appendix experiments comparing probe baselines, transfer strategies, and hyperparameters.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized grammar and terminology corrections, updates the affiliation and publication footer, and adds an Impact Statement and short Qwen3 appendix subsection. The original section order and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 15, relocates Table 8 from page 6 to page 7 and Table 9 from page 7 to page 8, and adjusts surrounding layout. Table 10 corrects the final POET-Xfast label from b=256 to b=512. Figures 1–7 retain their content.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds brief positioning among stable optimizers and new references to Jordan et al.'s Muon, SSO, and Pion. The sparse-training and low-rank research positioning remains intact. Updated Jaiswal and Hoffmann bibliography entries refer to the same previously cited works.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(10), the backward-gradient derivation, spectrum-preservation reasoning, and Cayley-Neumann approximation are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical definition appears in either appendix.

improvement.justification: The added Qwen3 dense and MoE comparisons modestly strengthen evidence of applicability beyond Llama, while the Table 10 correction improves reporting accuracy. The gain is limited by the unexplained removal of the gradient-clipping detail and sparse documentation of the new experiments. The central method and original empirical evidence remain stable.

A1.justification: Both complete PDFs describe the same POET-X work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B support reliable comparison, including matching relocated tables and identifying v2's additional appendix experiment.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds Qwen3 dense and mixture-of-experts pretraining results in Appendix B, Table 15.

before.justification: V1 reports original kernel benchmarks, C4 pretraining perplexities, memory measurements, and throughput-scaling experiments in the main text and Appendix B.

title: POET-X: Memory-efficient LLM Training by Scaling Orthogonal Transformation

C1.justification: Alongside the retained claims of separating behavior-related dynamics and scaling to large neural recordings, v2 adds prominent claims of interpretability advantages over latent-state readouts and post hoc dLDS analysis. The abstract and introduction also elevate previously unreported hindbrain asymmetry into a principal biological contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets comparable reconstruction with sparser behavioral mappings as support for dynamics-based readouts, develops a biological interpretation of hindbrain asymmetry, and discusses possible imaging artifacts. It explicitly limits the CLDS comparison's scope and acknowledges that robustness does not guarantee a unique identifiable decomposition. The original explicit nonstationarity interpretation of trial-type segmentation is softened.

D1.justification: v2 supplies detailed settings for the added model comparisons and TaskRNN experiments, optimization budgets, trial-type definitions, and expanded model-selection guidance. Table 3 adds runtime and memory estimates with measurement caveats. New availability statements promise zebrafish data upon request and simulation data/code upon publication; they do not establish an existing public release.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on delayanti task-trained RNN activations, with processing, memory, and response phases and 23 input/output behavior traces (Figure 4). This substantially broadens coverage beyond the retained two-system simulations and zebrafish recording. The revised 14,000-neuron wording does not establish new zebrafish coverage: Appendix B retains the original recording and preprocessing counts.

E2.justification: The CLDS and PSID comparisons remain. v2 adds explicit zebrafish comparisons against unsupervised dLDS with post hoc behavior correlations and b-dLDS-x, including regularized and separately optimized variants (Table 3). b-dLDS-x also provides the comparator in the new TaskRNN experiment.

The retained simulation and zebrafish parameter tables largely preserve v1's settings.

New asymmetry analyses examine imaging-related baselines. These directly test components and failure conditions previously receiving little experimental scrutiny.

E5.justification: v2 adds baseline-asymmetry t-tests, reporting p<0.04 and p<0.001, and descriptive standard deviations in Table 2. It also documents three-seed TaskRNN runs and provides seedwise results and averages for new zebrafish comparisons and sensitivity sweeps. The original ten-seed CLDS comparison is retained; an increase in its run count is not reported.

E6.justification: New results include TaskRNN behavior R² of 0.99 versus 0.95 for b-dLDS and b-dLDS-x, extensive variant/sensitivity results, and six of 25 operators exceeding the 17% asymmetry baseline. The single-behavior zebrafish fit is replaced: v1 Figure 4 reports R²=0.90, whereas v2 Figure 5 reports neural R²=0.91 with different learned operators. Retained appendix displays also change operator 23's Psi value from 0.59 to 0.44 and operator 24's behavior R² from 0.22 to 0.11.

M1.justification: v2 introduces the experimental b-dLDS-x variant, moving the behavioral readout and associated reconstruction objective from dynamics coefficients c to latent states x. The central b-dLDS architecture and inference procedure remain; Frobenius regularization and step-size rescaling were already present in v1.

P1.justification: The six-section main-text organization and much of the existing prose remain. v2 refines state-versus-dynamics explanations, rewrites the conclusion, reorganizes appendix subsections, and replaces acknowledgments with availability sections and an impact statement. Editorial changes are concentrated around the larger scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 adds the TaskRNN Figure 4, Supplementary Figures 5 and 11, and six tables covering comparisons, asymmetry, settings, and sensitivity. It replaces the single-behavior zebrafish visualizations, revises Figure 3's labels, and reformats parameter tables with row separators. Original Tables 1–2 become Tables 5 and 7, while several simulation figures remain identical.

These are mathematical corrections beyond typesetting. Appendix A's connectivity derivation and assumptions remain unchanged, and no identifiability theorem is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1 through comparisons within the dLDS family, the TaskRNN experiment, component ablations, and sensitivity studies (Figure 4, Table 3, Supplementary Figures 5 and 11). The new asymmetry claim remains based on one fish, and resource estimates are acknowledged as rough, but these limitations do not outweigh the methodological validation gains.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds TaskRNN experiments, model comparisons, ablations, sensitivity studies, and quantitative zebrafish asymmetry analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation experiments, comparisons with CLDS and PSID, and b-dLDS analyses of zebrafish hindbrain recordings in Section 5 and Appendix B.

These refine existing components.

Section 2.4 more explicitly connects Fu et al. (2025b) to cognitive failure. The broader related-work organization and principal positioning remain.

before.justification: V1 reports original CARLA probing experiments, activation-steering outcomes, nuScenes transfer evaluations, and analyses of generated logits.

title: Stem: Rethinking Causal Information Flow in Sparse Attention

D1.justification: Appendix D documents configurations for the added experiments and explains control costs and fixed-depth cache storage. The original hyperparameters, A800 hardware statement, code link, and supplementary code/video availability statement remain unchanged.

New Tables 7–9 reuse subsets of existing methods: HERO is absent from these additions, and DuCa is also absent from Table 9; neither is removed from the original comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix D introduces LingBot-14B evaluation at two resolutions with 49 frames and 70 steps, Voyager evaluation at 30 and 70 steps, and LingBot evaluation at 81 and 161 frames. It also adds control-time and context-dependent memory profiling. The original evaluation settings remain intact.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether caching advantages persist across backbones, resolutions, denoising schedules, and longer contexts, and examine control overhead and memory scaling. These substantially broaden robustness and efficiency analysis. Tables 5–6 contain unchanged ablations moved from the appendix into the main text.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the statement that latency is averaged over multiple trials after warm-up. The additions introduce no seed or repetition counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 retain identical results, while Tables 7–11 add substantial numerical evidence. Examples include Voyager PSNR 25.49 and 4.09× speedup at 70 steps, control overhead of 0.047–0.060%, and extra memory of 0.02–0.03 GB. Appendix figures are regrouped and repositioned, including paired qualitative comparisons. HiCache's updated publication information refers to the same work. The related-work taxonomy and novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

(19)'s single-point Taylor remainder is not generally valid for vector trajectories, but that localized proof issue does not outweigh the broader empirical and explanatory gains.

New Appendix C identifies instruction-based visual editing as a future extension through data and model scaling.

Table 3 reports 28.57 versus 1.29 seconds for 256 versus 10 text-to-image steps; this is a newly reported step comparison, not a version-to-version performance gain.

P1.justification: v2 makes scattered grammar and terminology corrections, expands related-work explanations, shortens the conclusion, and adds impact and acknowledgment sections. Appendix B becomes an experimental section with subsections, retaining the original image gallery in B.5, followed by a new limitations appendix. The main narrative organization is preserved.

before.justification: v1 reports original ASR, TTS, visual understanding, image-generation, sampling-step, and qualitative multimodal results in Section 4 and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original human-labeling results and experiments measuring judge accuracy, attack success, optimization trajectories, and benchmark reliability in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original IMSE and IMSE-Retrieval experiments, ablations and robustness analyses in Sections 4–6 and the appendices.

title: IMSE: Intrinsic Mixture of Spectral Experts Fine-tuning for Test-Time Adaptation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: extending local BO to constraints, polynomial dimensional dependence of KKT convergence, and superior benchmark performance. The new analyses support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Appendix B develops the stagnation mechanism while explicitly acknowledging that trust-region methods can recover through restarts; the concern becomes their cost under limited budgets. Appendices C.2–C.3 add substantive interpretations attributing gains to the core penalty mechanism and explaining normalization, penalty trade-offs, and robustness without task-specific tuning.

D1.justification: Section 6.1 newly specifies standard one-sided penalties for inequality constraints. Hardware, GP fitting details, normalization, and Table 1 hyperparameters are retained. The HalfCheetah objective and energy threshold added to the main text were already documented in v1's appendix.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate 25D, 50D, and 100D synthetic problems, 25D truss design, 50D beam design, and 102D HalfCheetah. The added analyses reuse the truss and 50D synthetic tasks without introducing new task requirements or environments.

E2.justification: CEI, EPBO, SCBO, and HDsafeBO remain the external baselines. New ablation comparisons add LCBO variants without individual auxiliary components and variants with fixed penalties of 1, 10, 100, and 1000 in Figures 6–7.

E3.justification: Appendices C.2–C.3 add controlled experiments that individually remove local GP fitting, local search boxes, or gradient normalization, and compare growing against fixed penalties. Existing benchmark initialization, evaluation budgets, noise, metrics, and batch-schedule protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1 examines only batch scheduling. V2 retains that study as Appendix C.1 and substantially expands diagnostic evidence through component ablations, penalty-schedule sensitivity tests, and SCBO restart analysis addressing the proposed explanation of trust-region stagnation.

E5.justification: The ten-run median/interquartile-range benchmark reporting and five-seed batch-schedule study are retained. Figures 6–7 explicitly follow Figure 1's reporting conventions; the added restart summaries also use medians and interquartile ranges rather than introducing a new statistical procedure.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and batch-schedule results are retained. Figures 6–7 add substantive findings about component removal and weak versus excessive fixed penalties. Appendix B newly reports at least two SCBO restarts in every truss run, with first and second restart medians of 350 and 747 evaluations and interquartile ranges of 338–383 and 657–756.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same exploration acquisition, repeated evaluations, quadratic-penalty surrogate, and projected gradient update. The Z2 wording and newly stated one-sided inequality handling clarify implementation without establishing a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. V2 adds Section 6.4 and a mechanism appendix, reorganizes the previous batch study into an expanded ablation appendix, and renumbers the setup appendices. Other edits clarify terminology and update affiliations, correspondence, publication information, and acknowledgements.

P2.justification: V2 adds a substantial mechanism illustration in Figure 3 and two paired ablation displays in Figures 6–7. Main Figures 1–2 remain unchanged; the old batch plots become Figures 4–5 with minor resizing, and the unchanged hyperparameter table is relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds Tang et al. (2025) and Brunzema and Trimpe (2026) when discussing second-order local BO, adds Nesterov et al. (2018) for smoothness, and removes Robinson (1976) alongside the revised constraint-qualification statement. The broader research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Remark 5.4 replaces the claimed equivalence to MFCQ and strict comparison with LICQ with an LICQ implication and a connection to the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz condition. Assumption 5.3 itself, the convergence bounds, and the entire Appendix A proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The new restart measurements and targeted ablations strengthen explanations that v1 supported mainly through benchmark curves, while the revised theoretical qualification and implementation clarification improve precision. These are useful, incremental gains: the central algorithm, proofs, and benchmark results remain unchanged, and the additional diagnostic evidence concerns two retained tasks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Local Constrained Bayesian Optimization (LCBO). Their main text, equations, figures, table, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds component and penalty-schedule ablations and an empirical analysis of SCBO restarts.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic, engineering-design, and HalfCheetah experiments, plus a batch-schedule ablation in Appendix B.

title: Local Constrained Bayesian Optimization

The headline compression claim changes from 52.5% average compression in the abstract, and 52.2% in the introduction, to 52.6% compression without the average qualifier. The 16.6% AIME25 accuracy gain is explicitly identified as relative, refining the quantitative claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that OOD gains reflect beneficial reasoning paths rather than additional mathematical training, and that sparse outcome rewards improve reasoning structure. Appendix C.1 additionally argues that mostly unimodal non-Gaussian distributions remain usefully described by means and variances. The original limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v2 discloses training-data provenance for reused baseline models and identifies DeepSeek-V3.2 and the ShorterBetter prompt source for the new judge analysis. E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same base-model, truncation, ShorterBetter, ThinkPrune-4k and LASER-DE-4096 comparisons. Table 2 retains AutoThink and staged ThinkPrune comparisons, while Figure 7 retains its 1.5B OOD comparators. No comparison method is added or removed.

New supplementary protocols extend OOD evaluation to Qwen3-4B and classify reasoning on 50 randomly selected MATH500 problems using DeepSeek-V3.2.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites polish the abstract, introduction, method explanations and conclusion, with terminology and subsection-title corrections. v2 adds OOD and reasoning-structure subsections, acknowledgements and another correspondence contact, while retaining the overall narrative organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3, 5 and 8; Table 3 redisplays existing 1.5B OOD results alongside new 4B results. Existing figures are retained, with caption corrections and page reflow. Older tables are renumbered or relocated rather than replaced by substantially redesigned displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds BubbleSpec and removes O1-Pruner from the references, correcting the OpenAI o1 attribution to the already-cited system card. Most other reference changes update publication metadata for the same works. SmartThinker’s positioning around dynamic length calibration remains.

T1.justification: The equal-variance inequality corrections in Equations (5) and (7) resolve disagreement with the existing Appendix A.2 derivation. Equation (4) replaces the formulation involving step-level semantic density with a per-trajectory accuracy/length reward. Appendix A.3 corrects the KL target from the old policy to the reference policy. The central Gaussian theorem and proof remain.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves several equation and reporting inconsistencies and adds useful generalization, reasoning-structure and distribution diagnostics. These incrementally strengthen the retained study. Benefits are tempered by the erroneous 'except SmartThinker' statement in Appendix C.3 and Section 4.5’s causal attribution, which exceeds what the OOD comparisons establish.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SmartThinker work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds 4B out-of-domain evaluations, quantitative reasoning-structure analysis and unimodality tests.

title: SmartThinker: Progressive Chain-of-Thought Length Calibration for Efficient Large Language Model Reasoning

Noise robustness reporting expands to NQ/Quora FLOPs and latency plots; the original capacity and training-dynamics analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.10 adds kernel-density estimation and empirical mean/median summaries for distributional characterization. This expands descriptive statistical reporting, while Table 1's averaging over 100 timing runs is unchanged. No new seed-variability reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests appear.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial routing, backend, latency, encoder, BioASQ, ablation, and distributional results. For example, Figure 15 reports relative transport error declining from approximately 0.40 at 1B training samples to 0.365 at 7B. These are new experimental conditions; the original timing table and several relocated plots retain their results.

M1.justification: The SupportNet and KeyNet architectures, homogenization wrapper, losses, query augmentation, clustered formulation, and inference procedures remain substantively unchanged. Additional backends and configurations evaluate the existing method.

P1.justification: The overall main-section structure and most method prose remain. V2 rewrites the abstract, conclusion, and selected experimental passages, moves the MRR/transport tradeoff discussion to Appendix A.4, promotes robustness into the main text, and adds an author contribution statement.

P2.justification: V2 adds a deployment schematic and new routing, ablation, scaling, and distribution figures. Retrieval displays expand into grids covering FLOPs, search budget, and latency; existing plots are relocated or reformatted, and Table 1 receives a revised layout while retaining its values.

R1.justification: V2 adds references on amortized optimization, learned/query-aware indices, additional backends, and BioASQ. It refines v1's blanket characterization of prior indices as query-agnostic by acknowledging approaches that use query statistics during construction, while retaining the central research positioning.

T1.justification: The support-function formulation, homogeneity construction, Euler-based loss motivation, network-sizing derivation, and relative transport-error definition remain equivalent. V2 adds explanations but no substantive theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical correction.

improvement.justification: Added ablations, larger-cluster tests, and multi-backend latency comparisons make training choices and deployment limits more assessable than v1's largely FAISS/FLOPs-based validation. The net gain is limited by reporting inconsistencies: Figures 12–13 repeat identical curves under NQ/Quora labels, Appendix A.9 discusses BioASQ S/M results absent from Figure 28, and broad dominance claims exceed the SOAR FLOPs evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SupportNet/KeyNet research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds larger-scale retrieval, additional indexing backends, encoder experiments, ablations, and distributional analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original retrieval, cluster-routing, timing, training-dynamics, and noisy-query experiments in Section 4 and Appendix A.

title: Amortized Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about capacity-aware prediction, compute-aware sampling and large-model extrapolation, including 50% optimization-cost savings and benchmark improvements of up to 3%.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly explains intrinsic domains as latent capability components accommodating validation data with unknown domain composition. It also adds conditional reasoning connecting proportional capacity scaling to similar loss-improvement ratios, while retaining the original dynamic-allocation interpretation.

D1.justification: Architecture, training hyperparameters, mixture construction and fitting details in Appendices A–C are unchanged. The added training-FLOPs wording in Figure 1 and Section 3.2 clarifies compute accounting already documented as 6ND in Appendix B.4; access information is unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five training domains, 14 downstream benchmarks, specialized training objectives and Math/Knowledge scenario. The added ratio analysis uses the existing Figure 3 experiment.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain DML, SODM, the model-size-agnostic method and the human-designed mixture where originally evaluated. The newly cited Olmix work is not added as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Section 2.1 adds a diagnostic metric: the ratio of small-to-large to small-to-medium loss reductions, evaluated at training step 2000. This extends the analysis protocol; existing model scales, data splits, training budgets and benchmark evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 extends the qualitative Figure 3 discussion with a quantitative check of whether effective capacity scales proportionally across domains. The intrinsic-domain ablation, sampling-strategy comparisons and other supplementary analyses are unchanged.

E5.justification: Appendices B.1 and B.4 retain the same 20 sampling repetitions and 10 independent runs, respectively, with averaging. The new ratio analysis adds no uncertainty estimates or formal significance test.

M1.justification: The CAMEL scaling law, loss-to-benchmark mapping, benchmark-weighted optimization and Hourglass sampling procedure are unchanged. The expanded intrinsic-domain explanation and capacity-allocation analysis do not alter the method.

P1.justification: v2 locally expands Section 2.1, makes small grammatical and terminology edits, adds an Impact Statement and replaces the preprint footer with conference publication text. The overall section organization and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 4 and 5 exchange numbering, several graphics are enlarged or relocated, and Figure 8 and Table 2 move from page 7 to page 8. Figure 1's caption clarifies the cost measure. No figures or tables are added or removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chen et al. (2026), Olmix: A framework for data mixing throughout LM development, to the introduction and references. The remaining related-work discussion and positioning are unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 introduces loss-improvement and ratio definitions and derives the expected ratio under proportional capacity scaling, explaining its similarity across domains with close power-law exponents. Assumption 2.1, Theorem 2.2 and the Appendix D proof remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the capacity-allocation motivation more explicit through a defined diagnostic, a conditional derivation and reported Math/Knowledge ratios. The intrinsic-domain explanation also improves clarity. These are limited gains: the central method, benchmark evidence and complete appendices remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAMEL study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–D. Corresponding content can be matched despite layout changes and figure renumbering; the appendix pages are identical.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports numerical loss-improvement ratios in its analysis of capacity allocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, scaling-law prediction errors, sampling-strategy comparisons and downstream benchmark results, including evaluation on a 55B-A1.2B model.

title: Capacity-Aware Mixture Law Enables Efficient LLM Data Optimization

C1.justification: The central contributions remain training-free, layer-adaptive saliency selection and approximate attention for faster diffusion inference. The headline throughput claims remain 7.6× for LLaDA and 9.6× for Dream. Adaptive-decoding compatibility was already asserted in v1 Appendix F.1; v2 adds supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit discussion of extra cache memory, throughput saturation at small batch sizes, and dependence on temporal sparsity and threshold selection. Appendix D.2 additionally interprets stepwise saliency patterns as support for robustness across response lengths and schedules, although it does not directly test different lengths.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses PyTorch implementation with custom CUDA attention/cache kernels, a FlashAttention-like fused design, and the baselines' FlashAttention implementations. It specifies greedy prediction and model-specific unmasking rules, expands algorithm explanations, and replaces the anonymous code link with a named GitHub repository pointer. These are documentation additions, not evidence that retained experiments changed implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GSM8K, MBPP, MATH, and MMLU-Pro. The additional hardware, decoding, and ablation experiments reuse this coverage without introducing different data populations or task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the original implementation, Fast-dLLM PrefixCache, Fast-dLLM DualCache, and dLLM-Cache. New Tables 3 and 7 use subsets of these existing comparators. Newly cited acceleration methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds a separate confidence-aware adaptive-decoding protocol and reports average tokens unmasked per step, whereas v1 explicitly excluded this decoding scheme from its experiments. Appendix D.5 adds B200 evaluation with batch size 16, and Figure 9 extends the tested threshold range. The original H100 comparison remains retained.

E4.justification: Table 1 extends the FFN-only versus approximate-attention ablation to MATH and MMLU-Pro. Appendix D.2 adds saliency measurements across denoising-step intervals, Figure 9 broadens threshold sensitivity analysis, and Section 4.2.5 tests compatibility with adaptive parallel decoding. These substantially expand the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Added saliency averages and decoding-confidence scores do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2's numerical results are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results under separate conditions. Table 3 reports Dream at tau = 0.995 achieving 78.62 accuracy with 3.89 tokens unmasked per step; Table 7 reports B200 LLaDA GSM8K results of 78.09 accuracy and 196.24 tokens/s at tau = 0.99. Expanded ablations and stepwise saliency tables add further outcomes.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes the initial sparse-step index set from all response positions in v1 to decoded positions in v2. This is a localized change to the specified procedure; the central saliency criterion, caching mechanism, warmup, and exact/approximate attention paths remain intact.

P1.justification: There is extensive prose revision across the introduction, attention explanation, evaluation discussion, and Appendices A–C. Background and algorithm descriptions are substantially rewritten and clarified within the retained overall section structure. v2 also adds evaluation subsections, acknowledgements, and an impact statement.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a conference template and extensively redraws or reformats figures, legends, captions, and tables. Figures 5–7 are reordered, Figure 3 gains clearer token-state labels, Table 1 expands, and Tables 3, 4, and 7 introduce new displays. These changes go substantially beyond pagination.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to FlashAttention, d2Cache, Dynamic-dLLM, and Hierarchy Decoding, supporting its implementation discussion and positioning alongside adaptive decoding. The broader relationship to caching and sparse-attention research remains stable; publication updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: The main statement of Proposition 3.2 drops v1's small-temporal-variation assumption, while Appendix E retains the same bound and proof. The conclusion also introduces an explicit cache-memory overhead calculation relative to KV-only storage. There is no substantial new theoretical development.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's asserted adaptive-decoding compatibility into an empirical test and strengthens transparency through implementation details and explicit memory limitations. Additional hardware and ablation evidence improves validation. These gains are tempered by inaccurate new comparative prose: Section 4.2.2 claims 2.16–3.67× speedup over dLLM-Cache, but Table 2 gives approximately 1.82× for LLaDA/MBPP at tau = 0.99 (169.62/93.04). The revision offers a useful but limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same DyLLM research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete Appendices A–F are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds adaptive-decoding experiments, B200 measurements, and analyses of saliency across denoising steps.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy, throughput, attention-error, and saliency experiments on LLaDA and Dream, including appendix ablations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same claims about robust joint temporal/channel modeling and forecasting performance on 12 datasets.

T1.justification: Equations 1–15, including graph construction, training objectives and the appendix MLP fusion formulation, are unchanged. No mathematical assumptions, derivations or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: Explicitly crediting TimeFilter for the existing sparsification step improves attribution transparency, while the typo and table-header corrections modestly improve presentation. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GCGNet research. All 23 pages, including equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–B, are available for reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the original forecasting results, ablations, robustness experiments and supplementary analyses in Section 4 and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on 12 datasets, component ablations, missing-input robustness tests and parameter analyses in Section 4 and Appendix B.

title: GCGNet: Graph-Consistent Generative Network for Time Series Forecasting with Exogenous Variables

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same scientific contributions: deterministic mask-only pruning, expanded mask expressivity, improved optimization and pruning quality, applicability to dense and MoE models, and practical inference speedups.

C2.justification: V2 newly interprets limited LoRA recovery as evidence that initial sparse structure is a bottleneck because recovery cannot revise pruning decisions. It also interprets mask distributions as evidence of component rescaling and explains training overhead through adapter computations and the teacher forward pass.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository hyperlink and public-availability statement. It revises training-time estimates and Appendix C hyperparameters, and documents the new cost comparison's rank-8 LoRA, per-device batch size, gradient accumulation, and activation checkpointing. Higher-sparsity distillation coefficients remain unspecified after narrowing the eta=2 statement.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same training and evaluation coverage: FineWeb-Edu, C4, LaMini, WikiText-2, the downstream benchmark suite, and ShareGPT prompts. V2 adds model checkpoints and pruning configurations, without adding datasets, tasks, or input-environment scenarios.

E2.justification: V2 substantially broadens the evaluated alternatives: Table 8 introduces Týr-the-Pruner, Table 7 adds HEAPr with LoRA recovery and extends the existing LoRAP recovery comparison, and Table 9 compares training costs against LoRA and full fine-tuning. Appendix C also changes the reported lambda2 learning rate from 0.8 throughout to 0.4 at 20% sparsity and 0.8 at higher sparsity, and restricts the eta=2 statement to 20% sparsity. These reporting revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds targeted analyses of whether longer LoRA recovery compensates for pruning decisions, the training overhead of distillation, and whether learned masks exploit continuous rescaling (Figure 7). Existing component, granularity, token-budget, dataset, and sparsity-pattern analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new mask histograms describe variation across components, rather than uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results in Tables 7–9 and Figure 7 while retaining the original benchmark values. For example, Table 7 reports 62.98 accuracy for LoRAP with 120M recovery tokens versus DDP's retained 64.82 at 30M tokens; Table 9 adds training-cost measurements. Section 5.1 also revises reported run times from approximately 20 to 40 minutes for LLaMA-7B and 40 to 60 minutes for DeepSeekMoE-16B. Added results should not be interpreted as same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The ReLU forward masks, annealed retention surrogate, sparsity and binarization objectives, distillation, MoE extension, and group-level sparsity formulation remain unchanged. Appendix A retains the same algorithm; revised experimental hyperparameters do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: V2 inserts sections on LoRA recovery, additional comparisons, and computational cost, and expands the mask-analysis discussion. It also clarifies latent-parameter terminology, fixes grammar and notation, and updates publication, funding, and conflict-of-interest text. The overall narrative structure remains intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds three tables and a three-panel mask-distribution figure. Existing speedup and appendix tables are renumbered, and appendix tables and sparsity figures are redistributed across pages. Existing visual content and the overall presentation style are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds the Týr-the-Pruner reference and positions DDP against it experimentally in Section 5.6. The related-work taxonomy and existing novelty framing remain unchanged; HEAPr's citation-year suffix changes only to disambiguate references.

T1.justification: The theoretical assumptions, propositions, theorems, and proofs remain substantively unchanged. Proposition B.2 corrects the recalled budget symbol from T to P, aligning it with Equation (21); this repairs notation without changing the mathematical argument.

However, unexplained discrepancies limit the benefit: for LLaMA-2-7B at 50% sparsity, retained Table 2 reports WikiText-2 perplexity 26.34, whereas new Table 8 reports 10.34 without explaining a setting difference. The useful additional evidence supports a modest overall improvement, rather than a substantial strengthening of the paper.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds recovery-budget experiments, additional baseline comparisons, training-cost measurements, and learned-mask distributions.

title: Deterministic Differentiable Structured Pruning for Large Language Models
