E1.justification: New Appendix A adds LIBERO-10 and joint multitask learning, including language-conditioned π0 experiments. This substantially extends the evaluated task requirements beyond v1's individual Robomimic and real-robot tasks, all of which are retained.

E2.justification: The original comparisons with IBRL, DPPO, EXPO, DSRL, and ResFit remain intact. The new LIBERO experiments reuse DSRL and pretrained-policy comparisons; π0 is an additional backbone, not a new competing finetuning method. The expanded ResFit description does not establish a changed implementation.

E3.justification: Appendix A introduces a substantial multitask experimental design: BC pretraining on 500 demonstrations across ten tasks, random task selection during online collection, and task-averaged evaluation with 100 rollouts per task in Figure 10. The π0 experiment adds supervised finetuning with 30 demonstrations per task before RL. These are additional protocols; the original experimental settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The component ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, pretraining analyses, trajectory-divergence analysis, and action-noise tests are retained. V1 Figures 10-19 become v2 Figures 14-23 with unchanged plotted content. The new LIBERO per-task curves provide benchmark results rather than distinct ablations or robustness analyses.

E5.justification: Five-seed averaging and variability reporting for the original comparisons and ablations remain unchanged. Appendix A specifies evaluation rollouts but introduces no explicit new seed count, significance test, or uncertainty-estimation procedure; the original five-seed statements cannot automatically be extended to these additions.

E6.justification: V2 Figures 10-13 add aggregate and per-task learning curves for both LIBERO settings. They report better aggregate sample efficiency than DSRL and improved π0 performance following RL. These substantially expand the reported evidence under new conditions; the original benchmark, real-robot, and ablation results are retained rather than improved or replaced.

M1.justification: V2 adds a specific π0 integration: image and language tokens produce an action-free, pooled latent for the residual actor and critic, while base actions come from separate π0 inference. This is a limited input/representation adaptation; Algorithm 1, residual learning objectives, filtering, and action selection remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Changes include a localized related-work rewrite, the new multitask/VLA appendix, updated cross-references, corrected running-header terminology, and conference/acknowledgment formatting. The main narrative and existing appendix explanations remain largely verbatim.

P2.justification: V2 adds four LIBERO figures showing aggregate and per-task results, while retaining the original graphical content and table structures. Existing appendix figures are renumbered and repositioned, Algorithm 1 moves, and Figure 7's caption replaces the misleading matched-initial-success description with the pretrained-policy comparison actually shown.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for RL-100 and LIBERO and replaces the NIST webpage reference with Kimble et al. (2020). Related work more precisely distinguishes policy-gradient and reward-weighted approaches, removes the blanket costly/brittle characterization, and clarifies ResFit's lack of chunked Q learning. Overall positioning is retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, objectives, filter definition, finetunability metrics, trajectory-divergence measure, and flow-matching equations are unchanged. V2 adds no theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens evidence for multitask and VLA applicability through LIBERO-10 experiments and documents the π0 interface, extending v1's individual-task validation. It also corrects the misleading Figure 7 caption and refines related-work descriptions. The gain is limited by sparse statistical documentation for the new experiments and an unchanged conclusion that still presents multitask VLA finetuning as future work.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DICE-RL work, with readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. V1 Appendices A-C are retained as v2 Appendices B-D, alongside a new Appendix A.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds LIBERO-10 multitask experiments using a multitask BC policy and the pretrained π0 model.

before.justification: V1 reports original Robomimic experiments, three real-robot manipulation experiments, robustness analyses, and extensive appendix ablations.

title: From Prior to Pro: Efficient Skill Mastery via Distribution Contractive RL Finetuning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claims about manifold correction, convergence under fixed and adaptive step sizes, and reconstruction quality. The added code-availability sentence does not redefine the scientific contributions.

C2.justification: Mechanism explanations, experimental interpretations and limitations are unchanged. Section 7 retains the qualifications concerning nonconvex constant-step convergence, recoverability, heuristic noise schedules and score-evaluation cost.

D1.justification: v1 states that source code accompanies the supplementary material. v3 retains that statement and adds an explicit public GitHub repository location in the abstract, improving access information. Hyperparameters, implementation details and hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same FFHQ and ImageNet coverage: super-resolution, Gaussian/motion/nonlinear deblurring, random/box inpainting, HDR and phase retrieval. The additional perceptual-regularization example in Appendix I.3 is also retained.

E2.justification: Comparator membership within each experiment is unchanged. Tables 1 and 4 and Figures 10–15 retain the same task-specific comparisons involving DPS, DAPS, DDRM, DiffPIR, RED-diff, DPIR, DCDP and PMC where evaluated.

E3.justification: Section 6, Table 3 and Appendix H retain the same validation-image sampling, measurement operators, noise settings, pretrained models, metrics and optimization settings. No evaluation protocol is added or revised.

E4.justification: The DC-step ablation in Figure 5, correction ablation in Table 5, empirical assumption checks in Appendix I.2 and decay-window/NFE analysis in Appendix I.6 are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions average benchmark metrics over 100 images and report mean plus standard deviation over 100 FFHQ images in Figures 10–15. Repeated-run, seed and uncertainty-reporting information is unchanged.

E6.justification: Numerical results, plotted trends and qualitative reconstructions match throughout the main text and appendices. For example, Table 1 retains Ours-tweedie's FFHQ 4× super-resolution scores of 30.439 PSNR, 0.857 SSIM and 0.178 LPIPS.

M1.justification: The three-stage denoiser, ADMM updates and Tweedie/ODE variants are unchanged. Algorithm 1 changes w^(0) and w^(J) to w^(k,0) and w^(k,J), making the existing outer-iteration index consistent without changing the procedure.

P1.justification: v3 adds the code-availability sentence, makes two Algorithm 1 indices consistent and expands the acknowledgment to include Oregon State University's SciRIS funding. The remaining narrative and section organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: Added text slightly reflows the abstract and the reference pages following the acknowledgment. Figures and tables retain their content, design, numbering and placement.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning are unchanged, including Section 5. The bibliography contains the same entries; some move between pages after the acknowledgment expands.

T1.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A–F retain the same definitions, assumptions, theorems, derivations and proofs, including finite-DC-step and ODE-denoiser results. Algorithm 1's index edits are notation corrections.

improvement.justification: The explicit repository location improves code discoverability beyond v1's supplementary-material statement, and consistent iteration indices improve Algorithm 1's clarity. These provide a limited gain in reproducibility guidance and presentation; the scientific evidence and stated limitations remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both complete 46-page PDFs describe the same AC-DC denoiser and ADMM-PnP framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A–I support reliable comparison; all appendix pages match in text and rendering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original reconstruction experiments and supplementary analyses, including the results in Tables 1, 4 and 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-reconstruction experiments on FFHQ and ImageNet, including baseline comparisons, ablations and diagnostic analyses in Section 6 and Appendix I.

title: Taming Score-Based Denoisers in ADMM: A Convergent Plug-and-Play Framework

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: analytic transitions enabling RL training, refinement for targeted exploration and strong graph-generation and molecular-optimization performance. The headline 95.0% and 97.5% synthetic results and the scope of the central claims are unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 now distinguishes dynamic-prior gains from RL and explains refinement's benefit without RL. Appendix E.2 attributes instability to the mismatch between endpoint prediction and sampling transitions; E.3 interprets memory and runtime scaling. Figure 7 interprets molecular diversity as evidence against collapse. The broader applicability discussion remains unchanged.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a link to Graph-GRPO's own code. New studies disclose comparison hyperparameters and per-graph resource-measurement details. Section 4.1 aligns the backbone terminology with the existing RRWP specification. The original hardware, architecture configurations, optimizer and refinement implementation details are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Appendix E.3 adds computational-cost evaluation on Tree graphs with 32, 48, 80 and 96 nodes beyond the original 64-node synthetic setting. This modestly extends input-size coverage for cost evaluation. Planar, Tree, the five docking targets and the 23 PMO tasks remain the substantive benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: v2 introduces an evaluated REINFORCE variant without analytic transitions on Tree graphs in Table 6. Table 4 also adds DeFoG variants using refinement and refinement with prescreening. Comparator membership in the main benchmark tables and retained extended comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: The new Tree comparison uses matched settings including learning rate 10^-5, group size 20, 50 denoising steps and 120 sampled groups per epoch, with reward and gradient diagnostics. The cost study introduces controlled graph-size and trajectory-length sweeps with runtime and memory metrics. These are added protocols; the original benchmark splits and oracle budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 4 substantially expands component isolation, testing refinement without RL and separating dynamic-prior effects from RL, refinement and prescreening. New Appendix E.2 examines training stability against REINFORCE, and E.3 studies computational scaling. Figure 7 adds qualitative diversity evidence. The original renoising sensitivity study is retained and moved to Appendix E.1.

E5.justification: The five-run synthetic and three-seed molecular reporting remains. However, relocated Table 5 loses v1's explicit seed=0 qualification. New runtime measurements are averaged over five epochs. Table 4 newly describes values as averaged over 23 tasks although they match Table 3's sums, leaving aggregation wording ambiguous.

E6.justification: Substantial new component, stability and computational-cost results are reported. Table 4 retains 17.450, now explicitly associated with dynamic priors, and adds 16.901 without them; this is not a same-setting decline. Table 6 reports step-500 rewards of 0.312 for REINFORCE and 1.537 for Graph-GRPO. Table 3 retains every mean but revises eight uncertainty values, including Mol GA's Zaleplon result from 0.519±0.358 to 0.519±0.029.

M1.justification: The analytic transitions, GRPO objective, refinement, dynamic priors and molecular training curriculum are retained. Dynamic priors already appeared in v1 Appendix B. Section 4.1 changes RWSE to RRWP, matching the architecture already specified in v1 Appendix C.2; this does not establish an architecture change.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized terminology and prose edits, rewrites the component-ablation discussion and introduces Appendix E for supplementary ablations. The renoising discussion moves there, while later appendices are relabeled. Author notation, publication text and an acknowledgment are updated, without extensive restructuring of the main argument.

P2.justification: Table 4 becomes a larger component matrix; Tables 6–7 and the molecular montage in Figure 7 are added. Table 5 moves to the appendix, and the existing molecular-evolution figure is rearranged into one row and renumbered Figure 9. Table 2's category headings are clarified. The overall visual format and most existing displays are retained.

R1.justification: Section 3.1 removes the Jang et al. Gumbel-Softmax citation and adds three works concerning vision-language-action safety, tool attacks and video metaphor understanding. These are limited citation changes; Section 5 and the paper's central positioning relative to graph generation and RL research remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, equations and Appendix A derivation are retained. Proposition 3.1 now explicitly calls its formula an off-diagonal entry, but v1 Appendix A already imposed that restriction and specified diagonal entries separately. The new scaling discussion interprets measurements rather than supplying a new formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 improves component attribution through the expanded Table 4 and adds useful stability and computational-cost evidence in Appendix E, alongside a code link. These strengthen evaluation of an otherwise stable method. The gains are partly offset by losing Table 5's seed-0 qualification and introducing ambiguous averaging language in Table 4. Overall, the revision provides a limited but clear improvement in evidential support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Graph-GRPO research. All 17 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds component ablations, a REINFORCE comparison, computational-cost measurements and molecular samples.

before.justification: v1 reports original Graph-GRPO experiments on synthetic graph generation, protein docking and molecular optimization, including ablations and additional appendix results.

title: Graph-GRPO: Training Graph Flow Models with Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion extend the claimed empirical scope to SE(3) robotic grasping. The central contributions—intrinsic average-velocity modeling, practical tangent-space supervision, conflict-aware optimization, and CFG—retain their previous meaning.

C2.justification: Appendix B newly explains that the practical JVP surrogate omits a connection correction and may incur greater error for high curvature or long transport intervals. The SE(3) discussion distinguishes distribution fitting from physical grasp feasibility, while Appendix G interprets capacity and limited-data findings as lacking a consistent memorization signature and explains the omitted torus nearest-neighbor diagnostic.

D1.justification: New Tables 13–14 disclose parameter counts and dataset scales, including 50K training samples per hypersphere setting and 732K–860K parameters. The original hyperparameter values remain unchanged in renumbered Tables 18–19. Conversely, explicit NOAA and EOSDIS data-source URLs present in v1's references are removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds rigid-body grasp generation on SE(3), using the grasp dataset attributed to Eppner et al., and promoter DNA generation using FANTOM5 sequences of dimension 1024×4 (Sections 5.2–5.3). These substantially broaden task and domain coverage beyond the retained spherical, torsion-angle, rotation, and synthetic hypersphere experiments.

E2.justification: The new DNA comparison in v2 Table 7 includes Dirichlet FM, Fisher FM, and Woo et al.'s Eulerian, Lagrangian, and Semigroup RMF variants. None was a reported experimental comparator in v1; Woo et al. appeared only in the research discussion. Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include grasp success at 1–7 steps, DNA MSE and k-mer correlation, spherical KLD, and sampling sweeps from 1 to 128 steps. Tables 15–17 add reduced model sizes, 100%/10%/1% training-data conditions, and leave-one-out nearest-neighbor comparisons. The existing 8/1/1 split and original hyperparameter settings remain stated as before.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 7 adds sampling-step sensitivity analysis. Tables 15–17 investigate capacity reduction, performance with limited training data, and possible memorization through train-generated versus test-generated nearest-neighbor comparisons. These substantially extend the retained gradient-conflict, CFG, and hypersphere analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds formal MMD permutation testing across datasets and training-data fractions (Appendix G, Table 16), specifying 1000 generated versus 1000 held-out samples, 100 permutations, and a minimum reported p-value resolution of 0.01. The existing five-seed means and NLL standard deviations are retained; no increase in repeated-run counts is reported.

E6.justification: Matched pre-existing numerical results are unchanged, but substantial new results appear. Table 4 reports one-step grasp success of 65% for RMF, 60% for G-LSD, and 3.2% for RFM; Table 7 reports RMF DNA MSE 0.030 and k-mer correlation 0.94. New KLD scores, sampling curves, and capacity/data-fraction results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same transported average velocity, geodesic interpolation, JVP target, decomposed objective, PCGrad updates, and CFG formulation. The new applications and surrogate-error analysis do not document a changed algorithm or new method component.

P1.justification: v2 expands the probability-path background and experimental discussion, inserts the curvature-analysis appendix and proof subsection, and makes localized wording and heading corrections. It also adds acknowledgments and changes the publication footer. The main narrative and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: New Tables 4, 7, and 12–17 add application comparisons, KLD, capacity disclosures, and statistical diagnostics; new Figure 7 provides a substantial multipanel sampling-step comparison. Existing figures are retained and repositioned or renumbered, and the two hyperparameter tables are brought together on the final page.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Brewin, Eppner et al., Hon et al., Fisher Flow Matching, and Dirichlet Flow Matching for the new theory and applications. Section 4's positioning against GFM, alpha-Flow, and Woo et al. is largely retained. Publication metadata updates for existing references do not introduce different works.

T1.justification: New Appendix B introduces bounded-curvature, speed, and velocity assumptions, a normal-coordinate Christoffel estimate, and Proposition B.2 bounding surrogate error by C0 U K V²(t−r)². Appendix D.3 supplies its proof. This is a substantive theoretical addition beyond v1's retained identity, loss decomposition, and geodesic derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's efficiency and applicability claims: Figure 7 directly tests sampling-budget tradeoffs, Tables 15–17 examine capacity and limited-data behavior, and the grasp and DNA experiments extend practical validation. Appendix B also makes the surrogate's local approximation limits explicit, addressing an important qualification missing from v1. Detailed configurations for the new applications remain sparse, but the broader validation and clearer limitations provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Riemannian MeanFlow work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds grasp generation, promoter DNA generation, sampling-step comparisons, and capacity, limited-data, and memorization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments on spherical, toroidal, and SO(3) data, including MMD, NLL, conditional generation, dimensionality studies, and training throughput.

title: Riemannian MeanFlow for One-Step Generation on Manifolds

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain the same claims about oracle-free preference construction, conditional alignment, and utility in difficult data regimes. The conclusion retains the same central contribution. Additional validation and qualifications do not redefine the core proposal.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly qualifies ReTabSyn as target-aware rather than fully task-agnostic and explains regression weakness through its discrete-label perturbation design. Section 3.3 clarifies feature perturbation as regularization rather than estimation of P(A|B). New backbone, target-transfer, and sensitivity results receive substantive mechanism and applicability interpretations, extending the discussion beyond v1.

D1.justification: The code-access pointer changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository. v2 adds dataset eligibility criteria and an audit, specifies the new model identifiers, and clarifies that interpolated training rows are excluded from downstream evaluation. Existing hardware, runtime, and baseline implementation details are retained. Repository availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Appendix M adds 12 alternative prediction targets across Churn, Obesity, Titanic, and Indian Liver Patient, substantially extending evaluation beyond each dataset's alignment target. Table 2 also adds Shoppers to the 1% prevalence evaluation. These expand task and scenario coverage within the retained datasets.

E2.justification: The original six generator baselines remain. Table 15 adds comparisons with prompted GPT-5.4 and a pretraining-only Qwen3.5 control on Wilt and Churn. This is a bounded expansion of the evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include Qwen3.5-2B evaluation, alternative-target macro-OVR AUROC averaged over five classifiers, full-data Adult and Magic experiments in synthetic-only and augmented settings, and beta/lambda sweeps. These substantially extend the experimental design. The original Section 4.1 split, small-data size grid, and synthetic sample count remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices L, M, and O add tests of backbone dependence, transfer beyond the alignment target, and sensitivity to DPO temperature and regularization. Table 22 specifically tests removing the regularizer. These address substantial additional robustness and mechanism questions; the original Table 6 ablations and Figure 5 analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 2-5 gain standard errors across utility, fidelity, and privacy results, and Appendix K supplies small-data standard errors. New backbone and full-data tables report standard deviations. v1 already specified 10 random seeds, so this establishes expanded uncertainty reporting, not an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: New results include Shoppers PR-AUC of 0.670 for ReTabSyn versus 0.649 for SMOTE, backbone comparisons, eight wins among 12 alternative targets, full-data results, and sensitivity outcomes. Table 3 changes TVAE's Liver AUC from 0.563 to 0.565. Most retained table means are unchanged. Newly tabulated small-data means in Table 14 do not fully agree with the retained Figure 3.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the stated target-perturbation probability from 0.7 to 0.5. This reconciles the sampling rule with the 50/50 default already described in v1 Section 4.7; it does not establish that experiments were rerun. The augmentation procedure, base framework, and DPO-Positive objective otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted method and results rewrites, expands explanations, and adds limitations, funding disclosures, and appendix sections. The original section sequence and most existing prose remain, so the language and narrative changes are limited rather than a wholesale reorganization.

P2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 expand from single-column to full-width displays, Tables 2-5 gain uncertainty formatting and revised captions, and Appendices J-O add Tables 13-22. This substantially expands and reorganizes the tabular presentation. All five original figures are retained, with some relocated.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning against oracle-guided tabular methods remain the same. GReaT, TabSyn, and AutoDiff references receive publication metadata updates. The explicit statement that Theorem 1 belongs to Xu et al. reinforces attribution already present in v1.

T1.justification: The utility-gap definition, attributed utility bound, assumptions, and optimization objective remain mathematically unchanged. New equations for perturbations and autoregressive factorization formalize previously described procedures. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful evidence about backbone dependence, target transfer, and regularization, supplies previously missing uncertainty, and states limitations more clearly. However, new reporting inconsistencies limit these gains: Section 4.3 claims non-overlapping Adult standard-error intervals although 0.906 ± 0.013 and 0.891 ± 0.010 overlap. Table 14 also places ReTabSyn below real-data training at 64 rows, contrary to the unchanged Figure 3(a). The broader assessment supports a limited net improvement, but central result reporting remains insufficiently reconciled.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReTabSyn and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original Appendices A-I can be matched across versions; v2 adds Appendices J-O. The material supports a full comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds backbone comparisons, alternative-target evaluations, full-data experiments, and hyperparameter sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original downstream utility, fidelity, privacy, ablation, constraint-satisfaction, and regression experiments in the main text and appendices.

title: ReTabSyn: Realistic Tabular Data Synthesis via Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The three central contributions—biological tokenization, contextual representation learning, and label-efficient transfer—remain. v2 adds sensor-noise robustness to the principal conclusions in Section 5, extending the claimed practical properties without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: The expanded Discussion adds substantive limitations concerning omitted gravitational context during pretraining, demographic and cultural bias, and untested free-living generalization. It develops applicability arguments for additional sensors and body locations. Activity-confusion interpretation also expands from temporal order to segment identity, replacing the earlier emphasis on persistent stair-versus-walking ambiguity.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an explicit code-and-weights access link, single-core timing information, and reasons for benchmark omissions from existing sweeps. Appendix D reconciles parameter counts with Table 1. Conversely, cycle-specific NHANES references and access URLs are replaced by a generic survey citation. Most implementation settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: NHANES and the same six wrist-accelerometer HAR benchmarks are retained. v2 adds evaluation under synthetic sensor-noise conditions on five benchmarks, modestly extending input-environment coverage. Other modalities, body locations, and clinical applications remain proposed extensions.

E2.justification: The main HAR baselines and unseen-transition controls are unchanged. Appendix H expands the earlier Bio-PM-versus-TF-C confusion comparisons with Bio-PM-versus-without-gravity comparisons in Figures 14–18. This comparator already appeared in the aggregate ablation table.

E3.justification: The core subject-disjoint splits and frozen linear-probe protocol remain. Added protocols include test-time Gaussian noise at approximately 27–3 dB, a 0.2–1.0 Hz cutoff sweep with the pretrained encoder fixed, and single-core tokenization timing for batches of 32 MHealth windows.

E4.justification: Section 4.6 introduces substantive tests of sensitivity to sensor noise and gravity-separation cutoff. Appendix H adds five class-level analyses of removing gravity, beyond the existing aggregate ablation. Reconstruction case studies are also replaced with three-axis examples, substantially expanding robustness and diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v2 adds a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank comparison against TF-C over 41 pooled folds, reporting p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.61, and mixed per-dataset significance. Existing mean-and-standard-deviation reporting remains; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises AugPred’s average Macro-F1 from 0.44 to 0.54, including HAD from 0.41 to 0.69; its label-budget curves also change. Table 2 corrects naive-tokenization UMH from 0.38 to 0.39. Reconstruction distributions change, including MR25 mean MSE from 0.085 to 0.097, and examples are replaced. Robustness, gravity-confusion, and timing results are added. Bio-PM’s main average remains 0.65.

M1.justification: The movement-segment tokenization, 32-sample CNN inputs, five-layer Transformer, masking and corruption procedures, weighted reconstruction loss, and downstream gravity fusion remain. Appendix F.2 retains the detailed hysteresis rules; expanded main-text explanations do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methods, and results undergo extensive rewriting. Signal preprocessing becomes a separate subsection, ablations are reorganized, and a substantial Discussion replaces the brief limitations section. Accelerometer terminology replaces IMU terminology throughout much of the document.

P2.justification: Pipeline and tokenization illustrations are redesigned, learning-curve and transition plots are reformatted and relocated, and reconstruction examples switch to three-axis displays. A robustness figure and five gravity-comparison figures are added. Tables and appendix layouts are reorganized; the original TF-C confusion matrices retain identical content.

R1.justification: v2 adds tokenization literature by Rajaraman, Gastaldi, and Schmidt and references supporting noise modeling and submovement applicability to head, ankle, and locomotor movements. These strengthen specific motivation and extension arguments while retaining the existing wearable-SSL positioning and central novelty claim.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(3), the submovement decomposition, token construction, and temporal-encoding mathematics are retained. The explicit explanation of shared submovement onsets and durations clarifies existing notation. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v2 strengthens practical validation through robustness tests, statistical comparison, and gravity diagnostics, while making limitations and access information clearer. These gains are tempered by unexplained result revisions and stale captions: Figures 7–8 retain old numerical descriptions, and Figure 8’s caption describes an obsolete plot structure. The net improvement is useful but limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Bio-PM and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–H. Renamed datasets and relocated analyses can be matched, with no material gaps preventing comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and additionally reports noise robustness, filter-cutoff sensitivity, computational timing, and class-level gravity-ablation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original NHANES pretraining results, six-benchmark HAR evaluations, ablations, label-efficiency experiments, and unseen-transition prediction results.

title: Bio-Inspired Self-Supervised Learning for Wrist-worn Accelerometer Data

C1.justification: The abstract's central non-robustness claim remains. The introduction and conclusion qualify Theorems 1 and 11 as adversarial constructions, identify Theorem 7 as the principal practical contribution, and restrict the general-target claim through the strengthened Assumption 10.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits the learned-score simulations to qualitative support rather than verification of every theorem assumption, and leaves whether the adversarial constructions arise through practical learning as an open question. It adds reasons for the low-noise DDPM objective and removes the earlier extended argument about annealing being crucial.

D1.justification: The added simulation documents use of the analytic score construction, alpha=25, and 1000 iterations. Existing network widths, optimizer settings, step size, hardware, and Sinkhorn implementation details remain in Section 9. The new main-text description of dynamically sampled training noise reiterates the earlier appendix procedure.

E1.justification: The original Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture targets remain. Table 1 extends evaluation to Gaussian target/start separation scenarios with target N(mu, I_d), d=50, and ||mu||=k sqrt(d) for k=1 through 7, including much larger mean shifts.

E2.justification: Table 1 introduces Langevin dynamics with the true score as a comparator against the analytic perturbed score. The original vanilla, fresh, and train initialization comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The added experiment specifies d=50, alpha=25, 1000 iterations, and evaluation of L2 score error alongside KL divergence. The original experimental settings remain in Sections 4 and 9. However, Sections 3.1–3.2 change references to simulated dimensions from 25/50 to 50/200, contradicting those settings; a dimension-200 experiment cannot be established.

E4.justification: The new mean-shift sweep tests when small target-distribution score error coexists with poor sampling, providing a sensitivity analysis supporting Theorem 1. The initialization comparisons and supplementary Gaussian Wasserstein analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Section 4 newly states that the full original sampling procedure is averaged over ten trials and reports ten-trial means for the added experiment. v1 already displayed error bars and documented ten Sinkhorn subsampling trials in Section 9. These disclosures do not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds seven rows of results. At ||mu||=49.5, it reports score error zero to displayed precision and KL 3.08e4 with perturbed scores versus 8.39 with true scores. All three original plot images, including their values and error bars, are unchanged; the table supplies new results rather than same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The score counterexample constructions, neural-network score learning, and Langevin sampling procedure are retained. Theorem 7 rewrites the existing piecewise construction with explicit outside-all-balls and unique-index conditions; this clarifies the construction rather than introducing a different method.

P1.justification: The introduction is condensed, Theorem 7's construction becomes a numbered explanation, its main-text proof sketch is removed while the appendix proof remains, and the cone definition moves to Appendix 8. Simulation explanations and qualifications expand, but the overall section organization and most text remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds a schematic of Theorem 7 as Figure 1 and the new simulation table. The original figures are renumbered 2–4; the two main-text plots are reduced in size and relocated into the simulation discussion. Their graphical content is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Raginsky et al. (2017) for dissipativity and removes Chen, Kontonis and Shah (2025) and Nijkamp et al. (2019, 2020). It more explicitly positions Theorem 1 as showing sharpness of Lee et al. (2022), while retaining the main relationship to prior data-based initialization work.

T1.justification: Assumption 10 adds dissipativity, substantively narrowing the target distributions covered by Theorem 11. before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark comparisons in Table 2, component ablations in Table 3, transfer experiments, and open-source model evaluations in Appendix A.

title: XSkill: Continual Learning from Experience and Skills in Multimodal Agents

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the demonstrated scope to nine agentic tasks, including tool use, and change the headline gain from '60%' to '60-point' gains. The central claims about self-locking, coupled AS/BT bottlenecks, and AREW remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of user-side repair dependence as a shortcut and corrupted positive critiques as inducing critique chasing. Appendices A and D explain the distinction between actor-side reweighting and changing critic targets, qualify the comparison to direct additive weak rewards, and discuss dependence on belief readouts and evaluation proxies.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access statement and telecom model, simulator, and critique-construction details. Existing hyperparameters and prompt templates are retained. However, Section 4.2 omits v1's explicit instruction to zero the auxiliary term when either positive or negative critiques are absent.

E1.justification: v2 retains the seven original tasks and adds tau2-bench-Telecom in solo and dual-control settings. These introduce actual tool execution and coordination with a user who can perform repair actions, substantially extending coverage beyond the original query-based tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 3–4 add direct intermediate-reward shaping using the same critiques, providing an important comparison with matched supervision absent from v1. This tests the contribution of the injection mechanism itself. The original comparators remain; on-policy distillation is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include 7B solo and 14B dual-control telecom agents, a GPT-4o user, and a matched 70-step dual-control comparison. v2 also adds tool-error, token-use and turn metrics, GPT-5 rubric evaluation, and structured critique-corruption controls. The original seven-task settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds BT-only and critique-position/sign ablations, an alternative belief-elicitation prompt, false-positive corruption tests, and GPT-5 checks of proxy validity. Telecom analyses examine execution errors and reliance on user-side repair. The existing reweighting-strength analysis is relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional results continue the existing point-estimate and training-curve reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their values. New results include telecom rewards of 0.20 for vanilla PPO versus 0.50 for AREW under matched 70-step dual-control training, reward-shaping and corruption results, and GPT-5 AS/BT scores. Some AREW and proxy entries in Tables 3 and 5 reproduce earlier results.

M1.justification: The likelihood-margin objective and additive advantage correction are retained. Section 5.3 adds a tool-use adaptation of critique generation, assigning negative signals from execution failures and repetition and positive signals from newly matched expected actions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, and substantial portions of the theory and method exposition are rewritten, with more consistent AS/BT terminology and notation. v2 adds a contents section, reorganizes the appendices, and moves the reweighting-strength discussion out of the main text.

P2.justification: v2 adds telecom and robustness plots and Tables 3–5, and splits the old Figure 5 between Figure 6 and the relocated, reformatted Figure 9b. The intervention panel is correctly relabeled MediQ. New Figures 8 and 9a nevertheless contain misleading axis labels.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands positioning relative to on-policy distillation and direct intermediate-reward shaping, distinguishing their feedback sources and objectives. New citations cover distillation, telecom evaluation, tool agents, and credit assignment; the earlier related-work discussion is largely retained.

T1.justification: v2 normalizes the virtual channel updates by H and H+1, revises the oracle-information assumptions through the residual-budget condition in Assumption C.6, and changes associated bounds and proofs. Appendix A also adds mathematical comparisons with on-policy distillation and direct reward shaping. These exceed notation changes.

improvement.justification: The same-critique reward-shaping control tests the contribution of advantage reweighting, GPT-5 labeling checks dependence on the original proxies, and telecom experiments test practical tool interaction. These address important evaluation gaps in v1. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and new axis-label errors and an omitted edge-case rule weaken reporting, but the net evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same SeL/AREW study. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices can be matched despite substantial expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds telecom tool-use experiments, robustness tests, reward-shaping comparisons, and rubric-based evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original training and evaluation results across seven tasks, including performance comparisons, AS/BT measurements, and critique-noise experiments.

title: On Information Self-Locking in Reinforcement Learning for Active Reasoning of LLM agents

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the synthesize-and-reground framework, SciMDR training dataset, SciMDR-Eval benchmark, and improved scientific QA through fine-tuning. The shortened title and wording edits do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v1 briefly mentions proprietary-model dependence and STEM focus. v2's new Limitations section explains how teacher errors and biases can propagate into training signals and explicitly states that applicability to Humanities and Social Sciences remains unvalidated.

D1.justification: Training hyperparameters, input limits, preprocessing, evaluation software, synthesis and judge prompts, annotation documentation, and code/data links remain unchanged. The new audit's sampling and judgment procedure is an evaluation-protocol addition.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same SciMDR training corpus, SciMDR-Eval, ChartQA, CharXiv, SPIQA, and context-noise scenarios. The new manual audit samples existing training data without expanding dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 3–5 retain the same comparator sets, including SPIQA fine-tuning, the open multimodal models, and GPT-4o/5.1/5.2. The newly cited SciRIFF work is not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix A.3 introduces author review of 100 examples per QA modality using correctness and relevance criteria. Table 6 also changes the reported localization flag for the 16.9-score ablation from present to absent, indicating removal of both localization and reasoning. This does not establish that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a direct manual audit of synthetic-data correctness and grounding. The existing data-quality comparisons, ablations, noise tests, and 100-question failure analysis remain; Section 5.3.4 summarizes failure analysis already present in v1 Appendix A.4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new manual audit reports sample counts and judgments without adding uncertainty or annotator-agreement estimates.

E6.justification: Appendix A.3 newly reports all 100 VQA and 100 TQA examples as correct and grounded, and 91/100 MQA examples as high-quality and fully accurate. The other nine MQA examples are described as factually correct but verbose or high-level. Numerical scores in Tables 3–8 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The claim-centric synthesis, visual grounding, backward reasoning generation, document-scale regrounding, and staged fine-tuning procedures are unchanged. The synthesis prompts in Appendix C also match.

P1.justification: v2 shortens the title, standardizes benchmark typography, nests the existing analyses under Section 5.3, and adds a main-text failure-analysis summary, acknowledgements, and limitations. Most existing prose and the overall narrative order are retained.

P2.justification: Tables 5–7 are resized and rearranged, several captions are shortened, and appendix material shifts. Figures 9–13 retain the same examples and layouts but have sharper graphics and extractable text in v2.

R1.justification: v2 adds Wadden et al. (2025), SciRIFF, to the introduction and bibliography. The broader related-work discussion and positioning around scale, faithfulness, and realism remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The new limitations discuss informal assumptions about teacher-model reliability without introducing mathematical definitions, derivations, or formal assumptions.

improvement.justification: The new 300-example audit provides limited direct evidence for synthetic-data quality, while explicit teacher-error and domain limitations improve qualification of the claims. Clearer ablation labeling and sharper appendix figures also help. The audit remains author-conducted without reported agreement or uncertainty, so the overall gain is modest.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SciMDR work. The main text, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D support reliable comparison; visual inspection confirms that the rasterized appendix examples in v1 correspond to those in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds a manual evaluation of 300 synthetic training examples in Appendix A.3.

before.justification: Tables 3–8 report original benchmark evaluations, fine-tuning comparisons, ablations, context-noise experiments, and failure analysis.

title: SciMDR: Advancing Scientific Multimodal Document Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims: an HSL-like three-dimensional FLUX color subspace, latent color observation, and training-free mechanistic color intervention. Additional validation does not redefine these stated core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix H newly explains that early interventions can alter fine details and semantics, sometimes improving realism but hindering editing, and discusses mitigation through later intervention and cleaner boxes. v2 also qualifies cross-architecture generality as preliminary and narrows the early-observation superiority claim to 'sometimes.' The principal mechanistic interpretation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents a preservation variant using approximately timesteps 20–25 with cleaner bounding boxes and supplies prompts for new qualitative cases. It clarifies mask compatibility while retaining the existing layer-18 segmentation approach. Code-access information, color definitions, existing prompt/seed pairs, and timestep calibration arrays remain unchanged; improved-box construction is not specified.

E1.justification: The existing GenEval, wall-color, and PRECISE coverage is retained. v2 adds qualitative scenarios requiring simultaneous, differently colored interventions on adjacent or overlapping objects (Appendix C), plus a complex crystal-ball scene involving reflections and smoke (Figure 7). This modestly extends task requirements and scene coverage.

E2.justification: Best-of-N, ColorPeel, and ReNO were already evaluated in v1 Table 4 and remain in v2 Table 5. v2 adds IP-Adapter to quantitative evaluation. It also substantially broadens structure-preservation comparisons beyond prompting to Best-of-N, ColorPeel, ReNO, and IP-Adapter through new Table 4 and revised Appendix I/Figure 15.

E3.justification: The reported PCA sample count changes from 512 to 400, and PCA evaluation expands to SD3.5, FLUX.2, and Qwen-Image. New protocols assess SSIM/LPIPS on the existing 300-image PRECISE subset, HCL/CIELAB color errors, and later interventions with cleaner bounding boxes. These substantially expand evaluation settings; the sample-count revision alone does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of simultaneous interventions, cross-model LCS structure, and fine-detail preservation using jointly improved bounding boxes and later intervention (Appendices C, L, and H). It also expands qualitative structure comparisons and examines lighting coherence. These supplement the retained intervention-type/timestep study and color-subgroup analyses with substantial new diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Figure 15 newly identifies the prompt-based qualitative comparison as using the same seed, adding a seed-control disclosure. The four-seed main PRECISE evaluation, one-seed reduced comparison, and fixed plain-image prompt/seed pairs remain unchanged. Neither version reports confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Numerous LCS and baseline scores change in Tables 1–2 and matched appendix tables. Table 2 changes local/global GenEval accuracy from 70%/73% to 68%/72%, natural-image local color error from 17 to 14, and plain-image global error from 9 to 11. Table 3 is unchanged. New comparative, color-metric, and qualitative results substantially extend the evidence. The PDFs do not explain all score revisions, so these are not established same-procedure performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 substantially revises the specified core color mapping. Polygon-edge encoding becomes spherical interpolation of centered anchor directions, with a separately interpolated radius and revised saturation normalization. These are non-equivalent encoder/decoder definitions used by observation and intervention; the surrounding Type I/II interpolation framework remains.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the VAE preliminaries, geometric mapping, and mask usage. Interpolation is named Type ⋆, method labels become LCS, and Section 5.6, appendix headings, and an Impact Statement are added. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds multi-object, preservation, cross-model, and geometric illustrations, plus Tables 4 and 8. It replaces the earlier structure-comparison grid, revises observation panels and Figure 7, corrects Figure 4's intervention labels, and marks the selected setting in Figure 6. This substantially expands and revises visual presentation beyond relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds the FLUX.2 reference and connects it to broader architectural applicability. The related-work narrative and novelty positioning otherwise remain stable. Renamed author entries, publication updates, and consolidated duplicate references correspond to existing works rather than substantive additions or removals.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 substantively changes the mathematical construction through an anchor center, vector-angle hue interpolation, a hue-dependent equatorial radius, and spherical encoding. Section 3.1 also replaces the reconstruction-plus-KL background objective with an LPIPS/KL/adversarial min–max formulation. The LCS–HSL bijection remains assumed rather than newly proved.

improvement.justification: v2 provides a clearer geometric specification, corrects intervention labels and an overbroad early-prediction claim, and strengthens validation with additional preservation controls and cross-model checks. These improve understanding and empirical support. However, widespread score replacements remain unexplained and some new settings lack implementation detail, limiting the additional confidence they provide. The net improvement is supported by clearer exposition and evidence, not uniformly better performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LCS research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds multi-object interventions, preservation comparisons, alternative color metrics, and PCA analyses of additional models.

before.justification: v1 reports original latent-space PCA analyses, color-observation experiments, GenEval/PRECISE evaluations, and qualitative color interventions.

title: The Latent Color Subspace: Emergent Order in High-Dimensional Chaos

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three principal mechanisms, cross-platform and custom-task contributions, and approximately 2.3-fold SYCL speedup claim. The additional experiments support existing contributions without redefining their core scope or novelty.

C2.justification: Appendix H newly interprets lower-performing individual iterations as exploration, while Appendix J interprets recurring prompt similarities as convergence toward stable guidance tailored to problems. Section 5.2 adds an interpretation of meta-prompting's benefits during longer searches. Existing benchmark-filtering and runtime-measurement qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a KernelFoundry repository address, a concrete optimization-hint and resulting code-change example, and token-use and API-cost details. Existing dependency versions, default hyperparameters, hardware descriptions, and prompt templates are retained. These additions improve documentation without establishing changes to the underlying implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same filtered KernelBench coverage, representative L1/L2 subsets, 12 robust-kbench tasks, oneDNN operations, and Llama 3 case study. The added analyses reuse existing KernelBench operations; no new task domain, dataset, or hardware environment is established.

E2.justification: v2 adds internal comparison methods with prompt evolution or gradient guidance disabled, explicitly evaluated against the full system in Tables 2 and 10. The external baseline roster remains unchanged. The added torch.compile mention does not have separately identifiable reported results establishing a new evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce 20-iteration component controls, prompt updates every two versus ten generations, and 100-iteration comparisons for operations 46 and 82. Appendix I specifies a five-task token-use analysis. Existing benchmark filtering, correctness criteria, hardware, timing procedures, and main optimization budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands investigation of the central mechanisms through component ablations and prompt-frequency sensitivity tests, extended convergence studies, a concrete gradient-guidance example, and prompt-similarity/manual analyses (Appendices E.3, F.4, H, and J). Appendix I also adds cost analysis. These go beyond v1's retained hardware crossover and application case studies.

E5.justification: Timing-repeat procedures are retained. Neither version reports independent-search seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added ablation tables and convergence plots provide point results without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark, hardware, oneDNN, and GPT-OSS results are retained, but substantial new component-level results appear. At 20 iterations, Table 2 reports average speedups of 2.539 for the full system, 2.505 without prompt evolution, and 2.178 without gradient guidance. New results also include frequency comparisons, 100-iteration trajectories, prompt-change observations, and cost estimates; these are additions under new conditions, not improvements over v1's scores.

M1.justification: The proposed MAP-Elites archive, behavioral descriptors, gradient guidance, templated parameter tuning, meta-prompt evolution, and distributed execution procedure are retained. The new disabled-component experiments and illustrative prompt example test or explain existing mechanisms rather than revise the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 lightly revises the abstract and scattered prose, adds publication/correspondence information and disclosure statements, and extends the appendix structure with new analyses. The main section order and most existing explanations remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The single-column manuscript becomes a two-column main text and reference layout, with widespread resizing and relocation of figures and tables. Table 2 gains ablation rows, a new ablation Table 10 is inserted, and Figures 5–7 add convergence and prompt-similarity displays. Existing figures and result tables are largely reused rather than replaced.

R1.justification: Appendix I adds limited cost-based positioning against robust-kbench and METR. The main related-work taxonomy and novelty framing remain stable; updated attributions and publication entries, including CodeEvolve and OpenEvolve, do not establish a broader expansion of cited approaches.

T1.justification: The behavioral grid, fitness function, gradient expressions, and correctness and hardware-speedup definitions remain mathematically unchanged. v2 adds no substantive formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the central mechanisms more assessable through ablations and prompt analyses, while adding a repository location and practical cost information absent from v1. The gain is limited by missing run-to-run uncertainty and mixed benefits across ablation metrics and the two long-run examples, which warrant narrower conclusions than Section 5.2's broad wording. Overall, the revision provides useful additional support and transparency while retaining the original scientific results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KernelFoundry research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting. v1 contains Appendices A–G; v2 extends them through J.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component ablations, longer optimization trajectories, token-cost measurements, and analyses of generated prompts.

before.justification: v1 reports original CUDA and SYCL experiments, hardware crossover measurements, comparisons with oneDNN, and a Llama 3 acceleration case study, with additional results in Appendices F and G.

title: KernelFoundry: Hardware-Aware Evolutionary GPU Kernel Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the stated empirical scope from three to five foundation models. The central claims—a unified online-learning framework, a formal regret–acceleration connection, three principal instantiations and up to 24% speedup—remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: New Appendix E qualifies the experiments as adaptation from drafts trained from scratch, rather than released checkpoints, and emphasizes framework contributions over benchmark-specific gains. v2 also interprets the new scaling and warm-up findings, revises the theoretical discussion to describe saturation, and corrects Appendix C.1's explanation from small to high acceptance rate for an accurate draft.

D1.justification: New disclosures include draft architecture and parameter counts for Hydra, EAGLE and EAGLE-3 (B.7), TPS aggregation as the mean of per-question throughput (B.10), and from-scratch initialization (E). These document existing implementation choices without establishing changed procedures. Most optimizer settings, hardware, prompts and code-access information were already present.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, the mathematical MMLU subset, Code-Search-Python, Spider, MBPP and Alpaca-finance. The added experiments reuse existing task coverage; larger model configurations and different warm-up counts do not introduce new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds standard autoregressive decoding to comparisons with Opt-Hydra and Ens-EAGLE-3 on GSM8K (Tables 3 and 7), extending its earlier participation in reasoning evaluations. Ens-Hydra is also added as an alternative comparator in Tables 4 and 9. The comparator sets in retained Tables 1 and 2 are unchanged.

E3.justification: The evaluation configurations expand from three to five target models through Vicuna-13B and Qwen3-32B, with Qwen3-1.7B drafting for the latter. New protocols sweep 500, 1000 and 1500 warm-up samples and approximate environmental variation using consecutive prompt-embedding distances. These substantially extend the evaluation design; retained experiments keep their documented settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds warm-up sensitivity (Table 8), ensemble-versus-optimistic updating for Hydra (Tables 4 and 9), and an empirical illustration of theoretical trends (Figure 11). Existing learning-rate, online-duration and training-overhead analyses are retained. Figure 11 has an attribution ambiguity: its caption names Ens-EAGLE while its legend names Ens-EAGLE-3.

E5.justification: Table 2's caption changes from results averaged over three runs 'with standard deviations' to simply averaged over three runs. Neither version displays standard deviations in that table, so this corrects the reporting description rather than removing uncertainty values. Three-run reporting and the uncertainty entries in the other retained tables remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Numerical results in Tables 1–2, the original hyperparameter and overhead tables, and the existing plots are retained. New Table 3 reports 1.46× and 1.84× speedups over autoregressive decoding for Ens-EAGLE-3 and Opt-Hydra on Vicuna-13B, and 1.31× for Online-LR on Qwen3-32B, with accepted length 9.98 and accuracy 95.68%. Additional tables and Figure 11 report new comparison and sensitivity results, extending the evidence under new settings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the principal Online-LR, Opt-Hydra and Ens-EAGLE updates remain unchanged. v2 adds Ens-Hydra, applying the existing ensemble strategy to Hydra as an alternative to optimistic updating, in Tables 4 and 9. This is a limited additional instantiation.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording improvements, adds an organization paragraph, expands acknowledgements and introduces impact and limitation sections. The dynamic-regret rationale and theorem remarks move from appendices into Section 2.2, while some existing implementation information moves into Section 4.1. Most prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The single-column workshop format is replaced by a two-column main text and references, with extensively reflowed and resized tables, figures, equations and headers. v2 adds Tables 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 and Figure 11; Tables 4 and 9 display the same analysis. Figures 1–10 are retained and repositioned rather than scientifically redrawn.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds brief coverage of diffusion-language-model acceleration and citations on distribution-shift adaptation and distillation; the introduction also cites Wang et al. (2026). The MATH citation changes to Hendrycks et al. (2021b), and the SRT citation is removed. The central positioning against task-specific online adaptation remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 receive substantive corrections. The acceleration lower bound becomes (k+1)/[(alpha*k+1)*(1+(k+1)*sqrt(Reg_T/(2T)))], and the upper bound changes from k/(alpha*k+1) to (k+1)/(alpha*k+1). Corollaries 1–3 now include saturation through min{k+1,...}. Appendix D replaces the central lower-bound derivation and propagates these changes through the proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a serious inconsistency in the central theoretical contribution: v1's acceleration lower bound could exceed its finite upper bound, whereas the revised bounds and proofs explicitly account for saturation and the additional output token. Larger-model evaluations, direct autoregressive comparisons, new sensitivity analyses and clearer initialization limitations strengthen empirical support and transparency. These gains outweigh residual reporting issues such as Figure 11's mismatched method labels.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OnlineSPEC work and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Content can be matched reliably despite substantial reformatting, relocated explanations and additional material in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds larger-model evaluations, autoregressive-decoding comparisons, warm-up sensitivity and alternative-update experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, deployment trajectories, hyperparameter analyses and training-overhead measurements in Section 4 and Appendix B.

title: When Drafts Evolve: Speculative Decoding Meets Online Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same simplicity-bias, diffusion-information-exponent, sample-complexity, correlated-latent speedup, and spherical-constraint claims. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 newly explains that Adam-trained richer networks and the single-neuron online-SGD theory should agree qualitatively rather than match exact timescales. Section 3.2 also adds a Fourier/Gabor interpretation connecting the synthetic directions to natural-image statistics.

D1.justification: Figure 8 supplies limited setup information for the new results: SGD, an overparameterized two-layer ReLU autoencoder, and the plotted dimensions. Its exact width, learning rate, and latent-correlation construction are not specified. Existing Appendix A details and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: The datasets and synthetic model family are retained. Figure 8b explicitly evaluates correlated MCM latents, but v1 Figure 1c and Appendix A.3 leave their joint latent distribution unspecified. Whether this expands data-scenario coverage or evaluates an existing scenario more explicitly is therefore uncertain.

E2.justification: The existing activation, architecture, and optimizer comparisons retain their participants. Figure 8 uses the previously evaluated SGD-trained ReLU autoencoder without introducing a new comparison method.

E3.justification: Figure 8 adds dimension sweeps: d = 50, 100, 200 for a single cumulant spike and d = 100, 200, 250 for correlated latents, with training steps normalized by d^3 and d, respectively. Existing experimental protocols in Appendix A are unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figure 8 examines whether recovery trajectories across dimensions support cubic versus linear learning-time scaling. The earlier width, depth, activation, and optimizer analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Existing initialization counts and standard-deviation reporting are retained. Figure 8 also averages five random initializations, extending the existing MCM reporting practice without introducing a new uncertainty estimator or increasing runs for retained results.

E6.justification: Figure 8 adds six dimension-specific overlap trajectories approaching unit recovery in the single-spike and correlated-latent settings. The previously reported plots and generated samples are unchanged; the addition supplies results supporting existing scaling claims.

M1.justification: The denoiser, loss, projected and unconstrained SGD procedures, and experimental architectures are retained. Restoring the x factor in v2 Equation (9) agrees with the derivation already present in v1 Appendix B.4; it does not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: Most prose and section ordering remain intact. Changes include local copyediting, corrected figure references, brief explanatory additions, a new asymptotic-notation subsection B.1, updated front matter, and a generic impact statement.

P2.justification: The single-column manuscript becomes a conference layout with two-column main text and references, redesigned front matter and headings, and resized or repositioned figures. Figure 8 is added; Figures A.1–A.4 become Figures 4–7 with their visual content retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hyvärinen et al. (2009) for the natural-image interpretation and refines its characterization of Li et al. (2024) as studying Gaussian/linear denoiser bias during generalization. Other references largely undergo formatting or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: v2 restores the missing x factor in the printed spherical-gradient formula and removes Assumption 4.5's assertion that the stated derivative bounds make F globally Lipschitz. The principal propositions, sample-complexity thresholds, and appendix proof structure are retained.

improvement.justification: Figure 8 adds empirical support for the existing scaling predictions, while the gradient correction and explicit theory–experiment qualification improve precision. These are limited gains: the central results remain unchanged, and incomplete setup documentation limits the strength and reproducibility of the new scaling evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same diffusion-model study. Their main text, figures, equations, and complete experimental and theoretical appendices can be matched despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds dimension-dependent spike-recovery results in Figure 8.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10, CelebA, and mixed cumulant model experiments, including learning curves and architecture and optimizer comparisons in Figures 1, 3, A.3, and A.4.

title: A theory of learning data statistics in diffusion models, from easy to hard

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: training-free attention-based dependency selection improves accuracy–steps trade-offs and enables globally dispersed decoding. The expanded conclusion reiterates the existing graph-coloring perspective rather than redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: New Appendix D explicitly qualifies the MRF as a heuristic conflict graph rather than exact probabilistic inference and acknowledges dependence on threshold schedules and attention-layer choices. Appendix A adds interpretations of Direct's latency trade-off, length scaling, and the loss of global parallelism under blocking.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies averaging all attention heads over the final 30% of layers in the main models, documents DAPD-Direct's task-specific threshold schedules, and supplies a project-access link. These improve disclosure; the layer specification alone does not establish that the earlier implementation changed. Existing hardware and toy-training details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic MRF data, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, Math500, IFEval, ParallelBench subtasks, and aggregated TriviaQA questions. Longer generation budgets and different block counts change settings within retained tasks, rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Original confidence-based token-by-token decoding to the HumanEval throughput comparison (Table 6); v1 evaluated it in the TriviaQA analysis. Fast-dLLM, EB-Sampler, and KLASS remain the principal comparators. Newly discussed DAWN and Li et al. are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds tokens-per-second evaluation, generation budgets of 512 and 1024, DAPD block-count comparisons, and controlled attention-layer selections. Reported ParallelBench settings also change: DAPD's threshold schedule changes from [0.001, 0.005] to [0.01, 0.2] for Staged, and KLASS's KL threshold changes from 0.001 to 0.01. These are substantial protocol additions and revisions, without establishing which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 tests direct confidence commits versus staged decoding, efficiency at longer generation lengths, the accuracy-throughput consequences of block-wise decoding, and dependency recovery using different attention layers (Tables 3–4, 7–8, and 10). These substantially extend the existing threshold-distribution and decoding-trajectory analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions describe 30 independently trained synthetic models and 100 random sampling paths, retaining the same mean-and-standard-deviation reporting in v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 9. The added experiments do not introduce new seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for DAPD-Direct, throughput, generation length, block count, and layer selection. For example, Table 6 newly reports DAPD HumanEval throughput of 106.0 TPS, and Table 10 reports AUC 0.93 using the last two layers versus 0.73 using the first layer. Figure 4 changes alongside revised ParallelBench settings, so its differences are not same-setting gains. Figure 3 and Table 2 retain their earlier results.

M1.justification: v2 introduces optional DAPD-Direct, which commits confidence-1.0 tokens before dependency-aware selection at every step (Remark 4.1; Appendix A). title: Steering at the Source: Style Modulation Heads for Robust Persona Control

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v2 provides useful additional evidence about warm-up sensitivity and client insertion, clarifies positioning against layer-aware resource allocation, and supplies explicit code-access information. before.justification: v1 reports original GLUE accuracy and FLAN ROUGE-1 experiments, motivational studies, ablations, and additional BLOOM results in the appendices.

title: FedTreeLoRA: Reconciling Statistical and Functional Heterogeneity in Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning

E5.justification: Both versions report accuracy means and standard deviations over five seeds, timing averages over 100 batches and three runs, and five-run work diagnostics. Changed accuracy standard deviations are revised estimates, not a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

MNIST accuracy and Appendix F timing/memory results remain unchanged.

Additional copyediting, terminology adjustments, and publication/acknowledgment updates are limited; the overall section structure remains.

Figures 11–13 have revised curves, axis ranges, and captions, while Table 2 gains a regularizer row. Existing figures and tables shift with reflow, but the overall display organization is retained.

Section 4.4 reverses the stated generative transfer asymmetry and replaces its web-pretraining explanation with an explanation based on field training tolerating laboratory conditions. Section 5.1 adds residual near-duplicate risk and explains how domain imbalance limits class estimates and aggregate interpretation.

Existing framework, LoRA, inference and parsing details remain.

This adds substantial evidence about a confound in the existing robustness comparison. Appendix B adds a parameter-efficiency comparison, while the generative failure analysis is reorganized and loses its quantitative hallucination breakdown.

Figures 3–4 are recomposed; Figure 4 substitutes a different potato photograph while retaining identical prediction values. The distribution plot and both confusion-matrix graphics remain unchanged.

after.justification: V3 reports original model evaluations, including additional ConvNeXt-Tiny experiments and a new class-level domain-composition analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification experiments, cross-domain evaluations, hyperparameter sweeps and failure analyses in the main text and appendices.

Existing plots are unchanged but some are relocated, renumbered, and recaptioned; Algorithm 1 is condensed. before.justification: v1 reports original interference microbenchmarks, synthetic serving experiments, ShareGPT/WildChat evaluations, and appendix scaling and failure-rate results.

Added discussions address morphology–structure complementarity and selection, density, and staining confounds. These introduce cross-compound mechanism retrieval and labeled pathology classification beyond v1's perturbation retrieval, spatial-transcriptomics regression, natural-image reference, and synthetic tasks.
