Pooled nuclear-morphology features are also evaluated against structure-only representations in Table 17. Table 16 separately reproduces GrapHist and other reference comparisons from prior work; these are not reported as newly rerun baselines.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce well-level Spearman-based percent-replicating and percent-matching evaluation, and patient-level cancer classification with graph-availability filtering, patch-size-dependent sample exclusion, multiple spatial scales, and macro F1 reporting (Appendix H). The retained RxRx3-core top-5% metric and three-fold protocol were already documented in v1 Appendix B.2.

E4.justification: v2 Table 10 adds sensitivity analysis of untrained ViT size, patch size, token aggregation, and depth. Appendix H.2 also examines patch scales and complementary structure-only versus morphology-only inputs. The earlier PCA, retrieval-cutoff, cell-count, and synthetic-structure analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix H.1 adds empirical null calibration using 20,000 non-matching Spearman correlations and a 95th-percentile threshold. The existing three-seed experiments and their uncertainty values remain unchanged; the additional fold-based standard deviations largely continue the established reporting practice.

E6.justification: Substantial new results appear in Tables 10, 13, 14, and 17. Examples include CellProfiler Recall@5% of 0.17±0.01, MoA matching of 12.8% for untrained SingleConv versus 11.4% for OpenPhenom, and cancer-subtyping macro F1 results. The retained HEST, synthetic-classification, and random-seed tables have unchanged numerical entries.

M1.justification: The original feature extractors, graph construction, GCN/EGNN architectures, and synthetic pretraining remain unchanged. Appendix H.2 extends the tissue pipeline with region-of-interest aggregation using MIL or mean, median, and mean-plus-standard-deviation pooling, adding a procedural stage beyond v1's patch-level tissue regression.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially reorganized: the abstract and introduction are revised, contributions become explicit, benchmark and PCA explanations expand, and new benchmark-design, Implications, Software and Data, and disclosure sections appear. Appendices are reorganized, some material moves into the main text, and the Meaningfulness and LLM-use sections disappear.

P2.justification: The single-column workshop presentation becomes a two-column main paper with reformatted appendices. Composite figures are split or regrouped, the JUMP compound and depth plots are combined, v1 Table 6 becomes main-text Table 2, and a tissue example is redisplayed as Figure 1. New tables are added and the duplicate enlarged-figure appendix is removed.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion newly distinguishes systematic evaluation-task diagnosis from studies of training dynamics, citing Kang et al. New references support SPACe, BRACS/BACH, GrapHist, and MIL evaluation. The CellProfiler citation changes from Carpenter et al. to Stirling et al.; the overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: The synthetic intensity-function definitions, geometric assumptions, and GCN/EGNN invariance reasoning are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced; the added retrieval-metric descriptions explain adopted evaluation procedures.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central diagnostic argument by testing annotated mechanisms and cancer subtyping, adding evaluated morphology controls, and checking sensitivity to untrained-model configuration. Its narrower abstract better reflects the mixed evidence, while the reported code release and additional protocol details improve reproducibility documentation. These gains outweigh the loss of some earlier documentation. Patch-dependent pathology samples and unresolved cell-count confounding still limit causal and cross-study interpretations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same microscopy-representation benchmarking study. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and added experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds CellProfiler evaluation, a ViT sensitivity study, mechanism-of-action retrieval, and breast-cancer subtyping experiments. Its separately attributed GrapHist reference results are distinguishable from these original experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval experiments, HEST gene-expression prediction, layer-wise analyses, and classification results on a synthetic tissue-structure dataset.

title: Deep Learning for BioImaging: What Are We Really Learning?

C1.justification: The abstract, four introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: few-step gradient-based memory writing, advantages over forward-only writing at fixed memory size, capacity scaling, and transfer to natural-language tasks. Added experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 3.5 corrects the earlier Short SQuAD K=1 superiority claim and qualifies larger-K gains as task-dependent, including no bAbI improvement. The retained SQuAD scores are 38.1 for K=1 versus RMT's 42.6, with 54.9 at larger K. New appendices explain memory bottlenecks, qualify input-memory advantages when per-layer capacity increases, and acknowledge unequal comparator state sizes and coarse reconstruction-capacity estimates.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds detailed per-model settings and total memory-state sizes in Table 6, clarifies WRITE-head initialization and curriculum stabilization, and specifies previously unspecified larger-K settings. Appendix K supplies Algorithm 1 and minimal PyTorch-like code. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation; the repository was already linked in v1.

E1.justification: The original KV-retrieval, bAbI QA1–QA5, Short SQuAD, and WikiText-103 tasks are retained. Appendix I adds PG19 text reconstruction from compressed memory, a limited additional dataset and task beyond the previous continuation and question-answering evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated TTT-Linear and LaCT comparators on the existing KV-retrieval task in Table 8. Figure 8 additionally compares latency against TTT-Linear, TTT-MLP, and LaCT. These substantially extend comparison with competing test-time-training methods; the original baseline set is retained.

E3.justification: New protocols sweep memory size and WRITE steps, vary Mamba state configurations, and compare input-level versus per-layer memory under matched and enlarged budgets. Added latency tests use larger models, 4k–16k contexts, and batch size 1. PG19 evaluation introduces reconstruction-capacity thresholds over 8–64-token sequences. These extend evaluation design rather than establish reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained WRITE-step extrapolation, meta-learning ablation, and reconstruction-loss analyses, v2 adds memory-size sensitivity tests in Appendix F, constrained-state Mamba comparisons in G, and memory-placement ablations in J. Appendix D extends latency scaling analyses. These directly probe memory bottlenecks, parameter efficiency, and compute amortization.

E5.justification: The existing mean-and-standard-deviation reporting over three runs is retained. Table 8 additionally reports LaCT's best of three runs alongside its mean and standard deviation because of high variability. This changes the reported summary practice without establishing increased run counts for existing experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1's scores are unchanged, while Table 2 fills the previously missing higher-K GradMem language-modeling result with 2.91±0.01 cross-entropy. Tables 7–9 and Figures 8, 10, and 11 add substantial comparison, capacity, latency, and ablation results. For example, Table 9 reports 99% reconstruction accuracy through 32 tokens with Llama-3.2-3B, K=2, and one memory vector. Appendix D's new latency prose conflicts with Figure 8, limiting exact timing interpretation.

M1.justification: The core reconstruction-based WRITE updates and second-order meta-training remain unchanged. Appendix I adds an adaptation using learned LoRA adapters during WRITE with a frozen, adapter-free READ model. Appendix J also tests directly optimized per-layer KV memory as an alternative parameterization.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose are preserved. v2 makes targeted language corrections, clarifies memory initialization and second-order ablation terminology, updates author/publication information, and adds an impact statement, acknowledgements, and appendix contents guide. The added scientific sections do not constitute wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4 and 6–9, latency Figure 8, memory-analysis Figures 10–11, and Algorithm 1 with code Figure 12. Existing displays remain, including v1 Figure 8 as v2 Figure 9. Figure 3 moves, Figure 6 is reflowed, and captions are refined, producing a substantial expansion of visual and technical presentation.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds LaCT/TTT Done Right and Nested Learning references and expands the existing TTT discussion with Table 4's comparison against Titans, Atlas, and LaCT. This sharpens distinctions in memory level, update granularity, and objectives while retaining the original research positioning. Other bibliography changes largely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: The formal setup, objectives, update equations, and computational break-even derivation in Equations 1–11 are retained. Algorithm 1 restates the existing procedure. Correcting Figure 2's WRITE-loop label from outer to inner clarifies terminology already correctly explained in v1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through previously missing TTT comparisons and controlled memory-budget and placement analyses, while expanded settings and pseudocode improve reproducibility. Section 3.5 also corrects interpretations inconsistent with Table 2. Larger-model accuracy evidence remains limited to short reconstruction, and Appendix D's 8B latency prose conflicts with Figure 8: 1870 ms versus roughly 700 ms at 4k for one WRITE plus READ. This reporting flaw limits the efficiency evidence but does not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative validation and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GradMem work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, memory ablations, larger-model latency measurements, and PG19 text-reconstruction experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original KV-retrieval, bAbI, Short SQuAD, and WikiText-103 results, alongside memory-writing analyses and runtime measurements.

title: GradMem: Learning to Write Context into Memory with Test-Time Gradient Descent

C1.justification: Both versions claim the same dual-component contribution, mitigation of semantic drift and structural incoherence, superior PEFT performance especially at low ranks and limited data, and zero additional inference cost.

C2.justification: The explanations of filtering and coordination, interpretations of robustness and generalization, and claimed applicability remain unchanged. Both retain the same limitation concerning training overhead at larger scales.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link on the title page. Implementation details, hyperparameters, software, and hardware disclosures remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish an additional code or data release.

E1.justification: The language, vision, and multimodal datasets remain unchanged, as do the low-data, varying-rank, long-context, and MT-Bench scenarios. Newly added benchmark citations do not introduce additional coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the benchmark tables, filtering comparisons, coordination alternatives, and compatibility experiments. Newly cited methods such as AuroRA and UoRA are not added to the reported evaluations.

E3.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A and I retain the same models, adaptation targets, ranks, data fractions, context lengths, splits, metrics, optimization settings, and parameter-budget controls.

E4.justification: Both versions contain the same component, GNN-design, filtering, and coordination ablations, plus the same long-context, singular-value, attention, gradient-similarity, and instruction-response analyses.

E5.justification: Figure 2's caption drops the statement that error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. The identical plot contains no visible error bars, so this corrects its description. Three-seed averaging and the paired two-sided tests described in Appendix A remain unchanged.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–13 match. The six embedded figure images are identical, and Figure 7 retains the same responses and GPT-4 scores. No reported results or rankings change.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same IB-guided gates, graph construction, residual message passing, training objectives, and merging procedure for inference. Capitalizing the method name does not change its procedure.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits the abstract and introduction, revises the title and author information, standardizes the method-name styling, and adds acknowledgments. The existing Impact Statement moves from Appendix M to the main text; most prose and section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Existing tables receive grouped headings, metric-direction arrows, and formatting refinements. Appendix table captions move above their tables, Figure 2 is enlarged and relocated, and Figure 6 moves. The underlying illustrations, plots, and table contents are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the cited literature with benchmark sources, additional representation-learning citations, and numerous PEFT, reasoning, retrieval, multimodal, and generative-model references, principally in Appendix L. This broadens the bibliography while retaining the existing research-positioning narrative.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, drift-energy definitions, variational derivations, Theorem 1 and its proof, and oversmoothing and complexity arguments are retained. Equation reformatting does not alter their substance.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly improves presentation and documentation through clearer table headings, copyediting, and a project-page link. It also corrects Figure 2's misleading confidence-interval description, matching the unchanged plot without error bars. The expanded bibliography leaves the central positioning intact, while experiments, results, and theory remain unchanged; the overall gains are therefore limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same StructLoRA study. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and matchable despite formatting changes and relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experimental results, including benchmark comparisons, component ablations, and appendix analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, ablations, efficiency measurements, and qualitative analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

title: Not All Directions Matter: Towards Structured and Task-Aware Low-Rank Model Adaptation

C2.justification: The explanations of planning and execution failures and the design recommendations are unchanged. Limitations still cover restricted configurations, absent multimodal evaluation, and dependence on annotated reference plans.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future framework release; v2 states that the framework and data are released and supplies a repository link in footnote 1. Existing implementation descriptions and appendix prompts are otherwise unchanged. The PDFs do not establish the repository's contents.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Mind2Web-Live web-task coverage. No dataset, task, domain, or test scenario is added or removed; the new data-release statement concerns access rather than experimental coverage.

E2.justification: The human/NL/PDDL plan comparisons, action-representation comparisons, and evaluated models remain the same: gpt-5-nano, claude-haiku-4.5, and gemini-flash-2.5. Comparator membership is unchanged in corresponding main-text and appendix experiments.

E3.justification: Both retain the 104-task test set, text-based DOM observations, action settings, gpt-5-nano judging, evaluation metrics, and single replanning round. The 50-example judge-validation checks in Appendix A.3 are also unchanged.

E4.justification: The decomposition/executability analysis, action-space comparisons, replanning analyses, failure examples, and judge-validation study are retained. No ablation, robustness test, or supplementary analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Statistical reporting remains unchanged. Both present point estimates without reporting repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Matched numerical results and qualitative findings are unchanged throughout the main text and appendices. For example, Table 2 retains 60.6% NL and 67.7% PDDL perfect-match rates, while Appendix A.3 retains 82% and 86% judge agreement.

M1.justification: The NL/PDDL planning procedures, low-level execution, LLM postcondition checking, and replanning mechanism are unchanged. Appendix A retains the same operational prompts apart from a quotation-mark correction.

P1.justification: v2 revises the release sentence, adds a short funding-acknowledgments section, and corrects an appendix quotation mark. The scientific narrative and main section organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The added footnote and acknowledgments cause text reflow. Table 4 changes columns, Table 5 moves from PDF page 6 to page 7, and printed page numbers disappear. Figure and table contents, structures, and numbering are retained.

R1.justification: Section 7 and the reference list retain the same cited works and research positioning, including the novelty claim about incorporating formal planning representations into web agents.

T1.justification: The definitions of plans, trajectories, postcondition checking, and evaluation metrics are unchanged. Neither version adds or revises formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: The repository pointer and explicit framework-and-data release statement modestly improve access and reproducibility documentation over v1's unlinked future promise. Scientific evidence and conclusions are unchanged. This is a documentation gain; the supplied PDFs cannot verify repository availability or completeness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 24-page versions of the same study. The main text, figures, tables, mathematical definitions, and Appendices A and B can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results, including the main experiments, additional model results in Appendix B.4, and judge-validation outcomes in Appendix A.3.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and the appendices report original evaluations on 104 Mind2Web-Live tasks, including planning, execution, replanning, model comparisons, and manual validation of LLM judges.

title: Why Do LLM-based Web Agents Fail? A Hierarchical Planning Perspective

C1.justification: The central framework, regularization, robustness, and performance claims remain. The abstract explicitly includes MARS, and the introduction extends the stated empirical scale from 820M to 1.5B. Section 6 also removes v1's broad assertion of fixed learning rates and clipping thresholds without tuning across experiments.

C2.justification: v1 explains disabling pre-clipping through its marginal benefit relative to cost. v2 instead emphasizes isolating post-clipping and adds a substantive discussion of when pre-clipping helps, its narrower role in filtering gradient spikes, and threshold-scheduling limitations. Appendix F.3 also explains declining relative overhead through increasing forward/backward computation.

D1.justification: v2 adds Spectra-MARS and larger-scale SOAP configurations, numerical-precision details for the iteration ablation, and a specific scripts link for 1.5B µP experiments. However, it removes the final-learning-rate rows from baseline configuration tables, including the previously explicit cosine endpoint of 0.01 times the peak learning rate.

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic matrix logistic regression, FineWeb-Edu and SlimPajama language-model training, and the same ten downstream tasks. SlimPajama already appears in v1 Appendix F.2. Larger models, µP configurations, and smaller batches change settings within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates SOAP at 160M and describes larger-scale experiments as pending. v2 adds SOAP comparisons against SPECTRA-Signum at 780M and 820M, with three learning rates in Table F.7. The existing baseline roster otherwise remains.

E3.justification: v2 adds 1.5B µP training for 8B tokens, 780M baseline runs with 5–20% more steps, batch-size-8 pre-clipping experiments, and GPT-with-µP diagnostics. It varies clipping thresholds, Newton–Schulz iterations, and numerical precision. The reported 780M/820M post-clipping schedules also change from standard/wsd-sqrt options to standard only; this does not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic testing: threshold sensitivity and Newton–Schulz iteration ablations in Tables 3–4, constant versus decaying pre-clipping thresholds in Table F.4, computational-cost comparisons, and GPT-with-µP spectrum/noise analyses in Figures F.16–F.17. Existing synthetic robustness and post-orthogonalization comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: New Table F.2 specifies that timings are averaged over 180 post-warm-up steps, adding an explicit measurement-averaging procedure. These are not 180 independent training runs. Neither version reports training-seed uncertainty or confidence intervals for the main validation results; the existing 50-noise-sample analysis is retained.

E6.justification: Figure 1 adds Spectra-MARS losses of 2.573 at 780M and 2.589 at 820M; Table F.5 adds a 1.5B Spectra-AdEMAMix result of 2.635. New SOAP, budget-extension, timing, and ablation results substantially expand the evidence. Figures F.16–F.17 report weaker or later spectral spikes for GPT with µP. The original downstream Table 1 scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: The SPECTRA wrapper, optional pre-clipping, post-clipping, and Newton–Schulz soft spectral clipping algorithms are retained. Applying the existing wrapper to MARS adds an evaluated instantiation; the revised threshold schedules are experimental settings rather than new optimizer components.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence largely persist. v2 relocates the proposition proof and inverse-square-root pseudocode to the appendix, removes the appendix contents page, adds an Impact Statement, and updates affiliation and funding text. Most existing scientific prose receives limited editing.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column formatting to a two-column conference layout, with extensive resizing and rearrangement. v2 adds experimental tables and µP figures, extends Figure 1, changes the axes of Figures F.7–F.8, and transposes the post-orthogonalization table. The separate warm-up figure and redundant perplexity plot are removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds Yang et al. (2021) for µP and removes Hu et al. (2024), the MiniCPM citation associated with WSD. Appendix A's research positioning is otherwise retained. The Guo citation's year update concerns the same work and does not constitute a new reference.

T1.justification: The convergence statements, assumptions, spectral-noise bounds, and appendix derivations are retained after renumbering. For example, Theorems 1, 5, and 6 become 3.4, 4.6, and 4.7. Proposition 1's existing proof moves to Appendix E.1 rather than being newly introduced.

improvement.justification: The new sensitivity ablations, completed larger-scale SOAP comparisons, and budget controls strengthen assessment of robustness and practical efficiency beyond v1's performance curves. These gains are tempered by removed cosine-endpoint settings and an unexplained 780M AdamW baseline discrepancy between new Table 2 (2.608) and retained Figure 1 (2.611). Overall, the evidence supports a limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPECTRA research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–F are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds larger-model experiments, ablations, timing measurements, and GPT-with-µP gradient analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic optimization experiments, LLM pretraining results, gradient-spectrum analyses, and downstream evaluations.

title: Enhancing LLM Training via Spectral Clipping

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add substantive claims that PDPS-generated failures improve safety hardening and that standalone input-space attacks are less effective and more expensive than output-space exploration. Combining the two search paradigms becomes an explicit contribution. The original efficiency and diversity claims remain.

C2.justification: New Section 7 explains that semantic separability is empirical rather than guaranteed, identifies impractical sampling requirements for far-tail failures, and discusses hidden-state access requirements and unevaluated black-box extensions. v2 also attributes improved fine-tuning outcomes to broader failure coverage and explains complementarity through prompt-induced distribution shifts.

D1.justification: A code-repository link replaces v1's promise to release code after acceptance. v2 documents LoRA/GRPO, AdamW and 25 training epochs for the new experiment, while retaining Appendix F's sampling, classifier and embedding specifications. The fine-tuning model identity, data split and several training settings remain unspecified.

E1.justification: The four original benchmark datasets remain unchanged, but v2 substantially expands task coverage to adversarial safety training and subsequent robustness evaluation. Sections 6.7 and 7 also introduce evaluations on optimized and explicitly suffix-perturbed prompts. Discussed black-box and RAG applications are not evaluated.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained IID and Diverse Beam Search comparisons, v2 evaluates GCG, PiF, ASETF, PAIR and TAP in Section 6.7 and Figure 8. Section 7 also compares greedy decoding with sampling on a perturbed prompt. These comparisons were absent from v1, although some methods were already cited.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 25-epoch LoRA/GRPO fine-tuning experiment using AdamW and IID64 evaluation, single-response input-space attack comparisons, and temperature-1 response-budget sweeps. It also evaluates Qwen3-32B-Instruct with a specified suffix intervention. The original 100-example benchmark setup and PDPS population/block schedules are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether discovered failures improve downstream safety training, how response budgets affect GCG/PiF/ASETF attacks, and whether prompt perturbation overcomes poor sampling coverage on Qwen3-32B. These substantially extend the diagnostic evidence. The original diversity analyses, qualitative examples and hyperparameter studies remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added experiments retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Table 4 reports ASRs of 0.75 before fine-tuning and 0.36, 0.41 and 0.24 after tuning with IID64-, DBS64- and PDPS64-generated samples. Figure 8 and Section 7 add attack, runtime, response-budget and perturbation results. Original Tables 1-3 and the matched appendix tables retain their numerical values; the additions concern new experimental conditions.

M1.justification: PDPS retains the same expansion-and-selection procedure, Algorithms 1-2, quality-diversity objective, hidden-state embeddings and token-likelihood quality score. Safety fine-tuning is an added downstream experiment using the unchanged sampler. Judge-guided selection and black-box extensions remain discussion or future work.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution list are substantially rewritten around semantic separability, early pruning and downstream safety training. Method explanations, the results roadmap and conclusion are expanded, with new results subsections, a standalone limitations/discussion section, broader-impact statement and appendix contents.

P2.justification: v2 introduces a document-wide redesign with new typography, colored headings, running headers, a compact author block and boxed abstract and appendix contents. It adds safety-hardening Table 4 and input/output-search Figure 8. Existing displays are retained and reflowed; v1's appendix Figure 8 and Tables 4-8 become Figure 9 and Tables 5-9.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning toward iterative safety training, adding a dedicated safety-hardening/adversarial-training discussion and references including Constitutional AI, Safety-Tuned Llamas and adversarial training work. It also expands input-space research coverage with PAIR, ASETF and PiF and develops a stronger comparative relationship to prompt optimization.

T1.justification: The sampling-probability argument, quality-diversity equations and Theorem 4.1's one-half approximation guarantee are retained. Changing the unsafe-event probability symbol from p to rho and rewriting initialization notation do not alter the mathematics. No new proof or formal result is introduced.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's discovery-focused evidence, v2 adds useful downstream validation in Table 4, direct input-space comparisons and sampling sweeps in Figure 8, and explicit applicability limits in Section 7. These improve practical relevance and qualification. However, the hardening experiment leaves its model, train/evaluation data and training-sample controls unspecified and reports no uncertainty, limiting support for the stronger causal and iterative-hardening claims. The supported net improvement is therefore limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PDPS research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A-F are readable and can be matched despite substantial additions, reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original safety-fine-tuning results, input-space attack comparisons and combined input/output-search experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Llama and Qwen experiments measuring attack success, response diversity, runtime and hyperparameter sensitivity, including additional analyses in the appendices.

title: Exposing Long-Tail Safety Failures in Large Language Models through Efficient Diverse Response Sampling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about scalable dynamics learning, morphology-informed generalization, prediction accuracy, and downstream control. The added experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds a precision-versus-computation rationale for retaining 256 bins and interprets the physical-space errors as supporting physically meaningful prediction gains. The deployment discussion replaces the rationale for excluding physical baselines with an interpretation linking the comparative Go1 outcome to more stable MPPI action selection. The stated lack of visual observations remains unchanged.

V2 also adds two appendix tables and expands Table 9.

R1.justification: The same cited works and related-work positioning are retained. Conversion from numbered to author–year citations and additional bibliographic URLs do not introduce new research comparisons or novelty claims.

C2.justification: V2 narrows the high-dimensional forward-prediction limitation specifically to DTLZ, arguing from the added benchmarks that it is not a generic dimensionality failure. It also interprets surrogate and solver robustness as supporting the reliability of the reported rankings and Zero-Deviation signal, and explains detection of infeasible lift/drag combinations despite individually in-range labels.

Appendices C and F substantially expand technical documentation with new forward-map definitions, splits, preprocessing, CNN/MLP configurations, and training schedules; Appendices D–E specify robustness procedures. The code-access claim is documented in the PDF, without external verification.

E1.justification: V2 adds thin-film optical coating with 128 layer thicknesses and 64 reflectance labels, and FashionMNIST inverse generation from five image statistics with 784 pixel variables. It also adds Unifoil tests involving negative drag, extreme lift-to-drag ratios, below-polar targets, and shifted Mach/angle-of-attack conditions. The original three datasets remain.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparator set remains standard CFM and INN, including on the added datasets. Retained UQ comparisons continue to evaluate Ensemble Variance and FM Loss, with random/oracle references where applicable. These add variability estimation for the robustness experiments without establishing an increased run count for the original experiments.

The select-best improvement range is corrected from 13–31% to 5–31%, and Zero-Deviation rejection improvement from 10–27% to 8–27%, matching existing tables. New Table 13 reports gas-turbine hard-OOD AUC 0.773, while retained Figure 8 shows 0.754; this discrepancy is unexplained.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain SafeChain, RealSafe, STAR, SafeKey, IPO, and ReasoningShield, plus the base models. The new LlamaGuard comparison uses the same comparator set. Updated publication years do not indicate changed baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds LlamaGuard evaluation on JailbreakBench and full-space and before/after geometry protocols, including Qwen3-0.6B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct configurations. Existing prompt counts, benchmark metrics, and decoding settings retain their reported values. Appendix G mentions extended training without specifying a revised training budget.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands diagnostic evidence: Table 3 adds removal of R_txt; Sections 6.4–6.5 test RETHINK geometry beyond PCA and examine representations before and after training; Appendix H adds model comparisons; Appendix F tests sensitivity to the safety evaluator. The existing GPTFuzzer/AutoDAN analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both state that experiments use three distinct random seeds and report mean and standard deviation. Tables 1–3 retain the statement that variances are omitted because they are at most 0.2%. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure or increased run count is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace CRAFT scores while retaining baseline values: DeepSeek/Qwen defense averages change from 0.074/0.117 to 0.062/0.099, and Pass@1 averages from 0.468/0.585 to 0.481/0.602. Table 3 changes the full-model average from 0.082 to 0.099 and adds the R_txt ablation at 0.279. Tables 4–5 and Figures 5/7 add geometry and evaluator-validation results. Figure 4 remains unchanged; the PDFs do not specify the training-budget difference underlying the replaced scores.

M1.justification: The LCLR stage, its three losses, and the GRPO-based R2L stage with latent, textual, and consistency rewards remain unchanged. Clarified trace labeling and the added textual-reward ablation do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: Most method and experimental prose and the main section sequence are retained. The LLM-alignment discussion moves into the main related-work section, the shortened LRM survey moves to Appendix A, and references move before the appendices. V2 also corrects wording and expands acknowledgments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, replaces the separate cover and main contents arrangement, and extensively redistributes retained displays. It adds Tables 4–5 and Figures 5 and 7, expands Table 3, and reformats the retained evaluation-prompt figure from Figure 5 to Figure 6.

R1.justification: V2 condenses the general reasoning survey, removing references such as Tree-of-Thoughts, Graph-of-Thoughts, and self-refinement work. It adds citations including TIDES, autonomous jailbreak agents, adversarial reasoning, Llama Guard, and GenoArmory. Positioning against the principal reasoning defenses remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 5.1 becomes Proposition 5.1 with a substantively different guarantee: an error bound attributed to reward variance and policy entropy is replaced by C times the latent perturbation radius, with C depending on Lipschitz constants. Appendix C replaces the earlier proof with an expanded derivation. Section 6.4 also introduces formal centroid, safety-axis, and projection-coefficient definitions.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful checks absent from v1: the R_txt ablation, alternative-evaluator validation, and quantitative geometry analyses. Explicit limitations improve transparency, and the full-model rows in Tables 1 and 3 now agree. These gains remain limited by unresolved reasoning in Appendix C: continuity does not establish that consistency-reward gains outweigh possible R_ls losses. Appendix F also overstates Table 5, where CRAFT's DeepSeek response score of 0.004 is worse than RealSafe and SafeKey at 0.003.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CRAFT research, with matching authors, methods, and core experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial formatting changes.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and ablation results, additional latent-geometry experiments, and LlamaGuard evaluation in Tables 1–5 and the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original CRAFT safety and reasoning results, component ablations, and evaluations against GPTFuzzer and AutoDAN in Tables 1–3 and Figure 4.

title: Contrastive Reasoning Alignment: Reinforcement Learning from Hidden Representations

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims about soft-rank diffusion, hybrid reverse sampling, contextualized denoisers, and long-sequence advantages. The introduction adds jigsaw as supporting evaluation without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 introduces explanations involving autoregressive error accumulation, local versus global corruption, and the accuracy/runtime tradeoff. Appendix C adds interpretations of reference insensitivity, representation costs, and chamber-based robustness, and identifies constrained-permutation experiments as future work. These substantially extend the scientific interpretation beyond v1.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents KV caching and teacher-forced parallel training, identifies the uniform reference used in the main experiments, and supplies settings for reference tests and timing measurements. Existing Appendix A implementation details remain unchanged. Detailed jigsaw training and preprocessing instructions are still sparse.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-10 jigsaw reconstruction at 3×3, 4×4, and 8×8 grids. This introduces natural-image spatial reconstruction beyond the retained numerical sorting and routing tasks, substantially broadening evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: The learned comparator sets in MNIST and TSP remain unchanged, and jigsaw reuses SymmetricDiffusers. The new spatial error analyses additionally compare against an explicit random-assignment reference in Figures 4 and 7. The alternative relaxation spaces in Table 7 are discussed without experimental evaluation.

E3.justification: v2 adds matched and mismatched training/evaluation reference-distribution protocols at 4×4 with noise scale 0.5 and T=5, per-position and Manhattan-displacement diagnostics, and cached/uncached timing on 10,000 samples using one H100. The new jigsaw comparison matches seven-layer backbones. Original MNIST and TSP splits, budgets, and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the unchanged MNIST component ablation, v2 tests sensitivity to uniform versus Gaussian references and train/evaluation mismatch in Appendix C.1. Figures 4 and 7 analyze positional errors, while Figure 6 and Table 9 examine caching benefits and accuracy/runtime tradeoffs. These add substantial robustness and failure-analysis evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's description of differences as 'within noise' supplies no uncertainty estimate; Figure 6's shading represents cache speedup, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Original MNIST, TSP, and component-ablation values are unchanged. New Table 3 reports 8×8 jigsaw exact-match accuracies of 0.0000 for SymmetricDiffusers, 0.0924 for cGPL, and 0.2700 for Pointer-cGPL. Tables 5–6 and 9 and Figures 4, 6, and 7 add reference-sensitivity, timing, and spatial-error results, substantially expanding the reported evidence.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a KV-cached inference option for cGPL and Pointer-cGPL, reusing attention keys and values across prefix positions; Table 9 compares cached and uncached decoding. The reflected bridge, denoiser architectures, training objective, and core sampling algorithms are otherwise retained.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are preserved. Local expansions add the caching discussion, Section 4.3, and an analysis appendix, moving the former Appendix C to D. Other edits include standardizing much of n to N, changing bibliography style, and updating the publication and correspondence text.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with positional heatmaps, displacement distributions, an accuracy/runtime plot, and new benchmark, robustness, representation-comparison, and timing tables. Existing displays are retained with relocation or renumbering, including architecture Figure 4 becoming Figure 5 and ablation Table 4 becoming Table 8.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for CIFAR-10, KV caching, Sinkhorn projection, and Hungarian assignment: Krizhevsky, Pope et al., Sinkhorn, and Kuhn. Appendix C.2 also positions rank-vector relaxation against Birkhoff and orthogonal representations. The main related-work discussion and original positioning are largely retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B's reverse Gaussian-bridge derivation is unchanged. New Appendix C adds supplementary mathematical content, especially the chamber definition in Eq. 29 and assertions about equal volumes, the induced uniform prior, and margins. Its claim that LiftToGrid produces the chamber centroid conflicts with the endpoint-inclusive grid in Eq. 2.

improvement.justification: The new spatial-task evaluation, reference robustness tests, and measured inference costs improve empirical support and make the accuracy/runtime tradeoff assessable. The benefit is tempered by sparse jigsaw training documentation and the new centroid claim in Appendix C.3, which conflicts with Eq. 2's grid containing 0 and 1. The original results and reverse-kernel derivation remain intact, supporting a limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Soft-Rank Diffusion work. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original CIFAR-10 jigsaw results, reference-distribution tests, spatial error analyses, and inference timings.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST sorting and TSP experiments in Tables 1–2 and component ablations in Table 4.

title: Learning Permutation Distributions via Reflected Diffusion on Ranks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and concluding discussion retain the same scientific claims: conditional memory access extends context to 128K while preserving performance, improving efficiency, and enabling KV-cache reduction. The code-release announcement changes access information rather than the core contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explains lower sparsity under shared projections as reduced specialization, identifies preprocessing overhead as a limitation at short contexts, and interprets the new experiments as supporting pruning across scales and efficiency when training from scratch. These qualify and extend the existing interpretation without replacing it.

D1.justification: The abstract newly announces an Apache 2.0 code release and repository location. Appendix D.1 clarifies that existing kernel timings include query compaction and index construction, and E.1.1 specifies the new experiment's corpus, token budget, and context schedule. The original Appendix F hyperparameters are unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds DCLM training-data coverage through its new from-scratch experiment in Appendix E.1.1. HELMET, BABILong, MRCR, and the short-context evaluation tasks are retained; the added studies introduce no new downstream task families.

E2.justification: Section 4.2 expands the end-to-end training-throughput comparison to include S2-Attn and NSA, whereas v1's corresponding comparison covered L2A and CLP. These methods already participated in accuracy evaluations, whose comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds a distinct training-from-scratch protocol: 100B DCLM tokens at 4K context followed by continued pretraining at 128K. Additional experimental controls cover shared projections, 7B pruning at the existing 95% threshold, and 4K/8K kernel timings with preprocessing breakdowns. These expand the experimental design without revising the original training protocol.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands diagnostic analyses: projection sharing tests parameter duplication, training from scratch tests dependence on pretrained initialization, runtime decomposition examines compaction overhead, and 7B pruning tests scaling beyond 1.5B. The existing routing, window-size, regularization, threshold, and parameter-freezing ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Existing sparsity bands and error bars are retained. The new shared-projection discussion invokes externally reported HELMET variability, but adds no uncertainty estimates, run counts, seed information, or statistical tests for the paper's experiments.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and throughput values remain unchanged, including v1 Tables 3–6, now Tables 8–11. New Tables 3–7 report sharing, overhead, from-scratch, and 7B-pruning results; Section 4.2 adds baseline training throughputs. For example, the new scratch-trained models score 11.8 for L2A versus 10.1 for the Transformer at 128K, while 4K kernel speedups range from 0.70× to 1.13× across tested sparsities.

M1.justification: Section 4.5 introduces an evaluated L2A-shared variant that shares QKVO projections between Local and Global Attention. The default architecture, routing rule, training objective, kernel algorithm, and pruning procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the overall section structure are retained. V2 adds localized explanations and a from-scratch ablation subsection, tightens several passages and captions, and updates the conference header and cross-references rather than extensively rewriting the paper.

P2.justification: V2 adds tables displaying projection sharing, runtime components, from-scratch short- and long-context performance, and 7B pruning. It also reorganizes existing displays: the main-text pruning plot moves to Appendix Figure 18, the isolated random-routing figure moves alongside discussion, and window-size plots are resized and grouped together. Existing plotted findings are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds the DCLM citation and a HELMET variability reference. Section 2 newly positions L2A as potentially complementary to key/value sparsification through a two-stage combination. The broader related-work survey and distinction between when and what to retrieve remain intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, routing and loss equations, and Appendix A gradient derivation are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, assumption, or substantive mathematical correction is introduced.

improvement.justification: The added controls and preprocessing breakdown strengthen the efficiency evidence and clarify where speedups fail; code-access information also improves reproducibility documentation. These are useful, bounded gains to an otherwise retained paper. Reporting precision is weakened by a new error: Section 4.2 states a 20.5-point NSA deficit, although Figure 2 reports CLP 40.7 and NSA 21.7, implying 19.0 points.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same L2A research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–F are readable and can be matched despite relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds parameter-sharing, runtime-overhead, training-from-scratch, and larger-model pruning experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original long- and short-context evaluations, training and inference measurements, pruning experiments, and routing ablations.

title: Learning When to Attend: Conditional Memory Access for Long-Context LLMs

C1.justification: The central cached-retrieval and beyond-log-probability claims remain. v3 explicitly extends the conclusion to reasoning models and qualifies cached retrieval as the dominant rather than sole pathway in the tested settings. These refine the scope and exclusivity of the original contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of answer-colon inactivity and Magistral's null PANL ablation, attributing the latter to redundant confidence information across reasoning traces. It newly identifies untested paraphrases and persona framing as limitations. It also introduces an OOD-artifact exclusion interpretation, although Table 1 does not support the assertion that all reported shifts lie within its natural percentile ranges.

D1.justification: C.4 adds substantial Magistral reproducibility information: checkpoint, attention implementation, decoding limit, filtering to 4998 trials, stratified activation collection, calibration selection, and trace-position extraction. C.1.9 newly specifies the three regression fits, feature combinations, and Ridge regularization of 1.0. These document the added analyses rather than demonstrate changes to previously stated settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates factual question answering on TriviaQA. v3 adds mathematical problems from BigMath and multiple-choice questions from MMLU, plus a TriviaQA scenario with explicit reasoning traces preceding answers. These substantially broaden task and input-context coverage (2.9; Figures 25–28).

E2.justification: The central variance-partitioning comparison expands beyond mean answer log-probability to include minimum, maximum, variance, first-token, and last-token log-probabilities, individually and jointly. These are evaluated comparators with reported results, substantially broadening the tested alternatives to activation-based confidence prediction (C.1.9, D.3; Figure 14).

E3.justification: v3 introduces distinct protocols for Magistral, including two-phase reasoning/confidence prompts, a 1024-token generation limit, and stratified sampling. New controls additionally corrupt the answer-colon position and share its selected probe regularization across positions; steering sensitivity tests add strengths 1 and 10. These extend the evaluation design without establishing reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether the pre-answer answer-colon position causally contributes to confidence, whether conclusions survive alternative log-probability summaries, and whether intervention shifts resemble natural activation variability. v3 also adds steering-strength sensitivity and decoding across reasoning-trace positions (Figures 13–14, 26, 29; Table 1).

E5.justification: Table 1 newly reports empirical 5th–95th percentile reference ranges for natural cosine similarities and norm ratios using 3000 activation trials. Existing SEM reporting and fivefold cross-validation remain. Neither version documents an increase in repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Original results are largely retained. New results include BigMath accuracy of 40.2%, MMLU accuracy of 76.8%, and Magistral's null PANL-noising effect despite effective patching. The expanded baseline analysis reports combined-baseline R² = 0.100 and additional PANL R²unique = 0.38 (D.3). These are added findings under new analyses or settings, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The intervention and probing framework is retained, with limited procedural adaptations for reasoning traces. Magistral patching corrupts the question and full reasoning/answer block instead of only answer embeddings, and donor matching uses reasoning-trace length instead of answer length (C.4).

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative are retained. v3 inserts dedicated OOD and answer-colon subsections, reorganizes the variance-partitioning methods, expands the generalization and conclusion passages, and adds limitations and an impact statement. These are targeted structural edits accompanying new content rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with an experiment roadmap, answer-colon and baseline-analysis plots, reasoning prompts and results, additional dataset panels, a steering sensitivity figure, and Table 1. Original figures are largely retained and renumbered; Figure 2 is redrawn with revised typography and tick labeling while preserving its plotted results.

R1.justification: v3 adds BigMath and MMLU references, Yang et al. on verbalized confidence, Teplica et al. on shared uncertainty circuits, and Kumaran et al. on error detection. The latter two provide additional positioning, while the main relationship to prior mechanistic and neuroscience work remains intact.

T1.justification: The existing intervention and metric equations are preserved in substance. The newly explicit variance-partitioning formula explains an existing empirical analysis; it does not introduce new theoretical reasoning. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's broad mechanism account relied on TriviaQA without explicit reasoning and a single log-probability summary. v3 substantially strengthens its evidential basis through additional task types, a reasoning model, answer-colon controls, and broader baselines, while acknowledging alternative pathways and prompt limitations. A material weakness remains: the new OOD discussion claims all shifts fall within natural ranges, although Table 1 lists scale-5 cosine similarities of 0.992–0.995 below the corresponding lower bounds of 0.997–0.998. This weakens that particular argument but does not outweigh the substantial gains in controlled evidence and demonstrated applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence? Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering, with no essential reading gaps.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds BigMath, MMLU, Magistral reasoning-model experiments, and further control and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original calibration, activation intervention, probing, and attention-blocking experiments on Gemma 3 27B and Qwen 2.5 7B using TriviaQA.

title: How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence?

C1.justification: The generator and benchmark contributions remain central. The introduction and conclusion extend the prompt-optimization claim to domains outside the optimization distribution and explicitly emphasize validation of task-difficulty controls. The advertised billions-scale task space was already documented in v1 Appendix C.

C2.justification: For the revised benchmark, v2 replaces v1's strong All-Edit model-ranking statement with caution about low success rates. It interprets baseline initialization as easier but liable to preserve the initial implementation, and explicitly identifies prompt-only optimization and limited model/scaffold coverage as remaining limitations.

D1.justification: v1 Appendix O's extensive domain, dataset, and module prompt specifications are removed and replaced by repository access guidance in v2 Appendix D.1. The documented five-task learned prompt also changes, without explaining whether this is a correction or a new run. v2 adds MARL's four-GPU requirement and updates estimated total compute from 23,000 to 35,000 GPU-hours.

E1.justification: Evaluated coverage expands from ten to fourteen domains, adding neural cellular automata, offline RL, on-policy MARL, and trajectory prediction. These were described but not evaluated in v1. v2 includes their DiscoBench results and uses them for explicitly held-out-domain prompt evaluation.

E2.justification: The three LLM-backed agents and all-fixed DiscoBench baseline are retained. However, v2 Appendix J.9–J.10 adds all-fixed baseline references to per-task comparisons of tuned prompts; v1's corresponding prompt-tuning results compared the four task-count conditions without that reference.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation on four domains outside the retained ten-domain prompt-training distribution. The module sweep expands from 15 configurations of four modules to 63 configurations of six modules. The new initialization experiment controls starting code across eight selected domains using DeepSeek-v3.2. Existing benchmark action budgets and dataset splits are retained.

E4.justification: Section 8.2 adds an empty-versus-baseline initialization ablation and qualitative examination of resulting algorithms. Section 8.1 substantially expands v1 Appendix G's module sweep, while dropping its detailed maximum-score summary. Section 7 adds an explicit analysis of generalization beyond the prompt-training domain distribution.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three meta-seeds, additional attempts until three successful runs where feasible, and 95% Elo intervals from 100 bootstrap rounds. Per-task stratified bootstrap intervals and interquartile means are retained, as are eight-inner-seed means and standard errors for the single-task prompt-tuning curves.

E6.justification: Benchmark aggregates, success@3 values, and numerous per-task results change. For example, DeepSeek's Single-Edit success rate changes from 80.0% in v1 Table 2 to 71.3% in v2 Table 3 on expanded coverage, not a comparable-setting decline. New results include held-out-domain prompt scores and initialization success rates of 92.4% versus 75.4% in Section 8.2.

M1.justification: The task generator, two-stage meta-train/meta-test construction, MLGym scaffold, and Claude/DeepSeek prompt-tuning procedure remain unchanged. The additional domains and on-policy target/activation modules emphasized in v2 were already specified in v1 Appendices B–C.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: design analyses gain a main-text section, domain appendices are consolidated, successful-run results move out of the main comparison, and the task-prompt appendix is removed. Method and research-direction passages are condensed, and evaluation terminology and section titles are revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds the benchmark-property table, restructures main result tables, replaces module-summary tables with Figure 2, and extensively expands appendix plots. Some presentation becomes less specific: many combination panels in Figures 32–39 use 'OnPolicyRL all' instead of v1's explicit module-combination labels.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to ProgramBench, Hyperagents, and process reward models, and presents benchmark positioning in a new property-comparison table. The underlying related-work argument remains stable; most other bibliographic revisions update publication metadata rather than introduce different works.

T1.justification: The task-count formula, its inclusion-exclusion derivation, the model-unlearning extension, and Elo equations are unchanged between v1 Appendices E–F and v2 Appendices C–D. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical validation covered ten domains and pooled prompt-tuning performance. v2 evaluates the four previously untested domains, explicitly separates transfer beyond the training-domain distribution, and adds controlled initialization comparisons and broader module ablations. These address important gaps in validating diversity, generalization, and controllable difficulty. The gains outweigh reduced self-contained prompt documentation and less informative combination-plot labels.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiscoGen/DiscoBench work and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Reordered sections and previously documented capabilities can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports expanded domain evaluations, held-out-domain prompt performance, and an initialization ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original DiscoBench evaluations of three LLM-backed agents, prompt-tuning experiments, module-combination analyses, and discovered algorithms.

title: Procedural Generation Of Algorithm Discovery Tasks in Machine Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: adapting diffusion LLMs through a unified delimiter-based corpus and domain adaptation, followed by SFT and RL, achieves strong small-data BBO performance. The added experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 broadens interpretation through the matched-backbone results, GP-prior sensitivity, mixed RNA findings and pretraining-knowledge audit. It explicitly acknowledges that unavailable pretraining data prevent an exact overlap audit. Section 4.6 also narrows the earlier interpretation about avoiding 'prompt hacking' to robustness under natural paraphrases that preserve task semantics and output format.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents stage-specific optimization steps and processed sample counts, inference-context resampling, single-pass greedy token filling, and duplicate rejection until 128 unique valid candidates are obtained. It adds representative paraphrases, GP implementation information and the ranking-probe procedure. The abstract's code hyperlink changes from an anonymous repository to the named DiBO GitHub repository; these are documented access instructions, not independently verified availability.

E1.justification: V2 retains the four original Design-Bench tasks and adds RNA-A/B/C from BootGen, involving length-14 RNA sequence optimization (Appendix A.6, Table 11). This substantially extends biological task coverage beyond the original DNA and robot-morphology evaluations.

E2.justification: V2 adds a matched LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct autoregressive comparator across all four original tasks and all three training stages (Table 2), providing a substantial new comparison against the diffusion backbone. The main table's named comparator set is retained. Inference-only dLLM with MCTS was excluded from quantitative comparisons in both versions; its discussion was moved.

E3.justification: V2 introduces matched-backbone controls, random versus evenly spaced pool sampling, Top-5/10/20 metrics, and ranking probes using 500 groups per task for K=2–5. It adopts dimension-scaled GP priors and changes the stated continuous-task DA learning rate from 1e-4 to 1e-5. That reported setting revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun; newly disclosed training budgets and decoding details are documentation additions.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses testing the backbone's contribution, sensitivity to offline-pool sampling, the effect of GP priors, and possible pretrained design-label knowledge (Tables 2, 6, 8 and 12). These address important questions absent from v1. The delimiter, training-stage, context-similarity and hyperparameter analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight random seeds and mean ± standard deviation for optimization results. V2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests or changed repeated-run counts. Additional result rows and the ranking probe's sample size do not establish a change in uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: DiBO's four headline maximum scores remain unchanged, but GP results and rankings change under revised priors; for example, Grad-EI's TF Bind 8 maximum changes from 0.673 to 0.864. DiBO's TF Bind 8 median changes from 0.599 in v1 Table 5 to 0.473 in v2 Tables 9–10, although v2 Table 8 retains 0.599. Numerous new results include mixed RNA outcomes: DiBO leads maximum scores on RNA-A/C but trails both comparators on every reported RNA-B metric.

M1.justification: Equation (3) revises the stated domain-adaptation loss indicator to include prompt masking alongside response masking. This is a localized loss-expression change: both versions already describe joint prompt-response reconstruction, so an implementation change is not established. The backbone, corpus construction, DA–SFT–RL pipeline and reward remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose remain intact. V2 makes targeted wording changes, expands implementation and appendix explanations, rewrites the prompt-robustness discussion and conclusion, and moves the inference-only comparison into Section 4.4. Author/affiliation and proceedings-header text also change; there is no wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial displays for the matched backbone comparison, pool sampling, prompt paraphrases, GP-prior comparisons, Top-K performance, RNA results and ranking audit. Existing ablation tables are regrouped and renumbered, and Figure 2 is relocated with a shorter caption. The two existing figures retain essentially the same visual content.

R1.justification: V2 adds literature supporting high-dimensional GP calibration and implementation, including Hvarfner, Binois and Wycoff, Garnett and BoTorch, plus BootGen and additional BBO/multimodal citations. The central positioning relative to autoregressive optimization and inference-only diffusion remains intact. Publication updates for existing works and removal of a duplicate ICT reference do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: Equation (3) adds a prompt-mask condition to the formal loss indicator, changing its mathematical expression rather than merely its typography. The other training objectives and similarity definition are retained, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The matched trained autoregressive control and calibrated GP comparisons substantially strengthen evidence for DiBO's advantages beyond v1's comparisons. Explicit training budgets and inference procedures resolve important reproducibility gaps, while RNA evaluations and a narrower paraphrase interpretation better expose applicability boundaries. These gains outweigh a material reporting defect: v2 gives conflicting TF Bind 8 medians, 0.599 in Table 8 versus 0.473 in Tables 9–10. The improvement concerns stronger evaluation and documentation, not increased headline DiBO scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiBO research work. The full main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material that was moved or renumbered.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds a matched autoregressive comparison, GP-prior and sampling analyses, RNA evaluations and a pretraining-overlap probe.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimization experiments on four Design-Bench tasks, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity studies and appendix median results.

title: Training Diffusion Language Models for Black-Box Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract revises acceptance-gain claims from approximately 12% on LLaMA3 and 8–12% on Qwen3 to 7–11% and 7–8%, explicitly identifying LADE as the comparison. It also specifies the strongest baseline for throughput gains. The five principal contributions and conclusion remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: New discussion attributes diminishing returns from additional masks to next-token training, interprets high update rates as over-adaptation, and discusses EAGLE3's speed-versus-training-cost trade-off. Appendix G.6 also qualifies the earlier generalization about writing tasks by identifying model-dependent preferences and near-ties for translation.

D1.justification: v2 revises hardware and output-length documentation, specifies branch configurations for new mask-count tests, and reports EAGLE3 training-cost and checkpoint-availability information. The implementation descriptions and baseline configurations in Appendices E–F remain unchanged. The conflicting setup descriptions limit reproducibility.

E1.justification: Figures 4, 5, and 8 extend the reported evaluated domains from eight task categories to ten by adding STEM and humanities. The original task categories and Dolly-Databricks analyses remain; no additional named benchmark is introduced.

E2.justification: Appendix G.5/Table 10 adds EAGLE3 as a training-based comparator for LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct at BC=30 and 60. Its Qwen3-32B entries are unavailable, not evaluated results. PLD, STAND, and LADE remain the main comparators.

E3.justification: The main timing metric changes from tokens per second to speedup over autoregressive decoding. v2 Table 1 specifies H100 hardware and 256-token outputs, replacing the earlier A100/100-token setting, although Section 4 inconsistently retains that earlier description. New experiments also introduce three-mask configurations, BC=120, and alternative update rates.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic evidence: Table 3 tests one to three masks at fixed BC=60, Table 9 jointly increases mask count and budget through BC=120, and Table 15 tests embedding-update-rate sensitivity. Existing sampling, pruning, initialization, and task-specific mask-count analyses remain despite appendix renumbering.

title: From Weak Cues to Real Identities: Evaluating Inference-Driven De-Anonymization in LLM Agents

C1.justification: The core contribution remains discounted historical reward estimation for sample-efficient RLVR. The abstract and conclusion qualify lower MSE by mild non-stationarity, while the introduction adds an appropriate-discount-factor qualification and claims statistically significant superiority over a broader baseline set.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of how nonzero advantages on all-correct/all-incorrect groups affect exploration and why DBB needs wider clipping. It adds interpretations of prior sensitivity, preservation of useful diversity, model-dependent discount selection and the tuning-versus-MSE tradeoff with empirical Bayes. Suggested settings for 30B+ models are explicitly extrapolations.

D1.justification: Appendix C clarifies clipping conventions and per-method settings and adds implementation guidance for GRESO and DAPO. Appendices H–I specify EMA initialization and online method-of-moments fitting for the empirical-Bayes prior. Existing hardware, data filtering, optimizer settings and framework links are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions train on DAPO-Math-17k and retain the same six mathematical and three general-reasoning evaluation benchmarks. The additional 0.6B model uses existing benchmarks; continuous and dense rewards are discussed only as future work.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated GRESO and DAPO baselines alongside GRPO and RePO. Appendices H–I additionally compare DBB with per-prompt EMA, Laplace smoothing and empirical Bayes on estimation MSE. These substantially broaden the comparator set.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include testing both GRPO and DBB under two clipping ranges, prior-parameter sweeps, Best@8 evaluation and a discount-factor search on Qwen3-0.6B-Base. The expanded main comparison explicitly matches total rollout budgets. Existing Table 5 training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices D–I investigate whether clipping explains the gains, sensitivity to prior strength, whether lower entropy harms useful response diversity, model-scale dependence of the optimal discount factor, and whether simpler estimators suffice. These address substantial questions beyond v1’s existing discount-factor, MSE and Dr.GRPO analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports scalar benchmark scores without stated replication or significance tests. v2 reports four independent evaluation seeds, means and standard deviations, and one-sided paired t-tests over per-prompt accuracies in Table 1. Appendix C clarifies that these are evaluation repetitions, not four independent training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces earlier scores with four-evaluation-run summaries. Reported DBB-minus-GRPO gains for 1.7B/8B change from 3.22/2.42 to 3.43/2.32 points in distribution and from 12.49/6.92 to 10.05/8.34 out of distribution. These are revised estimates, not demonstrated improvements from a changed method. New baseline, clipping, Best@8, prior-sensitivity and estimator-comparison results substantially expand the findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the discounted posterior updates, initialization and GRPO/Dr.GRPO integration remain unchanged. The wider DBB clipping range was already disclosed in v1; v2 investigates it without changing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the abstract, experimental discussion and Sections 5.1–5.2, with terminology and cross-reference corrections. v2 adds acknowledgements, updates affiliation/publication text and appends new analyses, while retaining the main section order and most methodological exposition.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially expanded with additional baselines, uncertainty values and significance rows. v2 adds Figures 4–8 and Table 6, providing new diagnostic plots, a prior-sensitivity heatmap and estimator comparisons. Figure 6 redisplays existing Mean@8 curves alongside newly reported Best@8 curves.

R1.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendices H–I newly position DBB against simpler shrinkage and shared-prior estimators. Section 6 and the cited-work set otherwise remain essentially unchanged; the Gelman reference switches editions of the same book rather than introducing a different work.

T1.justification: Appendices H–I add formal definitions and conditional MSE expressions for EMA, Laplace smoothing and empirical Bayes, including EMA’s historical weights. The original DBB equations and Appendix B derivation remain unchanged; the mathematical additions support the new comparator analyses.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v1’s limited comparator set and absent uncertainty reporting. Appendix D directly tests the important clipping-range confound, while prior-sensitivity, Best@8 and alternative-estimator analyses better support the central argument. Replication covers evaluation randomness rather than training variability, and reporting inconsistencies remain, such as Appendix G claiming six benchmarks while Table 6 lists five.
