E4.justification: Beyond v1's learning-rate sweeps and Transformer diagonal-dominance analyses, v3 tests whether advantages persist with twice the training budget and whether assigning embeddings and the LM head to the matrix optimizer matters (Appendices D.3–D.4). It also adds larger-model, Mamba and ResNet dominance diagnostics and gradient-clipping analyses (Appendices B and E).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed-based variability, confidence intervals or significance tests for the experimental comparisons. Raw and smoothed diagnostic trajectories and averages across parameters are not newly introduced uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Retained perplexity and timing tables preserve their values, while v3 adds substantial results. Examples include RMNP/Muon perplexities of 12.58/12.97 for GPT-2 1.5B and 13.75/14.13 for LLaMA-1B (Tables 18–19). New sweeps report best Mamba perplexities of 32.32/32.95 and CIFAR-10 accuracies of 94.33%/94.65% (Tables 20–21). Additional baseline and ablation results expand the evidence under new settings.

M1.justification: The proposed optimizer still updates momentum and applies row-wise L2 normalization. The revised Gram-matrix expressions reconcile the equations with the row normalization already specified in v1's Equation 4 and Appendix A. The expanded experiments and revised training prescriptions do not introduce a new core optimization mechanism.

P1.justification: Most existing prose, the six-section main structure and the proof appendix remain intact. v3 expands Section 2, replaces the former discussion at the end of Section 3.2, adds an appendix contents list and organizes new material into Appendices D.3–D.4 and E. These are localized editorial and organizational changes rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds a conceptual Figure 3, revises Figure 2's formulas, combines global dominance plots using relative training progress, and merges and expands the main performance charts. Numerous training, ablation and clipping displays are added, alongside expanded comparison tables. Several earlier plots and scores are relocated or redisplayed rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive discussion of Adam-mini, SRON, SCALE, SWAN, MNGD, Mano and MOGA. It acknowledges earlier row-normalization approaches and expands the distinction between curvature-based explanations and worst-case steepest-descent analyses. Pethick et al. was already discussed in v1; its relocation accompanies a broader revision of research positioning.

T1.justification: v3 corrects the order of diagonal extraction and matrix powers in Algorithm 2 and Equations 3–4, making the preconditioner expression agree with row normalization. It also marks finite Newton–Schulz orthogonalization as approximate and clarifies the matrix-dimension/transposition convention. The convergence theorems and Appendix A proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the added competitors, longer-training checks, vision experiments and corrected preconditioner equations improve the evidential basis and technical clarity. These gains are tempered by the stronger asymptotic-equivalence claim, which the finite-scale dominance diagnostics do not establish, and inaccurate new interpretations such as Appendix D.4's 0.13-PPL bound. The resulting net quality improvement is limited despite the substantial expansion.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RMNP research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds larger-model experiments, additional optimizer comparisons, ablations, Mamba pretraining and ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2 and LLaMA pretraining results, optimizer timing measurements, learning-rate sweeps and diagonal-dominance analyses.

title: RMNP: Row-Momentum Normalized Preconditioning for Scalable Matrix-Based Optimization

The introduction and conclusion remove near length-invariant perplexity as a headline finding, and the advertised parameter overhead changes from approximately 5.5% to 4–5%. The conclusion additionally claims superiority to ChunkLLaMA across all evaluated lengths, although Table 1 contains counterexamples.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3 newly acknowledges future-segment access and interprets the control results as evidence that hierarchical structure, rather than that access, drives gains. The new Limitations section explicitly identifies growing decoding KV-cache costs and untested benefits for models with native contexts of 128K or longer. The earlier interpretation linking attention stability to near length-invariant perplexity is removed.

D1.justification: Table 9 gains a Qwen3-8B pretraining configuration, documenting optimizer, LoRA, batch, slot, and bottleneck settings. Section 4.1 specifies 8×H200 GPUs for Qwen3 while retaining 8×H100 for LLaMA-2. Existing LLaMA-2 hyperparameters and the paper's code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use RedPajama and LongAlpaca-12k for training and PG-19, Proof-pile, passkey retrieval, LongChat topic retrieval, and LongBench for evaluation. Qwen3 adds a model configuration within existing tasks and context-length coverage, rather than a new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds unadapted LLaMA-2 and ChunkLLaMA comparisons, plus a base-Qwen3 comparison. Topic-retrieval Table 2 replaces GPT-3.5-Turbo-16K and Claude-1.3-100K with GPT-4o-mini-128K and Claude-3.5-Sonnet-200K, and adds Llama-3-8B-Instruct-8K. These substantially expand and revise the reported comparator set. GPT-3.5 remains in the unchanged LongBench comparison.

It also changes the stated evaluation mode for retained component/cardinality ablations from hierarchical attention to standard full attention despite unchanged scores. This establishes a reported protocol revision, not evidence of rerunning. Table 1's mode remains ambiguous: Section 4.1 specifies hierarchical attention, whereas Table 6 describes full attention as consistent with Table 1.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 adds a control testing whether access to future segments explains HiCI's gains; Appendix B.2 adds a component-wise FLOPs comparison. Conversely, v1's Table 5 comparing segment sizes, attention modes, and evaluation-length sensitivity is removed. The existing segment-size training-loss curves and layer-wise attention analyses remain, so this is a substantive change in analytical evidence rather than wholesale removal of segment-size analysis.

E5.justification: Removing v1 Table 5 also removes its standard-deviation summaries across evaluation lengths. This is a limited removal of descriptive dispersion reporting, not evidence of fewer training seeds or repeated runs. Both versions retain ten randomized passkey trials per context length; neither reports training-seed uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial result entries while retaining the existing LLaMA-2 language-modeling, LongBench, and component-ablation numbers. New Qwen3 results at 48K include PG-19 perplexity 9.73 and Proof-pile 2.26, alongside base-model values 11.32 and 2.46. Table 6 adds restricted-aggregation perplexities 7.28/7.00/6.94 versus shared-context 7.27/7.01/6.93. New comparator and FLOPs results are reported, while v1 Table 5's segment-granularity results disappear.

M1.justification: The main construction–integration–broadcast algorithm and Equations 1–13 remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 introduces a tested variant, Gi = Agg(L1, ..., Li), that restricts global aggregation to current and preceding segments instead of the entire sequence. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: v3 revises the abstract, contribution bullets, experimental discussion, and conclusion; separates language modeling and retrieval into distinct subsections; and adds dedicated related-work and limitations sections. The method exposition and most existing appendix prose remain substantially intact, making this a localized narrative revision rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands its model/comparator blocks, Table 9 gains a Qwen3 column, and Table 2 changes comparator rows. New Tables 6 and 10 display the causality and FLOPs analyses, while v1 Table 5 is removed. All five figures retain their designs and plotted content, with relocation and associated page reflow. The placeholder running header is corrected.

R1.justification: New Section 2.4 substantially expands positioning relative to global-workspace architectures and latent representations, including VanRullen and Kanai, Goyal et al., Zeng et al., concept-centric transformers, Coconut, and Large Concept Models. It distinguishes HiCI's within-layer context aggregation from inter-module coordination and latent reasoning or prediction. Additional references support the new model and baseline comparisons.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly formalizes Gi = Agg(L1, ..., Li) and identifies the original global aggregation's non-causal cross-segment pathway. The information-capacity bound, data-processing inequality, computational-complexity theorem, and their existing derivations remain unchanged. No new causality proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: The new model comparisons, related-work distinctions, causality discussion, and limitations improve breadth and transparency. However, Section 4.1 and Table 6 conflict over the attention mode underlying central perplexity results, while unchanged ablation scores receive a different protocol description. The new causal control leaves handling of within-segment future information unspecified, and the earlier segment-perplexity evidence is removed. These uncertainties affect the central validation, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HiCI with the same authors and core architecture. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original HiCI experiments and adds Qwen3-8B results, additional comparator results, and a global-context causality ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original HiCI language-modeling, retrieval, LongBench, ablation, training-efficiency, and attention-analysis results.

title: HiCI: Hierarchical Construction–Integration for Long-Context Attention

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central separation between rotation-invariant and spindly algorithms. The conclusion adds the empirical claim that the gap persists for anisotropic inputs, explicitly leaving a corresponding theoretical lower bound open.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds an interpretation involving target–eigenspace alignment and reduced prediction-risk contributions from low-variance directions, and explains why the isotropic proof does not directly extend. Section 5 also qualifies the previous minimax-match description as matching up to logarithmic simplification.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies a new synthetic-input specification: Gaussian sampling with diagonal covariance and power-law eigenvalues, with exponent values identified in Figure 6. This is limited additional reproduction information; sample sizes, target construction, training settings, and repeat counts for that experiment are not separately specified.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds anisotropic Gaussian input scenarios for the existing sparse-logistic task, with covariance-decay exponents 0.5 and 1.0 alongside an isotropic control. The preliminary Poisson and Exponential experiments mentioned in v1 are retained through relocation, not newly added.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison remains single-layer logistic regression versus the spindly parameterization, labeled Single and Spindle in new Figure 6. No additional comparator is evaluated; references to other algorithms remain discussion or future work.

E3.justification: The added experiment introduces a covariance-exponent sweep over 0, 0.5, and 1.0 and dimension sweeps extending to d = 500. The original Section 6 settings and Figure 5 sweep through d = 1000 remain unchanged. Appendix B does not establish whether its other experimental settings match Section 6.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests whether the performance gap survives departure from isotropic inputs and how dimension scaling responds to covariance decay. This adds a focused sensitivity analysis; the existing coordinate-dynamics analyses in Figures 3–4 remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions specify averaging Figure 5 over 10 independent dataset draws and display error bars. Figure 6 extends averaging and error-bar reporting to additional results without introducing a new uncertainty procedure or specifying additional run counts, seeds, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original Figures 3–5 are unchanged. New Figure 6 adds isotropic-control and anisotropic excess-risk curves: Single remains above Spindle, while its growth with dimension becomes sublinear under covariance decay. These are additional results, not established same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The logistic objective, single-layer procedure, Hadamard parameterization w = u ⊙ v, gradient-flow dynamics, and early-stopping approach are unchanged. The added experiments vary the input distribution without introducing a method component.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the conclusion and rate discussion, adds an Impact Statement, updates the publication footer, and moves the two existing open problems into new Appendix B. Subsequent appendices are renumbered; most prose and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the three-panel Figure 6 with covariance-dependent excess-risk curves. The existing spherical tangent-map diagram is relocated and renumbered from Figure 6 to Figure 7. Original experimental figures are retained, with otherwise limited layout reflow.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds Beck, Levi, and Bar-Sinai (2024) on grokking near linear separability. The sparse-recovery discussion is explicitly situated in the underdetermined regime and adds pointers to already-cited Warmuth et al. (2021). The central novelty positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 5 refines the stated sparse-logistic minimax benchmark from O(s log d/n) to O(s log(ed/s)/n), distinguishing it from the retained method bound. The formal assumptions, propositions, theorems, and proof appendices otherwise remain unchanged after renumbering; no anisotropic bound is proved.

improvement.justification: The added covariance-sensitivity experiment provides useful evidence beyond the original isotropic setting, while the conclusion clearly distinguishes that evidence from an unproved theoretical extension. Section 5 also qualifies the minimax comparison more precisely. These are modest gains: Appendix B leaves several reproduction settings unspecified, and the original proofs and experiments remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices. The proof appendices can be matched across renumbering from v1 Appendices B–E to v2 Appendices C–F.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, and Appendix B and Figure 6 add original simulations with power-law Gaussian covariance spectra.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 3–5 report original synthetic sparse-logistic-regression experiments comparing single-layer and spindly models, including training dynamics and excess risk.

title: Hard labels sampled from sparse targets mislead rotation invariant algorithms

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: PA-GRPO addresses permutation blindness through cross-permutation advantages and consistency rewards, with evidence from three backbones and seven benchmarks. The additional analyses support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Appendix H newly interprets prompt-variation results as evidence against dependence on one template and discusses why UniBias's better JudgeBench bias metrics do not imply better overall consistency. Section 5.5 also qualifies the coupled-permutation advantage as dataset-dependent. The explicit limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies evaluation temperature zero, clarifies baseline adaptations, and explicitly documents objective accumulation in Algorithm 1. The abstract changes code release from planned to reported availability at the same linked repository. Repository availability itself cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The training datasets, seven evaluation benchmarks, and task domains remain unchanged. Appendix H adds a prompt-variation scenario with explicit quality criteria and instructions to disregard answer order and labels, modestly extending the tested input conditions.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator set remains Base, GRPO, UniBias, PriDe, CalibraEval, and PIF; Table 6 uses this existing set. Appendix E clarifies task-format adaptations for CalibraEval and PIF, whose results already covered both task types in v1.

E3.justification: Appendix H adds RStd and CKLD evaluation metrics and a default-versus-modified-prompt comparison on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The existing full-permutation evaluation, main metrics, backbones, and training budgets remain unchanged. The newly stated evaluation temperature is a disclosure, not evidence of a revised setting.

E4.justification: New Appendices G–H substantially extend supplementary validation with a semantic-tracking case study, comparative distributional bias measurements, and a prompt-sensitivity test. The case contrasts GRPO preserving answer A after a swap with PA-GRPO following the same content from A to B. The earlier CoT and bias-decomposition analyses are retained in the main text.

E5.justification: Appendix F replaces the unspecified 'multiple independent runs' statement with three independent training runs using different random seeds. This newly specifies the reporting practice without establishing an increased run count. No confidence intervals or significance tests are added; RStd measures differences across answer labels, not run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 6 adds comparative RStd/CKLD results across seven benchmarks, including modified-prompt results. Table 5 revises the standard-permutation entries for all three MCQ benchmarks: ARC-Challenge Acc/Con/CA changes from 81.6/93.2/83.1 to 89.3/92.9/92.6, now matching Table 1. Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the permutation construction, semantic mapping, rewards, cross-permutation advantage, and optimization objective. Algorithm 1 makes instance-objective calculation and batch accumulation explicit, completing the documentation of the existing objective without establishing a changed method.

P1.justification: Sections 5.4–5.5 are rewritten to incorporate the earlier appendix analyses, while Appendices G–H receive new purposes. Algorithm 1 and baseline implementation paragraphs are edited, and acknowledgments are added. Most existing introduction, methodology, and conclusion wording remains intact.

P2.justification: Tables 4–5 move from the appendix into the main results section, with revised captions. v2 adds Table 6 and boxed prompts and response excerpts for the new analyses. The existing figures and principal table structures are retained, with local resizing and layout reflow.

R1.justification: The cited works and related-work positioning are unchanged. The new bias-metric discussion cites works already present in v1, and the paper retains its distinction between inference-time calibration, supervised debiasing, and permutation-aware reinforcement learning.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and derivations are retained, with no new assumptions, proofs, or theoretical results. Equation 14 replaces the abbreviated clipping interval with explicit lower and upper bounds, an equivalent notation change. The added bias metrics serve empirical evaluation.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens support for the debiasing interpretation through additional bias metrics and a prompt-sensitivity check, resolves Table 5's disagreement with the main MCQ results, and improves reproducibility disclosures. These are useful, bounded gains: the core experiments remain unchanged, and the new prompt test covers one alternative template on one backbone, limiting broader conclusions about prompt robustness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PA-GRPO work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–H are readable and support comparison, including matching analyses moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds bias-specific measurements, a prompt-sensitivity evaluation, and a qualitative comparison of GRPO and PA-GRPO.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on three model backbones and seven benchmarks, including component ablations, hyperparameter studies, CoT comparisons, and bias decomposition.

title: Mitigating Selection Bias in Large Language Models via Permutation-Aware GRPO

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: a general-purpose abductive framework, explicit graph/state-machine control, improved diagnostic performance, and publicly available code/prompts. The additional ablation supports these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly interprets the structured-text comparison as evidence that generic context management alone does not explain GoS's gains, attributing the remaining advantage to explicit graph relations and hypothesis updates. Appendix B limitations and Appendix D interpretations are otherwise retained.

These are access/provenance disclosures; the stated restriction on releasing raw incident data and interaction traces remains unchanged.

Naming Lenovo replaces the anonymized company designation. The added introductory MATH500, AIME2025, and GPQA figures are presented as previously reported performance, not new GoS evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds 'w/ structured state management,' which stores hypotheses, evidence, and support/refute status in structured text without an explicit causal graph. The eight single-agent/multi-agent CoT, ToT, GoT, and FoT comparators in the main experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4 retains GPT-5.1-2025-11-13, case filtering, the 0/1/2 judging scale, medical human evaluation, retrieval limits of three per expert and five for single agents, and three GoS interaction iterations. No separate change to evaluation procedures is documented for the added ablation.

E5.justification: Figure 8 retains the same five repeated judge assessments of ten medical cases. Neither version changes seed/run reporting, confidence intervals, significance testing, or other uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: The added Table 2 condition reports 18.12% Match, 59.42% Relevant, and $0.15 per case. All existing Table 2 entries, Tables 1 and 3–5, and plotted results remain unchanged; full GoS has no reported performance change.

M1.justification: The proposed GoS architecture, reasoning focus, causal graph, ReAct interactions, and backtracking/drill-down procedures remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix A. Structured-text state management is an added comparison condition, not a modification of full GoS.

P1.justification: v2 makes limited introductory edits, expands related work and the ablation discussion, adds Acknowledgement and Impact Statement sections, and revises affiliations and punctuation. The main narrative, section sequence, and appendix organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: ICML-style formatting changes the title/affiliation placement, running headers, spacing, and float placement and sizing. Table 2 gains one row. All ten figure graphics are retained, and the remaining tables preserve their structures.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds LINC, LOGIC-LM, and Aristotle, distinguishing their symbolic answer derivation from GoS's interactive investigation. The introduction adds Lightman and Rein benchmark citations and removes Peirce (1934). The OpsAgent title/year update refers to the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: The task and reasoning-focus definitions in Equations 1–2, graph/state definitions, transition conditions, and Appendix A algorithms retain the same mathematical content. No theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is added or revised.

improvement.justification: The structured-text control strengthens the causal-graph argument beyond v1's graph-removal comparison: it achieves 18.12% Match versus 31.88% for full GoS and 12.32% without the graph. Added neuro-symbolic related work also clarifies positioning. These are useful, bounded improvements while the primary results, method, and documented limitations remain intact.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Graph of States (GoS) work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–D support reliable comparison despite reformatting and changed pagination.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds a structured-state-management comparison in Table 2.

before.justification: v1 reports original medical and distributed-system diagnosis experiments, including accuracy and cost results, ablations, sensitivity analysis, and appendix error analyses.

title: Graph of States: Solving Abductive Tasks with Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central post-training claim becomes more specific: v4 attributes emergence to contrastive preference optimization, with standard SFT insufficient, rather than broadly to post-training. This algorithm-level conclusion enters the abstract, introduction, and discussion. The main claims about behavioral robustness, distributed detection mechanisms, and underelicited capacity are retained.

C2.justification: Appendix S substantially narrows the interpretation of learned-vector improvements: they do not transfer to broader self-knowledge, and shorter, more assertive responses accompany degraded faithfulness and prefill detection. v4 also qualifies zero-FPR findings to trial numbers 1-10, reports confabulation outside that range, and explicitly acknowledges that the mechanism of post-training emergence remains unidentified.

D1.justification: v4 supplies detailed LoRA hyperparameters, optimizer and schedule settings, preference-data access information, and an abliterated-model link. It clarifies model-matched concept vectors, shared transcoder usage, intervention token positions, and logit-based estimators. Some information is lost: v1's explicit refusal-ablation region boundaries and optimization search bounds are omitted.

E1.justification: v4 adds preference training using Dolci-Instruct-DPO and downstream evaluation on HaluEval, JailbreakHub, MMLU/GPQA-based chain-of-thought faithfulness tasks, and 1,900 self-written-versus-prefilled response examples. These substantially extend the represented data and task requirements beyond v1's concept-injection and generic-prompt evaluations.

E2.justification: v4 introduces comparisons among standard, reference-free, shuffled, and reversed DPO; chosen/rejected-response SFT; SFT with KL; margin-plus-KL training; and DPO without prior SFT (Table 3). Cross-model refusal experiments also add magnitude-matched random-direction controls. These are evaluated comparators absent from v1.

E3.justification: v1 aggregates OLMo results over layers 25, 32, 38, 45, and 51; v4 reports layer-specific evaluations at 19, 22, and 25 on 50 concepts. The attention-probe target also changes in the prose from steered/unsteered activations to successful/failed concepts, although v4 Figure 27 retains the old caption.

E4.justification: v4 adds training-objective and data-domain ablations, DPO beta sweeps, norm/unembedding controls, binary-classification analysis, trial-number sensitivity findings, and cross-model refusal controls. It also investigates downstream side effects. Conversely, the PLS2 steering analysis and v1 Figure 14b-d's circuit-importance analyses disappear; Figure 14a is retained as v4 Figure 33.

E5.justification: v4 newly specifies the existing 100 injection trials as 10 trial numbers with 10 samples each and discusses sampling and judge variability (Appendix B.3); this does not establish additional runs. Appendix H adds correlations controlling for other vector properties. Existing confidence-interval and cross-validation reporting largely persists, without new training-seed information.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include TPR-minus-FPR of +14.4 percentage points for standard DPO versus -13.5 for chosen-response SFT (Table 3). Newly reported downstream comparisons show MMLU faithfulness falling from 37.5% to 21.5% and prefill detection from 36.3% to 16.1% with the bias vector. These are new evaluations; the retained concept-injection gains are unchanged. OLMo results are replaced under revised settings.

M1.justification: The learned steering vector, renamed a bias vector, retains its training procedure. v4 adds a procedural variant for cross-model refusal ablation: a uniform per-model projection weight selected by a minimum-effective-dose rule (Appendix C.2), alongside the original approach using optimized regional weights.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, mechanistic explanations, and discussion receive extensive editing. Section 4 is reframed, Section 6 distinguishes the learned bias from injected concept vectors, related work is reorganized, and limitations become a separate section before discussion. The appendices are substantially reorganized, beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned, gate panels from v1 Figures 10-12 are consolidated into v4 Figure 11, and positive-attribution displays are regrouped in Appendix L. The circuit-distribution panel moves to Appendix O while other circuit-importance panels disappear. Layer-specific OLMo plots, new diagnostic figures, and multiple experimental tables substantially change the presentation.

R1.justification: v4 adds substantive comparisons with Pearson-Vogel et al., Lederman and Mahowald, and Rivera and Africa, relating cached-representation detection, probability matching, latent capacity, and trained steering awareness to its findings. Benchmark and faithfulness references also expand. This materially broadens the research positioning beyond v1's discussion.

T1.justification: The auxiliary circuit-importance definition, gate attribution multiplied by steering projection, is removed with the corresponding analysis. The central steering-attribution mathematics, including complete-cut conditions and Equations 1-3, remains unchanged between v1 Appendix M and v4 Appendix Q.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly associated introspection with checkpoint stage and assessed broader learned-vector effects through response style and length. v4 adds controlled training comparisons that substantially strengthen the preference-training explanation, and downstream tests expose important limits and adverse effects previously untested. Geometric controls further strengthen the mechanistic evidence. These gains outweigh the removal of some circuit-importance evidence and reporting inconsistencies, including Table 9's caption conflicting with the domain-sufficiency interpretation in Section 3.3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions and removals to be distinguished from relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds preference-training experiments, cross-model refusal-ablation tests, geometric controls, and downstream evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original concept-injection experiments, causal interventions on model components, feature analyses, and learned-vector training results.

title: Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a simple seven-prompt baseline, strong scaling performance, diversity collapse in RL-based augmentation, and the competitiveness of carefully designed single-stage prompting.

This adds a substantial analysis of potential costs beyond target-task effectiveness. Existing prompt ablations, diversity analyses, framework comparisons and generation examples are retained.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix C specifies diversity-sampling seed 42; v2 Appendix C.4 states only that a fixed seed is used. This removes specific seed information without establishing a changed seed. No new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests accompany the added results.

title: Visually-Guided Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning

C2.justification: The explanation of optimisation benefits shifts from disappearing barriers and connected manifolds to perturbative instability and changes in which fixed-point families attract trajectories. The stability appendix now describes escape toward lower-loss configurations rather than a global-minimum manifold. A sharper global geometric description becomes future work, and the direction-dependent connectivity discussion is removed.

title: Doc-V^*: Coarse-to-Fine Interactive Visual Reasoning for Multi-Page Document VQA

C1.justification: V1's abstract broadly states that offline CoT does not fundamentally increase expressiveness. V2 limits this claim to the communication lower-bound pipeline and explicitly confines the depth barrier to canonical explicit-table composition, including in the introduction and conclusion. These materially narrow the headline claims, while retaining the principal quantitative lower bound and research themes.

C2.justification: V2 explains that transferring the lower bound requires resource-preserving and stream-order-preserving reductions, and distinguishes generalized constructions from realizable S4/Mamba implementations. It adds limitations concerning vector-valued thought tokens, scan parallelism and computational cost. Section 8 also replaces v1's suggested preference for moderate width and standard precision with an explicit statement that the theory cannot rank practical performance.

D1.justification: No software or data access, hardware, hyperparameters or experimental implementation details are added. The canonical encoding and explicit SSM construction details relocated to the appendices were already supplied in v1; the two-step simulator was also already documented.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical evaluation scenarios. Function composition and pointer chasing remain theoretical problem families; making the existing canonical encoding explicit does not add evaluated task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods. S4, Mamba and transformer research appear as related work, not experimentally tested baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, metrics, training budgets or testing procedures. The revised streaming-memory accounting concerns theoretical guarantees.

E4.justification: Neither contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity studies or error analyses. V2's recommendation to study width and precision as separate ablation axes is prospective.

E5.justification: Neither reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical tests. The retained error-probability threshold of 1/3 is a theoretical guarantee.

E6.justification: No empirical numerical or qualitative results are added, removed or revised. V2's new figures are explanatory schematics; changes to formal resource bounds are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Corollary 2 changes the streaming algorithm from updating its lookup pointer immediately within a table to freezing the incoming pointer and committing the next pointer after the table ends. This is a localized algorithmic correction; the generalized SSM recurrence and two-step CoT simulator remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 moves lengthy proofs from Sections 4-7 into Appendices A-D and introduces main-text proof sketches and roadmaps. It also rewrites the abstract, expands the discussion and adopts the more explicit post-input/input-interleaved terminology. This substantially reorganizes the exposition.

P2.justification: V1 has no figures or tables. V2 introduces three explanatory diagrams covering forward communication, the gate-and-accumulate construction and CoT token timing, plus a boxed practitioner summary. These substantially expand the visual presentation of the central arguments.

R1.justification: The reference list is unchanged. Section 2 nevertheless refines the relationship to existing architectures: v1 describes an abstraction covering all known SSM architectures, whereas v2 presents a common upper-level lower-bound model that abstracts away architecture-specific parameterizations and constraints.

T1.justification: Theorem 4(A) replaces O(dpL + log n) memory with O(dpL + log T_n), where the newly defined T_n includes thought tokens and need not be polynomial in n. This correction propagates through Proposition 2, Corollary 4 and Appendices C-D. Corollary 2 repairs its correctness argument by freezing each table's lookup pointer. Definition 2 and Theorem 1 also make the canonical encoding explicit. These substantively revise central resource guarantees and proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs important weaknesses in the online-CoT analysis: Theorem 4 counts all processed steps in its memory bound, and Corollary 2 prevents unintended repeated lookups within one function table. Its narrower claims and explicit implementation limitations also reduce overgeneralization. Together with clearer diagrams and proof sketches while retaining detailed proofs, these changes substantially improve correctness and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same theoretical study and are readable throughout. V2's Appendices A-D largely relocate proofs from v1's main text, allowing comparison of the complete arguments.

after.justification: V2 and Appendices A-D remain theoretical. Its figures illustrate constructions, and Section 8 suggests future experiments without reporting original empirical outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports mathematical bounds, constructive simulations and algebraic proofs. Empirical findings are attributed to prior work; no original experimental or data-analysis outcomes are reported.

title: On the Expressive Power and Limitations of Multi-Layer SSMs

E3.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C retain identical sample sizes, preprocessing, architectures, losses, optimizer settings, and curvature-measurement procedures. No new evaluation protocol or revised experimental setting is reported.

E4.justification: The catapult, smoothing-parameter, and mini-batch analyses in Section 5.4 are unchanged. Appendix D retains the same ZO-Adam momentum sweep and empirical commutativity check.

E5.justification: Run information, statistical estimation procedures, and uncertainty reporting are unchanged. The plotted stability bands remain theoretical bounds; no seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Figures 1–13 and their reported findings are unchanged. This includes the EoS trajectories and the relative commutator decrease from 0.8–0.9 to below 0.05 reported in Appendix D.3.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the references retain the same cited works and positioning relative to earlier ZO optimization, EoS, and stability research.

improvement.justification: v2 updates publication metadata and modestly reflows the main text while preserving the scientific arguments, results, proofs, and reproducibility details. These presentation changes establish no meaningful net improvement or deterioration in overall paper quality.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and their results in Section 5 and Appendix D, including CNN, ResNet, ViT, LSTM, and Mamba training.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-network training experiments on CIFAR-10 and synthetic sequence sorting, including loss trajectories, Hessian curvature measurements, and sensitivity analyses in Section 5 and Appendix D.

R1.justification: Section 2, Appendix C, and the reference list are identical. No cited works or positioning relative to earlier detection and contrastive-learning approaches are added, removed, or revised.

improvement.justification: The revision changes affiliation information and its presentation but leaves the methods, empirical evidence, interpretations, limitations, and reproducibility information unchanged, including all appendices. title: DETR-ViP: Detection Transformer with Robust Discriminative Visual Prompts

Adding HumanoidBench to the supporting experiment list does not redefine that claim.

The new impact statement discusses prospective robotics benefits. The existing limitation that strong performance requires two sampling steps remains.

Existing ablations and hyperparameter analyses are retained under new numbering.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two, with substantially different typography, headers and placement of displays. v2 adds four figures and a component-results table, expands comparator legends and table columns, and renumbers appendix displays continuously. Some new captions contain incorrect panel references, notably Figures 8–9.

These rely on accurate likelihood estimation, sufficiently expressive function classes and an infinite-sample limit for velocity estimation. The earlier derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central claims: Table 3 quantifies component costs, Figure 6 tests likelihood accuracy on a control task beyond v1's toy visualization, and broader baselines plus HumanoidBench and AntMaze probe performance and multimodal exploration. before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracies, prototype-editing experiments, concept-intervention curves, and a prototype-count analysis.

title: Prototype-Grounded Concept Models for Verifiable Concept Alignment

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion redefine the architectural failure mode as high-frequency aliasing, contrasted with statistical damping, rather than primarily compression-induced information loss. They also narrow broad claims of avoiding compression to processing spatial interactions before coarsening and emphasize mesh alignment. Forecast skill, calibration and speed claims remain.

C2.justification: RQ2 and new Appendix C.10 attribute excess spectral power to aliasing and explain delayed onset through fine-scale information stored in feature channels by learnable interpolation. Appendix A reinterprets the unchanged compression penalty as spurious high-frequency energy rather than simply lost detail. Existing resolution and extreme-event limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a MOSAIC code URL in the abstract; v1's availability statement identified only the public training and evaluation data. The detailed architecture, hyperparameters, software stack, hardware and training schedule in Appendix C are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Both versions retain ERA5 and HRES-fc0, the same weather variables and benchmark coverage, and the Hurricane Ian case study. Revised spectral sample counts and forecast horizons operate within existing coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 2(a) adds the existing compressed variant, now named MOSAIC-C, to the spectral comparison and removes ArchesWeatherGen's ensemble-mean spectrum. AW-Gen is the retained ArchesWeatherGen method under an abbreviated label. Forecasting benchmark comparator sets are unchanged.

E3.justification: The central spectral evaluation is substantially redesigned: Figure 2(a) changes from a single 10-day forecast to 24-hour spectra aggregated over 720 initial conditions and 16 members for probabilistic models. Figure 2(b)'s stated horizon changes from 10 days to 6 hours; this establishes a reported setting revision, not necessarily rerunning. Main benchmark training and evaluation protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 extends the existing spatial-compression ablation with a spectral comparison testing whether compression produces excess power near the Nyquist limit. Table 2's ablation results, the Hurricane Ian analysis, mass-conservation study and other supplementary analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Spectral reporting changes from single-forecast examples to explicitly aggregated estimates over initial conditions and stochastic ensemble members. This adds a statistical aggregation practice, but no independent training-seed replication, confidence intervals or significance tests. Appendix B.4's existing mean and standard-deviation reporting is unchanged.

E6.justification: Under the revised spectral settings, RQ2 replaces MOSAIC's ratio of 1.00 with 0.97 and ArchesGen's 1.03 with 0.96, and adds MOSAIC-C's 1.02 near Nyquist. These are different-condition results, not same-setting performance changes. Forecasting, ablation, conservation and runtime table values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The HEALPix U-Net, block-sparse attention, learned perturbations, CRPS objective and inference procedure remain unchanged. MOSAIC-C corresponds to the N_side=32 compression variant already evaluated in v1 Table 2(g). Describing native-resolution processing before coarsening clarifies the existing architecture.

P1.justification: Focused rewrites affect the abstract, introduction, spectral discussion and conclusion, alongside new Sections 2.3 and C.10 and scattered copyediting. The Impact Statement and Acknowledgements switch order, but the overall method, experiment and appendix organization is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with revised curves and legends, changed spectral axes, a high-frequency inset, corrected wavelength labeling and speed-comparison annotations. Its caption is expanded. Other figures and tables retain their displays apart from reflow and relocation.

R1.justification: New Section 2.3 introduces aliasing research, while Section 2.4 acknowledges BLADE, LongCat-Video and ProxyAttn as closely related concurrent attention approaches. MOSAIC is distinguished through HEALPix NESTED indexing for spherical data. These additions substantively revise both the mechanism's research context and the attention contribution's novelty positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, attention equations, loss definitions and complexity expressions are unchanged. Appendix C.10 adds a qualitative Nyquist and aliasing explanation using the existing HEALPix pixel-count formula, without a new formal derivation, theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens spectral evidence through year-wide aggregation and the compressed-model comparison, clarifies the unchanged U-Net's operation, acknowledges close prior work and provides a code pointer. These are useful but limited gains. The revised Figure 2 uses shorter forecast horizons, although Figure 14 retains 10-day examples, and the observed spectral overshoot does not by itself establish the stronger causal aliasing explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MOSAIC research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and reports revised spectral comparisons, including spectra for the compressed MOSAIC-C variant.

before.justification: v1 reports original MOSAIC forecasting results, spectral analyses, architectural ablations, Hurricane Ian forecasts, mass-conservation measurements and runtime benchmarks.

title: (Sparse) Attention to the Details: Preserving Spectral Fidelity in ML-based Weather Forecasting Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about geometric verification, diagnosis, adaptive inference and alignment. The added experiments support existing generality claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly emphasizes domain-specific dissimilarity design, and Appendix A qualifies the theory's applicability to deployed models. Added passages interpret programming and architecture results as generalization evidence, and low score-confidence correlations as evidence of distinct dynamics. Stronger guarantee language elsewhere remains unchanged.

D1.justification: The additions identify code-scoring ingredients and the extra model checkpoints with their total/active parameter configurations. This provides limited new technical information. Appendix C remains unchanged, and the code experiments lack details such as the backbone, AST construction and score aggregation.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual evaluations on HumanEval and MBPP in Appendix D.3. This substantially extends coverage from mathematical and scientific question answering to open-ended program generation, while retaining GSM8K, MATH, ARC-C and GPQA.

E2.justification: Table 8 extends the existing error-diagnosis comparator set—Model Confidence, Self-Consistency and Self-Evaluation—to programming tasks. Existing comparisons retain their methods. Table 9 evaluates BMC on additional backbones rather than introducing competing verification methods.

E3.justification: Appendix D.4 adds GSM8K evaluations with LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B-Instruct, using 1B active parameters, and the 16B dense LLaDA2.1-mini. Appendix D.4 also tests consistency across model architectures and scales. Existing component ablations, sensitivity studies, geometric validation and qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports Spearman correlations with p-values and a chi-square test in Appendix E.1. Table 10 extends the existing correlation/significance reporting practice to another relationship. Neither version adds or revises repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 1–7 retain their results, but Tables 8–10 substantially extend the evidence with programming-task discrimination, additional-backbone performance and score-confidence associations. New BMC AUROCs are 0.687 on HumanEval, 0.662 on MBPP, and 0.858/0.853 on GSM8K with the two added backbones. Table 10 reports correlations ranging from 0.079 to 0.301. These are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v1. On MBPP, BMC AUPR is 0.668 versus Self-Consistency's 0.669.

M1.justification: Appendix D.3 introduces a code-specific BMC instantiation using AST Jaccard similarity and token-substitution rates without terminal-answer tokens. This changes the verification scoring for programming tasks; the original six-component estimator, reconstruction procedure, rejection sampling and alignment objective remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 adds a short methodological clarification, a theory qualification, two appendix subsections and a correlation-analysis paragraph. Affiliations, publication information, the appendix contents and one reference title are updated. Most prose and the overall organization are retained.

P2.justification: Three appendix tables are added for programming results, model architectures and correlations. Caption formatting, spacing and page flow change, including relocation of later qualitative figures. All seven original figures and their substantive visual content are retained.

R1.justification: The cited-work set and related-work positioning remain unchanged. The title of Tsui's Self-Correction Bench reference is corrected, but its author, year and arXiv identifier establish that it is the same cited work.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, propositions, assumptions, equations and proofs are retained. Appendix A adds a note describing the propositions as conditional motivation rather than deployment guarantees, but does not revise their mathematical statements or derivations.

improvement.justification: The added programming and architecture evaluations broaden empirical support, while the Appendix A note better qualifies the theory. The gains are limited by sparse code-experiment documentation and overstated interpretations: Table 8 does not support consistent superiority on MBPP AUPR, and Table 10's low correlations do not establish entirely distinct mechanisms. Stronger theoretical-guarantee language also remains elsewhere. These additions provide a modest net improvement without resolving the central limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BMC research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A–E are readable and support comparison, including matching content across pagination changes.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds programming-task evaluations, additional model evaluations and score-correlation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, supervised baseline experiments and human performance measurements, including results in Tables 3–7 and appendix Tables 10, 12 and 13.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about diffusion-based structural elucidation, scalable pretraining, targeted inference-time refinement, benchmark performance, and inference speed. T1.justification: The conditional-generation formulation, diffusion objective, atom-consistency scoring, and masking definitions in Equations 1-6 are unchanged. No mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised.

The PDFs do not explain whether the specification revisions correct earlier reporting or describe changed runs. This unresolved inconsistency in the scaling evidence prevents a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FRIGID research work. All 22 pages of each version, including Appendices A-C, figures, tables, and equations, are available and support a complete comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results in Section 5 and Appendices A-C, including benchmark performance and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original FRIGID experiments on NPLIB1 and MassSpecGym, computational measurements, scaling studies, ablations, robustness analyses, and prediction examples.

title: FRIGID: Scaling Diffusion-Based Molecular Generation from Mass Spectra at Training and Inference Time

C1.justification: The central lightweight noise-based fairness–utility contribution remains. The abstract and contribution bullets shift emphasis from dual-level debiasing and disentanglement toward fair classification supported by empirical leakage reduction. The conclusion qualifies complete disentanglement and the reliability of reusing task embeddings for other downstream tasks.

C2.justification: V2 explains residual sensitive information in the task branch, leakage recovery through averaging, and the interaction between batch size, imbalance and utility. Its conclusion adds substantive limitations concerning sensitive-label availability, stochastic predictions, representation reuse and incomplete disentanglement. Broader-impact discussion also distinguishes benchmark disparities from deployment fairness under distribution shift or unmodeled intersectional groups.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds baseline-specific tuning details for FairVPT, FairViT, FSCL and FairNet and revises the documented search grids. Appendix E newly describes micro-batch gradient accumulation and its limitation for fairness-loss estimation. Architecture dimensions, hardware, parameter counts and runtime disclosures remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same CelebA attribute pairs, UTKFace gender/age classification and BIOS profession/gender task, including the appendix benchmarks and gender-swapped biographies. New experiments vary training, representations and attacker procedures within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds FairNet to the image comparisons in Table 1 and appendix Table 13. The existing quantitative image and text comparators remain. FairVPT is removed from the saliency comparisons in v2 Figures 3 and 5, although it remains in the numerical comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation across hyperparameter configurations, attacks on individual branches and averaged noisy embeddings, batch-size variation, and fixed-checkpoint inference repeats. Appendix C changes learning-rate search spacing from half-orders to full orders of magnitude, clipping thresholds from {1,10,100} to {1,10}, and loss weights from {0,0.1,0.3,0.5,1,3} to {0.1,0.3,0.5,1}. These are reported protocol changes; they do not establish which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds Pareto analyses, staged adapter/loss ablations, branch-specific leakage and repeated-observation attacks, batch-size sensitivity, and isolated inference variability. Earlier noise-strength and deeper-attacker analyses are retained with revisions. The pure-noise-plus-task control and majority-vote inference study are removed, while the Big Nose/Age factorial ablation is replaced by staged comparisons.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run means and standard deviations for the main benchmarks. V2 adds three inference-only repetitions at a fixed checkpoint and explains the sources of main-result variability. It also explicitly labels several appendix ablations as single-run, same-seed results and removes uncertainty estimates from retained noise-strength, classifier-input and deeper-attacker comparisons.

E6.justification: Numerous Table 1 values and rankings change: FairNVT's Big Nose/Age Acc/DP/EO entries change from 82.1/10.9/1.9 to 83.4/22.9/11.1. The revised objective and search settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. New Table 3 reports Expression/Gender attacker accuracy of 52.1% with one observation versus 92.5% after averaging 50 perturbations. Cross-method attacker scores are removed from image and BIOS benchmark tables; BIOS accuracy/DP and existing supplementary image scores are otherwise retained.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the orthogonality objective from squared cosine similarity alone to cosine similarity plus HSIC between task embeddings and sensitive labels. This adds a direct statistical-dependence penalty to the task branch, materially changing its optimization. The dual adapters, Gaussian perturbation, concatenation and primary inference procedure remain.

P1.justification: Substantial paragraph rewrites span the abstract, introduction, preliminaries, framework explanations, results narrative and conclusion. Results are reorganized around Pareto trade-offs and representation-specific analysis, noise sensitivity moves into Appendix E, and limitations and broader-impact discussion are added. These changes exceed the accompanying title and publication-header edits.

P2.justification: V2 adds multi-panel Pareto figures, substantially restructures component and attacker tables, and introduces batch-size and inference-variability tables. Saliency grids are rearranged with FairVPT panels removed, benchmark tables lose attacker columns and gain FairNet rows, and the earlier majority-vote diagram disappears. Section 3.2 defines the added HSIC objective mathematically.

improvement.justification: V2 corrects a central mathematical error in Appendix B and substantially improves assessment of the method through Pareto comparisons, branch-specific leakage tests and explicit failure conditions. These changes make the fairness claims better bounded and supported. Removing comparative attacker scores, the pure-noise control and several uncertainty estimates weakens some evidence, and inconsistencies remain, such as approximately 80% task-embedding attacker accuracy in the prose versus 68.3% in Table 3. Nevertheless, the corrected reasoning and stronger examination of trade-offs and limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FairNVT, with matching authors, framework and benchmark tasks despite the revised title. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–E are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and ablation results, including additional Pareto analyses, representation-specific attacks, batch-size experiments and inference-variability measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original FairNVT experiments on CelebA, UTKFace and BIOS, including benchmark comparisons, component ablations, attacker evaluations and qualitative examples.

title: FairNVT: Fair Classification via Noise Injection in Vision Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about cognitive heterogeneity, human-like behavioral biases, agent stability, and the benefits of information sharing.

C2.justification: The interpretations involving myopia, self-interest, and system-level coordination are unchanged. The limitations concerning opaque model training, strategic adaptation, and generalization beyond the canonical game are also retained.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows compactness superiority from existing methods generally to basic event- and notation-based tokenizations, and replaces human-like variation with balanced variation tied to specific evidence. The conclusion removes the claim of unifying previously incompatible advantages. The abstract and central musical-quality and controllability contributions remain.

C2.justification: New Section 6 specifies limits involving unquantized performance MIDI, vocabulary growth, velocity detail, and pitch-encoding generality. Appendix A recasts relative pitch encoding as optional, treats ascending and descending orders as largely interchangeable, and explains larger temporal steps through sparse training of rare patterns. New analyses also support interpretations about encoding-specific gains, generalization, and near-lossless velocity averaging.

D1.justification: v2 adds source-code access instructions, dense-baseline implementation details, explicit absolute pitch encoding for synthetic diagnostics, fuller synthetic-data construction, and clarification of the 24 scales used for SC. It revises reported training resources. Conversely, it removes decoder Algorithm 3, the exact processed-dataset statistics table, and the MuseScore collection-method link. These substantially alter reproducibility documentation without establishing corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds POP909 as an unseen dataset for piano continuation, retaining the existing LMD/MuseScore coverage. The synthetic transposition task also changes its stated requirement from one semitone per bar to one semitone per beat in Section 5.2 and Appendix J.1. These are limited extensions within the existing music tasks.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds an evaluated Naive Piano-Roll comparator. Table 3 expands the compactness comparison to CPW, AMT, and Naive Piano-Roll, although CPW and AMT already appeared in other experiments. The previous continuation and accompaniment comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix D changes the reported training budget from 30 epochs and approximately 240 GPU-hours to 50 epochs and approximately 400 GPU-hours. The transposition diagnostic is also revised from barwise to beatwise shifts. These materially change the stated experimental settings; retained numerical results do not establish whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds three substantive checks absent from v1: a dense-grid control testing the importance of sparse encoding, an out-of-distribution POP909 evaluation, and a training-data analysis quantifying information lost through velocity averaging. These extend the evidence on mechanism, generalization, and representation fidelity beyond the existing ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the listening-study standard errors, within-subject ANOVA, pairwise tests, and Holm-Bonferroni correction. No new seed counts, confidence intervals, or uncertainty procedures accompany the added benchmark results. Appendix B.2's velocity standard deviation describes within-pattern variation, not uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: New results include Naive Piano-Roll scores of 0.051/0.106/582.3 in Table 2 and POP909 FMD of 365.9 for BEAT versus 401.1–512.6 for comparators in Table 9. Table 3 adds CPW's 1215.3 compound steps, AMT's 1950.6 tokens, and Naive Piano-Roll's 29340.9 tokens. Appendix B.2 reports exact velocity preservation for 99.5% of active patterns. Appendix A.2 adds an unquantified observation favoring absolute pitches with limited data. Existing numerical entries and main result plots are retained.

M1.justification: The sparse pattern encoding, default relative pitches, mean velocities, and Transformer objective remain. However, Section 3.1 replaces fixed-grid slicing with time-signature-defined beats resampled to τ steps, while Algorithms 1–2 retain the earlier slicing procedure. The PDFs do not resolve whether this reflects an underlying method change or a revised description.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized rewrites to the framework explanation, diagnostic motivation, ablation discussion, and conclusion; adds limitations and background sections; and updates affiliations and publication information. Existing appendices are renumbered around additions. The overall narrative and most existing prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Tables 2–3 gain rows, a POP909 table is added, and the dataset-count table and decoding algorithm display are removed. Figures 6–8 use replacement score illustrations, Figure 3 gains a more explanatory caption, and several displays move. The main plots, visual style, and overall layout remain largely unchanged.

R1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.3 add discussion of MusicVAE, Measure by Measure, Music Transformer, and streaming audio accompaniment. New Appendix K expands background with MidiNet, MuseGAN, and MidiTok, and POP909 gains a dataset citation. This broadens context while retaining the central positioning around sparse grid tokenization for autoregressive models.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix B revise the formal setup: N is no longer defined there as ceil(T/τ), and τ specifies resampled slots within musically defined beats. The earlier relation nevertheless remains in the pseudocode. Base-3 encoding, pitch-offset equations, and complexity statements are retained; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: The grid control, POP909 evaluation, and velocity-error measurements address specific evidence gaps in v1, while explicit limitations and narrower claims improve interpretation. The gain is limited by unresolved discrepancies between revised method prose and retained pseudocode, unchanged scores despite revised training/task descriptions, and removal of standalone decoding and exact dataset documentation. Overall, v2 provides useful additional support and qualification without resolving all reproducibility ambiguities.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BEAT research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, algorithms, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite additions, removals, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Naive Piano-Roll comparisons, POP909 evaluation, and measurements of velocity-averaging error.

before.justification: v1 reports original continuation experiments, listening studies, structural-pattern diagnostics, and ablations in Sections 4–5 and Appendix A.
