before.justification: v1 reports original FlowBot benchmark evaluations, an AFlow reimplementation, component and model ablations, and a unified-workflow experiment. Appendix B provides an execution and optimization example.

title: FlowBot: Inducing LLM Workflows with Bilevel Optimization and Textual Gradients

C1.justification: The central local-sufficiency and teacher-free selection contributions remain intact. The abstract and conclusion narrow the previously broad 24.1% improvement statement to a relative gain on the 1.5B model's Math Avg. score, making the headline claim more precisely scoped.

C2.justification: v2 replaces broad trigger-invariance language with a distinction between robust candidate coverage and trigger-dependent downstream accuracy. It adds interpretations of regularization tradeoffs, dynamic candidate-sizing failures, and benign versus harmful selector disagreements. It also qualifies DistilQwen2.5 as an off-the-shelf reference rather than a controlled training comparison.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access URL, baseline reproduction notes, fixed scoring anchors, an explicit regularization default, reserved-token compatibility guidance, and percentile calibration details for inference budgets. It clarifies that selector-training temperature differs from decoding temperature. However, v1's two-epoch selector-training statement and exact trigger-dataset counts are removed.

E1.justification: Appendix F.2 and Table A5 add actual evaluations on TruthfulQA, ARC-Challenge, and MT-Bench, extending coverage to factuality, science question answering, and open-ended instruction following. The MATH-only training domain and original six evaluation benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains its comparator set, including DistilQwen2.5, TSD-KD, Maj@8, Mul-T, TaH, R2R, SpecReason, and Takeover. New appendix comparisons add dynamic candidate-sizing alternatives against fixed K and fine-tuned greedy decoding as a control for selector gains. The expanded baseline descriptions do not establish changes to the existing methods.

E3.justification: New experimental settings include Llama and Phi student–teacher pairings, MT-Bench judge scoring, parameter sweeps, and a 900-case agreement-based analysis. For existing experiments, the reported Qwen0.5B reserved-bin count changes from 16 to 12, and selector LoRA dropout changes from 0.1 to 0.05. These are reported setting revisions; unchanged Table 1 scores do not establish whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds reserved-bin and regularization sweeps, dynamic-versus-fixed candidate sizing, trigger-coverage sensitivity analyses, and a selector-disagreement study relating errors to final correctness. These investigate training stability, candidate coverage, and failure mechanisms beyond v1's retained ablations and trajectory examples.

E5.justification: Both versions already state averaging over three random seeds. v2 newly reports mean ± standard deviation for Greedy and S2T-LOCAL across both Qwen scales and all six main benchmarks in Table A6. Appendix F.6 also adds a correlation significance result for selector disagreements. No increase in run count is established.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results, while v2 adds substantial domain, model, sensitivity, and error-analysis results. For example, new Table A8 reports Llama MATH500 accuracy of 27.8 for Greedy and 34.6 for S2T-LOCAL. Existing numerical corrections include the stated 0.5B math gain from 38% to 44.6%, MATH500 teacher entropy from 0.7 to 0.07, and appendix latency reduction from 75.8% to 74.8%.

M1.justification: The core inference algorithm, reserved-token selector, and training losses remain unchanged. Appendix D.1 newly proposes an auxiliary ranking head parallel to the language-model head for models without reusable reserved tokens. This is an optional architectural adaptation; its evaluation is not reported.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract and selected results passages, reorganizes training details, swaps the evaluation and related-work appendices, and reorders supplementary analyses. It also updates affiliations and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: The appendix gains nine tables covering sensitivity, new evaluations, uncertainty, and trigger diagnostics, substantially expanding the visual presentation. Existing tables are retained and renumbered, while figures are redistributed and several captions revised. The principal diagrams and plotted results remain visually stable.

R1.justification: Appendix B.1 expands the distinction between S2T and speculative decoding, and references are added for TruthfulQA, ARC, Llama, and Phi. The overall research positioning remains stable. TSD-KD's author attribution and numerous publication updates refer to existing works rather than new comparison methods.

T1.justification: Section 5.1 newly specifies the scoring-bin anchors mathematically as v_i = (i − 1)/(|R| − 1), where v1 only described predefined bin values. This is a limited formal specification addition. The error decomposition, proposition, and numbered equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the retained contribution: full S2T-LOCAL evaluation extends beyond Qwen, uncertainty is quantified for the main comparisons, and new sensitivity and error analyses expose when selection succeeds or fails. More precise claims and implementation disclosures address important weaknesses in v1. Reporting gaps remain, including unexplained Llama MMLU-Pro greedy scores of 19.5 in Table A7 versus 16.5 in Table A8 and some removed training details, but these do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same S2T and S2T-LOCAL research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–F support comparison; relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds non-math evaluations, non-Qwen experiments, hyperparameter sweeps, uncertainty estimates, and selector-error analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracies, selector-alignment measurements, latency results, and ablations in Tables 1–3 and Appendix F.

title: Select to Think: Unlocking SLM Potential with Local Sufficiency

C1.justification: v3 qualifies the performance claims: the introduction changes surpassing baselines to matching or surpassing them, and Figure 1 drops its blanket state-of-the-art assertion. The deterministic-control contribution, unification of existing methods and up-to-70-fold efficiency claim remain.

C2.justification: Section 3 adds a substantive explanation of transporting endpoint gradients back to the current time, how prior renoising procedures affect the guidance gain, and why FMRG-E tunes that gain without reprojection. Existing interpretations of reward hacking, early stopping and Jacobian guidance, and the stated limitations, remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies explicit code and pretrained-checkpoint access locations and distinguishes checkpoint ranks and distillation resolutions by experiment. The earlier alpha=16 specification disappears. Most task hyperparameters, hardware measurements and implementation instructions were already present in Appendix E.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate AFHQ-Dog and FFHQ inverse problems, style transfer, GenEval, aesthetic rewards and VLM-guided generation, including prompt-free inverse problems. Revised qualitative prompts remain within the existing generation tasks.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator sets remain unchanged, including DPS, FlowChef and FlowDPS for inverse problems/style transfer, and FLUX, unguided flow maps, best-of-N, ReNO and FMTT for generation. Adding DPS to the conceptual method-summary table does not introduce a new experimental baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix E.1 replaces the reported rank-16, alpha-16 adapter with rank-32 at 256 resolution and rank-64 at 512 resolution. Table E.22 changes best-of-N from N=8/400 NFEs to N=32/128 NFEs, matching the main benchmark configuration already described in v1. Qualitative NFE labels also change. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Figures 12, E.20 and E.21 revise and extend qualitative comparisons of aesthetic enhancement at low compute budgets, including additional FMRG-versus-ReNO examples. The early-stopping ablations, prompt-removal robustness analyses and Gaussian guidance analyses are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions specify four GenEval seeds with samples aggregated before calculating category accuracies. Neither adds confidence intervals, significance tests or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 9, 13 and E.15 retain their scores, but Figure 14 adds or revises low-budget points and omits the high-budget ReNO point. Aesthetic outputs and NFE labels change, including 6/10/14 to 5/9/13 in Figures E.20–E.21. Table E.22 replaces best-of-N's 41.0-second result with 13.1 seconds under a different configuration, not a same-setting speedup. Section 5.5 corrects the GenEval advantage from 3.5 to 3.4 points.

M1.justification: The control objective, FMRG-J/E updates, operator splitting, endpoint reuse, early stopping, warmup selection and VLM renoising procedure are retained. The expanded gradient explanation and revised checkpoint specifications do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Localized revisions tighten the abstract and introduction, reorganize contribution wording, expand the gradient-options discussion and update related work. The main section sequence and most theoretical and experimental prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Appendix E is extensively rearranged to group task-specific figures and tables with their corresponding discussions. Numerous displays are resized or relocated. The method-summary table moves and gains a DPS row; Figure 14 changes from logarithmic to linear NFE scaling; aesthetic grids are expanded and rearranged. These constitute substantial visual reorganization despite largely retained scientific content.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds Feng et al.'s On the Guidance of Flow Matching and distinguishes its posterior-variance approximation from FMRG's deterministic formulation. It also adds Variational Flow Maps and discusses its auxiliary noise-adapter training. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The central propositions, assumptions and proofs remain unchanged. A limited mathematical-summary edit changes MPGD's weight from t_+ c_t in v1 Table 4 to t_+ in v3 Table 8, while Appendix D.4–D.5 still gives t_+ c_t. This creates an unreconciled discrepancy rather than a new derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 improves reproducibility information through code/checkpoint locations and more specific checkpoint descriptions, and aligns the best-of-N timing row with the documented main evaluation. Added mechanism and related-work explanations improve clarity. These gains outweigh limited drawbacks, including the inconsistent MPGD summary weight and omission of the high-budget ReNO plot point. The unchanged core proofs and principal benchmark tables limit the overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FMRG work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–E. Content can be matched despite substantial relocation of appendix displays.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and reports revised quantitative plots and qualitative generation examples.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original inverse-problem, style-transfer, GenEval and VLM-guided generation experiments, including quantitative comparisons and ablations.

title: How to Guide Your Flow: Few-Step Alignment via Flow Map Reward Guidance

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution paragraph, and conclusion are unchanged in substance and wording. They retain the same claims about the cost-sensitive reformulation, margin guarantees, MILD, and empirical benefits.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of margin-driven expert selection, distinguishes controlled vision imbalance from natural MMLU imbalance, and attributes robustness to margin buffering. It also asserts negligible offline estimation cost, identical scaling across expert sizes, and that the ablation proves the theoretical bound drives success. These extend interpretation beyond v1, sometimes beyond the demonstrated evidence.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses 4,000 MMLU router-training queries, revises the vision model specification, and supplies settings for the added margin and noise experiments. The training count is additional documentation, not evidence of increased training data. Baseline adaptations, the precise noise construction, and extreme-scenario cost values remain incompletely specified.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, Tiny ImageNet, and the same mathematics/history MMLU coverage. Section 6.2 extends MMLU evaluation to imperfect cost estimates and a cost-induced 95%/5% expert-imbalance scenario, without adding datasets or domains.

E2.justification: The MMLU comparison expands substantially beyond TDEF to Standard CE, Class-Weighted CE, and LDAM. Section 6.1 reports their error-plus-cost losses as 0.985, 0.942, and 0.915, respectively, against MILD's 0.813. These are evaluated alternatives, whereas v1 only discussed alternative approaches.

E3.justification: Section 6 revises the stated vision predictor from ResNet-16 to ResNet-18, without saying experiments were rerun. New analyses introduce uniform/theoretical/tuned margin controls, 20% Gaussian cost-matrix perturbations, and skewed inference costs. Existing metrics, training budgets, and documented test-set size remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 6.2 tests whether theoretical margin initialization helps independently of tuning, whether noisy cost estimates degrade routing, and whether minority routing survives extreme MMLU imbalance. These substantially extend the earlier analyses; Appendix C.3's severe image-expert imbalance experiment and C.4's tuning discussion are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and standard deviations over five runs and omit standard deviations for deferral ratios. New results follow the existing reporting practice. No additional seed information, uncertainty-estimation procedure, or significance test is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results, but Sections 6.1–6.2 add substantial findings. Uniform/theoretical/tuned margins yield losses of 0.884/0.822/0.813; noisy-cost losses are 0.826 for MILD versus 1.054 for TDEF; extreme-imbalance losses are 0.885 versus 0.950. Additional CE, CWCE, and LDAM results broaden the comparative evidence.

M1.justification: The cost-sensitive reformulation, margin-dependent surrogate, theoretically guided margin selection, and MILD routing procedure remain unchanged. The restored sample summation in Section 5.3 agrees with the empirical expectation already stated in v1; it does not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: v2 adds an intuitive explanation and Section 6.2, moves and expands the standard cost-sensitive discussion from Appendix D, and makes localized grammatical and heading corrections. It also corrects Appendix H's theorem reference. The overall narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 and all four tables are retained. Table 3 moves from page 8 to page 9; Tables 1–2 reposition subtable labels and refine captions, while equations and surrounding text reflow. The new experimental findings appear in prose rather than new figures or tables.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds recent work on online, expert-conditioned, and nonstationary deferral, alongside additional consistency and balanced-classification references, while dropping the multitask example and replacing the cited robustness work. Section 6.2 expands positioning against LDAM and temperature scaling. Numerous other reference edits merely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: Section 5.3 restores the missing sum over training examples in the displayed objective. Appendix G corrects an equality to an inequality when replacing a maximum of exponentials with their sum. These are local mathematical corrections; the principal assumptions, theorem statements, and remaining proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: The added baseline comparisons and controlled analyses strengthen empirical support, and the objective and Appendix G corrections improve mathematical clarity. The gain is limited by incomplete specifications for the new experiments and overstrong causal and scaling interpretations. Overall, v2 provides more useful evidence without substantially resolving these documentation and interpretation weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MILD study. Their text, equations, Figure 1, Tables 1–4, and Appendices A–I are readable and support reliable comparison despite pagination changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds numerical comparisons with additional routing baselines, a margin-selection ablation, and robustness experiments in Sections 6.1–6.2.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification and MMLU routing experiments in Tables 1–3, plus severe expert-imbalance experiments in Appendix C.3 and Table 4.

title: Optimized Deferral for Imbalanced Settings

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion newly emphasize superiority over DPO and SimPO across datasets and architectures, plus the 58.5% downstream generation win rate. The central contributions concerning inconsistency, margin shifts, SA-DPO, and the loss-tail hierarchy remain the same.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 newly acknowledges that its equicontinuity condition is weaker and non-standard relative to uniform equicontinuity. Sections 6.1 and 7.3 add interpretations linking margin satisfaction to reduced capacity penalties and generation performance to prevention of hallucinated conversational artifacts. These interpretations were absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendix M adds Qwen settings: LoRA rank/alpha 32, 1,000 steps, batch size 16, learning rate 5×10^-5, and the 200-prompt PairRM evaluation. Conversely, Section 7.3 removes the explicit UltraFeedback median-distance cutoff of 0.1565 while retaining the median-split rule; this is reduced disclosure, not evidence of a changed split.

E1.justification: v2 adds Argilla DPO-Mix-7k preference evaluation and open-ended conversational generation using MT-Bench-style prompts. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained synonym, HH-RLHF, and UltraFeedback experiments by evaluating generated responses as well as preference ranking.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the retained experiments: DPO versus SA-DPO for synonyms, DPO/IPO/Poly-3 for capacity analysis, and DPO/SimPO/SA-DPO for UltraFeedback. Argilla and margin-satisfaction comparisons reuse DPO and SimPO; the new generation comparison reuses DPO.

E3.justification: The added evaluations introduce Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, an Argilla fine-tuning protocol, PairRM head-to-head win-rate evaluation on 200 held-out prompts, and a margin-satisfaction metric. These substantially expand the experimental design. The reported settings of the existing controlled and UltraFeedback experiments remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 6.1 adds a targeted diagnostic using margin satisfaction as a proxy for the approximation gap, reporting 58.0% for DPO, 63.0% for SimPO, and 72.3% for SA-DPO. The existing synonym-stability and loss-tail analyses retain their original questions and designs.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 change from point estimates without stated run counts to loss and accuracy summaries with mean ± standard deviation over five runs. Table 3 already used five-run uncertainty reporting in v1. This establishes expanded reporting, not an explicit increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds Argilla ranking results, margin-satisfaction results, and a 58.5% generation win rate against DPO. In Table 2, DPO/IPO/Poly-3 accuracies change from 71.8/94.7/100.0% to five-run means of 71.6/94.5/99.7%; Table 1's DPO loss changes from 0.1684 to 0.1695. UltraFeedback Table 3 remains unchanged. The additions and revised summaries do not establish a same-setting performance improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The margin-shifted surrogate and SA-DPO objective, including the semantic-distance margin Γ(y,y′) = τ∆(y,y′), remain unchanged. The Qwen experiments apply the existing method; the appendix preference-model renaming changes no algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, introduction opening, and conclusion; expands explanations of minimizability gaps and assumptions; numbers the contributions; and adds acknowledgments. It also consistently renames the appendix preference model. The main section and appendix order is preserved.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are enlarged, and Tables 1–2 receive revised captions and sizing for uncertainty reporting. Figures and tables reflow with the expanded text. Both versions retain the same three figures and four tables, with unchanged diagram and plotted-curve content.

R1.justification: Section 3.2 adds explicit attribution of the inconsistency result and proof technique to Mao et al. (2023c, Theorem 2.1). Appendix A expands recent consistency and deferral references, and new experimental resources receive citations. The main organization and research positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: The formal assumptions, theorems, derivations, and appendix proofs are retained. Section 4 expands the h± notation, and Definition N.2 renames the Generalized Bradley-Terry Model to the Surrogate-Induced Preference Model without changing its equations. The additional assumption discussion is explanatory.

improvement.justification: The Argilla/Qwen and generation evaluations broaden v1's existing empirical validation, while five-run uncertainty in Tables 1–2 and clearer assumption wording and attribution improve assessability. These are useful but limited gains: the new margin-satisfaction threshold is unspecified, and the aggregate PairRM win rate does not directly test the claimed prevention of hallucinated artifacts.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SA-DPO research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–P are readable and support reliable matching despite pagination and terminology changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original Argilla/Qwen ranking results, margin-satisfaction measurements, and a downstream generation comparison in Sections 6.1 and 7.3.

before.justification: v1 reports original synonym stress tests, Anthropic HH-RLHF loss comparisons, and UltraFeedback ranking results in Section 7, Tables 1–3, and Appendix M.

title: Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion newly assert priority as the first explicit smooth surrogate family with linear H-consistency across the three settings. V1's explicit energy-saving claims disappear. The central consistency, robustness and computational-efficiency contributions otherwise retain their scope.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the BERT results as locating the computational bottleneck strictly in the structured loss layer and broadens claimed applicability to exact F1 and BLEU in Appendix K. Appendix A also expands the explanation of how zero core curvature avoids the cited square-root barrier. These extensions receive no corresponding new limitations discussion.

D1.justification: V2 identifies AdamW for the new BERT experiment and corrects the CRF transition-interaction description from 4000 × 400 to 4000 × 4000. Existing implementation settings remain largely unchanged; the exact BERT configuration, timing hardware and code access information are not supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same binary problems, corrupted CIFAR-10, synthetic sequence tagging and artificially expanded Penn Treebank tagging task. BERT changes the model configuration, not the represented task or data. Appendix K mentions F1 and BLEU without evaluating them.

E2.justification: Section 5.5 adds an evaluated BERT-CRF comparator against BERT-Linear-Core alongside the retained BiLSTM comparison. The Cross-Entropy, Generalized Cross-Entropy, Hinge and Structured SVM comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: The added BERT comparison uses AdamW while retaining the 4,000-tag task, batch size 8, sequence-length filter and 83% accuracy target. Appendix E's convergence-plot caption changes from 10 to 200 labels, resolving its disagreement with the setup already stated in v1; this does not establish that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The new comparison across BiLSTM and BERT explicitly tests whether the efficiency advantage persists across encoders and whether the bottleneck resides in the structured loss layer. Existing gradient-distribution, optimization-stability and core-threshold analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies experimental run counts, seeds or significance tests. Existing shaded scalability plots are retained without new uncertainty definitions, and the BERT comparison adds no new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Section 5.5 and Figure 8 newly report 78.7 seconds for BERT-CRF versus 5.1 seconds for BERT-Linear-Core to reach 83% accuracy, a reported 15.4-fold speedup. These are additional results under a new backbone configuration. Table 2, the BiLSTM timings and the retained appendix results are unchanged.

M1.justification: New Appendix K proposes expanding sequence-model states to encode n-gram histories and constructing sampling proposals over weighted finite-state transducer paths. This is a limited methodological adaptation for non-decomposable metrics; the established losses and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged, and the adaptation is not experimentally demonstrated.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution roadmap, conclusion and related-work narrative are substantially rewritten around a theory-first progression through binary, multi-class and structured prediction. Appendix A becomes a numbered comparison, and new Remark 5.2 consolidates the rate comparisons. The main section sequence is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with reversed-margin standard losses and revised axes and legends. V1's appendix loss-surface figure moves into the main text as Figure 3. The combined efficiency figure is split, with a new BERT panel added. Other figures and tables are chiefly relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: Appendix A now explicitly identifies Cao et al.'s binary loss as a special case of the Linear-Core family, rather than merely structurally similar, and expands discussion of the universal square-root result. References are added for rational kernels, BERT, AdamW and further consistency research; the main prior-work relationships remain intact.

T1.justification: Appendix K adds an informal mathematical argument that a history-expanded transducer representation preserves linear consistency, bounded variance and computational efficiency for non-decomposable metrics. It supplies no complete derivation. Existing theorem statements and proofs remain unchanged; the variance theorem is merely renumbered from 5.2 to 5.3.

improvement.justification: The BERT comparison adds limited support for the efficiency claim, while the corrected label-count caption, clearer prior-work discussion and removal of unmeasured energy-saving claims improve precision. These gains are tempered by Appendix K's broad exact-F1/BLEU guarantees without a complete derivation or evaluation. The established proofs and experimental findings remain unchanged, so the overall improvement is modest.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Linear-Core Surrogates work. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds a BERT-based sequence-tagging timing comparison in Section 5.5.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 noise experiments, synthetic optimization and sequence-tagging experiments, and a Penn Treebank timing comparison in Sections 4–5 and Appendix E.

title: Linear-Core Surrogates: Smooth Loss Functions with Linear Rates for Classification and Structured Prediction

C1.justification: The benchmark contribution and conclusions about intent recognition and predictive precision retain their scientific scope. Replacing promotional phrases such as 'new standard' and 'shifts the paradigm' with more restrained wording does not change those claims.

C2.justification: The revised conclusion explains more explicitly why paired historical tables isolate predictive reasoning from data-search failures. That isolation rationale and the limitation concerning open-ended data discovery were already stated in v1; substantive result interpretations and failure mechanisms remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The explicit 1.0 clipping rule supplies additional information for reproducing batch-NMAE scoring. Repository access, prompt templates, judge configuration, model identifiers, and execution setup remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use 779 queries from 35 source tables across the same four tasks and three domains. Appendix B.1 corrects descriptive counts without establishing a change to the underlying coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the text-based, agentic, semantic-information, and predict-only comparisons. Newly cited related works are not added experimental baselines.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 now specifies batch NMAE with each normalized absolute error capped at 1.0 before averaging. v1 described averaging NMAE and supplied an uncapped base definition in Appendix C.3. This revises the reported scoring specification; the PDFs do not establish that evaluation was rerun.

E4.justification: The semantic-information and predict-only ablations, truncation comparisons, judge robustness checks, metric sensitivity study, tool-use analyses, and qualitative cases are retained without changed evidence.

E5.justification: Repeated-run, seed, and statistical uncertainty reporting are unchanged. Neither version adds uncertainty estimates or significance tests for aggregate performance; the existing audit and judge-agreement reporting is retained.

E6.justification: Reported performance values and rankings are unchanged. Appendix B.1 replaces 17 short, 17 medium, and 183 long-list queries with 34 short and 180 long-list queries, correcting the long-list share from approximately 68% to 84% and reconciling the counts with the retained total of 214.

M1.justification: The dataset-construction pipeline, intent-to-prediction formulation, text-based and ReAct workflows, and predict-only ensemble remain unchanged. The broader agentic applicability stated in Section 5.1 was already demonstrated in v1's Table 2.

P1.justification: v2 revises the title, corrects terminology and grammar, expands evaluation and conclusion wording, and updates the publication footer and bibliography. The section organization and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 receives wording, example-cell, and sizing corrections. Figure 3 changes 'Medical' to 'Healthcare' and moves earlier; Figure 5 and Tables 3–4 are repositioned. The underlying plots, table structures, and appendix displays are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: Sections 2.2–2.3 add seven cited works, including TabFSBench and VT-Bench, without substantially rewriting the research positioning. Several additions have apparently mismatched relevance: their listed titles concern waveguide filters, TSN network timing, or graph-inference encryption. Other changes largely update bibliographic metadata for existing works.

T1.justification: New Equation 3 explicitly defines clipped batch NMAE, bounding each normalized error contribution at 1.0, beyond v1's uncapped NMAE definition and verbal averaging rule. Other mathematical content is unchanged; replacing the width-penalty symbol tau with kappa is only notation.

improvement.justification: v2 fixes internally inconsistent candidate counts and makes batch-error clipping explicit, improving reporting clarity. However, newly added citations include apparently unrelated waveguide-filter and network-timing papers as support for TQA positioning. With unchanged experimental evidence and these competing gains and relevance problems, the PDFs do not establish a reliable net direction in overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TOPBENCH study. All 35 pages, including figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–E, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results, including the model comparison in Table 2 and ablations in Tables 3–4.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, semantic-information and predict-only ablations, judge audits, and supplementary analyses in Sections 5–6 and the appendices.

title: TopBench: A Benchmark for Implicit Predictive Reasoning in Tabular Question Answering

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same novelty, automation, physical-plausibility, controllability, and comparative-performance claims. No contribution is added, strengthened, or narrowed.

C2.justification: The interpretations and limitations remain unchanged, including omitted material degradation and mass loss, restricted scene scale, reconstruction and material-classification errors, and consistency problems from generative refinement.

D1.justification: Appendices A and B preserve the same prompts, hyperparameters, simulation grid, rendering samples, software, hardware, and runtime details. The project link and statement that code and data will be released upon acceptance are also unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six scenes: Firewood, Kitchen, Chair, Stool, Garden from MipNeRF360, and Playground from Tanks and Temples. The combustion and user-control scenarios are unchanged.

E2.justification: AutoVFX, Runway-V2V, and Instruct-GS2GS remain the comparison methods in Section 4 and Appendix B. No comparator is added, removed, or replaced within the corresponding evaluations.

E3.justification: The metrics, scene configurations, baseline prompts, and evaluation procedures are unchanged. Both user studies retain 86 and 88 participants respectively, 31 randomly sampled image/video pairs, and randomized left–right presentation.

E4.justification: The user-control analysis in Figure 7, material-reasoning error analysis in Appendix B.3, and generative-refinement consistency analysis in Appendix B.6 and Figure 11 are retained without changes.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same point estimates and user-preference percentages. Neither introduces repeated-run or seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 2–6 and the qualitative result images are unchanged. For example, FieryGS retains Table 2 scores of 0.624, 0.702, and 0.38, and Table 5 retains mean material accuracy of 89.31%.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A retain the same reconstruction and segmentation pipeline, GPT-4o material reasoning, combustion and charring simulation, unified renderer, and optional Wan2.1 refinement.

P1.justification: v2 consolidates six affiliation entries into Peking University and ByteDance Seed, removes the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence affiliation, and deletes the Beijing Science and Technology Program funding acknowledgement. title: Escaping Mode Collapse in LLM Generation via Geometric Regulation

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammatical and heading-capitalization edits, clarifies weighted-particle terminology, and updates publication information. improvement.justification: v2 improves mathematical consistency and adds useful quantitative checks of discrete simulation, approximation accuracy, and computational requirements, alongside code-access information. title: Dual-branch Robust Unlearnable Examples

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3–4 and the multipanel Figure 25. Figures 1–24 and Tables 1–2 retain their substantive displays, with limited caption edits, repositioning, and surrounding layout changes.

improvement.justification: v3 aligns the introduction, Theorem 5.1, and appendix conclusions with the almost-sure infinite-risk argument already present in v1. before.justification: v1 reports mathematical constructions, counterexamples, and proofs, but no original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis outcomes. Its random-bit constructions are theoretical arguments.

title: Realizable Bayes-Consistency for General Metric Losses

Appendix A.4 interprets the new controls as evidence that tags alone are insufficient. These additions substantially strengthen qualifications and mechanism interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds a SPARK code-repository link, cost-accounting definitions, and wall-clock and per-candidate training times in Table A.5. These improve access information and resource disclosure, while the existing pseudocode and listings remain unchanged. Detailed training and implementation recipes for the new benchmarks are still sparse.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluations on MNIST-1D, 20News, CartPole-v1, Mice Protein Expression, and Breast Cancer Wisconsin, substantially extending coverage beyond algorithmic reasoning. All 30 CLRS tasks were already present in v1's Table A.1; their increased prominence is not new coverage.

(2026). The related-work discussion and positioning relative to NAS, iterative refinement, and structured editing remain substantially unchanged.

after.justification: v3 retains the original empirical results and adds scope-control experiments and evaluations on five non-CLRS benchmarks.

before.justification: v1 reports original SPARK evaluations on CLRS, component ablations, five-seed search trajectories, and evolved architecture examples, including appendix results for 30 tasks.

title: Structured Progressive Knowledge Activation for LLM-Driven Neural Architecture Search

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about gradient-based planning, policy improvement, computational efficiency, uncertainty regularization and action reuse. Substantial new results appear for PQ/PQL and the added analyses: expanded-WebQSP CPR achieves 55.3% ECR with 10.10 APSS at alpha = 0.5, while no-hint CPR achieves 42.0% ECR with 2.54 APSS at alpha = 0.8. title: Mitigating Gradient Pathology in PINNs through Aligned Constraint

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about sparse adversarial dependence, hidden-state attribution, ranking consistency, low overhead and effective defense with preserved utility. The added appendix evidence does not revise these central claims.

C2.justification: Appendix F substantially expands applicability and mechanism discussions. It distinguishes spatially sparse benign objects from concentrated adversarial dependencies, acknowledges increased vulnerability under adaptive attacks while claiming partial protection, and explains soft-mask optimization instability. It also argues that textual steering and prefix injection make token alignment practically relevant.

D1.justification: The added analyses document image resolution, evaluation scope, adaptive loss construction, masking during optimization, perturbation bounds and iteration budgets. Exact regularization sweep values and soft-mask parameters are unspecified. Existing hardware information and the code-access statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds HR-Bench-4K, requiring recognition of tiny objects in high-resolution images, and a stronger threat scenario involving attackers explicitly adapted to GTM. UltraBreak also expands jailbreak coverage. JPS and AdvBench were already present; using the full AdvBench evaluation set is a protocol addition.

E2.justification: The new JPS comparison in Table 12 includes first-token logit-based masking, which was absent from v1's JPS comparison in Table 9. Logit attribution already appeared separately in Table 6. Existing comparator membership in Tables 1–9 is retained.

E3.justification: New adaptive evaluations introduce saliency regularization, defense-in-the-loop optimization and differentiable soft masking. Strategies 1–2 use 1,000 steps and bounds of 32/256 and 64/256, with strongest-ASR selection across regularization coefficients; soft masking is attempted for 10,000 steps. Appendix F.3 adds full-AdvBench evaluation on Qwen2-VL-7B. These are additional protocols; existing experiments retain their stated settings.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds substantial tests of three previously unexamined questions: whether masking harms tiny-object recognition disproportionately, whether defense-aware attackers circumvent GTM, and whether the attribution advantage extends to practical token-alignment attacks.
